pdf_index.anonymized_output_policy: Store separately verified anonymized copies under data_5conf/anonymized/pdf; preserve every original file.
pdf_index.is_anonymized_semantics: True only when a verified anonymized PDF and completed receipt are linked by this index; false means no verified copy is linked.

C1.justification: v1 emphasizes training-free mask matching and VLM distillation as alternatives to feature optimization. v2 makes an extrinsic paradigm separating geometry from semantics the central contribution, emphasizing overlapping object groups and lightweight semantic indices. The abstract, contribution list and conclusion substantially redefine the claimed conceptual novelty.

C2.justification: v2 adds explanations of sparse-view failure, VLM dependence, descriptor-induced semantic noise, neutral-point/rendering tradeoffs and memory-constrained parallelization. It expands the retained mask/VLM limitations into concrete failure mechanisms. Section 4.3 also changes the attribution of aggressive foreground removal from entropy-only filtering to opacity-only filtering.

D1.justification: Section 6 newly specifies detection intervals and thresholds, three-view selection, five generated nouns, the exact VLM prompt, matching/filtering thresholds, and ScanNet scene/category lists. Table 9 supplies timing and NVIDIA Tesla V100 hardware information. These substantially improve implementation documentation without establishing changes to the retained experiments.

E1.justification: Beyond the retained LERF and ScanNet evaluations, v2 adds qualitative object extraction on cluttered Grasp-Net scenes and a phone-captured office. It also demonstrates language-directed object removal, translation and stylization, substantially extending evaluated domains and task coverage (Sections 7.3–7.4, Figures 8–10).

E2.justification: Tables 1–2 add Occam's LGS, 3DVLGS, Segment-then-Splat, LAGA and LUDVIG to the resource/LERF comparisons. Table 3 adds LAGA and LUDVIG to ScanNet. Earlier comparators remain, substantially broadening comparison against both training-based and training-free methods.

E3.justification: The main LERF and ScanNet protocols are retained. New experimental designs introduce an opacity-only control, mask-view fractions down to 1/32, three VLM choices, descriptor counts of 1/3/5/10, filtering-threshold sweeps and component-level runtime measurements. These are added protocols, rather than evidence that the original benchmark settings changed.

E4.justification: v1's two component ablations are expanded with opacity-only filtering, sparse-mask robustness, VLM and descriptor-count ablations, and threshold sensitivity. v2 also adds runtime profiling, illustrated failures, neutral-point visualization, semantic-category counts and cross-view CLIP similarity analysis (Sections 7–10).

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, error bars or significance tests. v2's category-frequency histogram and feature-similarity heatmap add descriptive analyses, without introducing uncertainty-estimation procedures.

E6.justification: Existing benchmark and ablation scores are retained, including 54.3 LERF mean mIoU and 45.5/47.2/53.7 ScanNet mIoU. New baseline entries change comparative rankings: LAGA reports 64.0 on LERF, while the stated 3.9-point lead corresponds to LUDVIG's 50.4. Numerous new outcomes include opacity-only filtering at 52.6, VLM/threshold/descriptor results, 555.14 seconds total processing time, and additional qualitative findings.

M1.justification: The SAM/DAM2SAM masks, weighted back-projection, entropy/opacity filtering, VLM naming and CLIP matching procedures are retained. v2's extrinsic index layer explicitly organizes the object-to-feature associations and union-based retrieval already described in v1 Section 3.3; it does not establish a changed recognition algorithm.

P1.justification: The title and method name change, and the abstract, introduction, contribution list, portions of the results discussion and conclusion are extensively rewritten around extrinsic semantics. The method gains separate architecture/index-layer subsections, and the supplement organizes implementation, additional experiments, efficiency, failures and discussion.

P2.justification: The document switches from single-column to two-column layout. v1 Figure 1 is removed; its Figures 2–3 are redrawn as v2 Figures 1–2, including an explicit index-layer panel. Tables are expanded and reorganized, and supplementary Figures 5–14 and Tables 6–9 are added. Existing main qualitative comparison images are retained and renumbered.

R1.justification: v2 adds related works including LUDVIG, Occam's LGS, VoteSplat and SuperGSeg, and reframes prior approaches as embedding-based rather than uniformly dependent on expensive training. It revises Dr.Splat's description to pretrained product quantization and adds substantive positioning against boundary-refinement approaches in Section 10.1.

T1.justification: The rendering, accumulation, entropy and cosine-similarity mathematics remain equivalent. v2's index notation and Equations 6–7 express the thresholded group selection and union already specified in v1 Section 3.3. No substantive new assumptions, derivations, theorems or proofs are introduced.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially addresses v1's reproducibility and validation gaps through explicit implementation settings and prompts, controlled sensitivity studies, measured runtime and concrete failure evidence. These additions make the unchanged method substantially easier to reproduce and assess. However, the unqualified LERF SOTA claim conflicts with Table 2 (54.3 versus LAGA's 64.0), and Section 7.2's zero-opacity-threshold explanation conflicts with Section 3.3's filtering rule. These issues weaken particular interpretations, but the gains in technical transparency and supporting evidence provide a substantial net improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research pipeline and retain matching benchmark results despite renaming MUSplat to ExtrinSplat. Text, equations, tables and figures are readable. v1 has no appendix; v2 includes supplementary Sections 6–10, which were included in the comparison.

after.justification: v2 retains those empirical results and adds sensitivity experiments, runtime measurements, failure analyses, and qualitative evaluations on additional scenes and tasks.

before.justification: v1 reports original LERF object-selection and ScanNet segmentation results, qualitative comparisons, and component ablations in Tables 2–5.

results.title: ExtrinSplat: Decoupling Geometry and Semantics for Open-Vocabulary Understanding in 3D Gaussian Splatting

C1.justification: v2's main claims concern facial identity diversity, counting, and maintained image quality. v3's introduction and conclusion broaden the claimed contribution to clothing/body-type diversity and preserved or improved general compositional generation, supported by the new Section 4.2.3 and Appendix F.

C2.justification: v3 adds explanations linking RL's advantage over SFT to exploration and group-relative learning, attributing attribute transfer to broader learned distinctiveness, and attributing compositional preservation to HPSv3. It also interprets higher-count performance as generalization beyond memorization and explicitly excludes personalization from DISCO's scope. These extend the interpretations substantially, although some causal explanations lack isolating ablations.

D1.justification: v3 adds a project-page link, identifies the Fashion-SigLIP checkpoint, and documents torso cropping and Qwen3-VL body-type assessment for the new evaluations. Existing training hyperparameters, hardware, baseline settings, and reproducibility information remain unchanged.

E1.justification: v3 adds general compositional generation on GenEval2, out-of-training-range scenes with 8–10 people, clothing/body-type diversity evaluation, and per-person clothing and hairstyle prompts (Appendix F). The original training data, DiverseHumans, and MultiHuman-TestBench coverage remain.

E2.justification: Appendix E.1.4 adds a focused online supervised fine-tuning comparator, evaluated against DISCO in Table E.4. The original proprietary and open-source generator comparison sets remain unchanged.

E3.justification: New protocols include highest-reward-sample online SFT under the same prompts and curriculum, additional curriculum bounds, a blinded study with 25 participants judging 22 image pairs, and 270 samples spanning 2–10 people. Appendix F also introduces clothing-similarity and Qwen3-VL body-type scoring and GenEval2 evaluation. The original Appendix D settings are retained.

E4.justification: v3 adds analyses testing RL versus additional supervised training, curriculum-bound sensitivity, agreement with human judgments, extrapolation beyond trained person counts, transfer to other visual attributes, and per-person compositional control. The earlier reward-weight, aggregation-function, computational, and artifact analyses are retained.

E5.justification: Appendix E.1.8 newly reports correlation analysis between automated metrics and human judgments, although the correlation coefficient type and its uncertainty are unspecified. Existing shared image-index seeds and Figure 5's 95% confidence intervals remain unchanged; no increase in repeated runs is documented.

E6.justification: Original main-table and retained appendix scores are unchanged. New results include SFT versus DISCO UFA of 73.0 versus 98.6 (Table E.4), curriculum-bound outcomes, clothing similarity of 0.73/0.65/0.60 for Flux/face-DISCO/clothing-DISCO (Table F.1), and GenEval2 means of 24.6 versus 27.6 for Flux and DISCO (Table F.2). Human-study correlations and larger-crowd results further expand the findings.

M1.justification: The original Flow-GRPO procedure, four-component facial-diversity reward, curriculum, and Algorithms 1–3 remain unchanged. Appendix F.2 adds DISCO(Cloth), an adaptation replacing the ArcFace identity reward with Fashion-SigLIP clothing similarity.

P1.justification: The abstract and contribution narrative are revised, the mathematical preliminaries are substantially condensed, and the conclusion and limitations are rewritten. Appendix E is reorganized, a dedicated generalizability section is introduced, and ethics and reproducibility receive numbered appendix headings. These changes substantially reshape the narrative despite extensive retained technical text.

P2.justification: v3 adds four tables covering SFT, curriculum bounds, attribute diversity, and GenEval2, plus four figures showing human judgments, larger-crowd performance, clothing diversity, and compositional examples. Original figure artwork is retained and relocated where needed; Figure 1 is resized and Table 2 gains a highlighted final row.

R1.justification: v3 adds references for CLIP, Qwen3-VL, GenEval2, concurrent diverse-video policy optimization, and Ar2Can. It briefly positions DISCO relative to concurrent video-diversity work and as a foundation for Ar2Can, while retaining the earlier related-work framework.

T1.justification: Section 3.1 removes the explicit rectified-flow interpolation and target velocity, ODE–SDE drift relationship, and trajectory-policy factorization, replacing this formal background with a shorter description and reference to Flow-GRPO. The DISCO reward mathematics and optimization objective are retained; no new proof is introduced.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially strengthens validation by addressing v2's missing SFT control, human assessment of identity metrics, curriculum-bound sensitivity, and tests of extrapolation and general compositional capability. These additions support method choice and applicability while preserving the original main results. Reporting remains imperfect: the human-study correlations are incompletely specified, and the retained statement that no human subjects were used conflicts with the new 25-participant study. These limitations qualify, but do not outweigh, the broader evidential gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe DISCO and provide readable main text, equations, tables, figures, and appendices. Retained algorithms and experiments can be matched across the additions, relocations, and renumbering.

after.justification: v3 retains those original results and adds supervised fine-tuning comparisons, a participant study, curriculum experiments, and generalization evaluations.

before.justification: v2 reports original DISCO evaluations on DiverseHumans and MultiHuman-TestBench, component ablations, reward-weight experiments, and qualitative results.

results.title: Resolving the Identity Crisis in Text-to-Image Generation

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion replace the central claim about content-specific query representations and attention sharing with a claim that dominant singular components of the third feature encode style, motivating PFB and SAC. Training-free personalization from a single reference and efficient autoregressive generation remain the overarching goals.

C2.justification: v2 explains style/content separation through leading versus higher-rank singular components and interprets weaker spectral decay as increasing content leakage. It also adds an explicit limitation: heterogeneous reference styles can become blended because the method cannot selectively isolate sub-styles. v1 instead emphasizes query-based content control and ends with general future directions.

D1.justification: v2 adds Algorithm 1, the spectral-decay setting, and extensive baseline implementation information, including repository provenance, default configurations, the unofficial StyleDrop implementation, and a shared A6000/PyTorch environment. Table 1 and Appendix C explicitly explain that tuning-based runtimes include style-specific training plus one generated image. These substantially expand documentation without establishing that retained baseline experiments were rerun.

E1.justification: The 190-prompt Parti benchmark, ten quantitative reference styles, and image-guided and text-only generation tasks remain. Qualitative artistic-style coverage changes: v2 includes geometric flat illustration, metallic 3D, neon comic art, and retro sci-fi examples, while earlier Mesopotamian-relief examples disappear. Additional backbones change model settings rather than task coverage.

E2.justification: Table 1 and Figure 5 add CSGO and StyleAR to the six retained external baselines. B-LoRA joins the user-study comparison. For text-only style-aligned generation, v2 Figure 14 adds comparisons against StyleAligned and AlignedGen, whereas v1 Figure 8 displays only the proposed method.

E3.justification: v2 adds the harmonic mean of prompt and style fidelity as an evaluation metric. The user study changes from 40 participants choosing among four methods to 30 choosing among five. New experiments introduce mixed object/color prompt-pair controls and evaluation on Infinity-8B and Switti. The primary Infinity-2B benchmark, output resolution, and stated GPU remain unchanged.

E4.justification: The step-wise prompt-injection analysis is retained, but the query/key/value replacement analysis is replaced by baseline, full-feature replacement, and SVD-guided controls. Component ablations are redesigned around replacement, PFB, and SAC. Appendix A adds top-k singular-component and exponential-decay sensitivity studies, and Appendix D tests qualitative generalization across backbones.

E5.justification: Neither version reports random seeds, repeated-run counts, confidence intervals, error bars, or significance tests. Additional averaged CLIP results and the revised user-study sample size do not introduce uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: On the retained benchmark, Table 1 changes the proposed method's prompt fidelity from 0.330 to 0.334, style fidelity from 0.603 to 0.630, and reported runtime from 6.44 to 3.58 seconds; the six shared baselines' corresponding values remain unchanged. v2 adds baseline, harmonic-score, spectral-analysis, sensitivity, and backbone results. User preferences change from 57.5%/30.5% to 35.3%/32.0% for prompt/style fidelity, but the changed participants and candidate set preclude interpreting these as comparable gains or losses.

M1.justification: v1's three-path system uses feature initialization, Key Stage Attention Sharing at steps 2–3, and similarity-weighted Adaptive Query Sharing at steps 4–7. v2 replaces this with two generation streams conditioned on the same prompt, SVD-based Principal Feature Blending at the third feature, and Structural Attention Correction replacing content queries and keys at steps 3–12. These change the inference procedure, rather than merely renaming components.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, substantial introduction passages, mechanism analysis, method description, ablation discussion, and conclusion are rewritten around the SVD formulation. The appendix is reorganized into analysis, algorithm, implementation, backbone experiments, limitations, and qualitative-results sections. This substantially changes the narrative beyond adding scientific content.

P2.justification: v2 redraws the pipeline schematic and replaces the attention-feature illustration with a spectral-analysis display. It expands the comparison table, changes the ablation-table structure and placement, adds sensitivity plots and a user-preference table, and revises qualitative grids. Typography, author presentation, references, and overall page layout also change substantially.

R1.justification: v2 adds targeted references including CSD-VAR, FLUX, multimodal diffusion editing, CSGO, StyleAR, and AlignedGen, and connects the revised mechanism to prior feature decomposition and attention editing. Most of the three-part related-work discussion remains. Publication updates and duplicate entries for existing works do not constitute additional research coverage.

T1.justification: The mathematical construction changes from attention concatenation and cosine-weighted query mixing to principal/residual feature decomposition, an exponentially weighted SVD operator, and residual-preserving reconstruction in v2 Section 5.2. Appendix A additionally defines top-k decompositions and interventions. These substantively revise the formal definitions; neither version provides theorems or proofs.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens the evidence and documentation supporting its revised mechanism. Full-replacement/SVD controls, component ablations, and rank/decay sweeps provide more diagnostic support than v1's narrower attention-sharing analysis. Algorithm and baseline documentation address important reproducibility gaps, while timing clarification and explicit mixed-style limitations improve transparency. The smaller, redesigned user study cannot establish a preference improvement, and uncertainty reporting remains absent, but these limits do not outweigh the substantial gains in mechanistic support and reproducibility.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same training-free style-personalization work using scale-wise autoregressive models, despite retitling and substantial methodological revision. All pages, including figures, equations, tables, and appendices, support comparison.

after.justification: v2 reports original SVD intervention experiments, benchmark and ablation results, sensitivity analyses, a 30-participant user study, and qualitative experiments on additional backbones.

before.justification: v1 reports original prompt-injection experiments, benchmark results in Table 1, component ablations including appendix Table 2, and a 40-participant user study.

results.title: A Training-Free Style-Personalization via SVD-Based Feature Decomposition

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the same contributions: spatial data scaling, improved spatial performance, general-capability retention, emerging transfer, shortcut resistance, limited CoT benefits, and downstream utility. Additional evidence does not redefine these claims.

C2.justification: Appendix H introduces explicit hypotheses about CoT error accumulation and restrictive verbal supervision. Appendix F identifies object-recognition and manipulation-precision failure conditions. Appendices C and E add discussion of mixture balancing and general-task declines, materially extending the interpretation and limitations beyond v1.

D1.justification: Appendices A, B, and F newly document benchmark-to-capability mappings, annotation processing, filtering and sampling, overlap-controlled frame selection, detailed CogMap construction, and the robot's action interface and full prompt. These substantially improve implementation transparency; the existing code and model access links are retained.

E1.justification: Appendix E/Table 8 substantially broadens general-capability evaluation beyond MMBench-En by adding MMStar, AI2D scientific-diagram reasoning, and OCRBench text recognition. The original spatial benchmarks, manipulation task, and training-source coverage remain.

E2.justification: Table 1 adds Gemini-3-Pro-Preview as an evaluated comparator on all five spatial benchmarks. The previously reported comparator set is retained; the appendix largely provides further results for existing comparators.

E3.justification: Appendix C adds dataset-isolated training controls for ten InternVL3-8B variants. Table 10 additionally reports EASI-reproduced VST MMSI results alongside the paper-sourced aggregates retained in Table 1. The main training budget, optimizer, learning rate, and frame settings remain unchanged.

E4.justification: Table 6 substantially extends the earlier narrow single-source transfer examples into systematic training-source ablations. Appendices F and H add manipulation and CoT success/failure case studies, exposing recognition, execution-precision, and reasoning-consistency problems. The original robustness analyses remain.

E5.justification: Both versions describe Figure 1's bands as ±0.5 standard deviation across benchmark subtasks; Appendix A repeats this practice. v3 adds no repeated-run counts, seeds, significance tests, or new uncertainty-estimation procedure.

E6.justification: The original main-table scores remain, but Tables 6–13 add extensive ablation, scaling, general-capability, and subtask results. Gemini-3-Pro-Preview scores 45.2 on MMSI versus SenseNova-SI InternVL3-8B's 43.3. Some new aggregates conflict with Table 1, including MindCube's 41.2 versus 41.8 for SenseNova-SI InternVL3-2B; these are not established performance revisions.

M1.justification: The foundation-model architectures, data-centric training approach, and three CoT schemes remain unchanged. Appendix B elaborates the existing data-curation and CoT procedures; it does not establish a change to the implemented method.

P1.justification: The main narrative remains nearly verbatim, with localized wording and header edits. However, Appendices A–H substantially expand the exposition of existing work, developing brief descriptions into organized, stepwise accounts of data curation, CoT construction, and embodied-agent operation.

P2.justification: v3 adds Tables 6–13, Figures 5–8, an algorithm block, and detailed prompt/output displays. New visuals include annotated manipulation failures and CoT traces. Existing Figure 3 moves from page 7 to page 8, Figure 2 is resized with a clarified caption, and Table 1 gains a comparator row.

R1.justification: v3 adds references supporting MMStar, AI2D, OCRBench, and Gemini 3 Pro. Section 2's positioning around spatial data curation versus 3D-expert architectures remains essentially unchanged. The additional VLM-3R reference duplicates an already cited work.

T1.justification: Neither version develops theoretical results or proofs. The new frame-selection pseudocode and visualization-normalization explanation document procedures without establishing substantive changes to mathematical reasoning, assumptions, or formal properties.

improvement.justification: v1 only sketches the central data-curation pipeline and robot interface, and tests general-capability retention mainly through MMBench-En. v3 substantially improves auditability through procedural details, training-source controls, broader evaluations, and explicit failure cases. These gains outweigh remaining reporting problems: Table 7's base-model ViewSpatial score conflicts with Table 1, and the retained general-capability claims insufficiently acknowledge declines such as InternVL3-8B's AI2D score falling from 85.2 to 79.0 after spatial training.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same SenseNova-SI research. The supplied text, figures, tables, and supplementary material support reliable comparison. v1 ends with references; v3 adds Appendices A–H.

after.justification: v3 retains those original results and adds single-dataset experiments, general-capability evaluations, detailed benchmark results, and case studies.

before.justification: v1 reports original model evaluations, scaling experiments, shortcut and CoT analyses, and simulated robotic-manipulation results in Section 5.

results.title: Scaling Spatial Intelligence with Multimodal Foundation Models

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction's three contributions and conclusion retain the same claims: training-free transparent-object generation using physical refraction constraints and synchronized perspective/panoramic views. The expanded experiments support these existing claims rather than redefine them.

C2.justification: V2 Section 5.3 adds explanations for panorama synchronization's greater measured contribution relative to reflections and explicitly discusses relighting's trade-off between pixel accuracy and visual plausibility. Existing qualifications about Blender references, time-travel smoothing and future extensions largely remain unchanged.

D1.justification: V2 newly documents repeating relighting 20 times and selecting by object-region PSNR, provides additional scene prompts, specifies the retained ablation's six-scene sphere scope, and clarifies that the unchanged 126-second runtime excludes preprocessing. V1 does not establish whether the relighting selection procedure was already used.

E1.justification: Coverage expands from six indoor scene prompts to ten indoor/outdoor categories, adding cave, desert, karaoke and landscape scenes. V2 also evaluates captured indoor and outdoor photographs. The six object geometries are not newly introduced: v1 already includes the non-spherical objects in its appendix.

E2.justification: V2 retains FLUX inpainting and the original FLUX generation comparator, now labeled FLUX-dev, and adds FLUX.2-dev, Qwen-Image and Stable Diffusion 3.5 Large. Their participation is demonstrated in Tables 1 and 3 and Figure 9, substantially broadening comparison beyond the original two FLUX baselines.

E3.justification: V2 introduces an explicit design crossing five variations per prompt with six geometries, averaging results over 300 scene-object combinations. It also adds qualitative testing using fixed-camera photographs captured with and without a sphere. The existing metrics, 20 denoising steps, guidance scale and image resolutions remain unchanged.

E4.justification: V2 Table 2 and Figure 6 directly test reflection modeling and panorama synchronization, and Table 2 explicitly compares relighting effects. These substantially extend analysis of the central mechanisms. The original DPA, LPW and time-travel ablations are retained as Figure 13 and Table 4; refractive-index and time-travel sensitivity analyses also remain.

E5.justification: Both versions retain the same seed-matching statement and report point estimates without confidence intervals, dispersion estimates or significance tests. V2's prompt variations and newly disclosed repeated relighting concern evaluation coverage and output selection, not statistical uncertainty estimation.

E6.justification: The main aggregate comparison is replaced and expanded: Snellcaster's PSNR/LPIPS are 17.10/0.28 in v1 Table 1 and 16.51/0.24 in v2 Table 1 under different benchmark coverage, so these are not matched-setting performance changes. V2 adds baseline scores, mechanism-ablation results and captured-scene outputs. Its expanded comparison shows leading refraction metrics, but not leading CLIP or ImageReward.

M1.justification: Object placement changes from a geometry-based horizontal-surface heuristic with a 1.5 m floor-exclusion threshold in v1 Appendix C to SAM 3 segmentation of the prompt-specified surface in v2 Appendix B. The core ray tracing, cross-view synchronization, Fresnel blending and denoising procedures remain unchanged.

P1.justification: Experimental descriptions and the main ablation discussion are revised, prompt documentation is merged with object-parameter extraction, and the original ablation discussion moves to the appendix. References move before the supplement. Most introductory, methodological and concluding prose remains intact.

P2.justification: The empirical presentation is substantially redesigned: Figures 1 and 3 change examples, new Figures 5-6 show captured scenes and central-component ablations, and Figure 9 becomes a broader comparison grid. Table 1 changes to an all-method summary, the expanded per-scene table is split into two panels, and the original ablation figure moves to the appendix.

R1.justification: Four references are added for SAM 3 and the additional FLUX.2, Qwen-Image and Stable Diffusion comparisons. Section 2's related-work discussion and the positioning relative to synchronization and light-transport research remain substantively unchanged.

T1.justification: Equations 1-14, including flow matching, ray paths, Snell's law, synchronization and Fresnel blending, are unchanged. The single-object and uniform-refractive-index assumptions remain, with no added or revised theorem, proof or derivation.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially strengthens previously narrow empirical support through broader scene coverage, comparisons across additional model families, captured-scene examples and direct tests of the central reflection and panorama mechanisms. These address important validation gaps in v1. Reporting remains imperfect: Table 1's claim of preserving text alignment and aesthetics is not consistently supported by its CLIP and ImageReward scores. Nevertheless, the stronger evidence for the core refraction claim outweighs these localized interpretation problems.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe Snellcaster under the same title and authorship. All 16 pages of v1 and 17 pages of v2, including equations, figures, tables, references and appendices, support reliable comparison.

after.justification: V2 retains original experimental results and adds broader benchmark comparisons, captured-scene examples and further component ablations.

before.justification: V1 reports original image-generation comparisons, quantitative evaluations, component ablations and sensitivity analyses in the main paper and appendix.

results.title: Refracting Reality: Generating Images with Realistic Transparent Objects

C1.justification: The claims of training-free spatial acceleration up to 7× on FLUX and 3× on SD3 remain. However, v3 adds compatibility with timestep-distilled models and elevates combined acceleration up to 15.9× to an abstract claim and principal contribution. Table 2 identifies these speedups as FLOP-based, extending applicability beyond the earlier caching-integration claim.

C2.justification: v3 adds rationales for image-space Canny detection, fixed selection ratios, and nearest-neighbor interpolation. Section 6 introduces a tentative token-merging analogy while acknowledging that mixed-resolution self-attention remains unexplained. Appendix D emphasizes untested U-Net backbones instead of v2's explicit audio/3D examples, while retaining the limitation to flow-matching models.

D1.justification: v3 substantially expands execution and reproduction information: FP16, torch.profiler, FlashAttention except for ToCa, A6000 memory measurement, 5,000 MS-COCO images, explicit selection ratios, and configurations for new baselines and distilled-model integrations. These disclosures do not prove earlier settings differed. The front-page access pointer changes from a code repository to a project page, and the old custom-caching instructions disappear.

E1.justification: Appendix B.4 changes T2I-CompBench coverage from complex/texture to spatial/non-spatial/complex and narrows GenEval from six categories to four. CC12M remains. v3 newly identifies MS-COCO for image-quality evaluation, but v2 leaves that data source unspecified, so this alone does not establish an added dataset.

E2.justification: v3 Table 1 adds evaluated FLUX comparisons with Delta-DiT, TeaCache, and TaylorSeer, and SD3 comparisons with Delta-DiT, ToCa, and TaylorSeer. v2 principally compared against ToCa or RAS and Bottleneck Sampling. The integration comparison also replaces the earlier custom caching configuration with named temporal acceleration methods.

E3.justification: FID is replaced by ImageReward, and new artifact-rate and edge-energy evaluations are introduced. The FLUX 4× configuration with 18 RALU steps is replaced by a 5× configuration with 15 steps. New protocols include 100-image artifact analyses, four-step distilled-model integrations, and A6000 benchmarking. The retained FLUX 7× and SD3 stage counts merely change from per-stage to cumulative notation.

E4.justification: v3 substantially extends v2's qualitative upsampling-timing study and limited parameter ablations with systematic timing/JSD analyses, artifact rate versus FLOPs, and quantitative ratio sweeps. Appendix C adds image-space versus latent-space edge detection, fixed versus adaptive selection, interpolation comparisons, and edge-mask visualizations. These directly test previously unsupported design choices.

E5.justification: v3 adds error bars in Figures 2–3, a p < 0.001 statement for the ImageReward/JSD relationship, and FLOP mean±standard deviation in Table S4. GenEval reporting changes from fixed-seed wording to four different seeds per prompt. The error-bar definition and significance-test procedure remain unspecified; the wording does not establish increased repeated runs.

E6.justification: v3 adds or replaces extensive results, including ImageReward scores, expanded comparisons, distilled-model integrations, hardware measurements, and artifact ablations. For retained FLUX 7× RALU, reported latency changes from 3.37 to 3.75 seconds, while NIQE 6.87 and CLIP-IQA 0.681 remain unchanged. T2I-CompBench/GenEval change from 0.566/0.646 to 0.633/0.682 under revised task coverage, so these are not established same-setting gains.

M1.justification: The core procedure remains low-resolution denoising, selective early upsampling using decoded Canny edges, and full-resolution refinement, with correlated noise and JSD-based timestep matching. NT-DM becomes NT-Matching, but its underlying algorithm remains equivalent. Additional positional-embedding explanations and experiments with other acceleration methods do not establish a changed RALU algorithm.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction, artifact discussion, and method exposition are extensively rewritten. NT-DM is renamed NT-Matching, experiments gain dedicated artifact and edge-selection sections, and a Discussion section is introduced. Appendices are reorganized and references move after them, substantially changing the narrative structure.

P2.justification: v3 switches to a two-column layout, redraws the framework diagram, merges the main benchmark tables, restructures integration displays, and adds quantitative artifact plots and appendix tables. Qualitative comparison panels and captions are revised. Some SD3 and FLUX 7× appendix images are retained and relocated, rather than newly added results.

R1.justification: v3 adds context on Latent-SR and image-space super-resolution, forecasting methods, and token merging, alongside references supporting new metrics and implementations. FID and VQ4DiT references are removed. These additions refine the positioning, while the central distinction from training-dependent approaches and Bottleneck Sampling remains.

T1.justification: v3 Eqs. (5)–(6) correct the main-text matching target to a latent with isotropic covariance, replacing v2 Eq. (5)'s upsampled-latent target. Appendix A.1 adds consequences for intermediate and fully denoised endpoints. The rescheduling formulas otherwise remain equivalent, and the appendix's inconsistent covariance expressions in Eqs. (S2) and (S4) persist.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially strengthens the evidence for the central artifact-mitigation claims through controlled analyses and design-choice ablations, addressing v2's reliance on mostly qualitative artifact examples. Broader competitive baselines, integration tests, and execution details also improve assessment and reproducibility. FID removal and changed task subsets limit direct score comparisons, and reporting inconsistencies remain, such as FLUX 7× NIQE being 6.87 in Table 1 but 6.51 in Table 3. These shortcomings do not outweigh the substantial improvement in empirical support.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same RALU research despite different titles and extensive reformatting. All 28 pages of v2 and 29 pages of v3, including appendices A–E, provide readable text, equations, tables, and figures for comparison.

after.justification: v3 reports original benchmark results, controlled artifact analyses, design ablations, hardware measurements, and integrations with temporal acceleration and distilled models.

before.justification: v2 reports original RALU experiments on FLUX and SD3, including quantitative comparisons, caching integration, ablations, and generated images in the appendices.

results.title: Training-free Mixed-Resolution Latent Upsampling for Spatially Accelerated Diffusion Transformers

C1.justification: v1 emphasizes latent-likelihood scoring, feature-space benefits and a strong MVTecAD speed-AUC trade-off. v2 broadens the principal claims to plug-and-play applicability across diffusion AD models and state-of-the-art unified multi-class performance with approximately twofold acceleration without distillation. The reconstruction-free contribution remains, but its claimed applicability and comparative scope expand substantially.

C2.justification: v2 adds interpretations concerning feature quality versus diffusion architecture and why noise-residual prediction may favor integration with MDM over DeCoDiff. It extends applicability arguments to medical imaging. Conversely, v1's explicit caveats about Jacobian omission, theoretical interpretation and broader OOD applicability disappear; future work shifts toward single-step distillation.

D1.justification: Appendices A-B add dataset statistics, resizing and normalization instructions, architecture dimensions, detailed optimization and noise-schedule settings, software versions, hardware and throughput measurement conditions. v2 also supplies project and code links. These substantially extend v1's sparse implementation information, although its best-performing-checkpoint selection statement is no longer provided.

E1.justification: MVTecAD and VisA remain, while v2 adds MPDD and BMAD's six medical evaluation datasets, including brain MRI, liver CT and retinal OCT. It also adds unified multi-class evaluation alongside per-category comparisons, substantially extending the represented domains and evaluation scenarios.

E2.justification: v2 adds comparisons with RD4AD, UniAD, SimpleNet, DeSTSeg, HVQ-Trans and OmiAD in Table 2, plus medical comparators in Table 12. In the corresponding per-category MVTecAD comparison, DeCoDiff is added and DiAD is removed; DiAD remains in the new multi-class comparison. These changes substantially expand comparator coverage.

E3.justification: Training changes from 1000 to 300 epochs. The principal benchmark configuration changes from S=2 and category-tuned S in {2,3,4,5} to fixed S=3. v2 also introduces AP, maximum F1, AU-PRO and aggregate mAD evaluation beyond the earlier AUROC reporting. These are substantive revisions and additions to the evaluation design.

E4.justification: v2 adds feature-encoder and diffusion-architecture ablations and tests integration into DeCoDiff and MDM (Tables 5-7). Appendix F separately evaluates NLL, spatial range and their combination. Reconstruction-versus-inversion sensitivity testing remains with revised results, while v1's hazelnut score histograms are removed. Comparative localization case studies are also added.

E5.justification: Appendix B newly states that library random seeds were fixed and nondeterministic GPU operations disabled where possible. It supplies neither seed values nor repeated-run counts. Neither version reports confidence intervals or significance tests, so this is a limited reporting addition.

E6.justification: v1's tuned Ours* image/pixel AUROC averages are 99.1/94.8 on MVTecAD and 95.8/98.4 on VisA. v2's single-class tables report 99.1/97.3 and 97.0/99.0 under revised models and settings. These are replacement results, not controlled performance gains. New multi-class, medical, integration and ablation results substantially expand the reported findings.

M1.justification: The default diffusion architecture changes from UNet to class-unconditional DiT, described in v2's Implementations section and Appendix B. Algorithm 1 also changes the stated score aggregation from separately normalized terms to spatial range plus map sum. The underlying DDIM inversion, feature-space modeling and spatial-norm ideas are retained.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction and methodological narrative are extensively rewritten. v2 removes duplicated paragraphs from v1 Sections 3.4 and 4.3, consolidates related-work/background material, and reorganizes technical discussion into appendices. It also shortens the title, changes the author block and introduces the InvAD name.

P2.justification: v2 adds multi-metric benchmark tables, integration and architecture tables, implementation tables and extensive localization heatmaps. The original conceptual Figure 1 is retained but relocated and recaptioned. The score histograms disappear, the VisA comparison moves to the appendix with revised columns, and the properties table receives a substantially revised structure.

R1.justification: v2 replaces the broad memory/reconstruction/density survey with a diffusion-focused taxonomy covering conditioning, discriminators and adaptive timesteps. It adds substantive positioning against OmiAD and DeCoDiff and credits diffusion-based OOD work as inspiration. Several flow-related references and the earlier flow-connection argument disappear, changing the research framing beyond citation formatting.

T1.justification: Appendix E adds explicit DDIM posterior and noise-parameterization equations and a stepwise Euler inversion derivation. The central PF-ODE and inversion equations remain equivalent. v1's likelihood-Jacobian relationship and associated justification are removed, and the noise schedule is corrected from monotonically increasing to decreasing. No new theoretical guarantee is established.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens v1's limited validation and reproducibility: architecture ablations and integration tests directly examine previously untested dependence and portability, medical evaluation broadens applicability evidence, and Appendix B supplies much fuller implementation specifications. These gains outweigh remaining scoring-description inconsistencies and numerical reporting errors, including incorrect DeCoDiff deltas in Table 5. Changed architectures and protocols mean that cross-version scores themselves do not establish controlled performance gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same diffusion-based latent-inversion anomaly-detection work. Their text, equations, tables and figures are readable. v1 ends with references; v2 additionally contains supplementary sections A-G, which were included in the comparison.

after.justification: v2 reports original industrial and medical anomaly-detection results, architecture ablations, scoring experiments and integration tests, including results in its appendices.

before.justification: v1 reports original MVTecAD and VisA results, inference timings, and inversion/scoring analyses in Tables 2-4 and Figure 2.

results.title: InvAD: Inversion-based Reconstruction-Free Anomaly Detection with Diffusion Models

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the same central contributions: intrinsic 3D latent reasoning without manual geometric labels or external inference priors, two-stage training, recoverable geometric representations, and effectiveness across VLM backbones. The additional experiments support these existing claims.

C2.justification: The supplement substantially expands interpretation and applicability boundaries. Section 11 clarifies annotation-free supervision and VGGT dependence; Section 8.6 interprets geometric supervision versus special-token flexibility; Section 14.2 links a failure to inconsistent reconstruction under extremely sparse views. It also discusses general-image capability retention and early RL exploration. The original non-autoregressive-latent and iterative-reasoning limitations are retained in Section 13.

D1.justification: v2 identifies the larger training corpus behind the unchanged, now-starred Table 2 results: 237K samples from four sources, Gemini quality filtering, one supervised epoch, and a 57K RL subset. It also supplies generation prompts, a ten-attempt regeneration rule, hardware, batch size, training times, and vLLM usage. The abstract changes code status from promised to available; this is a reported availability change, not externally verified access.

E1.justification: v2 adds evaluated coverage on 3DSRBench (Table 9) and general image-understanding benchmarks MME, POPE, and SEED-I (Table 10). Section 8.3 explicitly extends the assessment to capabilities such as OCR and numerical reasoning, broadening the original spatial-reasoning evaluation.

E2.justification: Table 7 adds comparisons against five Qwen3-VL configurations, including the sparse 30B-A3B model. Table 9 newly compares against SpatialReasoner, SpatialReasoner-R1, and SpatialThinker. The LLaVA-OneVision-1.5 comparisons are retained unchanged in Table 8, having moved from v1's Table 1.

E3.justification: v2 adds dense/MoE Qwen3 configurations and a supervised alignment-loss-removal control. Section 3.1 also changes the reported CoT generator from GPT-4o to GPT-4.1. Existing accuracy/MRA metrics and MindCube hyperparameters remain unchanged; the newly disclosed curated-data settings do not establish that retained experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: v2 adds a supervised 3D-alignment-loss ablation (Table 11), a point-cloud-density analysis of prompt relevance (Section 8.4), training-curve analysis, and additional success and failure cases. These substantially extend the original latent-size, token-placement, projector, and reward ablations. Section 8.5 explains the existing projector comparison rather than introducing new ablation scores.

E5.justification: Neither version reports experimental seed counts, repeated-run uncertainty, confidence intervals, or significance tests. The added training curves show optimization trajectories, not uncertainty across repeated experiments.

E6.justification: The original table scores, including the relocated LLaVA rows, are retained. New results include 80.8% MindCube-Tiny accuracy for 3DThinker on Qwen3-VL-30B-A3B (Table 7), 65.6 versus SpatialReasoner's 60.3 on 3DSRBench (Table 9), general-understanding scores, and 54.1 without alignment loss versus 62.7 with it (Table 11). These are newly reported results, not improvements to the retained v1 scores.

M1.justification: The two-stage framework, latent tokens, projector, and geometric alignment remain intact. Section 8.1 introduces a localized procedural adaptation: sequence-level GSPO replaces token-level GRPO for MoE models.

P1.justification: The main narrative receives limited grammatical edits, author/affiliation updates, and an acknowledgment. Existing limitations move from the conclusion to supplementary Section 13, and the supplement receives its own roadmap and sections. The main exposition is largely retained rather than extensively rewritten.

P2.justification: v2 substantially expands the visual presentation with new result tables, density and projection illustrations, training plots, generation prompts, and detailed case-study panels. LLaVA rows move from Table 1 to Table 8, and Table 2 gains training-regime markers. Main Figures 1–4 retain the same images.

R1.justification: v2 adds four cited works: Adaptive Mixtures of Local Experts, DepthSSC, Swift Sampler, and Group Sequence Policy Optimization. The existing research positioning relative to textual cognitive maps, visual reasoning, and latent reasoning remains substantially unchanged.

T1.justification: The mathematical formulation in Equations 1–12 is unchanged. v2 adds no formal assumptions, propositions, proofs, or substantive derivations; the GSPO adaptation is described procedurally.

improvement.justification: v2 resolves an important reproducibility gap by identifying the substantially larger training corpus used for Table 2, which v1 did not distinguish from its MindCube training description. The new alignment-loss control, generation details, and explicit reconstruction failure substantially improve assessment of the method's support and limitations. Additional evaluations broaden that evidence. A new numerical inconsistency remains—Section 8.1 says 25.0 for Qwen3-VL-4B while Table 7 lists 26.0—but it is limited relative to these gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same 3DThinker research. Their text, equations, tables, and figures support reliable comparison. v1 ends after the references; v2 includes supplementary Sections 7–14, whose image-based prompts and case studies are readable.

after.justification: v2 retains the original empirical results and reports additional Qwen3-VL evaluations, benchmark comparisons, an alignment-loss ablation, training curves, and qualitative cases.

before.justification: v1 reports original benchmark evaluations, comparisons between training stages, ablations, and reconstructed point-cloud examples in Tables 1–6 and Figure 4.

results.title: Think with 3D: Geometric Imagination Grounded Spatial Reasoning from Limited Views

C1.justification: The central contributions remain multi-teacher 3DGS pretraining, transferable and data-efficient scene embeddings, and rendering-based adaptation. Adding Q&A to the abstract restates a capability already claimed and evaluated in v1. The introduction's contribution list and conclusion retain their scientific scope.

C2.justification: v3 adds a localized explanation of teacher compatibility through shared representations, separate projectors, and PHI-S balancing. It interprets the new robustness tests and explicitly discusses lamp/ceiling confusion and blurred boundaries after low-resolution adaptation in Appendix D.4. The existing point-cloud transfer hypotheses and offline pseudo-label-cost limitation remain.

D1.justification: The new supplement documents augmentation parameters, camera selection and cropping, teacher feature resolutions, Matterport3D reconstruction, InteriorGS label assignment and splits, prediction transfer, and downstream training settings. It specifies VLM optimization and two-H200 training hardware, among other details absent from v1. The abstract also replaces a future code/model-release promise with a linked code-release statement; repository availability is not independently established by the PDFs.

E1.justification: The datasets and principal tasks are retained. v3 extends evaluation to ScanNet++ iPhone RGB-D captures rather than only laser-derived point clouds, and adds tests on differently optimized Gaussian representations. These broaden input conditions within the existing indoor-scene coverage.

E2.justification: The comparator membership in corresponding main experiments is unchanged. SceneSplat's retraining changes its settings and scores, not its method identity. The added analyses use existing comparators such as Sonata and SceneSplat; teacher combinations are method ablations.

E3.justification: v3 reports retraining the joint-data SceneSplat baseline using updated Matterport3D reconstructions, revising a comparison control. Added tests vary Gaussian optimization, density, and capture source, while Appendix D introduces DINO-first probing and a specified UMAP sampling protocol. The main benchmark metrics remain unchanged. Most appendix training budgets, splits, and processing settings are newly disclosed rather than established changes to existing experiments.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained ablations, v3 adds optimization/density and iPhone robustness tests in Tables 10–11. The supplement adds DINO-first teacher ablations, visibility-crop analysis, UMAP comparisons, additional scene-feature examples, and before/after adaptation diagnostics. These substantially expand evidence about teacher contributions, input robustness, feature organization, and adaptation failures.

E5.justification: Neither PDF reports repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, significance tests, or experimental error bars. The added pose-sampling averages describe data characteristics, not uncertainty in performance estimates.

E6.justification: Table 1 replaces SceneSplat's joint-training scores: ScanNet200 f-mIoU/f-mAcc changes from 21.4/38.7 to 22.5/41.7, while Chorus remains 24.6/47.7. These accompany revised baseline training, not a same-setting Chorus improvement. v3 also adds substantial results in Tables 10–11 and C, including iPhone scores of 45.7/57.6 for Chorus versus 39.5/52.0 for Sonata, plus new qualitative findings. Most retained main results are unchanged.

M1.justification: The core encoder, teachers, losses, augmentations, and rendering-based adaptation remain unchanged. However, v3 Appendix C.2 describes reducing the VLM task-guided sparsifier to one attention block, whereas both versions' Section 4.1 says components other than the backbone remain unchanged. This inconsistency prevents distinguishing an architectural revision from a newly disclosed implementation detail.

P1.justification: v3 expands brief descriptions and references to supplementary material into organized, step-by-step explanations of adaptation, augmentation, dataset construction, and evaluation, with a contents list and Sections A–E. This substantially changes the explanatory structure. The main narrative order remains stable, alongside grammar, terminology, notation, affiliation, and acknowledgement edits.

P2.justification: v3 adds robustness Tables 10–11, supplementary Tables A–C, Algorithm 1, and Figures A–I covering pipelines, data processing, and feature analyses. The expanded PCA gallery includes a reused main-paper example alongside additional scenes. Existing main figures are largely retained; Figure 6 moves, Table 4 gains an explanatory caption, and the runtime table becomes Table 12.

R1.justification: v3 adds citations including Occam's LGS, SAM 2, UMAP, OPT, evaluation metrics, Rosetta Neurons, and the Platonic Representation Hypothesis. The latter two support a new discussion of shared representations across teachers. The principal positioning relative to SceneSplat, point-cloud pretraining, and multi-teacher distillation is retained.

T1.justification: v1 motivates the augmentations qualitatively and refers to unavailable supplementary equations. v3 Appendix A.3 supplies a Taylor-expansion and covariance argument for rendering-equivalent perturbations, and a projection/Fourier derivation relating scale inflation to Gaussian blur. These add substantive mathematical justification beyond notation changes or standard metric formulas.

improvement.justification: v3 resolves an important documentation deficiency: v1 repeatedly refers to supplementary method equations and implementation details absent from the supplied PDF. The added derivations, data-processing instructions, training details, robustness tests, and failure analysis substantially strengthen reproducibility and evidential support. Documented SceneSplat retraining also improves comparison transparency. The unresolved VLM connector inconsistency limits clarity but does not outweigh these gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe Chorus and retain matching methods, experiments, and figures. All essential material is readable. The supplied v1 ends after its references; v3 includes supplementary Sections A–E, allowing their newly included content to be assessed.

after.justification: v3 retains original Chorus results and reports additional robustness experiments, teacher ablations, and qualitative analyses in the main text and supplement.

before.justification: v1 reports original Chorus segmentation, question-answering, probing, data-efficiency, adaptation, and ablation results in Tables 1–10 and associated figures.

results.title: Chorus: Multi-Teacher Pretraining for Holistic 3D Gaussian Scene Encoding

C1.justification: The abstract and contribution summary replace the 1.25–2.00× acceleration claim with 1.43–1.71× and expand the distilled-model claim from 15.92× to 15.9–20.9×. These ranges reflect different reported configuration coverage. The central data-free post-training, selective-transfer and ADM contributions remain the same.

C2.justification: Appendices B–C explain how alpha changes the regularizer's gradient landscape and interpret the new ablation as supporting schedule robustness. Appendix F makes the training-stability rationale for sequential linearization and distillation explicit. These extend the interpretation without changing the main mechanism claims or introducing a substantially different applicability boundary.

D1.justification: Appendices A and G disclose the OpenVid prompt source, 81-frame inputs with 21 latent frames, FSDP, 10% warm-up, batch sizes 48/64, initial learning rate 0.0001, alpha decay from 20 to 2, and the 128-prompt heuristic-selection procedure. Evaluation counts of five videos per VBench prompt and three or twenty per VBench-2.0 prompt are also supplied. These substantially improve reproducibility, chiefly through additional disclosure.

E1.justification: Both versions study text-to-video generation using synthetic model trajectories and evaluate VBench and VBench-2.0. OpenVid is newly disclosed as the prompt source, without evidence of a dataset replacement. Model size, resolution and frame-count differences concern experimental configurations within this retained coverage.

E2.justification: The main comparators remain FlashAttention2, DFA, XAttention, SVG and SVG2; the Manual, Heuristic and objective controls also remain. Appendix F quantifies the direct-distillation failure already reported qualitatively in v1 Section 4.3. SLA receives an explicit exclusion explanation but is not evaluated in either version.

E3.justification: Section 5.1 adds a substantial configuration: Wan14B at 720p, replacing 22/40 attention layers and training on 32 H100 GPUs, alongside the retained Wan1.3B configuration. Appendix C specifies annealed and fixed-alpha comparison settings. Conversely, v1 Figure 7's latency sweep over 81, 161 and 321 frames is removed. Newly disclosed settings for retained experiments do not establish that those experiments changed or were rerun.

E4.justification: The appendix supplies alpha-schedule sensitivity results, visual evidence of temporal jitter under the naive objective, and a quantitative comparison of direct versus sequential distillation and linearization. Several questions were mentioned in v1, but their supporting appendix evidence was absent. V2 also removes the frame-length scaling analysis from v1 Figure 7.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-training-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, significance tests or uncertainty estimates. Appendix A's videos-per-prompt counts disclose evaluation sample sizes rather than a new uncertainty-reporting practice.

E6.justification: The Wan1.3B quality scores in Tables 1–4 are retained. V2 adds Wan14B results, including 1127-second inference at 1.71× speedup and 92.56-second distilled inference at 20.9×, plus VBench-2.0 totals of 59.62 and 58.22 respectively. Appendix Tables I–II add alpha-ablation and direct-distillation scores, while the longer-frame latency results disappear. These are additional or removed results, not same-setting improvements over v1.

M1.justification: The Hedgehog kernel, learnable layer-selection scores, constraint and regularization losses, ADM objective, score estimator, and optional subsequent DMD2 distillation remain unchanged. Applying the framework to Wan14B and documenting the existing two-stage procedure do not introduce a new proposed method.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction and method prose receive localized rewriting, and related work is shortened. The separate Efficiency Discussion is absorbed into Main Results, the ablation subsection is renumbered, and supplementary material is organized into Appendix A–H. The main narrative and method exposition remain largely intact.

P2.justification: Figure 4 changes from a radar chart to labeled bar panels for both model sizes. Table 1 gains latency columns and model groups, while Table 2 incorporates latency information previously plotted separately. The frame-scaling plot is removed, and the appendix adds Figures I–IV and Tables I–II. V1 Figure 8 is retained as v2 Figure 6, rather than constituting a new analysis.

R1.justification: V2 shortens the early-video survey and removes citations including Stable Video Diffusion, Tune-A-Video and Make-A-Video, while adding OpenVid and FSDP. It corrects the implementation paragraph's DMD2 citation and explains SLA's exclusion through its stated GPU-kernel restriction. The central positioning against sparse attention and intra-layer mixed attention is retained.

T1.justification: Appendix D adds the previously unavailable derivation of Equation (13), starting from the general score–velocity relationship, substituting the rectified-flow schedules and subtracting the two scores. The main equations and formal assumptions remain unchanged.

improvement.justification: V2 resolves an important reporting deficiency: v1 repeatedly points to an absent appendix for training settings, derivation and supporting analyses. These are now inspectable, and Wan14B comparisons test the efficiency–quality tradeoff beyond the original small model. Removing the longer-video latency sweep and introducing a default-score discrepancy—26.57 in Appendix Table I versus 26.52 in the main tables—are drawbacks, but the gains in reproducibility and verifiable support are substantial.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same LINVIDEO work, with readable text, equations, figures and tables. V1 ends with references despite referring to an appendix; v2 includes Appendix A–H. The supplied contents support reliable comparison of what each version documents.

after.justification: V2 retains original Wan1.3B experiments, adds Wan14B benchmark and latency results, and includes numerical ablations and generated examples in its appendix.

before.justification: V1 reports original Wan1.3B generation-quality evaluations, inference and training timings, and layer-selection and objective ablations in Section 5.

results.title: LinVideo: A Post-Training Framework towards O(n) Attention in Efficient Video Generation

C1.justification: The abstract, contribution list and conclusion retain the same claims about structured visual advantages, annotation-free perceptual allocation, improved preference alignment and lightweight compatibility with GRPO. The supplement adds support without redefining these contributions.

C2.justification: Appendix A adds interpretations of DINOv2's semantic emphasis, ResNet's texture responses and SAM's boundary emphasis, including cases where SAM weights backgrounds more strongly than foregrounds. Appendix B additionally suggests that semantic alignment improves indirectly despite excluding text alignment from the training reward.

D1.justification: Appendices A and C substantially expand reproducibility information previously deferred to unavailable supplementary material in v1. Additions include precise map computations, ResNet-50 layer4 extraction, learning rates, SDE noise parameters, a 0.6 gradient-timestep fraction, shared group initialization, a 1e-4 clipping range and video generation/reward-processing frame rates. These are newly documented details, without evidence of changed training settings.

E1.justification: Both versions use HPD image prompts, VidProM video prompts, VBench evaluation and the redness-reward setting. Additional qualitative examples and VBench breakdowns retain this coverage without introducing a distinct dataset, domain or task.

E2.justification: DanceGRPO and the untuned Flux/Wan2.1 models remain the comparison methods, with the same PSM backbone variants. The supplement reuses these comparators. Figure 10 explicitly labels the Flux reference for redness optimization; Figure 5 already displayed the shared starting outputs.

E3.justification: Table 5 adds an efficiency evaluation using training-step time, per-sample PSM latency and peak memory. Existing splits, resolutions, sampling steps and quality-evaluation settings remain unchanged. Appendix C discloses additional settings for the retained experiments without stating that those settings were changed.

E4.justification: v3 adds resource-overhead analysis in Table 5 and mechanism diagnostics through backbone-specific allocation maps and individual PCA components in Figure 8. Figures 9–10 further examine backbone-dependent outputs and semantic preservation under redness optimization. These substantially extend efficiency and mechanism analyses, while the quantitative ablations in Tables 3–4 remain unchanged.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, experimental seed lists, confidence intervals or significance tests. Appendix C's shared initialization noise within each sample group describes sampling control rather than statistical uncertainty estimation.

E6.justification: Tables 1–4 retain their scores, but v3 adds substantial efficiency and detailed performance evidence. Table 5 reports image training-time overhead of 1.0–1.8% and video overhead of 4.8%. Table 6 adds nine VBench dimensions: Dynamic Degree is 63.89 for ViPO, 45.83 for DanceGRPO and 52.77 for Wan2.1; ViPO nevertheless trails Wan2.1 on Color, Appearance Style and Scene. Additional figures report further qualitative outputs and allocation maps.

M1.justification: The PSM, spatial advantage assignment and ViPO objective in Sections 3.2–3.3 remain unchanged. Appendix A specifies computations for the already evaluated DINOv2, SAM and ResNet variants; it does not establish a change to the implemented method.

P1.justification: The main narrative and section order are largely unchanged. v3 corrects the author spelling Haibing to Haibin, several typographical errors and a duplicated phrase, and organizes the supplementary explanations into Sections A–C. There is no extensive rewriting of the existing argument.

P2.justification: v3 adds Tables 5–6 and Figures 6–10, providing extensive image/video comparison grids, allocation-map and PCA visualizations, backbone comparisons and additional redness examples. These substantially expand the visual presentation while preserving the main tables and figures; Figure 1 also receives a spelling correction.

R1.justification: The cited works and research positioning remain the same. Reference 21 changes from preprint metadata to its journal publication, and the supplement reuses existing backbone citations; neither constitutes a new related-work contribution.

T1.justification: Appendix A adds explicit mathematical definitions for inverted min-max normalization and CNN channel aggregation using softmax weights derived from global average pooling. Other appendix equations restate the existing PCA and variance-weighted construction. The original equations and reasoning remain unchanged, with no new theorem or proof.

improvement.justification: v1 defers essential PSM computations and training settings to supplementary material absent from the supplied PDF. v3 supplies those details in Appendices A and C, substantially improving reproducibility. Measured overhead and allocation-map diagnostics also provide concrete support for previously asserted efficiency and mechanism claims, while detailed VBench scores expose performance boundaries. The headline experiments remain unchanged and statistical uncertainty is still unreported, but the documentation and supporting-evidence gains are substantial.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same ViPO work and have readable text, equations, tables and figures. v1 ends after the references; v3 retains the main paper and adds supplementary Sections A–C. The supplied material supports a reliable comparison.

after.justification: v3 retains those original experiments and additionally reports computational overhead, detailed VBench results and further qualitative analyses in the supplement.

before.justification: Section 4 reports original Flux and Wan2.1 experiments, including quantitative comparisons in Tables 1–2, ablations in Tables 3–4, and qualitative redness-reward experiments.

results.title: Seeing What Matters: Visual Preference Policy Optimization for Visual Generation

C1.justification: The central replication/interpolation and simple-baseline findings remain. However, the abstract, introduction, and conclusion now foreground limited data, overparameterization, and underused structural priors as potential explanations, and introduce data scaling as a successful mitigation in G.pt. This materially expands the central contributions beyond v1's emphasis on unsuccessful mitigation.

C2.justification: v2 develops explanations involving dataset size and capacity, qualifies scaling benefits through Hyper-Representations' failure, and distinguishes downstream diversity from checkpoint diversity. Appendix H explicitly identifies architectural and training confounds in the image-versus-weight comparison. Conversely, v1's explicit limitation that unexamined methods may behave differently is removed.

D1.justification: v2 discloses more exact checkpoint/run counts, G.pt's 200 checkpoints per run, and HyperDiffusion's occupancy-field and mesh-extraction details. New experiments specify Kaiming Uniform initialization and an MLP stopping rule of 50 epochs without improvement. The existing project/code access information and CIFAR-100 training recipe remain.

E1.justification: Appendix I adds p-diff evaluation using ImageNet classification checkpoints, extending the earlier CIFAR-100 coverage. Existing classification, ShapeNet, Flowers, and intrinsic-dimension datasets remain; the coverage extension stays within the existing task families.

E2.justification: The evaluated comparison methods remain Gaussian noise addition, checkpoint averaging, fitted-Gaussian sampling, and independently trained models where applicable. The new ImageNet experiment extends the existing interpolation comparison. Newly cited weight-generation methods are not added as evaluated comparators.

E3.justification: New protocols scale G.pt from 2.1M to 20.4M checkpoints and Hyper-Representations from 2896 to 24136. Other additions reinitialize individual or all MLP layers and compare independently initialized MLPs trained for 0, 200, 400, or full epochs. Appendix B adds holdout-based rank testing. These substantially expand the experimental design while retaining the original default experiments.

E4.justification: Section 4.1 and Appendix F add substantial analyses of checkpoint scarcity, memorization of random weights, and dependence on MLP training progress. Appendix I tests whether greater downstream image diversity changes p-diff's behavior. The earlier model-size, regularization, and training-duration ablations remain in Appendix F.3.

E5.justification: v2 introduces non-parametric data-copying tests with standardized Mann-Whitney Z_U scores for original models and several ablations. Appendix B supplies HyperDiffusion sample counts and cautions against comparing scores across methods with different holdout sizes. The existing 20-seed from-scratch comparison and its accuracy variation are retained.

E6.justification: The added G.pt scaling experiment reports generated/training nearest-neighbor distances of 2.78/2.70, versus 2.25/3.64 under the original data size, with accuracy remaining approximately 94%. New statistical results show Z_U changing from -8.5 to 3.5 with G.pt scaling, while Hyper-Representations remains at -13.6. Randomized-weight and ImageNet findings are also added. Some Figure 6 scatter samples change, while v1 Table 1 is retained numerically as v2 Table 9.

M1.justification: The four studied weight-generation methods and the noise, averaging, and fitted-Gaussian procedures remain unchanged. The additions evaluate these methods under further conditions and introduce an evaluation statistic, rather than modifying their generation algorithms.

P1.justification: The abstract and introduction are substantially revised, the generic generative-model background subsection is removed, and Section 4 is reorganized around explanations of memorization. Earlier modeling-factor discussion moves to Appendix F.3, new appendices are integrated, and the standalone Limitations and Broader Impacts sections disappear. Headings and citation style change throughout.

P2.justification: v2 adds scaling/random-initialization histograms, statistical and ablation tables, and ImageNet heatmap and trade-off figures. It relocates the original main ablation table to the appendix and redraws existing scatter/t-SNE displays, including axis and marker changes. Title, heading, and page styling are revised throughout.

R1.justification: v2 expands citations to recent weight-generation successors, data-copying detection, network expressivity, and policy-archive compression, while updating introductory image/video examples. It more explicitly challenges prior novelty claims, but retains its overall positioning as an empirical examination of weight-generation generalization.

T1.justification: Appendix B adds an extremal-score argument alongside the rank-test definitions: approximately -30.8 is the minimum attainable Z_U for n=606 and m=666, and the HyperDiffusion cases attain it. The existing symmetry discussion, IoU definition, and intrinsic-dimension estimator remain unchanged; no substantial theorem or proof is introduced.

improvement.justification: Compared with v1's unsuccessful mitigation tests, v2 establishes contrasting data-scaling outcomes, tests memorization of random weights, and adds holdout-based statistical and ImageNet checks. These substantially strengthen the evidence about when memorization occurs and what may alleviate it. The explicit confounds in Appendix H also improve interpretation. Although removing the untested-methods limitation weakens scope qualification, the added controls and more nuanced explanations provide a substantial net improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs are readable versions of the same study. Their main text, figures, tables, equations, and appendices support reliable matching of retained, relocated, and newly added material.

after.justification: v2 retains these empirical results and adds data-scaling experiments, randomized-weight and training-length controls, statistical data-copying tests, and an ImageNet evaluation.

before.justification: v1 reports original memorization evaluations, noise and interpolation comparisons, modeling-factor ablations, symmetry experiments, and additional empirical analyses in its appendices.

results.title: Generative Modeling of Weights: Generalization or Memorization?

C1.justification: The abstract, contributions, and conclusion now explicitly emphasize both FSIG and personalization across diffusion backbones. Claims of higher quality and outperforming two-stage pipelines are qualified to better or comparable quality and often outperforming. The central single-stage unification and component contributions remain unchanged.

C2.justification: V2 explains the personalization tradeoff between FT-DMD2's stronger identity scores and substantially lower diversity, and acknowledges reduced diversity relative to DreamBooth. It also qualifies distant-domain FSIG superiority and the multi-head discriminator's advantage, while adding a proposed explanation for WGAN instability. Existing GAN-sensitivity and training-cost limitations remain.

D1.justification: V2 supplies a code-repository URL instead of v1's promise of future public release. Appendix 8.4 documents initialization of the added personalization FT-DMD2 baseline, and Appendix 8.6 explains selecting a=0.75 through visual inspection without subject-specific tuning. Most hardware, hyperparameters, and training details are retained.

E1.justification: FSIG, personalization, and Starry Night style transfer already appear in v1. V2 Figure 8 adds explicit personalization scenarios requiring property changes, including purple and cube-shaped teapots, beyond the previously illustrated recontextualization and accessorization cases. The larger DreamBooth subject sample is assessed under E3.

E2.justification: V2 Table 3 adds FT-DMD2 and DMD2-PSO on SDv1.5 to the personalization comparison, materially strengthening tests against two-stage pipelines and PSO under matching backbone and sampling budgets. DreamBooth becomes FT, DMD2-DreamBooth becomes DMD2-FT, and the existing PSO becomes Turbo-PSO; these are retained comparators. FSIG comparator membership is unchanged.

E3.justification: Personalization evaluation expands from three selected DreamBooth subjects to all 30 and adds Intra-LPIPS and Inter-LPIPS alongside identity and text-alignment metrics. V2 also introduces a groupwise weighting-factor sweep. The 25 prompts × 4 generation seeds per subject, principal training settings, and existing FSIG evaluation protocol remain unchanged.

E4.justification: V2 adds personalization sensitivity analysis for the dual-domain weight, with qualitative examples and separate live-subject/object CLIP-I results, plus within-prompt and across-prompt diversity comparisons in Figure 10. These substantially extend diagnostic evidence for personalization. Existing FSIG component, checkpoint, shot-count, NFE, and GAN-loss ablations are retained and relocated.

E5.justification: V2 Table 3 introduces ± reporting for personalization diversity scores, absent from v1; Uni-DAD Intra-LPIPS is 0.51±0.09. The statistic represented by ± and its aggregation unit are unspecified. Four generation seeds per prompt were already reported in v1, and additional independent training runs are not established.

E6.justification: V1 Table 7's individual and three-subject personalization scores are replaced by 30-subject results in v2 Table 3, with additional baseline and diversity entries.
