Uni-DAD's DINO/CLIP-I/CLIP-T averages change from 0.631/0.771/0.271 to 0.47/0.73/0.29 under different subject coverage, not a directly comparable performance change. New sensitivity findings are reported; existing FSIG table values remain unchanged.

M1.justification: Section 3.5 revises the stated GAN objectives from hinge losses to sigmoid-based binary cross-entropy in Equations 8–9. V1 already selected BCE in Table 5, so this corrects the method specification without establishing changed implementation or retraining. The architecture, dual-domain DMD, training loop, and personalization conditioning are retained.

P1.justification: The narrative is substantially reorganized around two benchmarks: personalization moves from a supplementary chapter into the main setup and results, while most FSIG ablations and Algorithm 1 move into the supplement. The abstract, contributions, discussion, conclusion, and appendix organization are extensively revised, and acknowledgements are added.

P2.justification: V2 adds personalization comparison and diagnostic figures, expands the comparison grid with FT-DMD2, and replaces the three-subject table with a benchmark-wide quality/diversity display. Computational costs move into the main text, FSIG ablation tables move to the appendix, and supplementary image grids are rearranged. This is substantial display reorganization beyond renumbering.

R1.justification: V2 removes the separate Google Research DreamBooth repository reference while retaining the DreamBooth paper. The scientific reference set and positioning against Codi, PSO, and guidance-distillation approaches otherwise remain substantially unchanged. Moving and condensing personalization related work is primarily structural.

T1.justification: V2 formally defines sigmoid discriminator outputs and replaces the hinge expressions in Equations 8–9 with logarithmic BCE objectives, resolving their mismatch with v1's selected loss. This is a mathematical specification correction. The DMD derivation, weighting equations, and remaining formal content are unchanged; no new theorems or proofs appear.

improvement.justification: V2 addresses an important validation gap: v1's personalization evidence covered only three subjects and lacked an Adapt-then-Distill comparator and diversity measurements. Full-benchmark evaluation, added controls, and sensitivity/diversity analyses provide substantially stronger evidence for the central quality–diversity tradeoff. Corrected GAN equations and more qualified claims improve consistency. Undefined ± statistics, incomplete details for DMD2-PSO, and removal of individual subject scores limit transparency but do not outweigh these gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Uni-DAD research and include readable main text and supplementary material. Equations, tables, figures, and relocated sections can be matched reliably.

after.justification: V2 retains the original FSIG experiments and reports personalization results across 30 DreamBooth subjects, additional comparisons, and new sensitivity and diversity analyses.

before.justification: V1 reports original FSIG experiments, component ablations, computational measurements, and three-subject personalization experiments, including supplementary Table 7.

results.title: Uni-DAD: Unified Distillation and Adaptation of Diffusion Models for Few-step Few-shot Image Generation

C1.justification: The principal claims of strong novel/extreme-view reconstruction and disentangled editing remain. v2's abstract adds an explicit claim that the perceptual loss is a drop-in replacement for standard losses, and its contributions emphasize supervision solely through deep perceptual features.

C2.justification: v2 qualifies v1's temporal-coherence discussion by acknowledging flickering and adds CLIP-related identity limitations, localized-editing tradeoffs, and failures involving unusual glasses or unrealistic faces. It introduces substantive interpretations of layer/token supervision and complementary loss behavior. The earlier blanket limitation concerning non-real-time inference is removed.

D1.justification: v2 newly documents AdamW settings, epoch counts, architecture dimensions and attention heads, the 3,000-image FFHQ subset, view/occlusion filtering, and sharpening-module processing. It adds component timing and memory measurements and explicitly states that training code, inference code, and the GUI are available through the project website. Newly disclosed settings do not establish that those settings changed.

E1.justification: The Ava-256, NeRSemble, and VFHQ evaluation coverage is retained. v2 Appendix C.5 substantially broadens tested input conditions through held-out FFHQ images, UFDD examples, and SORA-generated inputs, including cartoons, unusual accessories, and difficult illumination.

E2.justification: v2 adds SphereHead to the Ava-256 and NeRSemble reconstruction comparisons, FaceLift to an additional Ava-256 comparison, and NeRFFaceEditing to geometric-editing comparisons. The original LGM, PanoHead, GAGAvatar, and LAM comparators remain.

Reported CNN/editing training durations change from 24/30 hours to 10/48 hours. New protocols examine epochs 1–3, token supervision after one epoch, and four-layer model configurations; SSIM is also omitted from the main ablation table.

E4.justification: v2 adds early-training comparisons across DINOv2 layers, patch-versus-class-token ablations, difficult-input tests of the loss and sharpening module, and lightweight-model cost/quality analyses. It also examines localized versus large geometric edits. Existing data/loss ablations remain, although the quantitative LPIPS+L1-without-CNN comparison is removed.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, error bars, or formal significance tests. The additional experiments retain point-estimate reporting.

E6.justification: Primary reconstruction and ablation values change beyond rounding. For example, Ava-256 novel-view PSNR changes from 16.08 to 16.4 while LPIPS changes from 0.2666 to 0.269 for the revised model. Under the changed CNN controls, LPIPS+L1 now beats the full model on ablation LPIPS, reversing v1's ordering. New comparator, robustness, early-training, and lightweight-model results substantially expand the evidence.

M1.justification: The core reconstruction and editing pipelines remain. Sharpening supervision changes from DINOv2, L1, and LPIPS in v1 Section 3.4 to only the DINOv2 layer-8 class token in v2 Section 3.3. Appendix C.6 also introduces four-layer lightweight variants; the expanded CNN and Gaussian descriptions alone do not establish architectural changes.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, method exposition, and experimental discussion are extensively rewritten. Separate encoder, decoder, and rendering subsections are consolidated, training receives its own subsection, and the supplement is reorganized into thematic sections A–G, retaining earlier processing and visualization material within that structure.

P2.justification: Figures 1 and 2 are substantially redrawn, comparison figures gain methods and examples, and the ablation display is redesigned. Reconstruction tables are reorganized by dataset, with NeRSemble moved to the supplement. Numerous new loss-analysis, robustness, editing, and computational-cost displays materially expand the visual presentation.

R1.justification: v2 expands discussion and citations for SphereHead, FaceLift, Avat3r, inversion/diffusion approaches, and perceptual representations, while dropping the GRM and Feng et al. (2021) references. The existing positioning relative to GAN/NeRF pipelines and conventional supervision remains broadly intact.

T1.justification: v2 explicitly defines tanh-bounded FLAME-relative Gaussian positions in Equation 3 and a multiplicative perceptual-loss combination in Equation 7, details left unspecified in v1. These are limited mathematical additions; the decoder recurrence is retained, and no theorems or proofs are introduced.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens experimental support and reproducibility through relevant new comparators, a separately trained LPIPS+L1 control, targeted loss diagnostics, robustness tests, and detailed training specifications. Its more explicit temporal and editing limitations also improve claim calibration. These gains address important weaknesses in v1 and outweigh local reporting problems, including Table 5's SSIM heading above values around 15–16.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe PercHead, with matching authors, core architecture, reconstruction tasks, and editing framework. Their text, equations, tables, figures, and appendices are readable and support comparison despite substantial revision.

after.justification: v2 reports original reconstruction and editing experiments, revised quantitative results, and additional loss diagnostics, robustness tests, and lightweight-model evaluations.

before.justification: v1 reports original reconstruction results on Ava-256 and NeRSemble, quantitative ablations, video reconstructions, and image- and text-conditioned editing examples.

results.title: PercHead: Perceptual Head Model for Single-Image 3D Head Reconstruction & Editing

C1.justification: The central dataset, benchmark, and multi-frame spatial-learning contributions remain intact. v2's introduction additionally claims comparability with specialized 3D perception models, scalability with trainable parameters, and preservation of general abilities. It also adds a first-time novelty claim for observing spatial emergence, extending the existing contribution framing.

C2.justification: v2 adds interpretations concerning the importance of vision-encoder tuning, the proposed orthogonality of spatial and general capabilities, and depth/correspondence as more fundamental spatial tasks. SpatialRGPT's results motivate a new claim about failure of single-image supervision to transfer. The limitations now acknowledge extra-frame generalization evidence while retaining the need for training beyond pairs.

D1.justification: Table 7 newly discloses task-wise corpus counts, while Appendices H–L document configurations and sample counts for added experiments. Existing code listings, core hyperparameters, and hardware details remain. v2 removes v1's project-page link and Appendix B's pointer to complete templates; the PDFs do not establish whether actual resource availability changed.

E1.justification: v2 expands held-out evaluation to synthetic indoor views rendered from 3RScan, spatial and embodied reasoning in CVBench-3D and ERQA, and broader general VQA coverage through MMMU, MME, and MMVet. Appendix L also tests camera-direction prediction with additional intermediate images, extending evaluation beyond image pairs.

E2.justification: Tables 2 and 3 remove InternVL-13B and add SpatialRGPT to the MultiSPA and BLINK comparisons; 13B remains in other experiments. Appendix I additionally evaluates VGGT for camera-vector prediction, Depth Anything for depth comparison, and LoFTR for image matching, substantially broadening the comparator set.

E3.justification: The default training setup and MultiSPA scoring rules are retained. New protocols vary trainable components and full versus LoRA tuning, normalize scale for the VGGT comparison, test 1K correspondence examples with 50K auxiliary-task examples, compare 400K-example auxiliary-task additions, and insert 1–4 intermediate frames. These are additional experimental settings, not evidence that the retained experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: Beyond v1's scaling, pooled multi-task, and Easy/Hard correspondence studies, v2 adds component-tuning ablations (Table 8), task-specific transfer analyses (Tables 12–13), a forgetting curve throughout training (Figure 6), and robustness to additional input frames (Table 14). These investigate previously untested sources of gains and failure concerns.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated experimental runs, confidence intervals, error bars, or formal significance tests. The statement about using different random seeds to sample image pairs is retained and does not constitute new experimental uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: The retained model's MultiSPA and BLINK averages remain 56.11 and 84.3. v2 adds extensive results, including a 66.72 fully tuned average in Table 8, 18.7/27.7 accuracy for 8B/26B on 3RScan, and scale-normalized VGGT-versus-ours scores of 86 versus 82 in Table 9. Figure 4 adds a full-tuning result near 72%; v1's reported 44% used a different tuning configuration, so this is not a same-setting performance gain.

M1.justification: The data-generation algorithms, architecture, objectives, and default InternVL2-8B LoRA procedure remain unchanged. The original appendix algorithms and Listings 1–4 are retained. Newly evaluated component-unfreezing and full-fine-tuning configurations are experimental variants rather than new proposed algorithmic components.

P1.justification: There are localized rewrites of the abstract, introduction, related work, and scaling discussion, plus author/header edits. The appendix gains sections H–L and moves the limitations from H to M. Most existing prose, the main section sequence, algorithms, and dataset examples are retained.

P2.justification: v2 redesigns the opening page, placing Figure 1 above a two-column abstract/introduction arrangement. Figure 4 is redrawn with a logarithmic data axis and explicit LoRA/full-tuning curves. Tables 7–14 and the forgetting plot are added, and existing tables are repositioned. The original appendix example figures are retained and renumbered.

R1.justification: v2 adds references including VLM-3R, Spatial-MLLM, OST-Bench, and the newly evaluated expert models and benchmarks. Flamingo, ShareGPT4V, and ShareGPT4o references disappear with shortened training-background discussion. Positioning expands toward specialist-model comparability and emergence novelty, while the principal distinction from single-image spatial methods and SAT remains.

T1.justification: The projection, visibility, overlap, and rotation definitions in Equations 1–8 retain their mathematical content. Section 3.3's explicit inequality restates the existing 20% relative L2-error criterion. No new theorem, proof, or substantive derivation is introduced.

improvement.justification: The expert comparisons, additional domain and benchmark evaluations, component/task ablations, and extra-frame tests substantially strengthen evidence for the central claims and address important gaps in v1's validation. Appendices H–L also clarify what drives performance. Removed resource pointers and some overbroad interpretations are drawbacks: for example, the introduction claims no degradation despite Table 11 showing MMVet falling from 62.0 to 58.1. These issues do not outweigh the substantial gains in empirical scrutiny.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe Multi-SpatialMLLM and MultiSPA. The complete main texts, equations, figures, tables, and appendices support comparison; retained material can be matched across reformatting and renumbering.

after.justification: v2 retains those original experiments and adds expert-model comparisons, additional benchmark evaluations, and training and robustness analyses in Appendices H–L.

before.justification: v1 reports original MultiSPA, BLINK, and general VQA evaluations, scaling and multi-task experiments, and robotics demonstrations in Section 4.

results.title: Multi-SpatialMLLM: Multi-Frame Spatial Understanding with Multi-Modal Large Language Models

C1.justification: V3 foregrounds customized-teacher distillation as a contribution addressing small-teacher supervisory bottlenecks. Its abstract removes the open-source qualifier from the superiority claim, and its introduction broadens state-of-the-art wording beyond pure decoder-only unified models. The central claims about unified understanding, generation, editing and efficient autoregressive inference remain.

C2.justification: V3 adds substantive interpretations connecting teacher instability to parameter misalignment, explaining the benefits of all-layer and joint visual/text distillation, and motivating the generation-token allocation through limited interference with understanding. Appendix C also reports early and late fusion as comparable in accuracy under its controls, qualifying the architectural advantage as computational efficiency. These interpretations were absent from v1.

D1.justification: Appendices A–B disclose exact aspect-ratio scale schedules and guidance equations and strengths: 20 for text-to-image, and image/text strengths of 1/3 for editing. V3 also identifies Qwen2-VL recaptioning, JourneyDB prompt provenance, detailed training-data sources and ablation recipes. These substantially expand reproducibility information without establishing a change in code availability.

E1.justification: The main evaluation benchmarks and tasks are retained. Section 5 revises the additional 3M Stage-3 examples from in-house synthetic instructions to public sources covering VQA, art, counting and documents. New ablations use LLaVA-665K instruction data. The expanded Stage-2 source list primarily supplies provenance rather than establishing that every listed dataset was newly introduced.

More substantially, v3 introduces controlled comparisons against EvE and VoRA distillation strategies in Table 9, an alternative Qwen2.5-VL teacher in Table 10, and encoder-based late fusion in Table 14. These extend comparison beyond v1's end-to-end benchmark and latency evaluations.

E3.justification: New experiments introduce controlled training protocols: 8B-token distillation followed by LLaVA-665K fine-tuning, fixed text/understanding budgets with varying generation budgets, and fusion comparisons using a randomly initialized vision encoder. Section 4.3 also revises the stated maximum generated-image side from 1728 to 1776 pixels, although Table 1 retains 1728. These reported changes do not establish that retained experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: V1 lacks component ablations. V3 Section 7.5 tests distillation targets, teacher choice, task-token ratios and SAA removal. Appendix C adds fusion, distilled-token and training-scale analyses; Appendix D adds feature-map and Fourier analyses examining the scale-dependent information motivating SAA.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, significance tests or uncertainty estimates. V3's new tables and curves retain point-estimate reporting; averages across benchmarks are not repeated-run uncertainty estimates.

E6.justification: OneCAT's headline scores in Tables 3–7 are unchanged, but v3 adds substantial ablation and scaling results. New controlled tests report average scores of 31.4 without distillation versus 35.3 with all-layer distillation, and GenEval 81.2 with SAA versus 78.1 without; these are not version-to-version gains. Comparator results and qualitative outputs are added. The 1024×1024 TTFT comparison, 0.216 versus 0.092 seconds, is removed, and Figure 7's final editing case changes its prompt and outputs.

M1.justification: Section 4.1.2 changes the reported distillation-loss weight from 0.2 to 0.02. The three-expert architecture, scale-aware adapter, attention mechanisms and staged training otherwise remain intact. Expanded descriptions of adapter placement, scale schedules and guidance do not establish additional algorithm changes.

P1.justification: V3 extensively rewrites the introduction and method/training exposition, organizes the introduction around architecture and training, consolidates the architecture discussion under Modality-MoE, and shortens the efficiency narrative. Qualitative evaluation receives a separate subsection, and structured appendices provide background and implementation explanations. This exceeds simple additions or renumbering.

P2.justification: Figure 3 is redrawn, Table 2 is restructured, Figures 6–7 revise prompt/panel displays, and the two efficiency tables are merged. New ablation tables, learning curves, fusion diagrams, frequency visualizations and qualitative panels substantially expand presentation. Some Appendix E editing examples redisplay images already present in Figure 2 rather than constituting new results.

R1.justification: V3 adds relevant work including VoRA, SAIL, Synergen-VL, native-multimodal scaling research and reconstruction alignment, alongside numerous data-source citations. It introduces a specific critique of small-ViT distillation teachers. The existing four-part related-work organization and overall positioning around encoder-free unified autoregression remain.

T1.justification: New Appendix A formally specifies recursive multiscale quantization, binary spherical quantization, autoregressive factorization, and the within-scale conditional-independence assumption. Appendix B supplies explicit guidance equations. This adds mathematical definitions and assumptions absent from v1, largely as background and implementation formalization, without new theorems or proofs.

improvement.justification: V1 claims benefits from distillation and SAA without component-level validation. V3's Section 7.5 and Appendices C–D substantially address that deficiency through controlled ablations, scaling studies and feature analyses; explicit schedules, guidance settings and data provenance also improve reproducibility. These gains outweigh the limited losses and inconsistencies, despite unchanged headline scores. Missing uncertainty estimates, broader superiority wording and the conflicting 1728/1776-pixel settings remain weaknesses.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe OneCAT, with matching authors, architecture and principal experiments. All 22 pages of v1 and 32 pages of v3 were readable, including figures and equations. V1 ends with references; v3 adds Appendices A–E.

after.justification: V3 retains those original benchmark results and adds distillation, teacher, token-ratio, adapter and scaling experiments, including analyses in Appendices C–E.

before.justification: V1 reports original OneCAT understanding, generation and editing results, qualitative outputs, and inference measurements in Tables 3–9.

results.title: OneCAT: Decoder-Only Auto-Regressive Model for Unified Understanding and Generation

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the same central contributions: an open-data volumetric transformer, complementary self-supervised and vision-language pretraining, and transfer across classification, segmentation, and retrieval. The additional evidence does not redefine these core claims.

C2.justification: v1 qualitatively notes small-lesion failures; v2 develops an evidence-based interpretation involving decoder choice and training budget. C.3 adds explanations of corruption sensitivity, attributes weak MedSigLIP retrieval partly to text truncation, and interprets longer-report advantages while acknowledging possible confounding by healthy subjects. These substantially expand the discussion of mechanisms and applicability limits.

D1.justification: C.2.3 changes the nnU-Net integration from a promised release upon acceptance to a stated public repository with an explicit address. C.3.1 newly discloses fixed retrieval spacing of 0.5 × 0.5 × 1.0 mm. The pretraining hyperparameters, model specifications, and hardware disclosures remain unchanged.

E1.justification: v2 adds broader anatomical segmentation on TotalSegmentator benchmarks covering 104, 117, and 20 structures, plus evaluations focused on lesions below 10 mm, corrupted reports, and native voxel spacing. AMOS is removed from quantitative segmentation benchmarking because it was used for pretraining; its pretraining use and Figure 6 examples remain.

E2.justification: Table 9 adds segmentation comparisons with SuPreM, CT-FM, Merlin, and SAM-Med3D with one or ten clicks. SuPreM, CT-FM, and Merlin previously appeared in other task comparisons, but these segmentation comparisons are new. C.3.1 also adds MedSigLIP to CT-RATE retrieval evaluation.

C.3 adds corruption procedures, a 500-token report-length threshold, and native-spacing evaluation. These are additional protocols; the retained headline experiments keep their previous settings.

The existing optimizer, deep-supervision, initialization, and crop-size ablations are retained as Table 8, formerly Table 7.

E5.justification: The existing 95% confidence intervals across cross-validation folds in Figure 3 are unchanged. New Figure 8 contains shaded bands, but its caption and accompanying text do not define their statistical meaning or report runs or seeds. Whether these introduce a different uncertainty-reporting practice cannot be established reliably.

E6.justification: Table 9 adds SPECTRE Dice scores of 87.34, 88.85, and 87.29 on its three TotalSegmentator benchmarks. New Table 10 reports, for example, 1.53% versus 11.12% tiny-lesion detection for SEoMT versus UNETR at 37.5k steps. Retrieval robustness and MedSigLIP results are also added. Retained headline scores and the original ablation values are unchanged; the AMOS Dice result of 87.55 is removed.

M1.justification: C.2.7 adds linear-head and UNETR-style segmentation adaptations of the pretrained encoder, changing the decoding procedure in these experiments. The SPECTRE backbone, two-stage pretraining objectives, and default SEoMT procedure remain unchanged.

P1.justification: There are localized wording and cross-reference edits, revised acknowledgments, two additional segmentation subsections, and separate CT-RATE and MERLIN retrieval subsections. Most existing prose and the main narrative structure are retained; the added scientific content does not constitute extensive rewriting.

P2.justification: The supplement adds result Tables 9–10 and the dropout plot in Figure 8, while expanding and numbering the dataset table as Table 7. Table 1 loses its AMOS column, although its caption still says four datasets. Existing figure content is retained with resizing and placement changes, including relocation of the UMAP plot.

R1.justification: v2 adds the MedGemma Technical Report citation in connection with MedSigLIP and discusses additional segmentation comparisons, including SAM-Med3D. The main related-work survey and SPECTRE's claimed relationship to prior transformer and CT foundation models remain substantially unchanged.

T1.justification: The mathematical architecture and loss formulations in Sections 3–4, including all 20 numbered equations, are unchanged. The added experiments introduce no new formal definitions, derivations, theorems, or proofs.

improvement.justification: v1 included AMOS in quantitative evaluation despite using it for pretraining and discussed small-lesion failures mainly qualitatively. v2 removes that overlapping quantitative comparison and directly measures decoder, training-budget, and tiny-lesion effects, addressing important validity and diagnostic gaps. Broader anatomical and retrieval robustness evidence further strengthens the evaluation. AMOS illustrations and reporting gaps remain, including unexplained Figure 8 bands, but the gains in empirical credibility and characterization of failure conditions are substantial.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same SPECTRE research work. Their main text, appendices, equations, tables, and figures are readable and support reliable matching of retained, revised, and added content.

after.justification: v2 retains those original results and adds TotalSegmentator evaluations, decoder and small-lesion experiments, and retrieval robustness analyses.

before.justification: v1 reports original SPECTRE results for biomarker classification, semantic segmentation, and text-to-image retrieval, together with optimization and crop-size ablations.

results.title: Scaling Self-Supervised and Cross-Modal Pretraining for Volumetric CT Transformers

C1.justification: The central ArtiHippo, zero-forgetting, benchmark-performance, and prompt-complementarity claims remain. v2 adds an explicit introductory distinction from methods using manually chosen task-difficulty thresholds. Its contribution list also drops v1's explicit efficient-forward-transfer claim, while retaining the other principal contributions.

C2.justification: v2 newly argues that conventional L2G search is ill suited to ViTs, identifies NAS runtime and scaling as a substantive limitation, and interprets CLIP generalization results in terms of forgetting and potential foundation-model adaptation. Task-ID dependence and weak task-agnostic inference were already documented in v1.

D1.justification: v1 promises a future code release; v2 reports supplied source code and training logs, identifies their locations, and explains that checkpoints remain deferred. It also adds CLIP hyperparameters and ten-A100 hardware information, L2G budgets and beta-loss weight, and the rationale for L2P's 12 tokens. These are documented disclosures; the accompanying files are not verified by the supplied PDFs.

E2.justification: v1 already compares against ResNet-based L2G in Appendix F. v2 adds ViT-based L2G with DARTS and beta-DARTS on both main benchmarks, retains the ResNet L2G comparison, and removes the ResNet Adapter row. The CLIP study additionally compares against zero-shot CLIP, full finetuning, LoRA, and Zero-Init Attention.

E3.justification: The original benchmark splits and ArtiHippo training settings remain stable. New protocols include S-Prompts lengths 5, 10, 12, and 15, and CLIP ViT-B/32 transfer at 224×224 with 100 supernet epochs, 12 evolutionary-search epochs, and 30 finetuning epochs. New L2G comparisons use 150 supernet epochs on VDD and 50 on 5-Dataset.

E4.justification: v2 adds prompt-count sensitivity studies on both benchmarks and CLIP robustness tests across four shifted distributions, including projection-versus-value comparisons. Existing hybrid-adapter, component, task-order, and task-inference analyses are retained or relocated. Figure 5 removes the 25-epoch condition from the displayed training-budget analysis.

E5.justification: The existing three-seed VDD averages, five-order 5-Dataset averages, and Figure 5's two task orders with three seeds each are retained, as are their uncertainty-reporting conventions. The new CLIP table provides point estimates without specifying repetitions or uncertainty; no new statistical procedure or revised existing run count is documented.

E6.justification: The original ArtiHippo scores in Tables 2-3 remain unchanged. Added results include VDD accuracies of 74.47±0.84 and 75.49±1.24 for ViT L2G with DARTS and beta-DARTS, prompt-count results, and CLIP projection results of 78.43 on IN-Val and 47.87 OOD average. The ResNet Adapter row and Figure 5's 25-epoch results are removed.

M1.justification: The main four-operation, hybrid-adapter, similarity-guided NAS method is retained. For the new CLIP application, Appendix D uses pure exploration because source training data are unavailable and initializes New operations from CLIP weights, whereas v1 describes random initialization. This is a limited application-specific adaptation.

P1.justification: The abstract is rewritten around four research questions, the introduction is substantially revised, and related work is incorporated into it. Ablations move from the main text to Appendix B, background material is consolidated, and dedicated Limitations and Broader Impact sections are introduced.

P2.justification: v2 changes the document template, typography, author layout, and figure placement. Method diagrams are redrawn, Figures 3 and 5 are rearranged vertically, and Figure 4 is reduced. Main comparison tables expand, Table 4 separates individual block columns, and new prompt-sweep and CLIP tables accompany relocated appendix material.

R1.justification: v2 expands discussion of task-driven priors and task-difficulty-based parameter allocation, and adds references supporting beta-DARTS, parameter-efficient adaptation, and the OOD evaluations. The Layer Normalization reference is removed. The central positioning relative to L2G, SPOS, and prompting remains intact.

T1.justification: The substantive task-similarity, sampling, accuracy, forgetting, NAS, and task-inference formulations are retained. Replacing the standard attention equation with prose and using FFN shorthand changes exposition, not mathematical substance. No substantive assumptions, theorems, proofs, or derivations are added or revised.

improvement.justification: v1 lacks a same-backbone comparison with its closest NAS predecessor; v2 addresses this with ViT-based L2G comparisons on both main benchmarks and strengthens prompting comparisons through capacity ablations. These additions substantially improve support for the central claims, alongside fuller reproducibility disclosures and explicit computational limitations. Unequal NAS budgets, preliminary CLIP evidence without uncertainty, and stale captions in Table 2 and Figure 5 remain weaknesses, but do not outweigh those gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same ArtiHippo research work. Their text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices support reliable comparison despite substantial restructuring and added experiments in v2.

after.justification: v2 retains original experiments and adds ViT-based Learn-to-Grow comparisons, prompt-count ablations, and CLIP transfer and out-of-distribution results.

before.justification: v1 reports original VDD and 5-Dataset experiments, component and sampling ablations, and preliminary class-incremental results, including Tables 1-5 and 11.

results.title: CHEEM: Continual Learning by Reuse, New, Adapt and Skip - A Hierarchical Exploration-Exploitation Approach

C1.justification: The main contribution changes from task-incremental learning through attention-projection memory to an exemplar-free class-incremental framework with internal parameter memory and external task-centroid memory. v5 emphasizes task-adaptive computation, FoM superiority, and approaching fine-tuning references on MTIL/VDD, replacing v4's projection-layer identification and first-ViT-on-VDD contribution framing.

C2.justification: v4's known-task-ID limitation and proposed future inference solution are replaced by evaluated routing-accuracy/compute tradeoffs in v5 Appendix G. v5 newly attributes poor baseline performance to local/global classifier-head mismatch and interprets architecture differences through backbone capacity. HEE's benefit is reframed around parameter economy when accuracy is comparable to uniform sampling, rather than v4's large accuracy advantage.

D1.justification: v5 adds a concrete project repository address, per-stage training times (Table 7), and documentation of revised checkpoints and dataset reconstruction (Appendix H). It does not retain v4's detailed batch sizes, evolutionary-search population and iteration settings, regularization recipe, or baseline-porting instructions from Appendices B–C and F. Reproducibility information is substantially revised, with both additions and losses.

E1.justification: Evaluation changes from task-incremental learning with known task IDs to class-incremental learning with unknown test-time task IDs. MTIL adds coverage including Caltech101, EuroSAT, Food101, Oxford Pets, Stanford Cars, and SUN397. The 5-Datasets evaluation disappears: CIFAR10, Fashion-MNIST, and not-MNIST are removed, while MNIST and SVHN remain through MTIL and VDD respectively.

E2.justification: The evaluated comparator set is substantially replaced. v5 retains EWC, L2P, and S-Prompts, adds CODA-Prompt, DualPrompt, DIKI, LoRA-CL, MoAL, Tuna, and full/LoRA fine-tuning references, and adds MoEAdapter4CL in Appendix G. v4's L2G variants, L2 regularization, experience replay, SupSup, EFT, and Lightweight Learner comparisons are absent.

E3.justification: v4 uses ViT-B/8 at 72×72; v5 uses 224×224 inputs with ViT-B/16, DEiT-Tiny/16, and additional CLIP experiments. Appendix H reconstructs VDD using original images and revised splits where available, specifies no augmentation, and changes the stated VDD supernet/fine-tuning budgets from 100/30 to 50/20 epochs. Accuracy and forgetting now exclude the ImageNet base task, and FoM is introduced.

E4.justification: v5 adds exploration-probability and compute-tolerance sweeps, lightweight task-recognition studies, CLIP generalization tests, and local-versus-global classifier-head analysis (Figure 10; Appendices F, G, I). Placement, HEE-versus-uniform sampling, and task-order questions receive revised experiments. v4's shortcut, prompt-length, and training-duration ablations are removed. The original component-identification analysis is largely retained in Appendix J.

E5.justification: Principal comparisons retain three-seed mean and ± reporting. However, v4 Table 13 reports task-order results averaged over three seeds with uncertainty values, whereas v5 Table 10 provides order-specific point estimates without seed counts or uncertainties. This is a limited reporting change; it does not establish that fewer runs were performed.

E6.justification: Most benchmark results are replaced or newly reported. For example, v4 Table 2 reports VDD accuracy of 83.44 ± 0.50, while v5 Table 12 reports 86.71 ± 0.23 for default CHEEM under changed conditions; these are not a same-setting performance gain. MTIL accuracy of 85.88 ± 0.29 and extensive forgetting, compute, and routing results are added. The eleven component scores from v4 Table 1 remain in v5 Table 20, but its frozen-backbone classifier row is removed.

M1.justification: The HEE core remains, but v5 replaces the MLP Adapt operation with LoRA, introduces MLPDown as the primary memory placement alongside attention projection, and changes architecture selection from best validation accuracy to a compute-sensitive search (Sections 3.2–3.4). It also adds centroid-based task-ID inference and a lightweight recognition variant, replacing v4's reliance on supplied task IDs.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction, contribution statements, and experimental narrative are extensively rewritten. The introduction adopts four organizing questions, related work moves before the method, and the original component-identification section moves to Appendix J. The appendices are reorganized around the revised experiments and new analyses.

P2.justification: v5 adopts a two-column main layout, redraws the method taxonomy and memory diagrams, and depicts learned architectures using separate attention and MLP blocks. Results are reorganized into backbone-grouped accuracy/forgetting/FLOPs tables, with new FoM displays and sensitivity plots. Numerous earlier architecture visualizations disappear, while the retained component-selection table moves to the appendix.

R1.justification: v5 substantially repositions CHEEM around class-incremental head design, task-dependent computation, and parameter-efficient adaptation. It adds discussion or citations covering LoRA, InfLoRA, SD-LoRA, DIKI, MoAL, Tuna, and mixture-of-experts adapters, while removing the broad replay/generative-replay survey. S-Prompts becomes the acknowledged source of external task-centroid memory, rather than primarily a comparator and prospective extension.

T1.justification: v5 adds Appendix I's formal local/global argmax setup, Gaussian-logit assumptions, and derivations of agreement probabilities involving competing out-of-task classes. It also introduces the mathematical FoM definition in Equation 6. These extend substantially beyond v4's method and evaluation equations; the retained ViT and HEE equations are not new theory.

improvement.justification: v5 addresses v4 Section 3.3's central applicability limitation by implementing and evaluating inference without supplied task IDs. Controlled LoRA-CL comparisons, classifier-head diagnostics, and measured recognition/training costs substantially strengthen evidence about the method's mechanisms and practical tradeoffs. These gains outweigh the loss of some implementation detail and older ablations. The improvement does not depend on comparing incompatible accuracy scores or accepting the very large FoM ratios, which are amplified by a near-zero fine-tuning gap.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe CHEEM and retain the four-operation hierarchical exploration-exploitation framework. Despite substantial revisions, their readable main text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices support a reliable comparison.

after.justification: v5 reports original MTIL and VDD experiments, including different backbones, task-ID recognition, search sensitivities, and classifier-head analyses.

before.justification: v4 reports original CHEEM experiments on VDD and 5-Datasets, including baseline comparisons, component ablations, and task-order studies.

results.title: CHEEM: Continual Learning by Reuse, New, Adapt and Skip - A Hierarchical Exploration-Exploitation Approach

C1.justification: v3 adds AML as a central methodological contribution in the abstract, introduction and conclusion, claiming improved role-specific grounding. It also foregrounds asymmetric roles and their separate evaluation from a single expression, replacing v1's emphasis on complementary expression pairs. Single-expression dual-output segmentation itself was already claimed in v1.

C2.justification: v3 substantially expands the mechanism account: attention alignment motivates AML, similar actor/target attention supports shared layer selection, and supervision is interpreted as benefiting unsupervised heads. Appendix C.1 newly qualifies standard-benchmark applicability by using an AML-only variant. Meanwhile, v1 Appendix G's limitations concerning interaction-rich source availability and blurred or corrupted imagery disappear.

D1.justification: v3 newly documents SAM2 mask-track precomputation, human correction of evaluation expressions and masks, and exact AML layer/head selections. Reported training times change from 4/10 to 12/16 hours for 1B/4B, with epochs, batch size and hardware retained. It omits v1's explicit video-disjointness and evaluation-filtering statements; this is lost documentation, not evidence that the split became overlapping. Annotation prompts and the project-page address remain.

E1.justification: Both versions cover interaction-aware and standard RVOS using the VidOR-derived dataset, MeViS, Ref-Youtube-VOS and Ref-DAVIS, with MeViS, ReVOS and Ref-SAV training comparisons. InterRVOS-8K/2K/5K become InterRVOS-127K/28K/71K through expression-count naming. Revised sample counts and additional evaluations remain within the existing data and task coverage.

E2.justification: v3 Table 2 adds VISA-7B and VideoLISA-3.8B to the main comparison while retaining Referformer, LMPM and Sa2VA-1B/4B from v1 Table 5. The new standard-benchmark comparison in v3 Table A1 includes LISA, TrackGPT and VISA at multiple model sizes, substantially broadening the reported comparator set.

E3.justification: v1 Table 5 separates Referring, Actor-Target and Overall samples; v3 Table 2 separately scores actor and target outputs on interaction expressions and reports RVOS over all expressions. The evaluation set remains 738 videos but changes from 5,126 to 5,048 expressions. Zero-shot comparisons switch from InterRVOS-5K to the full training dataset, and v3 adds standard-benchmark evaluation of an AML-only variant.

E4.justification: v3 adds component ablations for tokens and AML, layer/head sensitivity tests, attention–segmentation correlation analysis, actor/target attention comparisons and supervised versus unsupervised head visualizations. These substantially expand mechanism analysis. Conversely, v1's independent-versus-joint token comparison and caption-type breakdowns on InterRVOS and MeViS are removed (v1 Tables 4, 6 and A1).

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, error bars or statistical significance tests. The new attention averages describe model behavior rather than uncertainty across experimental runs.

E6.justification: The main results are revised: v1 Table 5 reports overall J&F of 59.7/60.0 for ReVIOSa-1B/4B; v3 Table 2 reports RVOS scores of 62.0/64.5 and newly separate target scores of 67.4/68.3. Changed evaluation settings prevent treating these as controlled cross-version gains. v3 also adds AML and standard-benchmark results and replaces zero-shot results under changed training-set size. The MeViS dataset comparison remains numerically unchanged between v1 Table 3 and v3 Table A2.

M1.justification: v1 already uses separate actor/target tokens with InternVL and SAM2. v3 adds attention mask loss: selected segmentation-token attention maps receive binary cross-entropy supervision against resized object masks. Selecting the strongest vision-attending layer and its top-four heads introduces a substantive new training component, beyond expanded documentation of the existing architecture.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, related work and architecture exposition are extensively rewritten. Dataset construction details and training-dataset comparisons move into reorganized appendices, while AML becomes a major narrative focus. Dataset terminology changes to expression-count names, and the title and author list are revised.

P2.justification: v3 adopts a two-column layout, redraws the teaser and architecture diagrams, restructures the main results table around separate actor/target outputs, and adds numerous attention plots and visualizations. Caption-type tables are removed and qualitative panels replaced. Retained dataset examples, statistics and annotation prompts are relocated or reformatted rather than newly introduced.

R1.justification: v3 adds references including LISA, TrackGPT and GLAMM and explicitly distinguishes InterRVOS from grounded conversation generation, arguing that noun-phrase grounding does not capture directional actor/target semantics. This refines the existing RVOS and interaction-reasoning positioning without replacing it.

T1.justification: v3 introduces the mathematical definition of AML and its incorporation into the total objective (Equations 6 and 8). This is a limited substantive mathematical addition. Much of the other new notation formalizes previously described prompting and mask prediction; neither version supplies theoretical guarantees or proofs.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially improves validation of the central actor/target distinction: Table 2 reports each output role separately, addressing v1 Table 5's lack of separate role measurements. Component and layer/head ablations also provide concrete support for the new AML design, alongside broader baseline comparisons. Removing caption-type analyses, explicit limitations and split-disjointness documentation weakens transparency, but the stronger task-specific evaluation and methodological evidence provide a substantial net improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same InterRVOS/ReVIOSa research. All 31 pages of v1 and 30 pages of v3, including appendices, figures, tables and equations, support comparison. Renamed datasets and relocated material can be matched.

after.justification: v3 reports original actor/target segmentation results, attention-loss ablations, attention analyses and benchmark evaluations in Tables 2–4, Tables A1–A3 and Appendix B.

before.justification: v1 reports original segmentation experiments, architectural ablations, training-dataset comparisons and zero-shot results in Tables 3–6 and A1–A2.

results.title: InterRVOS: Interaction-Aware Referring Video Object Segmentation

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the same principal claims about progressive filtering, coverage-based REFINE, theoretical properties, and improved active-learning performance. Added experiments and comparisons provide further support without redefining the core contributions.

C2.justification: Appendices C–E substantially expand interpretation of larger-batch benefits, weak-member ensembles, computational feasibility, applicability beyond frozen features, and the remaining gap to the BoSS oracle. Section 4.3 also newly acknowledges that the value-ordering assumption may fail in practice. The original dependence on ensemble quality remains acknowledged.

D1.justification: V2 replaces the anonymous code placeholder and future-release statement with a concrete dal-toolbox repository URL. It also documents acquisition/training timings and parallel-runtime assumptions, including an 85% parallelizable fraction and scheduling overheads. These improve access and resource documentation without establishing changes to the original implementation settings.

E1.justification: V2 retains the original image datasets and ESC50, while adding long-tailed Snacks and CIFAR-100 scenarios with imbalance ratios 10 and 50, plus BloodMNIST and DermaMNIST (Appendix D, Figure 12). These substantially expand class-distribution conditions and biomedical-domain coverage.

E2.justification: V2 adds AutoAL to the ensemble comparisons, including Figure 4 and the complete learning curves. It also adds the label-privileged BoSS oracle to both individual and ensemble comparisons (Figures 14–17), expanding comparison scope to include an oracle reference alongside practical competitors.

E3.justification: The original main evaluation protocol is retained. Added protocols include batch sizes 10, 25, 50, and 100 under a fixed budget of approximately 2,500 labels, exponential class-imbalance construction with balanced-accuracy evaluation, and fine-tuning the last two DINOv2 transformer blocks with hyperparameters tuned on CIFAR-10 (Appendices C–D).

E4.justification: V2 adds controlled weak-member ensemble experiments, batch-size sensitivity, alternative second-stage selection, pool-shrinkage measurements, acquisition-time analysis, and robustness tests for imbalance, biomedical data, and partial fine-tuning. These substantially extend the original filtering-parameter and preprocessing-benefit ablations.

E5.justification: Both versions report 10 independent trials, but v1 explicitly omits standard errors whereas v2 displays them. Appendix E additionally reports a Friedman test across 18 dataset-by-model blocks followed by paired Wilcoxon signed-rank tests with Holm correction at significance level 0.01. No increase in existing trial counts is established.

E6.justification: Existing Figure 2 and Table 2 values and the reported 100% wins against SelectAL/TAILOR and 98% against TCM are retained. V2 adds a 97% win rate against AutoAL, BoSS reference curves, robustness and ablation outcomes, timings, and pool-retention measurements, including 0.052 for CIFAR-10 after five rounds. Table 3's parallel timings are projections rather than measured speedups.

M1.justification: The main progressive-filtering algorithm and UHerding-based final selection remain unchanged. Appendix C adds tested second-stage variants that generate candidate batches with ensemble members and select among them using Fisher-information-ratio or expected-error criteria (Figure 11), constituting a limited procedural extension.

P1.justification: V2 makes localized grammar, terminology, affiliation, and conclusion edits. It expands appendix subheadings, inserts an Additional Results and Experiments section, and moves the previous Appendix D learning-curve collection to Appendix E. The main narrative structure and most existing prose remain intact.

P2.justification: V2 redraws learning curves with uncertainty bands and oracle overlays, expands Figure 4 for AutoAL, and adds Figures 10–13 and Tables 3–4. The original complete learning-curve Figures 10–13 become Figures 14–17 with expanded legends and plotted comparisons, substantially revising the visual presentation of evidence.

R1.justification: V2 adds discussion and citations for AutoAL and BoSS, plus references supporting batch-ranking criteria, statistical tests, MedMNIST, and hyperparameter sensitivity. The central positioning against strategy-switching ensembles and single-step filtering remains intact; bibliographic metadata updates do not constitute additional scientific changes.

T1.justification: Equations 1–2, Definition 1, Theorems 1–3, and Appendix A's proofs and numerical examples are unchanged. The added qualification about the practical validity of Theorem 3's assumption does not revise its formal assumptions or mathematical reasoning.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially strengthens empirical credibility and applicability. V1 omitted uncertainty displays and lacked targeted tests of imbalance, biomedical domain shift, and feature fine-tuning; v2 adds these checks, formal statistical comparisons, AutoAL and oracle references, and concrete code-access information. These address important evidential gaps while retaining the original results. Parallel speedups remain projections and some added-study settings are incompletely documented, but these limitations do not outweigh the substantial gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same REFINE research. Their main text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices support reliable comparison, including matching the relocated and renumbered learning curves.

after.justification: V2 retains these empirical results and adds biomedical and class-imbalance evaluations, fine-tuning experiments, and further comparative and diagnostic studies.

before.justification: V1 reports original active-learning experiments on six image datasets, an ESC50 audio classification study, and filtering ablations.

results.title: Cleaning the Pool: Progressive Filtering of Unlabeled Pools in Deep Active Learning

C1.justification: The main claims about holistic interpolation, temporal stability, and resolution generalization remain. However, v2 removes the explicit claim to be the first use of autoregressive generation for VFI and the introduction's assertion that computation is decoupled from image resolution. These narrow novelty and efficiency claims without redefining the central contribution.

C2.justification: v2 adds interpretations concerning chunk-boundary continuity, sampling-speed tradeoffs, sparse attention's resolution generalization, longer chunks, and applicability to non-integer ratios. The performance discussion now emphasizes best FVD and competitive LPIPS, replacing v1's mismatched hard/extreme-split claims. Conversely, the detailed explanation linking zero-padding artifacts to encoder capacity is removed while its empirical comparison remains.

D1.justification: v2 specifies H100 timing hardware, four-GPU USP use for 4K experiments, EDEN's recursive interpolation, and binary-mask alignment across chunks. The four-GPU disclosure supplements v1's statement that two 80GB GPUs suffice; it does not establish a hardware change between runs. The code-access information remains equivalent, while the explicit frame-wise/per-video LPIPS aggregation description is omitted.

E1.justification: Training remains on LAVIB, with evaluation on SNU-FILM at 4×/8×/16× and the high-resolution benchmark at 16×. XTest-entire is renamed X4K-entire, retaining the same XVFI source citation, construction, and original scores. Additional qualitative examples use existing coverage; non-integer ratios are discussed but not experimentally evaluated.

E2.justification: v1's main comparison contains four optical-flow baselines. v2 retains them and evaluates diffusion-based EDEN in Tables 1–2, qualitative comparisons, and the efficiency study, substantially filling the missing comparison against a generative VFI method. RIFE also joins the qualitative comparisons, where v1 showed only AMT, EMA-VFI, and BiM-VFI.

E3.justification: v2 adds VFIPS and FloLPIPS, adjacent-frame L1 analysis, and runtime measurements. New protocols vary sampling steps, compare attention at 6K training steps and four sampling steps, and compare chunk lengths using 32K versus 8K training steps under similar computation. Section 4.1 also changes the stated training timestep shift from 4 to 5; this documents a revised setting without establishing that retained experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: The original sampling-order, conditional-VAE, and upsampling ablations are retained. v2 adds non-AR versus skip-concatenate boundary analysis in Figure 6, sampling-speed sensitivity in Table 4, full versus sparse attention in Table 5, and chunk-length sensitivity in supplementary Table A1. These directly test previously unexamined aspects of coherence and scalability.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, error bars, or significance tests. The existing reconstruction average over 16 videos is retained. v2's mean adjacent-frame L1 curve measures temporal variation rather than statistical uncertainty.

E6.justification: Original benchmark LPIPS/FVD values and existing ablation values are retained, while v2 adds EDEN, VFIPS/FloLPIPS, runtime, attention, chunk-length, and qualitative results. For example, SNU-FILM-8× now includes EDEN at 0.040 LPIPS/26.03 FVD alongside retained LDF-VFI values of 0.045/15.01, revealing metric-dependent rankings. Supplementary Table A1 newly reports X4K FVD of 510.63 versus 121.29 for the two chunk-length configurations; this is not a version-to-version performance gain.

M1.justification: The DiT backbone, sparse attention, tiled/chunked VAE, conditioning, diffusion forcing, and skip-concatenate procedure remain unchanged. Added mask-alignment prose explains support for non-integer ratios without establishing a new component. The flow-matching equations receive a consistency correction, assessed under T1, rather than a demonstrated algorithm redesign.

P1.justification: v2 replaces the contribution bullets with a benchmark-focused paragraph, folds dataset and metric descriptions into implementation details, revises the conclusion, and makes localized wording corrections. It also updates affiliations/contact details and adds acknowledgments. Most methodological prose and the overall narrative order remain intact.

P2.justification: The original combined benchmark table is split and expanded into Tables 1–2. Qualitative comparisons are substantially redesigned, with retained examples partly moved into the supplement and additional methods/scenes included. New temporal-coherence, efficiency, attention, and chunk-length displays substantially expand the visual presentation. Existing component and upsampling tables remain as Tables 3 and 6.

R1.justification: Related work expands to kernel-based interpolation and additional corrupted-context autoregressive diffusion approaches. New citations also support VFIPS, FloLPIPS, and diffusion training. The explicit first-autoregressive-VFI positioning is removed, but the principal relationship to frame-centric VFI remains. Consolidating duplicate VIDIM and latent-diffusion references does not remove those works.

T1.justification: Section 3.1 corrects the path from x_t=(1-t)x_1+t x_0 to x_t=(1-t)x_0+t x_1 and reverses Equation 1's velocity target from x_0-x_1 to x_1-x_0. This resolves the inconsistency with x_0 denoting data, x_1 noise, and inference integrating from t=1 to 0. No new theorem or proof is introduced.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens validation of the central coherence and scalability claims. v1 lacked an evaluated diffusion baseline and direct runtime, attention, and chunk-length tests; v2 supplies these alongside motion-aware metrics and boundary analysis. It also repairs the flow-matching inconsistency and makes the performance discussion better match the tables. These gains outweigh the shortened metric and upsampling explanations. The improvement concerns evidential support and accuracy, with the original main scores retained.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same LDF-VFI research. All 11 pages of v1 and 12 pages of v2 support comparison through readable text, equations, tables, and figures. The supplied v1 ends with references; v2 adds a supplementary page containing Figure A1 and Table A1.

after.justification: v2 retains those original experiments and adds baseline evaluations, motion-aware scores, runtime measurements, temporal-coherence analysis, attention comparisons, and a supplementary chunk-length ablation.

before.justification: v1 reports original benchmark comparisons, qualitative interpolation results, and ablations of sampling order, conditional VAE decoding, and temporal upsampling in Section 4 and Tables 1–3.

results.title: Towards Holistic Modeling for Video Frame Interpolation with Auto-regressive Diffusion Transformers

C1.justification: The abstract and central introduction/conclusion claims remain a training-free, LLM-assisted framework that resolves contextual contradictions through stage-aware proxy prompting and improves semantic alignment. SAP is a new name for the retained contribution; the additional experiments primarily strengthen its support.

C2.justification: v2 adds an attention-based account of competing token influences and distinguishes coarse-stage sensitivity from tolerance to exact timestep boundaries. Its failure analysis attributes most failures to proxy selection rather than interval assignment. The revised two-proxy discussion now describes performance as close to the full method, replacing v1's emphasis on substantial underperformance.

D1.justification: v2 supplies the previously omitted full Whoops-Hard prompt list, adds a project-page address, describes human filtering of ContraBench candidates and discusses embedding overhead. Figure 7 also specifies steps 1 and 14 where v1 only said 'too early' and 'too late'. These are documentation additions; the core instruction and evaluation templates remain.

E1.justification: v2 adds evaluation on simple, non-contradictory prompts through PartiPrompts-Simple (Table 6). Whoops!, Whoops-Hard and ContraBench remain the principal contradictory-prompt benchmarks. ContraBench retains the same 40 prompt scenarios despite reordering and minor wording differences.

E2.justification: v2 Table 1 adds Annealing Guidance, VL-DNP, R2F on FLUX-schnell and a reimplementation of R2F on FLUX-dev. The original comparators remain. Annealing also joins the user study and qualitative comparisons, substantially expanding the methods evaluated against SAP.

E3.justification: v2 introduces controlled interval perturbations with fixed proxy texts and uniform windows of three or five steps. It also tests Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct and specifies reuse of the same proxies and intervals for quantitative SD3 evaluation. The existing 50-step generation budget and GPT-4o alignment-scoring rubric remain unchanged.

E4.justification: v2 substantially extends the original component and timing analyses with attention-map diagnostics, controlled interval perturbations, alternative-LLM evaluation, a non-contradictory-prompt check, and categorized failures with manual proxy correction (Figure 3, Tables 4–7, Figure 12). The qualitative multi-seed gallery is reduced from six prompt cases to three.

E5.justification: Both versions report averaging alignment scores over three fixed random seeds per prompt. Neither introduces confidence intervals, variability estimates or significance tests. The additional robustness scores and failure-category percentages do not establish a changed uncertainty-reporting procedure.

E6.justification: The original Table 1 scores remain unchanged, including 85.10/62.13/66.16 for the FLUX-based method. However, Table 3 changes the two-proxy score from 50.73 to 60.26 without explaining the revision. v2 adds extensive baseline, SD3, perturbation and alternative-LLM results, plus PartiPrompts-Simple scores of 93.46 for FLUX and 93.06 for SAP.

M1.justification: The method retains LLM-generated proxy prompts, concept substitution and injection at assigned denoising intervals. The decomposition instructions and in-context examples are retained. Naming the framework SAP, testing alternative models and adding diagnostic attention analysis do not establish a changed generation procedure.

P1.justification: Beyond introducing SAP terminology, v2 extensively condenses and rewrites the coarse-to-fine explanation, decomposition discussion, experimental narrative and conclusion. It inserts a dedicated entanglement-analysis section, moves the realism discussion into supplementary material, and reorganizes the appendix into separately titled sections.

P2.justification: v2 changes the document template and extensively restructures displays. It adds contradiction and attention diagrams, rearranges the coarse-to-fine figure, expands comparison grids and tables, revises the SD3 display, and distributes supplementary examples across larger figures. Existing instruction tables are reformatted, alongside new robustness tables and the Whoops-Hard list.

R1.justification: v2 adds references to the GPT-4 technical report, Dynamic VLM-Guided Negative Prompting and Navigating with Annealing Guidance Scale in Diffusion Space. Related work now mentions annealed guidance, but the positioning around spurious correlations, semantic alignment, multi-prompt conditioning and LLM guidance remains substantially intact.

T1.justification: The contextual-contradiction definition and mathematical description of proxy prompts and timestep intervals retain their meaning. Neither version supplies formal theorems or proofs. The new contradiction diagram and attention-map discussion provide conceptual and empirical explanations rather than new mathematical theory.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens empirical support by testing timing sensitivity, LLM dependence and behavior on ordinary prompts, while expanding comparisons across diffusion backbones. Its failure analysis clarifies practical limitations, and publishing the Whoops-Hard list improves reproducibility. These additions address important gaps in v1's validation. The unexplained two-proxy score revision and continued absence of uncertainty estimates limit confidence, but do not outweigh the gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research work. All 13 pages of v1 and 20 pages of v2, including figures, tables and appendices, are readable and support reliable matching despite substantial reorganization.

after.justification: v2 retains original empirical results and adds baseline comparisons, robustness experiments, non-contradictory prompt evaluation and failure analysis.

before.justification: v1 reports original image-generation experiments, benchmark alignment scores, component ablations and a user study involving 61 participants.

results.title: Image Generation from Contextually-Contradictory Prompts

C1.justification: v3 adds an explicit priority claim that this is the first demonstration of successful domain-level pretraining for video models, distinguishing it from target-dataset pretraining. It also newly claims that its curation pipeline uniquely requires neither seed datasets nor text captions. These substantially broaden the novelty positioning beyond v1's retained dataset, recognition and efficiency contributions.

C2.justification: v3 acknowledges mixed PanAf500 accuracy effects and cross-dataset forgetting, discusses joint training's compute tradeoff, and proposes motion-feature and crop-related explanations for class-level behavior. The ground-truth-box limitation is removed following the added evaluation. However, Appendix E's claim of no performance reduction overstates Table 8: joint PanAf500 training lowers ChimpACT mAP from 38.75 to 37.93.

D1.justification: The new supplement documents source datasets, labeling rules, model identifiers, filtering thresholds, MLP training settings, contamination checks and baseline reproduction procedures. v3 also specifies the existing DaLP stage's 10k-step budget and test-data handling. Its abstract supplies a project URL and reports resource availability, replacing v1's release promise; the private subset remains withheld.

E1.justification: The four benchmarks and 424-hour pretraining corpus are retained. v3 extends evaluation of the proposed method to ChimpACT without supplied ground-truth detections, changing its input requirements. Expanded source descriptions and revised species statistics do not establish that new training populations were added.

E2.justification: v3 Table 3 adds UniFormerV2-B to the BaboonLand comparison, reporting 63.45 accuracy and 28.67 balanced accuracy. AlphaChimp was already compared in v1; v3 retains it in a separate predicted-detection comparison rather than introducing it as a new baseline. Most comparator membership is unchanged.

E3.justification: Additional experiments substantially expand the evaluation design: sequence-level training subsets of 10%, 25% and 50%, evaluation with predicted detections, a single-test-view control, and joint pretraining for 75k steps using a 50:50 data mixture. These are added protocols; newly disclosed settings for retained experiments do not establish that those experiments changed.

E4.justification: v3 adds direct label-efficiency tests against X3D (Figure 5), a test-view ablation (Table 5), qualitative predictions and class-level error analyses (Figures 4 and 7), contamination screening (Appendix B), and joint-pretraining tests addressing catastrophic forgetting (Table 8). These substantially extend the original component and dataset-composition ablations.

E5.justification: Figure 5 introduces 95% confidence intervals estimated over three randomly sampled subsets per reduced training size. Appendix D newly discloses averaging AlphaChimp over five runs. Averaging five attentive classifiers was already stated in v1 and is retained; the PDFs do not establish an increase in that run count.

E6.justification: v3 adds substantial results for label efficiency, predicted detections, individual classes and joint pretraining. Table 4 reports SAM3 plus PriVi/DaLP at 30.76 mAP versus AlphaChimp's retained 25.35. Existing V-JEPA baseline entries also change, including ChimpACT mAP from 30.85 to 36.33, while PriVi's 39.25 remains unchanged. Table 1 revises marmoset statistics and separately reports squirrel monkeys.

M1.justification: The V-JEPA backbone, loss and narrow attentive classifier remain unchanged. v3 adds optional procedural extensions: SAM3 supplies predicted boxes, with empty-box examples added during classifier training, and Appendix E evaluates joint PriVi/target-dataset pretraining instead of sequential adaptation.

P1.justification: v3 rewrites the introduction and contributions around the domain-level/dataset-level distinction, standardizes CID terminology to DaLP, moves detailed benchmark descriptions into Appendix C, and relocates adaptation procedures into the experimental setup. It reorganizes the results, expands technical explanations in Appendices A-E, compresses the conclusion and removes the future-work paragraph.

P2.justification: v3 adds an overview graphic, prediction examples, label-efficiency plots, a dataset-image gallery and class-level plots. It merges v1 Tables 2-3 into Table 2, reorganizes the benchmark table, separates predicted-detection results, and adds appendix tables. The architecture illustration and title/author layout are also revised.

R1.justification: The introduction substantially reframes the work around domain-level versus dataset-level adaptation, adding connections to Gururangan et al.'s language-model adaptation and Mueller et al.'s primate pretraining work. It also introduces the seed/caption-free positioning against existing data engines. Additional references cover SAM3, UniFormerV2, ASBAR and the behavioral studies supplying R&O footage.

T1.justification: Equations 1-5 retain the same learning objective and classifier formulation. The token-matrix dimension ordering changes notation without introducing substantive mathematical reasoning. Neither version supplies new theorems or proofs.

improvement.justification: v3 resolves important evidentiary gaps: Figure 5 directly tests v1's label-efficiency claim, Table 4 evaluates operation without ground-truth boxes, and the supplement makes data curation and baseline comparisons substantially more reproducible. Contamination screening and forgetting analyses further strengthen scrutiny of the results. Some interpretations remain overstated, particularly complete avoidance of forgetting in Appendix E, but this limitation does not outweigh the substantial gains in validation and transparency.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same PriVi dataset and recognition framework, and their text, equations, tables and figures are readable. The supplied v1 ends after its references; v3 additionally contains Appendices A-E. All supplied material supports comparison.

after.justification: v3 retains original empirical results and adds predicted-box evaluation, label-efficiency experiments, class-level analyses and joint-pretraining results.

before.justification: v1 reports original pretraining, behavior-recognition and ablation results, including experiments across four benchmarks in Tables 2-5.

results.title: PriVi: Towards a General-Purpose Video Model for Primate Behavior in the Wild

C1.justification: The central contribution remains acceleration through pruning and shared motion. v2 additionally claims superior image quality to every non-neural baseline while exceeding baseline rendering speeds, whereas v1 principally emphasizes acceleration and compression with quality comparable to its neural baseline. Renaming ASP to TSS does not itself establish a new scientific contribution.

C2.justification: v2 substantially develops GroupFlow's interpretation as structural regularization that can improve reconstruction under noisy trajectories, supported by new Nerfies/iPhone discussions. It adds limitations for highly non-rigid regions with too few groups and restricts GroupFlow applicability to explicit-motion frameworks. v1 instead emphasizes inherited De3DGS pose errors and dependence on trajectory quality.

D1.justification: v2 specifies pruning beginning at iteration 6000 and recurring every 3000 iterations, distinguishes standalone and benchmark implementations, and explains comparator-result provenance. It removes v1's explicit dataset-provided COLMAP initialization statement and Lie-algebra parameterization detail. Documentation is imperfect: Appendix A.5 retains A4000 hardware wording that conflicts with Section 5 and the revised table captions.

E1.justification: v2 adds the 50-scene MonoDyGauBench evaluation, introducing four Nerfies scenes and fourteen iPhone scenes and evaluating seventeen HyperNeRF scenes. NeRF-DS and D-NeRF remain, and the eight-scene standalone HyperNeRF experiment already present in v1 is retained rather than newly introduced.

E2.justification: The comparison roster changes substantially. For D-NeRF, v1 Table 2 includes D-NeRF, TiNeuVox-B, K-Planes, HexPlane, FFDNeRF, and SC-GS; these are absent from v2's corresponding benchmark comparison, which adds STG and STG-decoder. EffGS and RTGS match v1's C-D3DGS and 4DGS (ICLR), respectively, and are not new methods merely because their names changed.

E3.justification: Reported defaults change from 80% to 60% densification-stage pruning and from 200 to 2048 motion groups, while retaining 30,000 training iterations. v2 adds the MonoDyGauBench training wrapper and MS-SSIM evaluation, tests TSS on D-NeRF, and changes the principal rendering GPU from A4000 to RTX 3090 and NeRF-DS/D-NeRF training GPU to A5000.

E4.justification: v2 Table 10 expands group-count analysis from unpruned D-NeRF to both NeRF-DS and D-NeRF with and without pruning. It adds TSS comparisons on D-NeRF and HyperNeRF, dataset-specific pruning sensitivity results, and Figure 6 case studies. Conversely, v1's rotation-versus-fixed-orientation and linear-blend-skinning ablations in Table 11 are removed.

E5.justification: Both versions report averages over three independent runs, including parameter ablations. v2 extends this existing practice to additional experiments without introducing seed reporting, confidence intervals, run-to-run error bars, or significance tests.

E6.justification: v2 adds benchmark results in Tables 2–7 and revises existing standalone results. For example, the full NeRF-DS pipeline changes from 23.42 PSNR, 366.73 FPS, and 4.48 MB in v1 Table 1 to 23.66 PSNR, 505.60 FPS, and 21.40 MB in v2 Table 1. These reflect changed configurations and hardware, not controlled performance gains. The separate four-scene HyperNeRF vrig quality results are removed.

M1.justification: The sensitivity score, annealed timestamp perturbation, trajectory grouping, and rigid alignment are retained; ASP is renamed TSS. However, v2 Section 4.2.2 applies group rotations to Gaussian orientations as standard, whereas v1 Appendix A.5.1 explicitly fixes orientations and evaluates rotation modeling only as an alternative.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction, related work, and substantial method explanations are rewritten. Experiments are reorganized around standalone and benchmark evaluations, and the appendices are extensively reordered. Terminology changes include ASP to TSS and De3DGS to DeformableGS.

P2.justification: The document changes from single-column to two-column presentation. The teaser is redesigned, existing diagrams and comparison panels are revised, Figure 5 becomes separate dataset-specific grids, and Figure 6 adds qualitative comparisons. Benchmark tables are added, component tables are expanded, and the earlier design-choice ablation table is removed.

R1.justification: Research positioning is substantially reorganized around MonoDyGauBench's fidelity–efficiency comparison and five motion-representation families. New references include MonoDyGauBench, STG, FisherRF, POP-GS, and the iPhone dataset work. The earlier static-pruning and grouped-motion foundations remain; renamed methods and publication-metadata updates are not counted as new research.

T1.justification: The sensitivity approximation, trajectory-distance score, and rigid-alignment objective remain. v2 expands the trajectory definition to include rotations in Equation 8, while removing v1 Appendix A.5.2's linear-blend-skinning deformation and normalized-weight equations. The rotation transformation was already described in v1's appendix; its relocation is not a new derivation.

improvement.justification: v1 claims applicability beyond De3DGS without testing its components in another backbone; v2 demonstrates integrations into both DeformableGS and 4DGS under a common benchmark, substantially strengthening evidence for transferability and revealing backbone-dependent fidelity losses. Expanded group/pruning interaction analyses further improve support for design tradeoffs. These gains outweigh the lost rotation/LBS ablations, although mixed-GPU training comparisons, inconsistent speedup ratios in Table 1, and conflicting hardware descriptions in Appendix A.5 weaken confidence in exact timing claims.

A1.justification: Both complete 17-page PDFs describe SpeeDe3DGS, with matching authors and core pruning/grouping methods. The text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices support comparison despite substantial rewriting and experimental revisions.
