after.justification: v2 reports original SpeeDe3DGS experiments and integrations into DeformableGS and 4DGS on MonoDyGauBench, alongside quantitative ablations and qualitative comparisons. Some comparator results are explicitly reproduced from the benchmark manuscript.

before.justification: v1 reports original reconstruction, rendering-speed, storage, and training-time results on NeRF-DS, D-NeRF, and HyperNeRF, including component and parameter ablations in Appendix A.

results.title: SpeeDe3DGS: Speedy Deformable 3D Gaussian Splatting with Temporal Pruning and Motion Grouping

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction's contribution list, and conclusion retain the same substantive claims: efficient iterative pixel-dense upsampling, semantic consistency through Local Attender, strong predictive performance, and competitive generative upsampling. Additional experiments support these retained claims.

C2.justification: v2 qualifies the efficiency interpretation by acknowledging AnyUp-v2's linear scaling and memory advantages over regular UPLiFT. It adds a stronger-inductive-bias hypothesis for Local Attender, capacity and chunking tradeoffs, and explanations of smoothness, feature bleed, and background artifacts. Appendix D.3 also cautions that visually cleaner features do not necessarily improve downstream performance.

D1.justification: v2 adds detailed tensor-shape and broadcasting pseudocode, specifies the encoder's ten and decoder's six convolutional layers, explains the fast-mode implementation, and reports approximately nine hours of UPLiFT training on one A5000. It also adds code/configuration access guidance. These substantially expand reproducibility information without establishing changes to the original training procedure.

E1.justification: The training datasets and evaluated tasks and datasets are retained. New ResNet-50 and ConvNeXt-S evaluations use the existing COCO/VOC segmentation coverage; their pretraining-corpus descriptions identify backbone configurations rather than newly conducted dataset experiments.

E2.justification: v2 adds AnyUp-v2 to the main predictive and efficiency comparisons, its chunked variant to the scaling study, and NATTEN-based windowed cross-attention alternatives in Table 9. These introduce efficient local-attention comparators important to the central efficiency argument. The original AnyUp remains as AnyUp-v1.

E3.justification: New evaluations vary encoder/decoder widths, remove the encoder, test windowed attention with 1/4/8/12 heads and 5×5 windows, and add convolutional backbones and fast-mode execution. The efficiency study replaces the 48-GB A6000 with an 80-GB H100 alongside the retained A5000, and tests AnyUp-v2 chunk size 10. Existing main-benchmark training and metrics are retained.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained training-depth, neighborhood, and VAE ablations, v2 adds encoder/decoder capacity and encoder-removal tests (Table 8), Local Attender versus windowed-attention tests (Table 9), and multi-baseline PCA case studies (Figure 9). The efficiency analysis also expands to examine fast-mode and chunking tradeoffs.

E5.justification: Both versions report point-estimate task scores and averaged latencies. Appendix B.2 retains three warm-up batches followed by averaging ten measurement batches. No new seed counts, repeated-training-run information, confidence intervals, or statistical tests are reported.

E6.justification: Table 1 adds AnyUp-v2 and UPLiFTFAST results. Under the retained 448×448/A5000 setting, FAST reports 41.6 ms versus regular UPLiFT's 79.4 ms, with VOC mIoU 85.08 versus 85.21. Tables 8–10 add architectural and convolutional-backbone results; scaling curves and qualitative findings also expand. Original generative and DINOv3 scores are retained. H100 results replace A6000 results, preventing a same-hardware comparison there.

M1.justification: v2 introduces UPLiFTFAST inference execution through BatchNorm folding, channels-last layout, a fused Triton Local Attender kernel, and graph compilation (Section 3.4, Appendix A.5). The architecture and training objective remain unchanged. Algorithm 1 documents the existing Local Attender rather than introducing another operator.

P1.justification: Editorial changes are localized: Section 3.2 is shortened, wording and typographical errors are corrected, Section 3.4 is added, and Appendix A gains numbered subsections. The main narrative and section order remain largely intact; most expansion documents new experiments or technical details.

P2.justification: Figures 3–5 are redrawn with clearer feature visualizations, labels, and scale relationships. v2 adds Algorithm 1, Tables 8–10, and the PCA comparison in Figure 9. Efficiency plots receive additional curves, wider axes, and revised hardware panels; Table 1 gains rows. Retained appendix exhibits are also relocated and renumbered.

R1.justification: v2 adds references to Neighborhood Attention Transformer and Segment Anything. Section 2.1 distinguishes Local Attender from AnyUp-v2/NATTEN, while the appendix discusses SAM supervision in LoftUp. The broader related-work structure and existing citations are retained.

T1.justification: The Local Attender definitions, O(nT) scaling argument, and training equations (1)–(5) are unchanged. Algorithm 1 restates the existing operations as pseudocode; no new theorem, proof, formal assumption, or mathematical derivation is introduced.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens evidence for the central efficiency and Local Attender claims through efficient AnyUp-v2 comparisons, controlled windowed-attention and capacity ablations, and fast-mode speed/accuracy evaluation. The pseudocode and architecture details address important reproducibility gaps in v1. These gains outweigh a limited reporting regression: Table 1's unchanged 'second best' depth-accuracy caption conflicts with the added AnyUp-v2 results.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same UPLiFT work. Their text, equations, tables, figures, and Appendices A–D are readable and support reliable matching of retained, revised, and added material.

after.justification: v2 retains those original experiments and adds fast-mode evaluations, architectural ablations, convolutional-backbone results, and qualitative comparisons.

before.justification: v1 reports original segmentation, depth-estimation, generative-task, efficiency, and ablation results, including Tables 1–8 and appendix visualizations.

results.title: UPLiFT: Efficient Pixel-Dense Feature Upsampling with Local Attenders

C1.justification: v1 claims superiority over published zero-shot checkpoints and, in its conclusion, training on any previous synthetic dataset. v2 acknowledges the stronger FoundationStereo checkpoint and instead claims competitiveness with its training dataset while retaining superiority over the conventional mixed-data baseline. The abstract and introduction reposition the contribution around dataset-design analysis, a resulting dataset and open generation code.

C2.justification: The object-type discussion shifts from suggesting that mesh diversity matters less to explaining performance through benchmark-specific object biases. New discussion interprets solver realism as potentially helping in-domain performance while hindering transfer, and associates render-noise benefits with KITTI's noisier captures. These refine the interpretation while retaining the central realism-and-diversity explanation.

D1.justification: v2 newly specifies ceiling-removal and lighting-alteration probabilities of 0.3 and 0.2, explicitly documents ETH3D's 1px threshold, and clarifies configurable window removal. It omits v1's NVIDIA L40 identification and explicit 1m camera-clearance detail. Unoptimized generation estimates change from 1902 CPU/960 GPU days to 275 CPU/900 GPU days. Most appendix implementation details and the code link are retained.

E1.justification: v2 adds the FoundationStereo training corpus and DrivingStereo evaluation data within the existing synthetic-to-real stereo task and indoor/outdoor/driving coverage. The additional Middlebury split and revised generated-dataset counts concern experimental settings rather than new task coverage.

E2.justification: Compared with v1 Table 3, v2 Table 2 adds StereoAnywhere and FoundationStereo checkpoints, removes Selective-RAFT, and adds RAFT-Mixed and paired Selective-IGEV training comparisons. FoundationStereo data also becomes a comparator in the dataset, sample-efficiency and appendix qualitative experiments. These substantially strengthen and restructure the comparisons.

E3.justification: v2 adds generation-compute matching using 30k versus 5k pairs, held-out evaluation excluding ten Middlebury validation scenes and sampling 200 DrivingStereo pairs, and EPE evaluation throughout the parameter study. Section 4 revises the dataset size from 152,890 to 163,666 pairs and adds Selective-IGEV training. Section 4.3 describes the sample-efficiency model as DLNR instead of RAFT-Stereo; this reported setting revision does not establish that retained results were rerun.

E4.justification: v2 adds a bush-only object ablation, full-versus-reduced solver evaluation, and compute-matched rendering/solver experiments testing the quality-versus-quantity tradeoff. Held-out benchmarks address generalization beyond parameter-tuning benchmarks, while Appendix A/Table 7 checks conclusions using EPE. The earlier ray-tracing ablation is largely relocated into Table 4, rather than newly introduced.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, experimental seeds, confidence intervals, uncertainty bars or significance tests for the empirical comparisons. The additional EPE measurements in v2 are performance metrics, not uncertainty estimates.

E6.justification: Many retained benchmark scores are unchanged, but substantial results are added. In v2 Table 2, FoundationStereo reports 1.10 Middlebury-2014-H error versus the retained DLNR-WMGStereo result of 3.76. New Table 6 reports held-out Middlebury errors of 12.61 for DLNR-WMGStereo and 14.23 for DLNR-FSD. Bush, compute-matched, EPE and FSD scaling results are added; the earlier Booster ray-tracing-ablation scores are omitted. Reported unoptimized generation-cost estimates also change.

M1.justification: The generation procedure is retained. Floating-object placement, problematic-object/material removal, window-glass geometry removal, the greedy room solver, denoising and scene mixing already appear in v1. The WMGStereo renaming, added implementation explanations and evaluation of another stereo architecture do not establish a new proposed method.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction and related work are extensively rewritten, including an explicit three-contribution summary and consistent WMGStereo terminology. Cost-optimization subsections are reordered, and atmospheric-effects and post-processing passages move from the main text into Appendix B. This exceeds routine copyediting.

P2.justification: The original generation-cost bar chart is removed, and ray-tracing rows move into an expanded cost-study table. Model comparisons are regrouped by architecture; held-out and appendix EPE tables are added. The scaling plot gains an FSD curve and a wider axis, and the appendix qualitative comparison gains FSD panels. Existing figures are also relocated and restyled.

R1.justification: v2 adds substantive positioning against FoundationStereo, emphasizing comparable training data alongside accessible generation code and parameter analysis. It also adds StereoAnywhere, SMD-Nets/UnrealStereo4k and DepthAnythingV2 citations. The dedicated real-world-dataset and deep-stereo-network discussions are removed, along with several associated references, substantially refocusing related work.

T1.justification: Neither version presents formal theoretical results or proofs, and no substantive mathematical assumptions or derivations are added. The expanded use of standard stereo-error metrics is an empirical evaluation change.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens validation: Table 6 tests benchmarks excluded from parameter tuning, Table 4 evaluates the generation-cost tradeoff under matched compute, and Tables 2 and 5 introduce stronger comparators and additional controlled training comparisons. The revised claims appropriately acknowledge FoundationStereo's stronger checkpoint instead of retaining broad superiority claims. Although some implementation details and Booster ablation entries are lost, the improved controls, generalization evidence and claim calibration provide a clear substantial net gain.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same procedural stereo-dataset study despite changes to the title and dataset name. All 16 pages of v1 and 18 pages of v2, including their appendices, were readable and supported comparison.

after.justification: v2 retains original empirical results and adds comparisons, compute-matched experiments, held-out benchmark evaluations and appendix EPE results.

before.justification: v1 reports original dataset-generation ablations, stereo benchmark evaluations, generation-time measurements, sample-efficiency experiments and qualitative predictions.

results.title: What Makes Good Synthetic Training Data for Zero-Shot Stereo Matching?

C1.justification: The first real-world aerial SSC benchmark and LiDAR-free generation claims remain. However, v2's abstract and contribution list add an explicit central claim of a consistent aerial domain gap across terrestrial SSC models and both 2D and 3D vision foundation models, substantially broadening the claimed scientific contribution.

C2.justification: v2 replaces v1's favorable interpretation of CGFormer under balanced classes with uniformly difficult aerial SSC and comparatively limited altitude effects. It adds arguments for classical reconstruction and manual annotation, removes the reciprocal-transfer interpretation, and corrects depth overestimation to underestimation. Its new SILog trade-off claim conflicts with Table 5, where both matched models improve after fine-tuning. Static-scene and cross-altitude temporal limitations remain.

D1.justification: v2 discloses Ingolstadt as the collection region, annotation costs of approximately 29 minutes per image and 1.3 days per scene, and specific variants of added models. Most generation hardware and hyperparameters remain documented. Conversely, the retained Depth Anything V2 experiment loses explicit batch-size and peak-memory information previously provided in v1.

E1.justification: v2 adds semantic-segmentation evaluation using a ConvNeXt comparator trained on seven aerial datasets, while removing v1's explicit Virtual KITTI 2 evaluation branch. OccuFly retains its nine scenes, environments, seasons, and altitudes, but its taxonomy drops FlyingAnimal, reducing coverage from 22 to 21 classes.

E2.justification: The evaluated SSC methods change from CGFormer to Symphonies and DISC, previously only cited. Depth comparisons add MapAnything V1.1, Metric3Dv2, and Depth Anything 3; reconstruction and annotation comparisons additionally evaluate Depth Anything 3, Semantic Segment Anything, and ConvNeXt. DAv2-metric and DAv2-OccuFly are retained under revised names.

E3.justification: Table 1 revises training/validation counts from 14,321/1,997 to 14,804/1,965; the test total remains 3,842, with changed scene-altitude allocations. Annotation-grid spacing changes from fixed 25 m to scene-dependent 23–28 m. New protocols assess reconstruction scale, segmentation mIoU, and pixel agreement against 135 additional annotations excluded from data generation. These reported changes do not establish that retained experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: v2 adds tests of foundation-model reconstruction and automated pseudo-label alternatives, independent geometric/semantic label validation, and environment-wise class-distribution analysis. It removes the reciprocal aerial–Virtual KITTI 2 transfer analysis. Altitude and class-wise SSC analyses remain, but evaluate different models; v1's grouped frequency-normalized performance plot is removed.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, significance tests, or uncertainty estimates for benchmark performance. New agreement percentages and averaged errors are point estimates, not new uncertainty-reporting practices.

E6.justification: CGFormer results are replaced by Symphonies and DISC results, including overall IoU/mIoU of 13.68%/0.58% and 29.52%/2.04%, respectively, in v2 Table 4. New findings include 526% average reconstruction scale deviation, 17.58% segmentation mIoU, and 92% annotation agreement. Depth-model results expand substantially, while v1 Table 4's altitude-wise DAv2 values are retained in v2 Table 12. These are expanded or replaced evaluations, not demonstrated same-setting gains.

M1.justification: The SfM/MVS reconstruction, semantic label lifting with voting and kNN, class-aware densification, and frustum-based sampling procedures remain unchanged in substance. Adding depth maps to the sample notation formalizes an existing output. Annotation-grid parameter revisions are experimental-setting changes.

P1.justification: The abstract, contribution list, dataset-evaluation narrative, and benchmark discussion undergo substantial rewriting. The supplement is reorganized to open with scene-level visualizations; depth-dataset comparison moves into the main text, while semantic-taxonomy comparison moves into the appendix. The central method exposition remains largely stable.

P2.justification: v2 replaces the grouped SSC bar chart with a reconstruction comparison, adds an environment-wise frequency chart, and replaces CGFormer qualitative panels with DISC examples. SSC and depth tables are substantially restructured and expanded. Dataset-comparison tables and scene-level visualizations are relocated rather than newly introduced.

R1.justification: v2 adds references supporting foundation-model and pseudo-label evaluations and explicitly acknowledges PointSSC as precedent for label lifting, explaining the camera-only aerial adaptation. References tied to Virtual KITTI 2, MobileStereoNet, and Dynamic NeRF disappear. The broader SSC survey and first-aerial-benchmark positioning remain largely intact.

T1.justification: The mathematical construction and equations remain substantively the same, with no new theorem, proof, or derivation. Correcting the coverage notation from rho(L) to rho(J) and explicitly including existing depth maps in sample notation are clarifications.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens the benchmark's evidential foundation: the independent 135-annotation check addresses v1's limited direct validation of label accuracy, while reconstruction alternatives, pseudo-label tests, and broader model comparisons better justify its design and usefulness. These gains outweigh localized reporting regressions, including omitted training details, inconsistent class frequencies between Tables 7 and 11, and the SILog interpretation contradicted by Table 5.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same OccuFly dataset and camera-based data-generation framework. Their main text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices are readable and support comparison, including matching relocated material.

after.justification: v2 reports original SSC and depth-estimation experiments, reconstruction and pseudo-label evaluations, and an independent annotation-agreement assessment, including additional appendix results.

before.justification: v1 reports original reconstruction statistics, CGFormer SSC evaluations, Depth Anything V2 experiments, and reciprocal cross-domain depth-transfer results in the main text and appendix.

results.title: OccuFly: A 3D Vision Benchmark for Semantic Scene Completion from the Aerial Perspective

C1.justification: The central contribution shifts from a three-stage Gaussian/particle simulation framework with specialized collisions and object-animation extensions to physics-guided score distillation and joint learned motion/appearance refinement. The abstract, introduction and conclusion newly claim that physics guidance and joint refinement are essential for coherent multi-particle generation; the structured-object generality claim disappears.

C2.justification: v2 adds explanations linking recurrent error accumulation and trajectory drift to regularization, including the tradeoff between insufficient and excessive physics constraints. Its ablations identify appearance regularization as critical and rotation regularization as relatively unimportant. The earlier manual-appearance mismatch limitation is replaced by limitations involving environmental lighting responses and unreliable guidance after trajectory divergence; the bidirectional-interaction limitation remains.

D1.justification: Appendix B adds neural architecture, CogVideoX-2B optimization settings, regularization weights, Claude Sonnet 4 initialization, prompts and evaluation details. Explicit manual appearance values and GaussianDreamer instructions from v1 disappear. Resource reporting changes from A5000 simulation/rendering at 7 FPS to A100 execution with approximately two minutes of simulation, one hour of optimization and subsequent rendering at 10 FPS; these describe different workloads.

E1.justification: The five scenes from Mip-NeRF360 and Tanks and Temples and the four weather effects remain. However, v2 removes the distinct structured-object tasks demonstrated in v1: falling leaves/feathers and landing drones, UFOs and bees. v2 instead presents text-guided appearance variants such as purple snow and magic particles, replacing the earlier manual controllability demonstrations.

E2.justification: ClimateNeRF and GaussCtrl remain in the weather comparison. v2 adds an evaluated, adapted Instruct-4DGS dynamic editing baseline with qualitative results and Table 3, while removing v1's AutoVFX comparison on feather/drone effects. This substantially changes the dynamic comparison evidence.

E3.justification: v2 adds ViCLIP-T and VE-Bench evaluation using 15 interpolated camera trajectories per scene, plus average trajectory drift for new ablations. The stated weather simulation length changes from 250 to 500 steps. The new Instruct-4DGS experiment trains a zero-initialized deformation field and specifies 3,000/5,000 optimization iterations. These introduce materially different evaluation procedures.

E4.justification: v1 provides a qualitative collision-handling ablation. v2 expands this into four qualitative and quantitative component variants, then adds fixed-versus-adaptive weighting, individual regularization-loss removal and trajectory-drift sensitivity studies (Table 2 and Appendix A, Tables 4–6). These test optimization mechanisms and failure conditions absent from v1.

E5.justification: Neither version documents repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, error bars or significance tests. v2's average trajectory drift is an evaluation metric, and its discussion of diffusion uncertainty motivates weighting; neither establishes experimental uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: Table 1 replaces the proposed method's all-weather CLIPSim/CLIPDir/VQAScore values of 0.25/0.09/0.80 with 0.28/0.11/0.89; the corresponding baseline image scores remain unchanged. v2 adds video scores, dynamic-baseline results and extensive ablation/drift findings, while removing object-animation results. The changed method and simulation duration prevent interpreting the higher scores as controlled same-setting gains.

M1.justification: v1 directly renders simulated motion using manually specified or GaussianDreamer-derived appearance. v2 introduces LLM initialization and recurrent neural dynamics jointly optimized through Video-SDS, physics/appearance regularization and adaptive weighting, retaining simulation as a motion prior. Appendix B.2 also adds ClimateNeRF-supervised background-snow finetuning.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction, contribution statements and conclusion are extensively rewritten around physics-guided score distillation. The method narrative changes from three simulation/rendering stages to a motion prior plus learned optimization. Related work is reordered, and the appendices are reorganized into additional experiments, technical details and visual results.

P2.justification: Figure 2 is substantially redrawn to show the neural optimization loop. The controllability and ablation displays are replaced or expanded, Table 1 gains video-metric columns, and Tables 2–6 and new experimental figures are added. Object-animation and AutoVFX figures disappear. The earlier appendix comparison figures are updated and relocated as Figures 11–12, rather than wholly new comparisons.

R1.justification: Research positioning is reorganized around score distillation, static editing and physics animation to motivate joint optimization. v2 adds substantial coverage of methods including Instruct-NeRF2NeRF, GaussianEditor and Instruct4D-to-4D/Instruct-4DGS, alongside video-diffusion and evaluation references. AutoVFX, GaussianDreamer and much of the earlier classical simulation and mesh-editing discussion are removed.

T1.justification: v2 introduces mathematical definitions for recurrent velocity, position, rotation and appearance updates and the combined Video-SDS/physics/appearance objective (Equations 5–8). These substantially extend v1's rendering, simulation-update and active-tracking formulation. v2 also explicitly assumes learned trajectories remain close to the simulation prior. Neither version provides theorems or proofs.

improvement.justification: v1's dynamic-realism claims relied on image metrics and a narrow qualitative ablation. v2 substantially strengthens their assessment through video metrics, a dynamic editing comparator, quantitative component and sensitivity studies, and explicit failure analysis, with much fuller optimization documentation. These gains outweigh reduced object-task coverage and added optimization cost. Performance attribution remains limited by changed simulation settings, absent uncertainty estimates and ClimateNeRF-supervised background snow, but the overall evidential and explanatory improvement is substantial.

A1.justification: The authors, retained Gaussian/MPM pipeline, scenes and weather tasks identify the same research work despite the changed title and substantial redesign. Both PDFs provide readable main texts, equations, figures, tables and appendices; rendered pages resolve extraction issues.

after.justification: v2 reports original weather-generation experiments, image/video metric comparisons, an adapted Instruct-4DGS comparison, and quantitative component, regularization and trajectory-drift ablations in Tables 1–6.

before.justification: v1 reports original weather and object simulations, quantitative comparisons with ClimateNeRF and GaussCtrl in Table 1, and qualitative collision-handling ablations and baseline comparisons.

results.title: Let it Snow! Animating 3D Gaussian Scenes with Dynamic Weather Effects via Physics-Guided Score Distillation

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion elevate parallel-decoding integration from proposed future work to a third central contribution. The headline speedup changes from approximately 1.7x to 5x, and claimed superiority expands from speculative-decoding baselines to parallel decoding, including ZipAR.

C2.justification: New Section 4.5 identifies memory costs from two checkpoints/KV caches and dependence on drafter-verifier distributional alignment, linking weaker LlamaGen gains to this limitation and proposing self-speculation as a remedy. v2 also explains choosing the training-free pixel upsampler despite weaker isolated performance, whereas v1 selected the learned PatchGAN variant for its trade-off.

D1.justification: v2 identifies HIT-SR as the pixel-space super-resolution component. It removes explicit Tar, ZipAR, and LANTERN repository links and v1's training-time/hardware disclosure and hinge-loss, LeCam, and augmentation details. Most learned-sampler architecture, optimizer, batch-size, training-step, and inference-hyperparameter information remains in the supplement; these omissions do not establish changed training procedures.

E1.justification: Both versions retain LAION-COCO-Aesthetic training data, GenEval and DPG-Bench evaluation, and MS-COCO 2017 validation images for perceptual metrics. Text-to-image generation at 512p and 1024p remains the task coverage. Adding Tar-7B and LlamaGen changes model configurations rather than datasets or tasks.

E2.justification: v2 removes Table 1's entire broad cross-model comparison block, including Chameleon, Lumina-mGPT, Transfusion, Show-O, Janus/Janus-Pro, D-DiT, Emu3, and Harmon. The comparison consequently focuses on acceleration within base generators. ZipAR-16, EAGLE-2, and LANTERN remain the principal acceleration comparators and are also evaluated on the added model configurations.

E3.justification: Evaluation expands from Tar-1.5B alone to Tar-7B at both resolutions and LlamaGen-XL at 512p. v2 also introduces parallel-versus-sequential evaluations at matched acceptance thresholds. The existing metrics, A100/batch-one timing setup, and supplementary 500-prompt latency protocol remain; the retained latency description still excludes MLLM conditioning time.

E4.justification: Figure 5d adds an ablation testing parallel decoding, and Figure 7 adds component-level latency breakdowns with parallel decoding enabled. Figure 5a removes the DINO-discriminator variant and adds the pixel-space upsampler comparison. Probability-pooling, local-expansion, and supplementary neighborhood-radius ablations are retained.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, significance tests, or uncertainty bands. The revised tables and plots retain point-estimate reporting.

E6.justification: Table 1 replaces MuLo-SD results with results for the revised default: Tar-1.5B/1024p changes from 1.68x speedup and 76.3 GenEval to 3.90x and 76.8. New Tar-7B/1024p results report 5.33x and 85.4. New LlamaGen results report 1.40x, below LANTERN's 1.59x and ZipAR's 1.88x. These involve changed method configurations; supplementary curves and qualitative outputs are also revised.

M1.justification: v2 adds whole-image drafting with ZipAR and parallel resampling across rejection islands, with ZipAR also operating within islands (Section 3.4). It additionally introduces a training-free pixel-space upsampling route and makes it the default. v1 used learned latent up/down-samplers with sequential drafting and resampling.

P1.justification: v2 condenses the preliminaries and multi-scale motivation, separates implementation details from experimental settings, and introduces parallel-decoding and limitations subsections. Much wording and the overall introduction–related work–method–experiments–conclusion–supplement structure remain recognizable.

P2.justification: Table 1 is reorganized around generator/resolution configurations. Figure 3 is redrawn to show rejection islands, Figure 4 expands from six to eight examples, Figure 5 gains a fourth panel, and Figure 7 becomes a sequential/parallel four-panel comparison. Figure 8 changes axis ranges, qualitative displays are refreshed, and document typography changes throughout.

R1.justification: v2 adds references for connected-component labeling and HIT-SR, while removing works supporting deleted comparisons or training discussion, including ImageFolder and Projected GANs. ZipAR is repositioned as an implemented component rather than only a prospective combination. The broader positioning relative to LANTERN and multi-scale autoregressive models remains substantially intact.

T1.justification: v2 Equation 8 newly defines rejection islands as disjoint 8-connected components partitioning the expanded rejection set. Existing acceptance rules, neighborhood definitions, and the theoretical sequential-speedup expression remain mathematically equivalent. No new theorem or proof is supplied.

improvement.justification: v2 turns v1's proposed remedy for sequential bottlenecks into a specified, experimentally tested contribution, supported by the new parallel-decoding ablation and component timings. Broader model validation, a training-free variant, and explicit memory/alignment limitations substantially strengthen practical relevance and evidential scope. Reporting remains imperfect: Appendix Section 8 retains the old ZipAR-dominance interpretation, some Table 1 deltas contradict their absolute values, and claims of consistent superiority overreach the LlamaGen results. These defects temper, but do not outweigh, the substantial gains in validation and applicability analysis.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same MuLo-SD research. Their main text, equations, tables, figures, and complete supplementary material are readable and support comparison despite substantial revisions.

after.justification: v2 reports original experiments on Tar-1.5B, Tar-7B, and LlamaGen-XL, alongside ablations, latency breakdowns, and qualitative results.

before.justification: v1 reports original Tar-1.5B benchmarking, latency measurements, component ablations, and generated-image comparisons, including supplementary experiments.

results.title: Multi-Scale Local Speculative Decoding for Image Generation

C1.justification: The principal benchmark, StaR effectiveness, generalization, and dynamic-applicability claims remain. The introduction newly claims that prompting cannot fundamentally improve toggle reasoning, strengthening the motivation for learned intrinsic reasoning. Describing StaR as a multimodal reasoning method and extending evidence to four agents do not themselves redefine its contribution.

C2.justification: v2 adds substantive interpretations of why prompting fails, characterizes oracle-state baselines as upper bounds on training-free collaboration, and argues for integrating all reasoning components. Appendix B.2 newly attributes AgentCPM regressions to coordinate drift and fixed visual tokens, whereas v1 merely acknowledged lower performance. These broaden the mechanism and failure explanations substantially.

D1.justification: Appendix A.5 and Table 8 substantially expand reproducibility information: full fine-tuning, unfrozen vision components, sequence length, batch size, accumulation, scheduler, warmup, precision, action-format conversion, and four-step UI-TARS history. v2 also documents source proportions, paired split membership, and additional agent and baseline prompts. These are largely new disclosures rather than demonstrated changes to existing experiments.

E1.justification: Both versions use the same six source datasets, binary toggle task, AndroidControl-H/L, AITZ, GUI-Odyssey, and 20 dynamic mobile tasks. GUIAct-Mobile specifies the earlier GUIAct source. Additional agents, prompting controls, and audits use retained task and data coverage.

E2.justification: v2 adds GUI-Owl-7B and four evaluated comparison approaches: state-focused prompting, StaR-style prompting, ground-truth state prompting, and ground-truth state combined with StaR-style prompting (Tables 1 and 9). Original comparators remain; proprietary-agent results move from v1 Table 1 to v2 Table 9.

E3.justification: v2 substantially extends the evaluation design with privileged ground-truth state inputs, explicit prompting controls, component-removal training experiments, and manual assessments of 100 annotation instances and 200 disjoint benchmark instances. Existing benchmark sizes, metrics, click-distance thresholds, learning rate, and epoch count remain unchanged; newly disclosed settings do not establish reruns.

E4.justification: v2 adds annotation-quality validation, OS-Atlas ablations removing perceiving or analyzing (Table 10), and analysis of 463 degradation and 287 improvement cases for AgentCPM (Appendix B.2). These address label reliability, component contributions, and failure causes absent from v1. The Wi-Fi case studies are retained and moved to Appendix B.4.

E5.justification: Appendix A.1 introduces sample-based estimates of individual annotator correctness and an independence-based estimate of retained-label accuracy (Table 4), absent from v1. This adds a limited statistical estimation procedure. Neither version reports repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, or significance tests for agent performance.

E6.justification: v2 adds extensive prompting, GUI-Owl, ablation, audit, and error-analysis results. UI-TARS state-control O-AMR entries change from 45.53% to 47.45% zero-shot and from 74.52% to 77.86% with training; the PDFs do not explain these revisions. Dynamic results remain unchanged. For GUI-Owl, Table 1 implies a 24.03-point gain, conflicting with the 21.64% stated in Section 5.2.

M1.justification: StaR retains the same trained perceiving, analyzing, and deciding chain, combined with refined toggle episodes and ordinary agentic training data. Appendix A.5 elaborates implementation, including handling non-toggling steps already illustrated in v1. The annotation-equation discrepancy noted under T1 does not establish an actual procedure change.

P1.justification: The main text is extensively rewritten and condensed. Reasoning-related work moves ahead of the other related-work subsections, terminology changes from toggle feature to functionality, case studies move into the appendix, and the experimental appendices receive substantial restructuring and expanded explanations.

P2.justification: v2 changes from a single-column to a two-column layout, redesigns Figure 1, expands Figure 3 with a prompting panel and consistently oriented axes, and reorganizes general-agent plots. It expands comparison tables and adds data-source, audit, action-space, hyperparameter, and ablation tables. Existing case-study figures and prompt displays are relocated or resized.

R1.justification: v2 adds related works including Insight-V, Argus, CogAgent, ShowUI, Magma, and multimodal chain-of-thought research, and foregrounds multimodal reasoning. The central positioning around improving intrinsic toggle reasoning instead of relying on external annotation remains, making this a limited expansion of research positioning.

T1.justification: v2 adds a localized annotation-reliability derivation under independent annotator correctness assumptions (Appendix A.1, Equations 5-6). Equation 1 also changes from conjunction to equality of the binary toggle indicators, admitting joint negative classifications and contradicting the retained prose. The added metric formulas otherwise restate existing definitions.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens evidence and reproducibility where v1 lacked prompting controls, component tests, and empirical label validation. Tables 9-10 directly examine alternatives and reasoning components, while Appendix A adds annotation audits and detailed training settings. These gains outweigh the new annotation-equation inconsistency, numerical reporting errors, and overly broad oracle upper-bound claims, which still limit confidence in some interpretations.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same StaR research work. Their text, equations, tables, figures, and complete Appendices A-C are readable and support reliable comparison despite extensive reformatting and reorganization.

after.justification: v2 retains these empirical results and adds GUI-Owl evaluations, prompting comparisons, annotation-quality audits, component ablations, and error analysis.

before.justification: v1 reports original evaluations of baseline and StaR-trained agents on the state control benchmark, three general agentic benchmarks, and 20 dynamic mobile tasks.

results.title: See, Think, Act: Teaching Multimodal Agents to Effectively Interact with GUI by Identifying Toggles

C1.justification: The largest-dataset claim and three principal dataset contributions remain. v2's abstract, introduction and conclusion additionally assert experimentally demonstrated effectiveness across controllable generation, world simulation and geometric reconstruction, strengthening the earlier largely prospective application claims.

C2.justification: v2 adds interpretations of downstream generalization and attributes VGGT's limited Dycheck response to strong pretraining and near-ceiling performance. It newly acknowledges non-metric pose properties and suboptimal masks in complex scenes. Most other MegaSaM failure conditions already appeared in v1 and are consolidated into Section 6.

D1.justification: v2 supplies full captioning prompts and pose-encoding instructions in Figures 11–12, plus checkpoints, trainable/frozen modules, optimizers, schedules, loss weights and hardware for downstream experiments in Section 5 and Appendix C.1. Some earlier information is omitted, including the four-anchor SAM2 detail and the project URL printed in v1; URL omission does not establish resource unavailability.

E1.justification: v2 expands from dataset and annotation assessment to three downstream tasks. Actual training/evaluation now includes RealEstate10K and Sekai-Real for generation, DL3DV for novel-view synthesis, and Sintel, TUM-dynamics and Dycheck for pose estimation, alongside SpatialVID. Earlier citations or dataset-description rows did not constitute these experiments.

E2.justification: New comparisons evaluate Wan2.2-based generators trained on RealEstate10K, Sekai-Real and SpatialVID-HQ; GS-LRM trained on alternative datasets; and CUT3R/VGGT controls for SpatialVID fine-tuning or data inclusion. The earlier six-method annotation comparison is retained as Figure 10. Cited methods such as Long-LRM are not separately evaluated baselines.

E3.justification: v2 introduces task-specific metrics, training budgets and held-out evaluation protocols, including 100/300/500 generation test sequences and equal-size 60K-clip reconstruction training with two input and four target views. The stated preprocessing resolution changes from 1920×1080 to 1280×720. These are reported settings; the PDFs do not establish that earlier analyses were rerun. GS-LRM initialization remains inconsistent between Section 5.2's fine-tuning description and Appendix C.1's training from scratch.

E4.justification: v2 adds a controlled VGGT comparison with and without SpatialVID-HQ training data, plus qualitative examinations of camera adherence, scene details and reconstruction consistency in Figure 6 and Appendix C.2. These extend the analysis beyond the retained filtering, caption-refinement and estimator-selection examples, without introducing a broad sensitivity or robustness study.

E5.justification: Both versions report aggregate statistics and distribution plots without repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals or significance tests. v2's averages over test sequences do not introduce uncertainty estimation; the new sample counts concern evaluation design.

E6.justification: Tables 2–4 introduce downstream results absent from v1. For example, v2 reports DL3DV PSNR of 27.80 for SpatialVID-trained GS-LRM versus 27.01 for RealEstate10K training, and TUM-dynamics CUT3R ATE of 0.040 after fine-tuning versus 0.049. Reported HQ size changes from 371,270 clips/1,146.06 hours to 365,362 clips/1,111.55 hours. The retained rotation and translation distributions also exchange metric labels in Figure 5, changing their reported numerical assignments without establishing recomputation.

M1.justification: The core filtering, MegaSaM/depth/SAM2 annotation and Gemini/Qwen captioning procedures are retained. Section 5.1 and Appendix C.1 add a downstream adaptation of ReCamMaster-style camera conditioning to Wan2.2, excluding intrinsics and injecting learned extrinsic embeddings into transformer blocks.

P1.justification: The introduction, related work and curation descriptions are extensively condensed and rewritten. Detailed filtering and semantic analyses move into Appendices A–B, a validation section is inserted, and the conclusion becomes a discussion-and-limitations section. This substantially reorganizes the narrative beyond the added experiments.

P2.justification: v2 changes from a single-column to a two-column layout, relocates and enlarges many retained figures, and adds three result tables, prompt panels and downstream qualitative comparisons. The dataset-quality panels are rearranged, with rotation/translation distributions reassigned to different labels. These are substantial display changes beyond renumbering.

R1.justification: v2 adds discussion or citations for Context as Memory, GameFactory, Wan, T5, VBench and Long-LRM, while removing references such as MotionSight, LGM and LVSM. The central positioning around bridging semantic video datasets and geometric datasets, including Sekai as concurrent work, remains.

T1.justification: Appendix C.1 adds an explicit reconstruction-objective definition combining weighted MSE, LPIPS and depth-smoothness losses, which is absent from v1. This is a limited mathematical addition for the new validation experiment. The existing trajectory-metric definitions are retained, and neither version provides theorems or proofs.

improvement.justification: Tables 2–4 address v1's central evidential gap: downstream usefulness was asserted largely from dataset statistics rather than demonstrated through model training. The new evaluations, including equal-size reconstruction comparisons, and detailed prompts/training documentation substantially strengthen validation and reproducibility. Claims of improvement across all VBench metrics exceed Table 2, and GS-LRM initialization and motion-plot labeling remain ambiguous, but these weaknesses do not outweigh the substantial addition of direct evidence.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe SpatialVID and are fully readable, including figures, tables, equations and v2's Appendices A–C. Much of v1's main-text documentation can be matched to material relocated into v2's supplement.

after.justification: v2 retains original dataset analyses and adds camera-controlled generation, novel-view synthesis and pose-estimation experiments, with quantitative results in Tables 2–4 and supplementary qualitative results.

before.justification: v1 reports original dataset statistics, caption analyses, camera-estimator trajectory comparisons and comparisons with processed Panda70M videos, including Figures 6, 11 and 13.

results.title: SpatialVID: A Large-Scale Video Dataset with Spatial Annotations

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, contributions, and conclusion expand the work from benchmark construction and evaluation to include a reinforcement fine-tuning baseline. v3 additionally claims cross-city generalization improvements and improved reasoning efficiency after training. The central transit-map benchmark and open-/closed-source performance-pattern claims remain.

C2.justification: v1 offers broader knowledge and visual integration as possible explanations for closed-source advantages. v3 emphasizes visual grounding and successful self-correction, contrasting these with open-source models overturning correct intermediate judgments. It also introduces interpretations concerning language bias, OCR insufficiency, and grounding versus spatial-reasoning failures. Existing generalization limitations remain, with expanded cross-view, agent-based, and embodied future directions.

D1.justification: v3 documents three-expert quality review, an approximately 16% initial annotation error rate, additional difficulty labels, name-normalization rules, local/English answer matching, and training hyperparameters. It also specifies a planned Apache 2.0 dataset release. These disclosures do not establish changes to retained experiments. Conversely, v1's eight-A100 inference-hardware specification is removed.

E1.justification: The 30-city, 1,008-pair dataset is retained, but Appendix C.3–C.4 adds substantially different input scenarios: complete network topology supplied as text, and English station aliases for Beijing and Hangzhou. These extend v1's visual-input and question-only settings. OCRBench contributes previously published scores for analysis, rather than a newly conducted evaluation.

E2.justification: Table 2 adds Qwen2.5-VL-7B-Instruct while retaining all 15 original models; Table 3 retains its six-model comparison. The new training comparison uses untuned 3B and 7B counterparts, and symbolic-map experiments reuse existing model families. Comparator coverage expands within the established model set.

E3.justification: v3 introduces cross-city fine-tuning with disjoint training and test maps, AdamW, learning rate 1e-6, KL coefficient 1e-3, eight sampled responses per query, and batch size 16. New analyses specify topology textualization, structure-preserving station-name substitutions, and alternative scoring schemes. The existing 312-sample test set, 2,048-token limit, and difficulty weights are retained.

E4.justification: v3 adds component-level error scores, map-score sensitivity tests, language substitutions, symbolic-input comparisons, and analyses distinguishing OCR, grounding, and spatial-reasoning failures (Appendix C). These substantially extend v1's masking, difficulty, city, and qualitative analyses. The original difficulty and city plots are retained as Figures A1–A2, not new experiments.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, experimental seeds, confidence intervals, error bars, or significance tests for its benchmark results. The eight responses sampled during GRPO training are an optimization setting, not uncertainty estimation.

E6.justification: All shared numerical entries in Tables 2 and 3 remain unchanged. v3 adds the 7B results, training outcomes, and Tables A3–A7. For example, Table 4 reports 7B short/long accuracy increasing from 13.28%/7.12% to 26.22%/26.04% after fine-tuning. Table A5 shows English-alias improvements for every long-question comparison but declines in four of six short-question comparisons. Symbolic-input results use different conditions from visual evaluation.

M1.justification: v3 adds a task-specific GRPO training baseline for Qwen2.5-VL-3B and 7B, using binary route-correctness and output-format rewards (Section 4.3 and Appendix B.4). v1 only constructs and evaluates the benchmark. The existing construction pipeline and correctness/map-score algorithms remain substantively unchanged.

P1.justification: The paper is retitled, the introductory benchmark-gap argument and performance interpretation are substantially rewritten, and the results discussion is reordered. The appendix is reorganized: preprocessing moves into evaluation details, supplementary experiments receive their own section, and case analyses and further statements are separated. Map Metadata is renamed Metro Data.

P2.justification: v3 adopts a two-column layout, substantially redraws the overview, construction pipeline, and case figures, and adds Table 4 and Tables A3–A7. v1 Figures 3–4 move to appendix Figures A1–A2. Redrawn case figures add endpoint annotations and error labels; Figure A3 also changes two retained Doubao response labels without explanation.

R1.justification: v3 substantially expands the cited literature and sharpens positioning around jointly testing fine-grained perception and spatial reasoning. It explicitly contrasts ReasonMap with MapBench and V*Bench, adds geospatial benchmarks such as Geo-Bench, GeoReasoner, and GeoChain, and connects future work to localization, agentic vision, and embodied research. Earlier cited works are retained, including those with updated publication metadata.

T1.justification: Appendix B.4 adds a formal centered group-advantage definition and reward-weighted log-likelihood objective, Equations 1–2, for the new training baseline. v1 contains no corresponding training mathematics. The original scoring algorithms are retained, and no theorem or proof is added.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially strengthens the benchmark's diagnostic value: symbolic-input and language controls test explanations that v1 largely discussed, scoring ablations examine metric sensitivity, and cross-city fine-tuning demonstrates use of the previously unused training partition. Added evaluation and annotation details also improve transparency. These gains outweigh localized reporting problems, including an overgeneralized English-language advantage despite mixed short-question results and inconsistent Doubao labels in Figure A3. The improvement rests on stronger validation and practical usefulness, rather than higher scores alone.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same ReasonMap benchmark despite the changed title. Their complete main texts and appendices are readable, and corresponding datasets, algorithms, tables, and relocated figures can be matched reliably.

after.justification: v3 retains those original results and adds fine-tuning experiments, symbolic-map evaluation, language substitutions, and scoring analyses. Table A7 separately identifies its OCRBench scores as collected from other works.

before.justification: v1 reports original evaluations of 15 MLLMs, visual-input masking experiments, difficulty and city analyses, and qualitative error cases.

results.title: ReasonMap: Towards Fine-Grained Visual Reasoning from Transit Maps

C1.justification: v1 centers its contributions on omission and fabrication as two causal sources of hallucination. v2's abstract, introduction, and conclusion instead foreground the claims that outcome-only GRPO rewards reinforce spurious background dependencies and that these dependencies promote hallucinations. Causal token rewards remain the central mitigation contribution, but the main explanatory claim is substantially redefined.

C2.justification: v2 develops new interpretations linking gradient saliency, outcome-only reinforcement, and decoding to background-driven hallucination, and interprets new experiments as supporting transfer across GRPO variants. Its efficiency conclusion changes from reduced training time to an acceptable performance-cost balance. The limitations discussion drops v1's qualifications concerning deployment scenarios, static datasets, and alternative RL algorithms, retaining primarily the model-scale limitation.

D1.justification: v2 newly discloses offline optimization over fixed, pre-collected rollouts and explains backbone matching, gradient computation, and saliency normalization for the diagnostic experiment. It supplies H=8 and revised reward weights. Most existing hardware, FSDP/vLLM, batch-size, sequence-length, learning-rate, and supplementary-code information is retained; the offline disclosure alone does not establish a change from online training.

E1.justification: MMBench evaluation is removed, while the new diagnostic study adds text-only descriptions as counterparts to image-question inputs. The high-resolution, grounding, and mathematics benchmarks were already evaluated in v1's appendix. v2 additionally lists ArxivQA and ThinkLite-VL as experimental datasets, but does not specify their experimental roles sufficiently to establish a distinct new training or evaluation setting.

E2.justification: v2 Table 1 adds Beam Search, Nucleus, VTI, HA-DPO, CLIP (OHD), POVID, CSR, and GCPO to the retained comparisons. The appendix decoding comparison replaces DeepEyes with DeCo, HA-DPO, and GCPO, while new experiments compare DAPO, Dr. GRPO, and GCPO with and without COPO. The training-efficiency comparison also replaces its comparator set.

E3.justification: v2 introduces a paired LLaVA/LLaMA GRPO saliency protocol and changes the decoding experiment from Qwen2.5-VL with split-specific POPE scores to LLaVA-1.5 with CHAIR and aggregate POPE. Reward weights change from 0.5/0.5 with eta=0.3 to independently tuned 0.35/0.35, with revised sensitivity sweeps. The principal CHAIR, POPE, and GPT-4o evaluation sample counts remain unchanged.

E4.justification: v2 adds gradient-saliency comparisons between multimodal and text-only models and between models with and without COPO. Appendix H adds GRPO-variant transfer, full-sequence versus reasoning-only reward placement, and continuation-count sensitivity analyses. Existing component, decoding, and efficiency analyses are revised, while several omission/fabrication examples are replaced.

E5.justification: v2 introduces averaging over H stochastic continuations to estimate causal sufficiency, explicitly addressing decoding variability and selecting H=8. This changes statistical estimation within reward construction; it does not establish repeated independent training runs. Neither version reports benchmark confidence intervals, error bars, significance tests, or seed-based variability.

E6.justification: Proposed-method results change extensively: LLaVA-1.5 CHAIR_S/CHAIR_I changes from 35.5/10.5 to 19.8/5.3, and POPE from 87.0 to 88.0. Appendix HR-Bench 4K overall changes from 78.0 to 76.7, while MathVerse changes from 48.8 to 50.6, surpassing the retained GPT-4o score of 50.2. Numerous comparator and analysis results are added. These are results for revised methods/settings, limiting attribution as controlled performance improvements.

M1.justification: v2 replaces single-continuation, correct-prefix-gated sufficiency with reward-gain estimation averaged over H continuations, and replaces optimized perturbation-based necessity with the reward drop caused by masking. It adds causal rewards directly to outcome-based GRPO advantages for reasoning tokens, replacing cumulative standardized rewards with an eta coefficient. The objective also gains trajectory-length normalization. These are substantive algorithm changes beyond the COPO renaming.

P1.justification: The paper is retitled and named COPO, with extensive rewrites of the abstract, introduction, problem formulation, and causal discussion. v2 introduces a dedicated empirical-analysis subsection, reorganizes method exposition, and adds numbered sections and lettered appendices. These changes substantially alter the narrative and document structure.

P2.justification: v2 replaces the opening illustration, adds saliency panels and a framework diagram, and incorporates the earlier dog/frisbee example into redesigned Figure 4. It merges the CHAIR and POPE tables, separates GPT evaluation from the former combined table, displays MME as a bar chart, and adds appendix tables and plots. Typography, headings, captions, and supplementary-material layout are also extensively revised.

R1.justification: The positioning shifts from general data-centric/model-centric hallucination mitigation toward reasoning post-training and limitations of GRPO. v2 adds substantial discussion and citations concerning RL, preference optimization, GCPO, and other newly evaluated methods, and revises its description of DeCo. The earlier comparison with causal chain-of-thought work remains, so it is not a new positioning element.

T1.justification: Although the SCM and PNS definition are retained, the operational mathematical definitions of sufficiency, necessity, and advantage are substantially revised. In particular, necessity becomes an explicit reward difference under removal rather than the reward of the perturbed answer, changing its mathematical relationship to indispensability. Neither version provides formal theorems or proofs.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens formulation and validation: the necessity reward now measures damage from masking, correcting v1's mismatch between its formula and claimed indispensability, while relevant preference/RL baselines and transfer and reward-placement controls address important empirical gaps. These gains outweigh the shortened limitations discussion and a new Algorithm 1 inconsistency that uses the same prefix for both sufficiency branches. The saliency evidence remains qualitative, and benchmark uncertainty is still unreported; higher scores alone do not drive this assessment.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same causal sufficiency/necessity-guided GRPO research, renamed COPO in v2. The complete main texts and appendices, including equations, tables, and figures, support comparison despite substantial revision.

after.justification: v2 reports original benchmark results, gradient-saliency experiments, ablations, and additional comparisons across GRPO variants and reward-placement implementations.

before.justification: v1 reports original benchmark evaluations, component ablations, parameter sensitivity, qualitative examples, and decoding comparisons in the main text and appendix.

results.title: COPO: Causal-Oriented Policy Optimization for Hallucinations of MLLMs

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the same central contributions: proprioceptive–privileged contrastive learning, the SRL4Humanoid framework, and improved humanoid learning efficiency and performance. Additional experiments support these claims without materially redefining them.

C2.justification: Appendix D adds explanations involving teacher-imposed limitations, restricted exploration, and joint evolution of representations and policies, plus interpretations of privileged-information and coefficient effects. The original limitations concerning additional SRL methods and visual inputs remain.

D1.justification: v2 adds an explicit code-repository link and identifies the experimental GPU as an RTX4090 with 24GB memory, whereas v1 specified only a single GPU. These are additional access and hardware disclosures, not evidence of changed original experiments.

E1.justification: Appendix D.2 adds LimX Oli velocity tracking on rough terrain and velocity tracking on the Unitree G1 robot. These substantially broaden coverage beyond the original flat-terrain tracking and motion-imitation tasks on one robot platform.

E2.justification: Figures 13–15 introduce TSD-Teacher, TSD-Student, and proprioception-only PPO comparisons, including on the original LimX tasks. This adds a distinct privileged-learning alternative and an information-availability control. The original PPO/VAE/SPR/SimSiam comparator set is retained.

E3.justification: The added experiments introduce a proprioception-only control, two-stage teacher–student comparisons, and wall-clock efficiency evaluation for G1 in Figure 16. Original task settings and PPO hyperparameters remain unchanged; relabeling existing training axes as iterations does not establish a changed budget.

E4.justification: Appendix D adds analyses of privileged-information dependence, distillation versus joint learning, rough-terrain performance, and sensitivity to the PvP loss coefficient. v1 already disclosed searching coefficients 0.1, 0.5, and 1.0, but did not report their comparative learning curves.

E5.justification: Both versions describe learning curves using means and standard-deviation bands. The additional figures follow that existing practice; neither version specifies run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, or significance tests.

E6.justification: Figures 13–17 add substantial results: PvP exceeds distilled students, proprioception-only PPO learns poorly, G1 converges faster with PvP, and coefficient 0.1 gives the highest final score in the coefficient sweep. Teachers sometimes achieve higher final scores than PvP. These are additional results, not demonstrated v1-to-v2 performance gains.

M1.justification: The zero-masking procedure, shared encoder, SimSiam-style objective, PPO integration, and interval updates remain unchanged. The new coefficient study does not change the baseline coefficient of 0.5 specified in Appendix C.2.

P1.justification: v2 makes localized grammar and terminology corrections, updates author affiliations and contact information, adds acknowledgments, and introduces Appendix D. The main narrative and section organization remain largely intact.

P2.justification: v2 adds a substantial set of comparison and sensitivity plots in Figures 13–17. Existing learning plots switch from percentage progress to iteration axes, erroneous 32dof titles become 31dof, and figures and appendix material are reflowed. Tables 1–6 retain their structure.

R1.justification: v2 adds citations to Kumar et al.'s RMA and Lee et al.'s challenging-terrain locomotion work, positioning PvP against teacher–student distillation in Appendix D. The existing related-work discussion is otherwise substantively retained.

T1.justification: The POMDP formulation, objectives in Equations 1–12, and reward formulas remain unchanged. Appendix D adds empirical findings and conceptual arguments, without new formal assumptions, derivations, or proofs.

improvement.justification: Appendix D substantially strengthens validation previously limited to SRL comparisons on one robot by adding distillation comparisons, privileged-information controls, rough terrain, and a second platform. Coefficient analysis and code/hardware disclosures further improve assessability. New experimental details remain sparse, and some superiority language exceeds the final-score advantages in Figures 15–16, but these limitations do not outweigh the broader empirical support.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same PvP/SRL4Humanoid study and contain readable text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices. v2 retains Appendices A–C and adds Appendix D, supporting a reliable comparison.

after.justification: v2 retains those original experiments and adds teacher–student comparisons, additional robot and terrain evaluations, and coefficient-sensitivity results in Appendix D.

before.justification: v1 reports original humanoid-control experiments, including learning curves, tracking performance, SRL ablations, and robot demonstrations in Section 5.

results.title: PvP: Data-Efficient Humanoid Robot Learning with Proprioceptive-Privileged Contrastive Representations

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction and new conclusion redefine the central contribution around building a suitable foundation model and systematically aligning it through progressive multi-task RL. Cross-task transfer and comprehensive instruction alignment become principal claims, replacing v3's emphasis on architectural separation, data construction and exploratory reflection as the contribution package.

C2.justification: v4 adds substantive interpretations about task synergy, OCR interference, reward hacking, editing-first supervision and generalization beyond training rewards. Some conclusions exceed the evidence: Section 9.9 claims superiority across every OOD metric, although Table 10 gives alternative curricula higher CLIP-I, DINO or CLIP-Out scores. The earlier language, input-quality and reflection limitations largely remain.

D1.justification: v4 newly documents foundation-stage resolutions and training steps in Table 6, RL data sources and sample counts, and task-specific budgets. It also specifies Flux-VAE, FlashAttention2 and a two-layer refiner. Its abstract reports resources as released rather than promising their release. Conversely, v3's explicit 32-layer diffusion-decoder and 2520 hidden-size specifications are omitted.

E1.justification: v4 replaces the reported DPG-Bench evaluation with OneIG-Bench, extending assessment beyond long-prompt alignment to text rendering, reasoning, stylization and diversity. It also adds an indexed multi-image reconstruction task and introduces RL training data from Flow-GRPO, EditScore and Echo-4o. The original understanding, editing and OmniContext coverage remains.

E2.justification: v4 adds Qwen-Image to T2I comparisons, Gemini-2.5-Flash-Image and Qwen-Image-Edit-2509 to GEdit/OmniContext comparisons, and DreamO/UMO to the overall comparison. BLIP3-o 4B disappears from the overall table but remains in the GenEval appendix. Removing v3's detailed ImgEdit table also removes its GPT-4o and UltraEdit comparisons on that benchmark.

E3.justification: New experimental designs include reconstructing a selected input image and measuring steps to loss below 0.014, plus controlled RL task/reward/order comparisons with 1,500 T2I, 700 editing and 200 in-context training steps. GenEval no longer reports a separate rewritten-prompt OmniGen2 variant. These additions are distinct from newly disclosed foundation-training settings; OmniContext retains its eight subtasks, 50 examples each and GPT-4.1 evaluation.

E4.justification: v4 adds quantitative RoPE comparisons and convergence curves, including an image-index-embedding variant (Table 1, Figure 9). Tables 5 and 10 examine task selection, reward choice, training order and transfer to benchmarks outside the training rewards. The earlier reflection examples and qualitative failure analyses are largely retained in the supplement.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, significance tests or comparable uncertainty estimates. v4's new loss curves show optimization trajectories rather than uncertainty across repeated experiments.

E6.justification: For its revised RL-aligned system, v4 reports GenEval 0.95 versus v3's 0.80 without rewriting and 0.86 with rewriting; GEdit overall is 7.21 versus 6.41 in the corresponding detailed tables, and OmniContext average is 7.95 versus 7.18. These concern differently trained systems. OneIG and ablation results are added, while DPG and category-level ImgEdit results disappear. v4's MULTIPLE-object score is internally inconsistent: 7.91 in Table 4 versus 7.80 in Table 8.

M1.justification: v4 introduces progressive online reinforcement learning after foundation training. Its Flow-GRPO curriculum proceeds through editing, GenEval and in-context generation, using EditScore, verifiable rewards and Qwen2.5-VL-72B respectively. This substantially extends v3's generative training and separate reflection fine-tuning; the underlying decoupled architecture is largely retained.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction and method narrative are extensively rewritten around instruction alignment. Dataset construction moves before the method, detailed pipelines and reflection material move into a separate supplement, related work is reorganized, and a conclusion is added. These constitute substantial narrative restructuring beyond the scientific additions.

P2.justification: v4 replaces the single-column report layout with a two-column main paper and supplement, substantially resizing and relocating retained figures and tables. It adds the convergence plot and RoPE, RL-ablation and training-schedule tables, redraws the reflection schematic, and removes the DPG and detailed ImgEdit tables. Most qualitative examples are retained rather than newly generated evidence.

R1.justification: A new related-work section substantially develops diffusion-model RL, discussing DDPO, DPOK, Flow-GRPO, DanceGRPO, Mix-GRPO and related approaches. The paper now positions its contribution against single-task or narrow-objective alignment methods. v3's specific comparison with ReflectionFlow and associated reflection-centered positioning are removed.

T1.justification: v4's positional-encoding equation restates v3's constant image identifier and local spatial-coordinate construction. The new curriculum tuple notation describes the training stages but adds no substantive mathematical assumptions, derivations, propositions or proofs.

improvement.justification: v3 provided limited controlled evidence for its design choices. v4 substantially strengthens that foundation through positional-encoding comparisons, task/reward/order ablations and transfer experiments, while adding useful training documentation (Tables 1, 5, 6 and 10). These gains outweigh the loss of DPG and detailed ImgEdit results. Reporting weaknesses remain material, particularly Section 9.9's unsupported all-metrics superiority claim and the inconsistent OmniContext entry in Tables 4 and 8.

A1.justification: Both PDFs are readable and describe the same OmniGen2 model, data pipelines and OmniContext benchmark. Text, tables, figures and v4's supplementary material support reliable comparison, including matching material moved from v3's main text.

after.justification: v4 reports original model evaluations plus positional-encoding experiments and reinforcement-learning ablations, including Tables 1, 5 and 10.

before.justification: v3 reports original OmniGen2 benchmark results, generated examples and reflection experiments, including Tables 2–9 and Figures 10–14.

results.title: OmniGen2: Towards Instruction-Aligned Multimodal Generation

C1.justification: The central claim that dense initialization removes the need for densification while accelerating reconstruction remains. v2 specifies LPIPS and SSIM when claiming faster matching of standard 3DGS, drops the prominent half-splat claim, and explicitly promotes integration with adaptive density control without increasing training time or Gaussian count.

C2.justification: v1 attributes weaker PSNR improvements to difficulty with reflective surfaces; v2 replaces that discussion with an explanation of how SH initialization improves view-dependent appearance, especially indoors. It also adds substantive interpretations separating geometric consistency, spatial coverage, and raw point count, plus arguments about initialization sufficiency under sparse supervision.

D1.justification: v2 substantially expands the implementation recipe: confidence and reprojection thresholds, NDC units, handling of underdetermined SH estimation, coefficient-unfreezing instructions, and ADC settings. Appendix A also supplies an approximately 120-second initialization breakdown, including matching, triangulation, and SH estimation, plus CPU preprocessing details. These materially extend v1's reproducibility information.

E1.justification: The three core datasets remain, but v2 adds systematic sparse-view reconstruction on seven Mip-NeRF360 scenes with only 12 or 24 training views (Appendix B). v1 had only a brief sparse, front-facing demo report. v2 also reports Synthetic-dataset evaluations in Appendix F, although their referenced videos are not embedded in the PDF.

E2.justification: v2 adds VGGT-X to the initialization comparison and evaluates RegNeRF, SparseNeRF, and SparseGS in the new sparse-view comparison; the first two were only cited in v1. Conversely, v1's quantitative efficiency comparisons against methods including gsplat, EAGLES, MiniSplatting, and 3DGS-LM on Tanks&Temples and Deep Blending are absent from v2.

E3.justification: Default initialization changes from 15K correspondences and one nearest neighbor to 20K and two neighbors. v2 adds 10K-step early stopping, explicit 12/24-view training protocols, and ADC integration using 140 reference views and 8.5K correspondences per view. Scaffold-GS resource reporting changes from anchors to generated splats. The standard test split and image downsampling are retained and moved to Appendix A.

E4.justification: v2 adds sampling-component and SH ablations (Table 6), a 3DGS-without-densification control (Table 4), denser COLMAP controls (Table A2), and quantitative nearest-neighbor sensitivity. v1's Gaussian-count trajectories and undercoverage case visualization (Figs. A5–A6) are removed. Motion, noise robustness, and extreme-viewpoint analyses are retained rather than newly introduced.

E5.justification: v1 Fig. A5 shows shaded bands around Gaussian-count trajectories described as averages across scenes; v2 removes this plot. Neither PDF defines what those bands represent, so their status as statistical uncertainty reporting is unclear. Neither version otherwise specifies repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, or significance tests.

E6.justification: For 30K EDGS+3DGS, Mip-NeRF360 PSNR/LPIPS change from 27.80/0.175 to 28.02/0.141, while LPIPS changes from 0.124 to 0.132 on Tanks&Temples and 0.219 to 0.223 on Deep Blending. These are revised-method results, not strictly matched-setting gains. v2 also revises RAIN-GS's Mip-NeRF360 PSNR from 22.23 to 27.23 and adds substantial sparse-view, component, and integration results.

M1.justification: v2 introduces degree-3 spherical-harmonics initialization from multi-view observations using a pseudoinverse (Sec. 3.5). Compared with v1's pair-averaged initial colors, v2 uses reference-view color plus fitted higher-order coefficients, materially changing appearance initialization. Triangulation and confidence-thresholded correspondence sampling were already present in v1.

P1.justification: v2 substantially rewrites and condenses the introduction and related work, including removing the artist/sculptor analogy. It reorganizes the method into five subsections, restructures the experimental narrative around quality, efficiency, and compatibility, reorders ablations, and extensively reorganizes the appendices.

P2.justification: The large combined comparison table is separated into quality and efficiency tables, with additional integration and component tables. v2 redraws the teaser and sensitivity plots, adds a motion schematic, moves v1 Fig. 2 to Fig. A3 and Fig. A7 to Fig. 5, removes Playroom qualitative panels and some diagnostic figures, and changes the appendix to a two-column layout.

R1.justification: v2 adds references to VGGT-X, VGGT, SparseGS, and Penrose's generalized inverse. It extends comparisons with learned geometry priors and sparse-view methods and emphasizes complementarity with adaptive densification. The broader positioning relative to NeRF, Gaussian splatting, acceleration, and initialization research remains intact.

T1.justification: v2 adds mathematical definitions for reprojection filtering, combined sampling distributions, and the SH least-squares/pseudoinverse formulation (Eqs. 8–13). The existing triangulation and Gaussian-motion mathematics remain essentially unchanged. No new theorem or convergence proof is introduced.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially improves support for the method's mechanism and its reproducibility. Table 6 and Appendix E provide controls separating appearance initialization, sampling cues, and point-count effects, while Appendix A supplies important implementation details missing from v1. The systematic sparse-view evaluation also strengthens evidence beyond the earlier demo report. Some cross-dataset efficiency comparisons and diagnostic visualizations are lost, but the targeted controls and substantially clearer initialization recipe provide a clear overall quality gain.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same EDGS research work. Their main texts, equations, tables, figures, references, and supplementary appendices are readable and support reliable comparison, including matching relocated material.

after.justification: v2 reports original reconstruction results, component ablations, integration experiments, and appendix experiments on sparse-view reconstruction and denser COLMAP initialization.

before.justification: v1 reports original EDGS reconstruction experiments, quantitative benchmark results in Table 1, initialization and matching ablations, robustness analyses, and appendix per-scene results.

results.title: EDGS: Eliminating Densification for Efficient Convergence of 3DGS

C1.justification: v1 principally claims preliminary viability despite an ImageNet accuracy gap. v2 presents two-stage alignment as a central contribution and claims competitive performance across a broad benchmark, retaining 90–98% mean dataset-wise relative RGB accuracy while providing substantial loading-speed benefits.
