This materially broadens the central effectiveness and efficiency claims.

C2.justification: v2 adds substantive qualifications about offline fitting cost, dependence on the RGB teacher, sensitivity to distribution shifts, and alignment using non-pruned FP16 splats. Its appendix interprets reconstructed-RGB experiments as evidence about compression-limited performance and architectural studies as evidence for a token bottleneck. These extend v1's discussion of the accuracy gap, weak scratch training, and omitted quantization.

D1.justification: v2 newly documents preprocessing iterations and batch sizes, estimated fitting GPU-hours, normalization statistics, Fourier frequencies, Perceiver dimensions and heads, and forward-pass pseudocode (Tables 3–4 and Section 11.2). These substantially improve implementation specificity without establishing that every newly disclosed setting changed. Code release remains prospective, with v2 expanding the promised release to the full preprocessing and CLIP pipeline.

E1.justification: Training retains the 12.8M DataComp dataset, but evaluation expands far beyond ImageNet-1K to fine-grained recognition, medical and satellite imagery, rendered-text sentiment, synthetic spatial tasks, and shifted ImageNet/ObjectNet inputs. v2 describes 38 datasets, although Table 5 contains 37 dataset rows; the substantial coverage expansion is clear despite that discrepancy.

E2.justification: v2 adds 98-token RGB comparisons without fine-tuning and with one or five fine-tuning epochs (Table 7), plus rendered-RGB, grid/convolutional-stem, and point-transformer comparisons (Figures 18–20). The ViT-L/16 comparator plotted in v1 Figure 7 is absent from the corresponding v2 studies. These change the evaluated comparator set, beyond extending existing models to more datasets.

E3.justification: The reported GS training budget changes from six adaptation epochs to two distillation epochs followed by five CLIP epochs. v2 adds explicit RGB token-merging/fine-tuning controls, cross-dataset absolute and dataset-wise relative accuracy summaries, load/decode timing on batches of 256, and pruning sweeps over 100 images per configuration. These are substantive protocol additions, while the main RGB training recipe remains largely retained.

E4.justification: v1 mainly examines initialization, qualitative pruning, splat/token budgets, and training from scratch. v2 adds quantitative pruning sensitivity and convergence analyses, plus controlled studies of distillation order and losses, normalization, learning rates, text freezing, alternative stems, point transformers, reconstructed RGB inputs, and direct Gaussian tokenization (Sections 9 and 11.5–11.6). These test substantially more explanations for performance and optimization behavior.

E5.justification: v2 Figure 4 newly uses KDE summaries to estimate empirical distributions of pruning and PSNR outcomes across configurations. This adds descriptive statistical estimation, rather than repeated-training uncertainty. Neither version reports seed counts, confidence intervals, or significance tests for its classification results.

E6.justification: v2 adds extensive dataset-level scores, timing results, and ablation findings. For example, Table 5 reports 16.87% ImageNet top-1 for GS-1600 with 196 tokens under the revised training procedure; this is not a same-protocol gain over v1's reported 13–15% range. The earlier top-5 summary is absent. Initialization PSNR examples also change alongside the illustrated image, whereas Figure 2 retains the original 90.3× fitting-speed result.

M1.justification: v1 directly adapts an RGB-initialized GS encoder through CLIP training. v2 introduces a preceding vision-only distillation stage matching normalized RGB and GS CLS embeddings, followed by CLIP adaptation with optional text-side unfreezing (Section 5.2). Its stem also changes from the gated, z-score/global-mean design in v1 Figure 5 to the simpler normalization and projection path in v2 Figure 1d and Algorithm 1.

P1.justification: v2 substantially reorganizes the presentation: it adds the GaussianVision name, condenses preliminaries, moves CLIP background from Section 3.3 to appendix Section 8.1, rewrites the alignment section around setup/training/protocol/results, and separates Discussion from Conclusion. The structured appendix further reorganizes technical explanations and analyses; this exceeds a simple content extension or renumbering.

P2.justification: v2 redraws and combines the overview and GS architecture into a first-page Figure 1, replaces the qualitative pruning display with quantitative plots and new examples, and replaces the ImageNet-only result display with a broad benchmark chart. It adds substantial comparative tables, profiling displays, and ablation panels throughout the appendix. These are extensive visual and layout changes beyond numerical updates.

R1.justification: The main positioning against pixel-based tokenization, INRs, GaussianImage, and earlier Gaussian recognition methods is retained. v2 adds references and discussion for CLIP Benchmark, VTAB, and contrastive representation distillation, principally supporting its expanded evaluation and loss studies rather than redefining its relationship to prior research.

T1.justification: v2 Section 4.4 newly specifies the exact batch-averaged reconstruction-plus-L1 objective, weighted absolute-RGB luminance score, and retained-splat index set, which v1 leaves verbally specified. This is a limited addition of mathematical definitions. The Gaussian reconstruction equation is unchanged, and neither version develops theoretical guarantees or proofs.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially addresses v1's narrow validation and limited support for its design choices through broader evaluation, token-matched RGB controls, and targeted distillation and architecture ablations. Detailed preprocessing and model specifications also improve reproducibility. Reporting defects remain: 38 datasets are claimed but 37 are tabulated, and Table 3's speedup column matches batch-time ratios rather than throughput speedups. These weaken particular summaries but do not outweigh the substantial gains in empirical support and technical transparency.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same work, with v2 adding the GaussianVision name and substantially extending the study. Text, equations, figures, and tables are readable. v1 ends with references; v2 includes an accessible appendix in Sections 8–11.

after.justification: v2 reports original cross-dataset classification results, profiling measurements, pruning studies, and extensive architecture and training ablations, including appendix results.

before.justification: v1 reports original CUDA speed measurements, initialization and pruning experiments, and zero-shot ImageNet results for its Gaussian-splat encoders.

results.title: GaussianVision: Vision-Language Alignment from Compressed Image Representations using 2D Gaussian Splatting

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the same central contributions: physics-conditioned PAVAS, VGG-Impact, APCC, and improved physical consistency and perceptual quality. The supplement principally supports and qualifies these existing claims.

C2.justification: v2 substantially expands interpretation and applicability discussion: velocity validation uses a displacement proxy; imperfect or missing physics cues permit fallback; text conditioning supports off-screen sounds; and CUT3R dominates computational overhead, with real-time operation not targeted. It also interprets missing-observation statistics and adds explicit material modeling as future work.

D1.justification: Appendices D–H disclose full VLM prompts, the Qwen checkpoint and decoding settings, 8-FPS reconstruction, confidence filtering, missing-observation handling, model dimensions, optimizer scheduling, EMA, H100 allocations, runtime measurements, and detailed user-study instructions. These substantially improve reproducibility without demonstrating changes to the existing implementation.

E1.justification: Appendix B newly documents evaluation on ABO-500 objects for mass estimation and STARSS23 scenes for metric-displacement estimation as a velocity proxy. This substantially expands the documented dataset coverage beyond VGGSound and VGG-Impact. VGG-NonImpact merely subdivides previously covered VGGSound data.

E2.justification: The main V2A comparator sets remain unchanged. Appendix B supplies an expanded estimator comparison: Table S1 includes Image2mass, 2D CNN, and LLaVA alongside NeRF2Physics. Figure S1 explicitly compares against SpatialVLM's pseudo-ground-truth construction pipeline, clarifying the expert-model comparison invoked in v1.

E3.justification: Table 2 explicitly increases participation from 15 to 27 people. Newly included evaluations specify 500 ABO objects, 256 filtered STARSS23 clips with shared masks and displacement-tolerance metrics, inference-time physics perturbations, and runtime profiling over 100 videos. The core training settings stated in both main texts remain unchanged.

E4.justification: v2 adds mass/velocity perturbation tests, complete physics-cue removal, APCC shuffling and noise checks, model-capacity comparisons, impact/non-impact breakdowns, and additional qualitative cases. These investigate robustness, metric validity, scaling, and applicability beyond the unchanged component ablations in Table 3.

E5.justification: Both versions report user-study means and standard deviations. v2 changes the participant count and resulting estimates but adds no repeated-run or seed reporting, confidence intervals, significance tests, or comparable uncertainty-estimation procedure.

E6.justification: Tables 1 and 3 retain their numerical results, while Table 2 is revised for the expanded study; PAVAS physical plausibility changes from 4.34±0.86 to 4.37±0.84. Substantial new results include estimator accuracy, fallback performance, scaling, subgroup comparisons, runtime, and APCC degradation from 0.378 to 0.655 under shuffling. These are additional findings, not improvements to the unchanged main benchmark scores.

M1.justification: The PPE, mass/velocity conditioning, FiLM modulation, gated pooling, residual Delta-modulation, and flow-matching objective remain unchanged. Appendix E supplies implementation and architectural details without establishing a changed generation procedure.

P1.justification: v2 adds a structured A–J supplement with extensive explanations of existing modules, conditioning, prompts, metric computation, training, and study procedures. This substantially expands the exposition. Main-text edits are smaller, including compressed related work, wording corrections, and a new acknowledgments section.

P2.justification: v2 adds Figures S1–S6 and Tables S1–S8, including estimator and robustness plots, a detailed transformer diagram, additional spectrogram panels, and configuration, runtime, result, and prompt tables. Figures 1–3 and the main table structures are retained with local layout reflow.

R1.justification: v2 adds references including StereoFoley, FoleySpace, additional audiovisual-alignment and VLM work, and sources supporting the supplementary benchmarks. The central positioning against appearance-driven generation and narrowly physics-conditioned approaches remains intact; the additions do not redefine the claimed contribution.

T1.justification: Appendix D.2 makes the previously verbal APCC definition mathematically explicit, specifying incoming/outgoing event velocities and the class-averaged absolute correlation discrepancy. This adds formal specification beyond a standard correlation formula. The original method equations remain unchanged, and no new theorem or proof is introduced.

improvement.justification: v1 asserts estimator reliability and refers to supporting supplementary details absent from the supplied PDF. v2 provides estimator benchmarks, APCC validation, missing/noisy-cue tests, and extensive reproduction instructions, while documenting computational and visibility limitations and enlarging the user study. These resolve substantial evidential and reproducibility gaps. Proxy velocity validation and absent repeated-run uncertainty remain limitations, but do not outweigh the gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same PAVAS work, with matching core equations and experiments. The supplied text and graphics are readable throughout. v1 ends after its references; v2 additionally contains Supplementary Material A–J.

after.justification: v2 retains original generation experiments, reports a 27-participant user study, and supplies additional estimator, robustness, runtime, and subgroup results in its supplement.

before.justification: v1 reports original audio-generation comparisons, a 15-participant user study, component ablations, and qualitative examples in Tables 1–3 and Figure 3.

results.title: PAVAS: Physics-Aware Video-to-Audio Synthesis

C1.justification: The abstracts, introductions, and conclusions retain the central claims: the first volumetric extension of functional maps, applications to signal and connectivity transfer, and improved surface correspondence. Both abstracts retain the claim of consistently outperforming surface-only spectral methods. Added validation does not redefine these core contributions.

C2.justification: v3 explains that VOL is relatively easy and benefits from volumetric information only with Orthoprods, and that SHREC’20 can favor surface methods unless CMH compensates for topological errors. Appendix F newly recommends LBO for small bases and CMH for larger ones; Appendix D qualifies boundary traces as useful but potentially suboptimal. These materially expand applicability qualifications beyond v1's predominantly favorable interpretation.

D1.justification: v3 supplies a code-access URL, pseudocode for all three procedures, explicit cotangent weights and Neumann conditions, and concrete basis settings. Examples include 20×20 maps expanded to 120×120 with ZoomOut steps of five and 500 eigenfunctions for untangling. These fill substantial documentation gaps in v1; they do not establish that previously reported experiments used different settings.

E1.justification: Both versions use Su et al.'s volumetric shapes, SHREC’19, SHREC’20, TOPKIDS, and the same brain-segmentation setting. The Nigolian/Garanzha untangling-failure scenario already appears in v1 Figure 7; v3 expands its evaluated sample. New appendix diagnostics use existing shapes rather than introducing another population or application domain.

E2.justification: Surface-matching comparisons expand from one reported basis per dataset in v1 Table 2 to LBO, CMH, and Orthoprods comparisons on every retained dataset in v3 Table 2. These add comparator variants within the corresponding comparisons. The principal FMaps, ZoomOut, ZoomOut Fast, Orthoprods, and Garanzha untangling methods are retained.

E3.justification: Appendix B introduces Weyl-adjusted spectral comparisons and changes the Laplacian-commutativity normalization. New protocols include 100,000 random point pairs per shape pair for geodesic distortion, boundary reconstruction across basis sizes 50–500, and additional continuity, coverage, Dirichlet-energy, and flip metrics. Section 5.2 reports evaluation over 1,405 untangling failures, where v1 supplied an illustrative rescue.

E4.justification: v3 adds analyses of surface-versus-volume geodesic distortion, boundary traces' ability to reconstruct surface eigenfunctions, and broader basis-dependent matching failures. Untangling validation becomes substantially more systematic. The original flip-versus-basis-size curves are retained in Appendix F, so their relocation alone is not counted as new analysis.

E5.justification: Appendix C and Figure 11 newly report mean geodesic distortion with standard deviations over sampled point pairs. These describe variation within the sampled data, not repeated-run uncertainty. Neither version reports multi-seed performance estimates, confidence intervals, or significance tests.

E6.justification: Table 2 adds many basis-specific results and revises existing entries: SHREC’19 LBO success changes from 100% to 53.15% despite unchanged reported AGEs, and SHREC’20 CMH success changes from 92.73% to 55.49%. New entries show surface methods outperforming volumetric LBO and Orthoprods on SHREC’20. v3 also reports rescuing 85% of 1,405 untangling failures and adds diagnostic results. Revised spectral histograms use changed normalization and therefore do not establish same-setting gains.

M1.justification: The tetrahedral cotangent-Laplacian framework, functional coordinate transfer, spectral extrapolation, and volume-aware surface correspondence remain the same. CMH, Orthoprods, and ZoomOut already appear in v1. Newly stated boundary conditions and pseudocode document the existing procedures without establishing an algorithmic change.

P1.justification: The main text is extensively condensed and rewritten. The former spectral-validation subsection moves into Appendix B, while dataset discussion and basis analysis are reorganized into Appendices G–H, alongside new explanatory and algorithmic appendices. Terminology, headings, citation style, and author ordering also change.

P2.justification: The document is comprehensively reformatted. Table 2 becomes a full-width three-basis comparison, and the four matching plots expand into twelve panels in Figure 15. v3 adds an extrapolation diagram, distortion and reconstruction plots, a metrics table, and algorithm boxes; it also splits, relocates, resizes, and rearranges existing illustrations.

R1.justification: Targeted additions acknowledge LDDMM volumetric registration and Raviv et al.'s volumetric heat-kernel descriptors, and cite additional work on Laplacian discretization, spectral approximation, and boundary traces. These broaden contextual grounding while retaining the existing positioning relative to piece-wise mappings and surface functional maps.

T1.justification: v1 infers a left inverse from the boundary matrix being tall; v3 adds a cited Neumann-boundary linear-independence argument. Appendix B introduces Weyl-law reasoning for transforming volumetric eigenvalues by a power of 3/2 and changes the commutativity denominator from ||C|| to ||CΛ_M||. These substantially extend mathematical justification and revise a formal metric definition without changing the mapping algorithm.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially improves reproducibility and scrutiny of the method by supplying implementation parameters and pseudocode, exposing basis-dependent failures through fuller comparisons, and testing assumptions about volumetric distortion and boundary representation. The aggregate untangling evaluation strengthens practical validation beyond v1's isolated example. Important weaknesses remain: revised success rates are unexplained, and the retained consistent-superiority claim conflicts with Table 2. Nevertheless, the increased transparency and targeted validation provide a substantial net quality gain.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe Volumetric Functional Maps and retain the same methodological and experimental backbone. All 13 pages of v1 and 19 pages of v3 are readable, including v3's Appendices A–I; v1 has no appendices. Figures, tables, and equations support reliable comparison.

after.justification: v3 retains original experiments and adds geodesic-distortion and boundary-reconstruction analyses, additional map-quality measurements, and an aggregate untangling evaluation.

before.justification: Section 5 reports original correspondence errors, runtimes, connectivity-transfer results, and brain-segmentation demonstrations, including experiments on 40 volumetric shape pairs and several surface-matching datasets.

results.title: Volumetric Functional Maps

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion expand the contribution from an eight-environment, two-dimension benchmark to ten environments and three dimensions. v2 adds the central claim that VLM perception is comparatively strong while strategic reasoning and decision-making remain deficient, and foregrounds human experiments.

C2.justification: v1 attributes multimodal underperformance primarily to inadequate visual extraction; v2 Section 4.1 emphasizes combined visual and strategic difficulties despite competent perception. Persona effects and human comparisons add substantive interpretations. Appendix A removes the missing-human-baseline limitation, updates the agent-count limitation after three-player tests, and drops the earlier accuracy-only metric caveat.

D1.justification: The new perception appendix documents sample sources, requested output structures, coordinate wrappers, scoring weights, and tolerances. Appendix F.3.2 supplies verbatim persona prompts, and new-environment settings and model-version identifiers are documented. v2 also adds direct code-repository access and licensing disclosures; both versions already claim public code and data.

E1.justification: v2 adds Knights Archers Zombies and MPE to the eight core environments, introduces perception-recognition tasks, and evaluates three-player Hanabi and Coin Dilemma. It also adds human participants. Tiny Hanabi and Tic-Tac-Toe were already described in v1 and are not new coverage.

E2.justification: The main comparisons add o3, gemini-2.5-pro, and ui-tars-1-5, while omitting o4-mini and reasoning-enabled gemini-2.5-flash from those tables. Both omitted models remain in v2 appendix Tables 6–8. A human baseline is newly evaluated; the existing MCTS, poker-equilibrium, and Pong opponents remain.

E3.justification: v2 introduces 400-sample perception evaluations per environment, task-specific recognition scoring, coordinate overlays and tolerances, controlled persona prompts, and human testing with matched observations and play counts. New environments receive their own protocols. Appendix B also changes reported Doubao model versions, without establishing which retained experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: Section 4.3 and Appendix F.3.2 add cooperative-versus-self-interested persona interventions for three reasoning models across three mixed-motive games, testing how prompts affect behavior and returns. This substantially extends the earlier observational social-behavior analysis. The multimodal/CoT analyses and six illustrative failure cases are retained.

E5.justification: v1 Table 2 reports normalized means with standard deviations; v2 Table 4 reports means alone, although appendix raw-result and ablation tables retain uncertainty values. v2 additionally presents the human-return distribution and percentile comparisons in Figure 6. The stated run counts for retained experiments do not increase.

E6.justification: v2 adds extensive perception, human, persona, new-environment, and three-player results. Retained entries also change: GPT-4.1's Kuhn Poker prediction accuracy changes from 54.0 to 58.2 in v1 Table 1 versus v2 Table 3. Headline maxima change from o4-mini's 47.8% accuracy and 24.3% return over eight games to o3's 46.6% and 31.4% over ten games; these are different model/coverage aggregates, not like-for-like gains.

M1.justification: The existing VLM observation/action interface and reasoning and decision-making procedures are retained. Neither version proposes a new agent architecture or training algorithm; the added perception tests and persona interventions extend benchmark evaluation.

P1.justification: The extended main-text environment descriptions are consolidated into a taxonomy and moved into Appendix I. Evaluation and analysis sections are reorganized, boxed findings become integrated prose, and the appendix structure changes substantially. The title and author block are revised, and ethics, reproducibility, and LLM-use statements are added.

P2.justification: v2 redesigns Figure 2, adds taxonomy and perception tables, expands comparison tables to ten environments, redraws social-behavior plots with personas, and adds human and three-player displays. The raw-results table becomes a rotated full-page table. Existing environment screenshots and failure examples are largely relocated and reformatted rather than newly introduced.

R1.justification: v2 adds Terry et al.'s PettingZoo reference and removes the references to Coulom, Littman, and Zinkevich. Section 5 largely preserves the original positioning against text-only multi-agent benchmarks and predominantly single-agent VLM benchmarks; the citation-style conversion does not constitute substantive repositioning.

T1.justification: Appendix C introduces quantitative definitions for perception scoring, including weighted recognition components and distance-tolerant coordinate credit; KAZ uses weights of 0.2, 0.2, 0.2, and 0.4 with a radius of 100. The POMG formulation, reward-category definitions, and poker equilibrium parameterization remain unchanged, with no new proofs.

improvement.justification: The 26-participant human study directly addresses v1's acknowledged lack of a human baseline, substantially improving performance calibration. Direct perception tests and persona interventions also strengthen diagnosis beyond v1's largely indirect explanations, while three-player experiments support broader applicability. These gains outweigh reporting problems: v2 Table 9 has game headings inconsistent with its caption and surrounding text, and o3's Breakthrough return differs between Tables 4 and 8. Those inconsistencies limit confidence in particular results.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe VS-Bench. Their complete main texts and appendices, including tables, figures, and mathematical formulations, are readable and support reliable comparison despite the revised title and organization.

after.justification: v2 reports original perception, reasoning, and decision-making results, plus new persona experiments, a 26-participant human study, and three-player evaluations.

before.justification: v1 reports original evaluations of fourteen VLMs across eight environments, including action prediction, online decision-making, and multimodal/CoT comparisons.

results.title: VS-Bench: Evaluating VLMs for Strategic Abilities in Multi-Agent Environments

C1.justification: The abstract and introduction revise the quantified headline claim from 49.89 AP and a 15.51-point advantage to 38.90 AP and a claimed 13.98-point advantage. The CoS, curriculum, dataset, state-of-the-art, and zero-shot contribution claims remain. However, Table 1 supports only a 4.52-point advantage over the ground-truth-2D baseline named in that headline claim.

C2.justification: Appendix A newly attributes the inflated original scores to erroneous matching. Section 4.1 narrows superiority over the privileged baseline to five of seven unified Omni3D metrics, and Section 4.4 removes the assertion that 10% training data nearly matches DetAny3D. The mechanism explanations and dedicated limitations remain largely unchanged, while some blanket superiority statements persist.

D1.justification: Appendix A adds a concrete disclosure about the evaluation implementation error and its correction. The implementation appendix otherwise retains the same tokenization, data processing, optimizer settings, 64-H100 training configuration, training duration, and resource-access information.

E1.justification: Both versions use the same six 3D datasets, outdoor and unified Omni3D settings, held-out-category evaluations, indoor grounding tasks, and 2D pretraining corpus. Appendix renumbering introduces no additional dataset or test scenario.

E2.justification: Figures 1 and 4 switch their DetAny3D reference from scores corresponding to the ground-truth-2D variant to the ordinary variant: 34.38 to 24.92 and 35.9 to 32.2, respectively, as identified by Table 1. The comparator sets in Tables 1–3 remain unchanged.

E3.justification: The new Appendix A reports correcting mAP evaluation from erroneous cross-image matches to matching within each image. This fundamentally changes detection scoring across the empirical evaluation. The stated splits, target-aware prompting, IoU thresholds, training budgets, and model configurations are retained.

E4.justification: Tables 4–5 and Figure 4 revise the evidence for ordering, factorization, serialization, data efficiency, and pretraining under corrected scoring. For example, the Hypersim interleaving advantage changes from 17.9 to 6.5 AP. The questions and ablation variants remain the same, as do the runtime analysis and failure case studies.

E5.justification: Neither version reports experimental seed counts, repeated-run uncertainty, confidence intervals, error bars, or significance tests. Correcting detection matching changes evaluation, not uncertainty-reporting practices.

E6.justification: Accuracy results are extensively replaced in Tables 1–5 and Figure 4. Table 1's overall Omni3D AP changes from 49.89 to 38.90; Table 2's novel-category KITTI AP changes from 29.98 to 25.87. In Table 3, SUN-RGBD category-only AP changes from 44.5 to 29.7, now tying Cube-LLM_large. Appendix Table 5's interleaved Hypersim AP changes from 30.6 to 11.2. These are evaluation corrections with unchanged training and inference.

M1.justification: The architecture, interleaved 2D-to-3D decoding, near-to-far ordering, center-size-rotation representation, and training objectives are unchanged. Appendix A explicitly states that training and inference are unaffected by the evaluation correction.

P1.justification: v2 adds the erratum, renumbers the existing appendices, lightly edits acknowledgments, and revises or shortens several performance paragraphs. The main narrative and section organization remain substantially intact.

P2.justification: Figures 1 and 4 are redrawn with revised scales and plotted comparisons. Table 1 changes highlighting to reflect stronger baseline entries, and the erratum causes limited appendix reflow. The table structures, architecture diagram, and qualitative examples are retained.

R1.justification: The same cited works and research positioning are retained, including the relationships to Cube-LLM, OVMono3D, and DetAny3D. Reference differences concern citation formatting and page back-references, not added or removed research.

T1.justification: The box definitions, autoregressive factorization, Chain-of-Sight equations, and geometric assumptions in Section 2 are unchanged. The evaluation implementation correction introduces no new formal definition, theorem, or proof.

improvement.justification: Appendix A addresses a fundamental defect in v1's empirical foundation: cross-image matching inflated accuracy. Disclosing that error and replacing results throughout Tables 1–5 and Figure 4 substantially improves validity and transparency. The correction remains imperfect: the abstract's 13.98-point margin uses the unprivileged baseline despite naming the privileged one, and Table 1's outdoor AP of 36.1 conflicts with 33.1 in Section 4.1 and Table 4. These inconsistencies temper, but do not outweigh, the substantial benefit of correcting the central evaluation error.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe LocateAnything3D and contain complete, readable main text, equations, tables, figures, appendices, and references. Corresponding material can be matched despite appendix renumbering and page reflow.

after.justification: v2 retains these original experiments and reports corrected accuracy results in Tables 1–5 and Figure 4.

before.justification: v1 reports original detection, zero-shot generalization, grounding, ablation, training-dynamics, and runtime results, including appendix experiments.

results.title: LocateAnything3D: Vision-Language 3D Detection with Chain-of-Sight

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction and conclusion retain the same central claims: textual conditioning can fail in robotic control, learned task and visual prompts enable adaptation without fine-tuning the diffusion model, and ORCA achieves state-of-the-art benchmark performance. Added experiments support these claims without redefining the main contribution.

C2.justification: v2 adds substantive discussion of adaptation costs and overfitting, possible SVD failure from input-length mismatch, multi-task applicability, and architecture-specific limitations in Appendix C. It also distinguishes specialist agents from generalist VLAs. However, the retained claim that larger timesteps benefit Reacher-easy contradicts the revised Table D.

D1.justification: v2 adds a project-page link, parameter counts for adaptation baselines, and frame/layer choices for added backbone experiments. It also explicitly describes TADP's single fixed-image conditioning. Existing compression-layer pseudocode and principal hyperparameters remain unchanged; the PDFs do not establish availability of downloadable code or data.

E1.justification: The original 12 tasks across three suites remain. v2 Appendix A.2 adds KITCHEN-3, LIVING-1 and STUDY-1 from LIBERO-Long, extending evaluation to long-horizon, language-conditioned manipulation and joint multi-task control.

E2.justification: v2 Table 3 adds fully fine-tuned VC-1 and SCR, VC-1 with RoboAdapter, and SCR with LoRA. Appendix Tables A and E add SVD, Stable Diffusion 3.0, standalone DINOv2, SigLIP and Theia comparisons. The original benchmark comparator sets remain unchanged.

E3.justification: New experiments introduce full versus parameter-efficient adaptation, alternative backbone feature-extraction settings, SVD restricted to three input frames, and joint training of three LIBERO tasks with a shared policy. The original demonstration counts, 100-epoch training budget and evaluation every 10 epochs remain unchanged; several added experiments have limited protocol detail.

E4.justification: v2 adds analyses testing prompting against downstream fine-tuning, sensitivity to diffusion architecture, and dependence on the visual-prompt encoder, including an SD-VAE alternative without an external encoder. Existing component, layer, attention and qualitative studies remain; the timestep study receives a revised default-result row.

E5.justification: Retained experiments continue reporting means and standard deviations over three seeds. Additional comparisons largely use the same reporting practice, without new significance tests, confidence intervals or an explicit change in repeated-run counts. Updated standard-deviation values belong to the changed results.

E6.justification: The original main benchmark scores remain unchanged, but v2 adds substantial results in Table 3 and Appendix Tables A–C and E. For example, ORCA's new LIBERO single-task and multi-task means are 65.5 and 46.6. The default timestep row changes from mean 70.8 to 74.3, including Reacher-easy changing from 71.9 to 87.6, now matching the main results.

M1.justification: ORCA retains frozen Stable Diffusion 1.5, learnable task prompts, dense visual prompts and behavior-cloning training. Sections 5–6 preserve the conditioning procedure and default components. The additional backbone and encoder experiments do not establish a revision to the proposed method.

P1.justification: Most original prose and the main section sequence remain intact. v2 locally revises the abstract and introduction, expands baseline explanations, reorders analyses and moves references after the supplementary material. Section 6.5 also repeats the task/visual-prompt visualization discussion almost verbatim.

P2.justification: v2 converts the document to two columns, moves Figure 1 onto the title page, merges the DMC and MetaWorld tables, and rearranges Figure 6 into a vertical frame sequence. It adds five experimental tables and extensively resizes or relocates retained displays. The appendix rollout visualizations retain their underlying content.

R1.justification: v2 substantially broadens positioning beyond frozen encoders and perception-oriented prompting to parameter-efficient adaptation, newer visual encoders, video/Transformer diffusion and VLAs. Corresponding references are added, and Appendix A.8 explicitly contrasts ORCA's specialist focus and image-text pretraining with generalist models trained on robot interaction data.

T1.justification: The diffusion equations, feature-extraction formulation and behavior-cloning objective remain mathematically unchanged. Neither version contains additional propositions, proofs or formal derivations that alter the theoretical content.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens the empirical case for conditioning: fine-tuning controls and encoder ablations address alternatives insufficiently tested in v1, while LIBERO experiments broaden validation beyond the original suites. Explicit architecture limitations also improve calibration. Sparse settings for some added experiments, duplicated prose and the stale timestep interpretation temper these gains, but do not outweigh the stronger evidence supporting the method.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same ORCA research. Their main texts, equations, tables, figures and complete appendices support reliable comparison despite substantial layout changes and renumbering.

after.justification: v2 retains those original results and adds fine-tuning comparisons, LIBERO-Long experiments, alternative-backbone evaluations and visual-encoder ablations.

before.justification: v1 reports original imitation-learning results on DeepMind Control, MetaWorld and Adroit, with component, layer and timestep ablations and qualitative analyses.

results.title: Exploring Conditions for Diffusion Models in Robotic Control

C1.justification: The title, abstract, and contributions broaden the central claim from improved MAE feature abstraction to generative representation learning encompassing diffusion models. v3 additionally claims improved diffusion generation quality. The original MAE accuracy and low-rank representation claims remain.

C2.justification: v3 qualifies the earlier persistent rank–accuracy narrative by acknowledging weaker ordering later in training and proposing compensatory feature-rank growth. It adds arguments about fine-tuning's limitations as a representation-quality measure and potentially suboptimal diffusion decay placement. Conversely, it removes v2's explicit discussion of incompatibility with contrastive objectives.

D1.justification: v3 documents U-ViT model sizes, VAE latent dimensions, default scheduler/sampler references, and COCO clustering choices, although detailed new settings are largely deferred to citations. Appendix A retains MAE hyperparameters, hardware, and training times but removes the explicit L2-loss disclosure for reconstruction visualizations; this does not establish a change to those experiments.

E1.justification: v3 adds COCO validation images for semantic grouping and unsupervised segmentation, plus CIFAR-100 diffusion experiments. ImageNet-100 coverage expands to unconditional and class-conditional generation and diffusion representation learning. The original ImageNet classification and appendix supervised experiments remain.

E2.justification: Table 1 removes MoCo-v2, SimCLR-v2, and iBOT from the reported comparison and adds ConMIM, ADDP with ViT-L, and Latent MIM. Section 5 also introduces unmodified U-ViT, represented by alpha_min = 1.0 in Table 4, as the diffusion comparator.

E3.justification: New evaluation protocols include end-to-end fine-tuning, COCO clustering/postprocessing evaluated with mIoU, and diffusion generation evaluated with FID. Diffusion probing selects the best feature layer and noise level, while ImageNet-100 diffusion uses pretrained-VAE latents. The existing MAE pretraining and linear-probing settings are otherwise retained.

E4.justification: v3 adds semantic feature-map analysis on COCO, diffusion decay-factor sweeps, generated-image comparisons in Figure 9, and quantitative rank–accuracy correlations in Figure 5c. These substantially extend the analysis of representation structure and decay behavior. Earlier MAE ablations, t-SNE results, reconstruction examples, and supervised rank analyses are retained.

E5.justification: v3 adds Pearson correlation estimates between feature rank and probing accuracy at seven training epochs in Figure 5c; v2 discusses this association qualitatively. Neither version reports repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, or significance tests.

E6.justification: Matched MAE probing and appendix tables retain their values. Newly reported results include COCO segmentation at 10.41 versus 4.10 mIoU, fine-tuning at 82.9% versus MAE's 83.6%, and class-conditional ImageNet-100 diffusion FID of 4.98 versus 6.93 for standard shortcuts. Section 4.1 also corrects the proposed method's prose score from 72.3% to 72.7%, while retaining a baseline typo of 67.3% instead of Table 1's 67.8%.

M1.justification: The decay formula, MAE encoder-only application, encoder–decoder skip connections, and zero initialization remain unchanged. Section 5 introduces a limited diffusion-specific adaptation: decay extends through the U-ViT decoder, reflecting the different location of useful semantic representations.

P1.justification: The title and abstract are revised, experiments receive separate MAE and diffusion sections, and embedding analysis becomes a subsection. Selected ablation and discussion paragraphs are rewritten, and citations switch to author–year style. Most existing introduction, method, conclusion, and appendix prose remains.

P2.justification: The opening presentation is redesigned into a results montage and a horizontal architecture diagram. Table 1 replaces its backbone column with separate fine-tuning and probing columns; new semantic visualizations, a diffusion table, and generated-image comparisons are added. The rank figure gains a correlation panel, while retained appendix displays are reformatted and relocated.

R1.justification: v3 adds references supporting U-ViT, diffusion representation learning, spectral feature visualization, and newer masked-modeling comparators, while removing the MoCo-v2 and SimCLR-v2 references. iBOT remains cited despite leaving Table 1. The established positioning around residual architectures and low-rank bias is largely retained.

T1.justification: Equations 1–6 retain the same residual recurrence, expansion, linear decay schedule, and entropy-based effective-rank definition. No new formal assumptions, theorems, proofs, or substantive derivations are introduced.

improvement.justification: Beyond v2's MAE-focused evidence and supervised appendix analyses, v3 directly tests semantic grouping on COCO and representation learning alongside generation in diffusion models. This substantially strengthens support for the abstraction and applicability arguments. It also quantifies and qualifies the rank interpretation and reports a fine-tuning disadvantage. Incomplete new experimental details, removal of the contrastive-learning caveat, and the remaining text/table inconsistency are drawbacks, but the additional empirical validation provides a clear substantial net gain.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same decayed-identity-shortcut research, despite the broader title and scope in v3. Their main text, equations, tables, figures, and Appendices A–B are readable and support reliable matching.

after.justification: v3 retains these experiments and adds original fine-tuning, COCO segmentation, and diffusion representation-learning and generation results.

before.justification: v2 reports original MAE representation-learning experiments, ImageNet ablations, reconstruction examples, and supervised ResNet analyses in Appendix B.

results.title: Residual Connections Harm Generative Representation Learning

C1.justification: The abstract and conclusion retain the principal registration, label-efficiency and backbone-generality claims. The introduction removes LDVN's 'first general' priority claim and replaces unbiased-gradient assertions with direction preservation and scale control. This is a limited narrowing of one central contribution.

C2.justification: v2 adds explanations involving hard-case reweighting, preserved stochastic exploration, posterior collapse and reward hacking when anatomical similarity constraints are removed. It also develops the interpolation and composition argument behind withholding SPAC NJD, supported by reconstruction tests. These materially expand mechanisms, failure conditions and qualifications beyond v1's brief discussion.

D1.justification: Section 10 supplies previously unavailable loss implementations, backbone-specific head placement, latent dimensions, clipping bounds, reward/loss weights, temperature annealing, training budgets, checkpoint selection and hardware/software details. Section 8 documents classical baseline configurations. Much of this fills v1's references to an absent supplement; it documents settings without demonstrating that the underlying implementation changed.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate brain MRI, liver CT and cross-modality abdominal registration using the same underlying datasets. The supplementary experiments examine retained coverage; they introduce no new task, population or input environment.

E2.justification: The main comparator set is retained, but v2 adds evaluated LapIRN-diff and LapIRN-disp stage3 baselines on OASIS (Table 7), plus SyN and deedsBCV on all three benchmarks (Table 8). These substantially broaden the reported comparisons beyond citations or promised supplementary results in v1.

E3.justification: Section 4.2 revises v1's assertion of uniform weakly supervised baseline training: v2 allows published protocols for CorrMLP, RIIR, SPAC and WarpDDF+RegCut when unification is unsupported. Added experiments introduce 50-epoch sensitivity tests, classical optimization schedules and alternative SPAC reconstruction procedures. Original pair counts and headline metrics remain unchanged; the revised description does not establish reruns.

E4.justification: v2 adds LDVN scaling ablations, empirical checks of weak dependence, hyperparameter sensitivity, posterior-collapse analysis and a failure case removing image similarity (Sections 7.2–7.6). Section 9 tests SPAC field reconstruction, and Section 11 adds anatomical-label breakdowns and visual comparisons. These substantially extend evidence about stability, mechanisms and failure conditions.

E5.justification: v2 newly reports 20 independent runs for warm-up stability, 1,000-sample Monte Carlo variance estimation, and Dice mean/standard deviation over ten latent samples of one input. It also specifies fixed seeds for label subsampling. Existing Wilcoxon reporting remains, but the relocated efficiency table loses v1's five-run averaging disclosure. These are reporting additions, not evidence that retained experiments received more runs.

E6.justification: Tables 1–3 and the relocated efficiency measurements retain their numerical values. Substantial new results include LapIRN-diff/disp OASIS Dice of 79.70/84.52, classical baseline scores, sensitivity and collapse outcomes, and SPAC reconstruction results. v2 also reports warm-up success rates of 33% versus 79% and convergence around 120 versus 75 epochs. These are newly reported comparisons, not version-to-version performance gains.

M1.justification: The Gaussian policy heads, deterministic warm-up, Dice/NJD rewards, LDVN scaling, multi-trajectory GRPO and greedy refinement procedure remain. v2 clarifies initialization and supplies implementation details without establishing a changed algorithm or architecture.

P1.justification: Most main-text prose and section order are retained. v2 condenses dataset descriptions, rewrites baseline-protocol wording, reorganizes LDVN exposition around the supplement and clarifies warm-up discussion. Author information and malformed numerical ranges are corrected. These are localized editorial changes rather than a wholesale narrative rewrite.

P2.justification: v2 replaces the separate title/abstract page with a compact front page and restyles the document. It removes v1's motivational Figure 1, improves labels on the retained qualitative comparison, expands captions and relocates efficiency Table 4 to supplementary Table 11. Seven new tables and four new figures substantially expand the visual presentation.

R1.justification: v2 adds Heinrich's self-similarity work and Mattes's multimodal registration reference, while removing six dataset/challenge source references, including OASIS, LiTS and Learn2Reg. It also drops the 'first general' LDVN positioning and expands comparisons with classical methods and SPAC. The main related-work narrative remains largely intact.

T1.justification: v1 provides a short affine identity and asserts unbiasedness and linear variance growth. v2 Section 7 adds Proposition 1 with an explicit gradient proof and a covariance-based variance derivation under bounded moments and weak dependence. The mathematical guarantee is narrowed to direction-preserving rescaling, substantially developing and correcting the earlier argument.

improvement.justification: v2 addresses important gaps in the supplied v1 by providing LDVN proofs, targeted stability and failure analyses, additional baseline evidence and substantial reproducibility details. Narrowing the unbiasedness claim also improves precision. These gains strengthen support for the central contribution despite unchanged headline scores. Reporting weaknesses remain, particularly the unexplained aggregation of 33%/79% success rates from 20 runs and the lost timing-repeat disclosure, but they do not outweigh the substantial gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same MorphSeek work, with readable text, equations, tables and figures. The supplied v1 ends with references; v2 additionally contains Supplementary Sections 7–11. The available material supports a reliable document-level comparison.

after.justification: v2 retains those experiments and reports additional baseline comparisons, Monte Carlo estimates, sensitivity tests, posterior-collapse measurements and qualitative analyses.

before.justification: v1 reports original registration experiments on OASIS, LiTS and Abdomen MR-CT, including benchmark comparisons, component ablations and efficiency measurements.

results.title: MorphSeek: Fine-grained Latent Representation-Level Policy Optimization for Deformable Image Registration

C1.justification: The largest-dataset and first RT-based HMR claims remain. The introduction's benchmark contribution and Section 4 now claim demonstrated downstream human motion prediction alongside HAR, broadening the claimed contribution without corresponding results in the supplied supplement.

C2.justification: The supplement adds specific limitations: unstable body-shape estimates attributed to weak appearance/geometric cues, reduced accuracy at close and distant ranges, and possible misuse for behavior monitoring. These refine applicability and failure explanations while retaining the main interpretations of radar, fusion, and generalization.

D1.justification: v3 supplies dataset organization, sparse compression and LMDB loading instructions, the full action list, training hyperparameters, hardware, training time, crop dimensions, preprocessing, and HAR implementation details. Its abstract replaces the future-release promise with a public-access statement and link. These substantially address information missing from v1.

E1.justification: Demonstrated coverage remains the same 661K-frame, 20-subject, 50-action dataset, evaluated for HMR and HAR. The new action/distance analyses subdivide existing coverage. v3 claims motion-prediction evaluation, but supplies no corresponding protocol or results establishing an additional evaluated task.

E2.justification: The HMR comparators remain mmMesh, P4Transformer, RT-Pose, RETR, and TokenHMR; HAR retains CNN, AGCN, and BlockGCN. Supplementary Table 6 expands reporting for existing methods, without adding a competing HMR model.

E3.justification: New analyses evaluate errors by individual action and sensing distance, and Section 8 reports a single-GPU, single-process loading-time comparison. The original splits, action-group protocols, and HMR metrics remain. Newly specified training budgets do not establish changes to existing experiments.

E4.justification: v3 adds per-action error distributions, distance sensitivity, HAR confusion matrices, and detailed modality/fusion and cross-subject/action case studies in Figures 10–15. Section 10.3 also reports a TokenHMR fine-tuning comparison. These substantially expand diagnostics beyond v1's scaling analysis and limited mesh visualizations.

E5.justification: Figure 13 newly reports per-action MVE distributions using box-and-whisker plots. This adds error-variability reporting, although the whisker convention is unspecified. Neither version reports repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, or significance tests.

E6.justification: Table 6 adds extensive joint, rotation, translation, and parameter-count results; supplementary figures add action, distance, and HAR findings. Table 3 revises S1 RPC MVE/MJE/MRE/TE from 89.5/76.6/9.2/48.6 to 90.4/77.5/9.3/49.4, although Table 6 retains the earlier values. Section 8 additionally reports loading time decreasing from over 18 to under 1 hour per epoch.

M1.justification: The four-frame input, two-stage BEV localization and local 3D reconstruction, SMPL-X outputs, and feature-concatenation fusion remain. The supplement specifies architecture, losses, and data-loading implementation without establishing a revised HMR algorithm.

P1.justification: The abstract and contribution bullets are extensively rewritten. A structured supplement adds substantial exposition of existing data organization, action design, implementation, applications, and diagnostic interpretation. The main section sequence remains, but explanatory coverage and document organization expand considerably.

P2.justification: v3 adds Figures 7–15 and Tables 5–6, covering data organization, loading, actions, detailed results, and diagnostics. It also revises the overview/system illustrations and redraws Figure 5 with changed axes, legends, and removal of numerical bar labels.

R1.justification: The bibliography expands from 52 to 72 entries, adding robotics, retargeting, imitation, radar motion prediction, and implementation references. The introduction strengthens robotics positioning, but the central comparison with existing radar datasets and the RT-based HMR novelty argument remain.

T1.justification: Sections 10.2–10.3 newly provide explicit mathematical definitions of the combined localization/mesh objective and component losses, plus crop-to-full-image and translation equations. v1 only sketches these components. No new theorem, proof, or theoretical guarantee is introduced.

improvement.justification: v1 refers to implementation details in an absent supplement; v3 supplies substantial training, loss, preprocessing, hardware, and dataset-access documentation. Detailed results and action/distance diagnostics also make the benchmark more assessable and usable. These resolve an important documentation deficiency. The gains remain substantial despite inconsistent values between Tables 3 and 6, conflicting sensing-range descriptions, and the unsupported motion-prediction claim.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe M4Human and RT-Mesh, with matching core experiments. All supplied pages, figures, tables, and equations are readable. v1 ends after the references; v3 includes supplementary Sections 7–11.

after.justification: v3 retains those empirical results and adds detailed benchmark scores, action- and distance-dependent errors, qualitative comparisons, and data-loading measurements.

before.justification: v1 reports original HMR comparisons, dataset-scale experiments, multimodal fusion results, and downstream action-recognition results in Tables 2–4 and Figures 5–6.

results.title: M4Human: A Large-Scale Multimodal mmWave Radar Benchmark for Human Mesh Reconstruction

C1.justification: v1 centers its contributions on high-quality, efficient transparent generation through a shared-latent VAE and curated data. v3 redefines the central contribution as shifting alpha distributions while preserving RGB generation, explicitly claiming stable and spatially controllable transparency. These new mechanism and capability claims appear throughout the abstract, introduction and conclusion.

C2.justification: v3 attributes transparency holes to RGB–alpha entanglement and explains why preserving RGB capability can retain unwanted backgrounds without mean sampling. It adds qualifications about weak control at small mean shifts and red bias at large shifts. v1's broader discussion of remaining unnatural content, background debris and inaccurate masks is no longer retained as a limitations assessment.

D1.justification: v3 specifies the Wan2.1-T2V-14B backbone, its I2V counterpart, and a typical mean-shift strength of 0.05. It omits v1's 272 × 272, 17-frame crop specification, caption-language/manual-refinement details and testing-prompt instructions. Common adapter ranks, batch sizes and the project link remain. These omissions establish documentation changes, not changes to the underlying preprocessing.

E1.justification: The underlying matting datasets and Internet-data domains remain. However, v3 adds mask-conditioned generation with controllable subject position and size, and trains Wan2.1-I2V-14B for image-and-text-conditioned animation (Section 4.4; Figures 9–10). These extend v1's text-to-video task requirements. Changes in training sample counts are settings changes, not new dataset coverage.

E2.justification: v1 evaluates TransPixeler's open and closed versions. v3 retains both and adds LayerFlow (Single) and LayerDiffuse + AnimateDiff to the comparisons in Figure 5 and Tables 1–2. Figure 6 additionally evaluates Wan + MatAnyone, introducing a generation-plus-matting alternative.

E3.justification: v3 introduces white-background evaluation with VBench and GPT-4o metrics, user-ranking evaluation, and PSNR/SSIM/LPIPS reconstruction tests. Reported VAE/DiT training budgets change from 60,000/1,500 to 75,000/1,750 iterations. The generation-training collection changes from 437 to 429 samples: images increase from 20 to 43, Internet-effects videos decrease from 116 to 85, and matting videos remain 301.

E4.justification: v1 provides illustrative failures but no component ablations. v3 adds reconstruction ablations for rendering and the bidirectional loss (Table 3), generation ablations for that loss and mean sampling (Figure 7), mean-shift sensitivity tests (Figure 8), and mask-geometry tests (Figure 9). The earlier astronaut and explosion failure examples are not retained.

E5.justification: Neither PDF reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, error bars or significance tests. v3's new scores and average user rankings are point estimates; they do not introduce uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: v3 adds the first quantitative comparison, user-ranking and reconstruction tables. Examples include text alignment 4.00 and aesthetics 0.649 in Table 1, transparency/overall ranks 1.23/1.11 in Table 2, and full-model RGB/alpha PSNR 41.47/42.22 in Table 3. Qualitative comparisons are replaced and control/animation findings added. These are newly reported results, not matched v1-to-v3 gains; the 128-second versus 32-minute timing comparison remains.

M1.justification: v3 adds a transparency-aware bidirectional diffusion loss using a frozen DiT during VAE training, beyond v1's reconstruction objectives. It also introduces alpha-derived Gaussian ellipse masks that shift noise means during training and inference, enabling spatial transparency control. These change the objectives and generation procedure while retaining the shared-latent VAE and LoRA/DoRA framework.

P1.justification: v3 retitles the paper and extensively rewrites the abstract, introduction, method narrative and conclusion. It creates a separate Related Work section, consolidates dataset discussion, compresses the reconstruction-loss exposition, and reorganizes experiments around comparisons, ablations and applications instead of v1's extended results gallery and limitations section.

P2.justification: The single-column presentation becomes a two-column layout. Framework diagrams are redrawn to include the new components, the detailed feature-merge diagram disappears, and several dataset illustrations are consolidated into Figure 4. Long comparison galleries are replaced by compact comparison panels, three quantitative tables, and new ablation, control and animation figures.

R1.justification: v3 substantially repositions the work around distribution separation, criticizing prior methods for entangling RGB and alpha rather than primarily emphasizing quality and efficiency. It connects its sampler to BBDM, TKG-DM, ShiftDDPMs and Shifted Diffusion, and expands the comparison and evaluation literature with MatAnyone, VBench and OpenS2V.

T1.justification: v3 introduces mathematical definitions for the signed transparency mask and bidirectional loss, conditional Gaussian noise, and covariance-based ellipse construction (Equations 1–3 and 12–19). No theorems or proofs are added. Equation 13 also writes the velocity target as Z_t minus shifted noise, unlike v1's noise minus Z; this is inconsistent with the stated interpolation.

improvement.justification: v1's superiority claims rely mainly on selected visual examples and timing. v3 substantially strengthens their support through broader comparisons and component ablations, especially Table 3 and Figure 7. Material weaknesses remain: study sizes and uncertainty are unspecified, reproducibility details disappear, and Equation 13 is inconsistent. Table 2's transparency ranks also total 14 rather than the 15 expected for complete untied five-method rankings, without explanation. These issues limit confidence, but the controlled analyses provide a substantial net improvement in experimental support.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Wan-based RGB-A video-generation project despite retitling and substantial revisions. All pages, figures, tables and equations support comparison. Neither supplied PDF contains an appendix; v3 references separate supplementary material that is not included.

after.justification: v3 reports original quantitative comparisons, user rankings and reconstruction ablations in Tables 1–3, alongside transparency-control and image-to-video demonstrations.

before.justification: v1 reports original generated-video comparisons, inference timings and failure examples in Sections 3.2–3.4 and Figures 10–20.

results.title: Video Generation with Stable Transparency via Shiftable RGB-A Distribution Learner

C1.justification: The unified image-and-skeleton generation claim remains, but headline contributions shift substantially. v2 drops independent condition masking and implicit skeleton-to-skinning learning as central contributions, emphasizes a scalable mixed-asset data engine, extends superiority claims to arbitrary-pose comparisons, and foregrounds skeleton-aligned asset generation for animation without manual retargeting.

C2.justification: v2 emphasizes dense structural priors, depth ambiguity and skeleton–mesh alignment as explanations for control and animation applicability, replacing much of v1's learned-physical-prior and CFG-generalization discussion. Limitations change from absent hand guidance and restricted data/model scale to difficult hand, hair and skirt details and the single-stage 512-resolution output. Texture mismatch remains acknowledged, with external editing, refinement and texturing now discussed as mitigation.

D1.justification: v2 documents pretrained/frozen components, interpolation and sampling details, encoder dimensions, synchronized augmentations, a 3:2 dynamic/static data ratio, UniRig-based skeleton extraction, static-view rendering and single-H20 timing hardware. The stated learning rate changes from 1e-4 to 1e-5. Conversely, v1's explicit training GPU count, DiT layer/parameter counts, VAE latent length and several rendering/sampling settings are no longer supplied for the revised system.

E1.justification: Training expands from Playbox-derived AnimePose to diverse animated and static humanoids from ReadyPlayerMe, VRoid, Objaverse, Objaverse-XL and HumanRig. Evaluation adds real photographs from DeepFashion and deliberately mismatched skeleton proportions/topologies. The separately reported Playbox quantitative benchmark disappears. CharacterGen's test set and synthetic-image examples already existed in v1 and are expanded or revised, rather than entirely new coverage.

E2.justification: v2 adds Hunyuan3D 2.1 to the canonicalization comparison and introduces arbitrary-pose comparisons against Trellis, CraftsMan and Hunyuan3D, including Qwen-Image-to-3D cascades. v1's qualitative Mixamo comparison is removed. CharacterGen and StdGen remain canonicalization and timing comparators; SKDream is discussed but not experimentally evaluated.

E3.justification: CD, Fidelity Distance and F1 are replaced by normal-map MAE/SIM and Uni3D-I/ULIP-I. Appendix 9.1 selects the best normal-map score over 36 ground-truth azimuths. Canonicalization now specifies 50 VRoid images, replacing the earlier Playbox/VRoid benchmark specification. New arbitrary-pose protocols give baselines ground-truth or Qwen-edited target-pose images, while PoseMaster receives a source image and target skeleton. These settings preclude direct cross-version score comparisons.

E4.justification: The joint-versus-bone study becomes a sparse-joint-versus-dense-point study. v2 adds an image-only versus skeleton-guided comparison, mismatched-skeleton robustness cases, and ground-truth versus Qwen-edited baseline-input analysis. It removes v1's CFG-strategy ablation and 10–90-degree arm-angle demonstration. Thus both the questions investigated and their supporting evidence change substantially.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, error bars or significance tests. Both present point estimates and qualitative examples without statistical uncertainty estimates.

E6.justification: The canonicalization result rows are replaced under different metrics, and v2 adds quantitative arbitrary-pose, skeleton-guidance and Qwen-cascade results in Tables 2–4. Reported timings change from approximately 3/60/180 seconds to 23.48/32.98/61.54 seconds for PoseMaster/CharacterGen/StdGen, respectively (v1 Table 2; v2 Table 5). Numerous qualitative results also change. These are revised results under changed or newly specified conditions, not controlled cross-version performance gains or losses.

M1.justification: v1's fine-tuned Dora VAE and separately trained DiT are replaced by a pretrained Hunyuan3D 2.1 backbone with frozen VAE. Bone-endpoint tokens become densified coordinate-and-direction points, sampled to 256 points and encoded by two point-transformer blocks. Hand bones are incorporated. The documented four-condition guidance becomes skeleton-conditioned two-branch guidance. The data-construction procedure also adds automatically rigged static assets and view pairs.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction, related work, method explanations and conclusion are extensively rewritten around pose stylization. Experimental sections are reorganized, animation receives a main-text Application section, and the appendix becomes separate Additional Details, Additional Experimental Results, and Limitation and Discussion sections.

P2.justification: v2 redraws the teaser and pipeline, adds data-engine, skeleton-densification and animation diagrams, restructures numerical tables, and redesigns qualitative comparisons with additional baseline and ground-truth columns. CFG, Mixamo and arm-angle panels disappear. The timing table moves to the appendix, while the existing 3D-printing diagram is retained and expanded with additional examples.

R1.justification: The broad SDS/LRM and character-generation survey is replaced by sections on 2D pose stylization, 3D pose stylization and native 3D generation. Substantial new discussion covers video animation, Qwen-Image, SKDream, newer native generators and UniRig/Puppeteer. The work is additionally positioned as a controllable alternative to skeleton-prediction-based rigging.

T1.justification: The mathematical definitions of the pose condition and guided vector field change: endpoint-based encoding and four-condition guidance in v1 are replaced by coordinate/direction encoding and skeleton-conditioned guidance in v2 (v1 Equations 4 and 8; v2 Equations 3 and 4). The flow-matching objectives remain equivalent, and neither version introduces theorem or proof results.

improvement.justification: v1's central arbitrary-pose capability relied mainly on visual examples and a Mixamo comparison with unmatched poses. v2 adds quantitative comparisons using both ground-truth and edited baseline inputs, explicit metric computation, real-photo evaluations and mismatched-skeleton tests. This substantially strengthens evidence for the paper's central purpose. Uncertainty reporting remains absent, and training/test separation is less explicit after VRoid enters training. These limitations temper the gains, and changed metrics and backbones prevent a controlled cross-version performance conclusion.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe PoseMaster's image-and-skeleton-conditioned 3D generation framework. Their complete main texts, equations, tables, figures and appendices are readable and support reliable comparison despite substantial revisions.

after.justification: v2 reports original canonicalization and arbitrary-pose comparisons, skeleton-guidance experiments, generation timings, robustness tests and additional qualitative evaluations.

before.justification: v1 reports original geometric evaluations on Playbox and VRoid, generation timings, pose-representation and guidance ablations, and qualitative generation results.

results.title: PoseMaster: A Unified 3D Native Framework for Stylized Pose Generation

C1.justification: The abstract and contribution list extend the state-of-the-art performance claim to NAVSIM, sometimes printed as 'NVISIM'. The central contributions concerning perception-retrieval interaction, the knowledge graph, and value-guided planning remain unchanged.

C2.justification: Appendix D newly attributes robustness to irrelevant knowledge to training the value model to assign such entries score 0. This explanation is not reconciled with retained Listing 1, which assigns non-applicable rules score 1. Existing interpretations of trajectory error and limitations of ethical-behavior metrics are retained.

D1.justification: v2 explains native candidate-generation support for DiffusionDrive/iPad and documents the inputs, heuristic substitution, and random-knowledge construction used in new ablations. The original implementation paragraph moves unchanged to Appendix A.1, including hardware and training settings. The promise of future dataset/model release is unchanged.

E1.justification: v2 adds NAVSIM to the retained nuScenes and Bench2Drive coverage. This extends evaluation to another real-world driving benchmark with non-reactive simulation, rather than merely adding configurations within the original datasets.

E2.justification: New Table 3 adds comparisons involving VADv2, Hydra-MDP, and iPad. The Bench2Drive ablations additionally evaluate SparseDrive-derived heuristic rules against learned valuation. Comparator membership in the original nuScenes and Bench2Drive benchmark tables is unchanged.

E3.justification: v2 introduces NAVSIM's four-second non-reactive evaluation, PDMS and its submetrics, and the stated 103k training/12k testing samples. Table 7 adds controlled knowledge-only, value-only, heuristic, noise-insertion, and random-retrieval settings. Existing benchmark protocols and the preference dataset's 80/20 split are retained.

E4.justification: Tables 5 and 7 newly separate knowledge and value contributions on Bench2Drive, compare heuristic rules, and test corrupted or randomly selected knowledge. Appendix D adds a retrieval-validity analysis on nuScenes validation data. The original nuScenes and value-model ablations remain unchanged as Tables 6 and 8.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, or significance tests. The added retrieval-category percentages are descriptive results, not a new uncertainty-reporting procedure.

E6.justification: New Table 3 reports PDMS 90.9 for KnowVal-DiffusionDrive versus 88.1 for DiffusionDrive, and 92.9 for KnowVal-iPad versus 91.7 for iPad. Table 7 adds component and noise results; Appendix D reports 50.1% key, 41.8% general, and 8.1% irrelevant retrieved items. All four original result tables retain identical values after matching relocations.

M1.justification: Section 3 retains the perception-retrieval framework, value-model architecture, losses, and trajectory scoring and selection procedure. The new DiffusionDrive/iPad applications use native candidate generators; they do not introduce a revised KnowVal algorithm or objective.

P1.justification: Most introduction and method prose is retained. Experimental discussion is locally revised, implementation details move to the supplement, and appendices are reordered around implementation, knowledge graphs, analyses, and examples. This is a limited narrative reorganization rather than extensive rewriting.

P2.justification: Experimental displays are substantially reorganized: NAVSIM Table 3 and Bench2Drive Tables 5/7 are added; the original system ablation is summarized in main-text Table 4 and retained fully in appendix Table 6; the value-model table moves to Table 8. Existing figures remain, with supplementary Figures 7/8 reordered.

R1.justification: v2 adds references to NAVSIM, VADv2, Hydra-MDP, and iPad. The broader positioning against end-to-end, VLA, and retrieval-augmented approaches remains stable; publication metadata updates for retained references do not add new works.

T1.justification: The diversity penalty, value-score definitions, and normalized weighted aggregation in Equation 1 are mathematically unchanged. Neither version supplies theoretical propositions or proofs that are added or revised in v2.

improvement.justification: v1 lacked direct tests separating knowledge from learned valuation and empirical checks of retrieval relevance and corruption. v2's Tables 5/7 and Appendix D substantially address these central evidential gaps, while NAVSIM evaluation strengthens support for compatibility across planners. Original evidence is preserved. The gains are qualified by absent uncertainty reporting and the unresolved irrelevant-rule scoring inconsistency, which limits the new robustness explanation.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same KnowVal research and contain readable main text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices. Relocated and renumbered material can be matched reliably.

after.justification: v2 retains those original results and adds NAVSIM evaluations, Bench2Drive ablations, retrieval-noise experiments, and retrieval-relevance statistics.

before.justification: v1 reports original nuScenes and Bench2Drive evaluations, component and value-model ablations, and qualitative trajectory assessments.

results.title: KnowVal: A Knowledge-Augmented and Value-Guided Autonomous Driving System

C1.justification: The introduction and conclusion add SVDS as a contribution addressing incomplete removal and color inconsistency. The central claims about attention-guided object-effect removal, background preservation, and OBER remain. The quantitative superiority claim is qualified from all test sets and metrics to nearly all.

C2.justification: v2 adds explanations of the denoising-strength tradeoff, interprets the blending control as evidence beyond background preservation, and discusses applicability to effect-free objects. Reflection generalization is narrowed to transfer from limited indoor reflection training to outdoor reflections. The limitations discussion replaces the explicit large/long-shadow warning with explanations and examples of under-removing target effects or over-removing neighboring effects.

D1.justification: v2 adds dataset and interactive-demo links, SVDS parameter details, and model-size and runtime information with resolution and hardware context. Most training and augmentation details are retained. Conversely, it omits v1's explicit baseline prompt, 'an empty scene,' and the precise SDXL-Inpainting checkpoint URL.

E1.justification: Section 8.2 adds evaluations on OmniPaint-Bench, OmniEraser-Bench, and an effect-free subset of MULAN; MULAN previously appeared only in discussion and dataset comparisons. Figure 13 additionally demonstrates simultaneous removal of multiple targets. Object insertion, movement, and coarse-stroke scenarios were already present in v1.

E2.justification: Table 1 adds OmniEraser, GeoRemover, and OmniPaint while retaining the earlier numerical comparators. The user study adds OmniEraser and OmniPaint, and several qualitative panels replace older comparators with these methods. Table 7 introduces baseline variants equipped with ground-truth-mask background blending.

E3.justification: The reported guidance scale changes from 7.5 to 1.0, OBER-Test from 160 to 163 samples, and OBER-Wild from 300 to 302. ReMOVE becomes ReMOVE†, comparing the removal region against the input rather than output background. New protocols include 500 effect-free MULAN pairs, resolution normalization, and ground-truth blending controls. User-study presentations increase from 40 to 80 per participant, retaining 30 participants. The reflection-bootstrap training description also changes from no reflection data to limited indoor reflections; these disclosures do not establish which retained experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: Table 2 and Figure 11 add comparisons of uniform denoising strengths against SVDS. Section 8.3 tests whether background blending explains the performance advantage, while Figures 13 and 17 add simultaneous-removal cases and explicit failure examples. The earlier mask-loss, simulated-data, fusion, and coarse-stroke analyses remain.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, error bars, or significance tests for the performance results. Expanded user-study sampling changes the evaluation protocol without adding uncertainty estimation.

E6.justification: Table 1 replaces ObjectClear's RORD-Val PSNR of 26.40 with 26.24 and OBER-Test PSNR of 32.98 with 33.04 under revised settings; these are not controlled version-to-version gains or losses. ReMOVE scores are replaced by ReMOVE† scores, with OmniPaint now ahead of ObjectClear on OBER-Wild, 0.8656 versus 0.8470. Tables 5–7 add benchmark and blending-control results. New user-study preferences for ObjectClear are 78.90% against OmniEraser and 70.33% against OmniPaint, while earlier preferences are retained. Runtime results are also newly reported.

M1.justification: v2 adds Spatially-Varying Denoising Strength (SVDS), using strength 1.0 inside the object mask and 0.99 outside, with background reinjection during inference. This is a localized inference extension to the retained architecture, embedding construction, mask loss, and attention-guided fusion.
