Renaming Object-Effect Attention to Adaptive Target-Aware Attention does not itself change the method.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion are extensively rewritten, with the narrative shifting from dataset-first to model-first. The title, attention terminology, and author header change. The appendix is reorganized into Sections 6–8, and the existing insertion/movement presentation moves out of the main text.

P2.justification: The main paper switches from single-column to two-column layout, moves Figure 1 to the opening page, and substantially revises qualitative comparison panels. Tables gain comparator rows and denoising columns, and new benchmark tables and analysis figures are added. The user-study table becomes a bar chart. Several original figures are retained and relocated, including insertion/movement.

R1.justification: v2 adds references concerning FLUX, SAM 2, video removal, and GeoRemover, and expands the dataset comparison to Video4Removal. The central positioning around explicit object-effect modeling remains. It also removes PhotoMaker, FastComposer, and PortraitBooth citations that v1 explicitly credited for the retained embedding and attention-loss designs.

T1.justification: Equations 1 and 2 retain the same alpha-map construction and attention-mask loss. Neither version supplies theoretical propositions or proofs, and v2's empirical denoising and metric modifications introduce no formal derivation or mathematical guarantee.

improvement.justification: The additional external benchmarks and newer comparators substantially strengthen generalization evidence, while Table 7 addresses whether the advantage mainly comes from background blending. SVDS ablations and illustrated failures further clarify effectiveness and boundaries. These gains outweigh reporting regressions: Table 5 incorrectly claims and highlights an across-metric win despite OmniPaint's better OmniEraser-Bench DINO score, and some methodological attribution and reproducibility details are removed.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe ObjectClear and OBER, with matching core methods, equations, and experiments despite the changed title. Their text, figures, tables, and complete appendices are readable and support reliable comparison.

after.justification: v2 retains original empirical results and adds benchmark evaluations, controlled comparisons, denoising ablations, and user-study comparisons in Sections 4 and 8.

before.justification: v1 reports original benchmark results, component ablations, qualitative experiments, and a user study in Section 4 and Appendix C.

results.title: Precise Object and Effect Removal with Adaptive Target-Aware Attention

C1.justification: The central claim of adapting pretrained video models to music while preserving textual control remains. v2 additionally claims generalization to nonhuman subjects and agreement between automatic evaluation and human judgments. Its increased emphasis on layer selection and single-GPU training largely foregrounds capabilities already described in v1.

C2.justification: v2 develops the rationale for measuring positive guidance influence rather than degradation from layer removal, including arguments about distribution shift and prior preservation. It interprets human preferences as supporting automatic metric reliability. The appendix's limitations concerning faces, fingers, and silhouette ambiguity remain unchanged.

D1.justification: v2 newly specifies the shallow-MLP audio projector with temporal downsampling, LoRA initialization, and four YouTube playlists containing over 3,700 source videos. These are additional disclosures rather than established implementation changes. Conversely, v1's explicit project/code availability statement and link are removed.

E1.justification: v2 adds qualitative generation tests on marmots, rabbits, and dogs (Figure 3), extending v1's human-subject coverage. AIST, YouTube training data, and SUNO music tests remain. The separately identified TikTok-track tests in v1 Appendix I are no longer documented as such.

E2.justification: v2 adds first-, middle-, last-, and all-layer adaptation comparisons in Tables 1 and 5, plus a qualitative EDGE comparison in Figure 2. The earlier no-layer-selection scores match the evenly distributed strategy; MM-Diffusion, Mochi, and the original component comparisons remain.

E3.justification: v2 adds Qwen3-Omni evaluation alongside VideoLLaMA 2 and an anonymized A/B study with 33 participants and four assessment questions (Appendix C). Long-video testing extends from twice the training duration to up to nine seconds. The original training budget, data split, and 100-video evaluation configuration remain.

E4.justification: v2 substantially expands tests of layer placement and adds a cross-attention zero-initialization ablation. It also evaluates omission of in-the-wild data on dance/video quality, beyond the earlier prompt-alignment analysis. The original numerical and qualitative component ablations are retained in the appendix.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run statistical estimates, confidence intervals, error bars, or significance tests. Qualitative seed variation remains, and the new human study reports point percentages without uncertainty estimates.

E6.justification: All numerical entries in v1 Tables 1–4 are preserved in v2 Tables 2–4 and 6. v2 adds substantial results in Tables 1 and 5 and human preferences in Figure 9, including 91.5% for video quality and 82.1% for music-dance alignment against MM-Diffusion. Qwen3-Omni scores are additional evaluations, not same-setting improvements over v1.

M1.justification: Both versions use zero-initialized audio cross-attention, rank-64 LoRA, Beta-Uniform scheduling, mixed training data, and caption diversification. Both select 16 of 48 layers using STG-based imaging quality. v2 expands and reorganizes the description without establishing a changed procedure.

P1.justification: The abstract and introduction are extensively rewritten, related work is condensed, and the method narrative is reorganized around layer adaptability. ZICA and LoRA explanations are combined, and comparison discussions and appendix sections are substantially rearranged.

P2.justification: v2 replaces the overall architecture diagram with a ZICA/layer-selection illustration and adds skeleton, animal, and human-evaluation figures plus new comparison tables. Existing figures are resampled or rearranged, the MM-Diffusion comparison and original ablation table move to the appendix, and supplementary layouts change substantially.

R1.justification: v2 adds citations to perturbed-attention guidance, Smoothed Energy Guidance, Qwen3-Omni, and ControlNet while dropping several background references. It sharpens the contrast with skeleton-based generation by discussing representational limitations and avoided post-processing, while retaining the original broad research positioning.

T1.justification: v2 Section 4.1 adds an explicit implicit-energy-gradient formulation of layer-skip guidance (Equation 4), absent from v1's prose description. It removes v1's specific homography-based rank argument. The core diffusion, CFG, attention, and Beta-distribution mathematics remain equivalent, with no new theorems or proofs.

improvement.justification: The expanded layer-selection controls, evaluation with a second model, and human study substantially strengthen evidence for the central adaptation strategy and quality claims, addressing v1's narrower validation. These gains outweigh the removed code link and localized reporting problems. However, human–automatic correlation is not quantified, and Figure 9's choreography percentages inconsistently total 102%, limiting confidence in that particular result.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe MusicInfuser and contain readable main text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices. The complete material supports reliable comparison despite substantial reorganization.

after.justification: v2 retains these original results and adds layer-selection comparisons, another automatic evaluator, and a human preference study.

before.justification: v1 reports original generated dance videos, quantitative comparisons, component ablations, and generalization experiments.

results.title: MusicInfuser: Making Video Diffusion Listen and Dance

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the same central claims: introducing high-resolution image editing, transferring source details through test-time feature optimization, synchronizing non-overlapping patches, and achieving strong editing performance. The added experiments support these existing contributions rather than redefine them.

C2.justification: v2 adds explanations for using empty prompts and selecting the final upsampling sub-blocks. Appendix G acknowledges substantial runtime overhead and frames full precision and NTI as quality–efficiency trade-offs. The existing limitations concerning pretrained-model weaknesses and propagated reference-image artifacts remain.

D1.justification: Appendix C substantially expands the previously sparse FLUX specification with sampling equations, synchronization adaptation, and attention-output caching. v2 also discloses 100 synthetic source images, clarifies 400 evaluation pairs per resolution, identifies the real-image source, and reports A6000 hardware, precision policies, runtime, and memory requirements. These are documentation additions, not evidence of changed underlying settings.

E1.justification: v1 evaluates synthetic images at 1K and 2K editing resolutions. v2 adds evaluation on 285 real-image/instruction pairs from Pexels in Appendix F and an 8K editing example in Figure 6, substantially extending the represented image domain and demonstrated resolution coverage.

E2.justification: The evaluated external comparators remain DiT-SR, DiT4SR, PiSA-SR, and TSD-SR. Table 4 extends this same set to real images. The new layer-placement and constant-mapping alternatives are internal ablations, not additional external baselines.

E3.justification: Section 5.3 adds LPIPS to the four existing metrics. New experiments introduce CLIP-Sim for the transfer-design ablation and runtime/memory measurements with different precision and NTI conditions. Appendix D changes its stated default from τ=35 to τ=15, matching the unchanged main-text default; the PDFs do not establish that existing experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: Appendix D adds a substantive comparison of transfer-layer placements and constant versus convolutional mappings in Table 3. The τ sensitivity results and preferred setting are revised, and Appendix G adds computational-cost analysis separating execution with and without NTI. The synchronization ablation is retained.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, error bars, or significance tests for the experiments. The additional results retain point-estimate reporting.

E6.justification: v2 adds real-image, transfer-design, computational-cost, and 8K results. Table 1 adds LPIPS and revises existing values, including ScaleEdit's 1K M-PSNR from 22.114 to 22.132. The new 2K LPIPS results favor PiSA-SR over ScaleEdit, 0.472 versus 0.496. Table 2 replaces the τ results, favoring 15 rather than 35 on the original metrics, although τ=25 has slightly better LPIPS than τ=15.

M1.justification: The patch-wise feature transfer and synchronization framework is retained. Section 4.4 and Algorithm 1 change the activation condition from t < τ to t ≤ τ, including one additional timestep in the stated procedure. FLUX was already evaluated in v1; its expanded implementation description does not establish a newly introduced backbone.

P1.justification: v2 makes copyedits and replaces overly broad uses of 'diffusion' with 'generative' terminology where appropriate. It expands implementation subsections, adds acknowledgements and a computational-cost section, and retitles the appendix as supplementary material. The main narrative and section sequence remain intact.

P2.justification: v2 adds Figures 6–7 for 8K and real-image editing and Tables 3–4 for design and real-image comparisons. Tables 1–2 gain LPIPS columns and metric-direction arrows, and Figure 3's latent labels are corrected. Existing appendix galleries correspond to Figures 8–10; the overall visual organization is retained.

R1.justification: v2 adds citations for ICM-SR, optimized-inference image editing, ResNet, flow matching and rectified flow, CLIP, and LPIPS. These provide additional context and technical attribution; the paper's positioning against low-resolution editors and super-resolution pipelines remains substantially unchanged.

T1.justification: Appendix B corrects the synchronization formulas by explicitly using resampled latents, restoring the temporal factor in the blending masks, and correcting the original-patch term in Equation 22. Appendix C adds FLUX's ODE updates, clean-sample estimate, and modified-vector-field formulation in Equations 23–27. These are localized mathematical additions and corrections, without new theorems or proofs.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially addresses v1's reliance on synthetic evaluation through the 285-pair real-image study in Table 4. The transfer-design ablation, corrected synchronization mathematics, explicit FLUX implementation, and computational-cost disclosure strengthen validation and reproducibility. These gains are qualified by the unexplained reversal of the τ results and superiority statements that overreach the new LPIPS findings.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe ScaleEdit, with the same title, authors, and core framework. Their main text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices support reliable comparison, including matching relocated and renumbered material.

after.justification: v2 retains original editing experiments and adds real-image evaluation, transfer-module ablations, computational measurements, and an 8K editing example.

before.justification: v1 reports original quantitative editing comparisons in Table 1, a timestep ablation in Table 2, and qualitative editing and synchronization experiments.

results.title: Low-Resolution Editing is All You Need for High-Resolution Editing

C1.justification: The central claims of accurate, photon-efficient hyperspectral imaging using simple optics and subsecond reconstruction remain. V2 additionally claims that prototype performance matches simulation and explicitly highlights a preliminary comparative advantage under photon-starved conditions. These extend the performance claims without redefining the main contribution.

C2.justification: V2 substantially expands mechanism and limitation discussion. Long-wavelength errors are attributed to flattening chromatic focal shift rather than v1's lower illumination explanation. It adds low-rank spectral oversmoothing, dark-region light leakage and dynamic-range failures, possible remedies, and the need for more realistic low-light noise models. It also develops interpretations of comparator-specific artifacts.

D1.justification: V2 substantially revises acquisition documentation, specifying a tungsten–halogen source, 100 µm pinhole, LCTF sampling, spectral ground-truth capture, flat-target absorption correction, and an 800×800 crop from 1920×1200 images. Conversely, v1's exact lens model identifiers and approximately 25-lux scene illumination are absent from the supplied v2 text. Both retain a general code/data availability statement.

E1.justification: Harvard, KAIST, CAVE and the same real-scene types are represented in both versions. However, v1's dataset declaration cites Brainard data, whereas v2 replaces that citation with Harvard, already evaluated in v1's Table 1. No identifiable Brainard-specific results establish whether this represents removed coverage or a citation correction.

E2.justification: Table 1 expands from six to eight comparators by adding Spectral DefocusCam and 2in1 Cameras, both also evaluated in Figure 3. The existing comparators remain. These additions substantially broaden comparison with closely related defocus imaging and diffractive optical systems.

E3.justification: Simulated photon flux changes from 4.6×10^17 to 7.5×10^17 photons/m²/s, and v2 adds a 2.9-second exposure condition. Prototype calibration changes from 12 bands spanning 400–694 nm at 12 lens positions to 29 bands spanning 440–720 nm at five positions. V2 also evaluates real reconstructions against LCTF-measured spectral ground truth, extending v1's chart-reference and RGB evaluation.

E4.justification: V2 adds a targeted low-exposure robustness comparison and ground-truth failure insets in Figure 3. Depth and measurement-count sensitivity analyses remain in Figure 5, with revised curves; v1's explicit three-versus-six-measurement image comparison is not reproduced. The newly mentioned denoiser-versus-l1 ablation is only referenced to the unavailable supplement.

E5.justification: Neither supplied PDF reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, error bars or significance tests. Additional averages and result entries in v2 do not introduce uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: Table 1 replaces SfD's PSNR/SSIM/SAM of 24.10/0.61/36.51 with 30.81/0.92/7.35, alongside extensive comparator-score revisions and new rows. These are not same-setting gains because photon flux changes. V2 adds per-channel real-scene scores and all 24 ColorChecker spectra, reporting average patch PSNR 29.54 dB and SAM 7.42°. Figure 3 and sensitivity curves also change.

M1.justification: The two-lens architecture, forward model, spectral eigenspace projection, deep denoiser and fast plug-and-play ADMM reconstruction remain unchanged. Algorithm 1 has identical updates. Revised calibration bands and measurement counts configure the existing method rather than introduce a new algorithm.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, related work, experimental discussion and conclusion undergo extensive rewriting. Experiments are reorganized into simulation settings, simulation results, data collection and real-data results, replacing the earlier system-specification and quantitative/qualitative subsection structure. Detailed colorimetry exposition is removed.

P2.justification: Figure 1 is relocated and its comparison chart changes axes and visual encoding. Figure 3 gains comparator columns, failure insets and a low-exposure panel. Figure 4 combines expanded real-scene and ColorChecker displays, replacing presentations previously spread across Figures 4 and 6. Figure 5 swaps panels and changes distance-axis coordinates; Table 1 expands structurally.

R1.justification: Related work expands substantially across CASSI reconstruction, diffractive and metasurface imaging, and focal-stack predecessors. V2 explicitly distinguishes SfD from Spectral DefocusCam and 2in1 Cameras and discusses earlier spectral recovery by He et al. and Zhan et al. This clarifies its positioning around robust reconstruction and simple optics.

T1.justification: The supplied forward model, optimization objectives, constraints and ADMM equations are unchanged, as are the principal optical assumptions. V1's explicit XYZ and color-difference calculations disappear, but these document standard evaluation computations rather than new theory. Neither PDF includes the referenced supplementary derivations.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially strengthens real-world validation: v1 mainly shows RGB scene reconstructions and three ColorChecker spectra, while v2 supplies measured spectral ground truth, per-channel comparisons across four scenes, and all 24 patch spectra. Relevant new comparators and explicit failure analysis further improve scrutiny of the central claims. Some reproducibility details are lost, and changed settings prevent interpreting higher scores as direct gains, but the stronger spectral validation provides a substantial overall improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Spectrum from Defocus work, with readable text, equations, tables and figures throughout. Neither supplied PDF contains an appendix or the separately referenced supplement; supplement-only material cannot be compared.

after.justification: V2 reports original simulations, a low-exposure comparison, prototype reconstructions against measured spectral ground truth, and sensitivity experiments in Table 1 and Figures 3–5.

before.justification: V1 reports original simulated reconstruction results in Table 1 and Figure 3, prototype measurements, ColorChecker evaluation, and robustness experiments in Figures 4–6.

results.title: Spectrum from Defocus: Fast Spectral Imaging with Chromatic Focal Stack

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction's contribution list and conclusion retain the same central claims about feature over-reliance, sharp loss landscapes and improved transfer through layer regularization and spectral rescaling. Additional evidence does not redefine these headline contributions.

C2.justification: v3 adds an optimization-shortcut explanation for high-frequency reliance, discusses modality-dependent strengths against GCG, and interprets noise robustness. Beyond v1's acknowledgement of low absolute commercial ASR, Appendix J explicitly states that FORCE remains impractical against early-fusion and commercial models and proposes a token-space/pixel-space explanation.

D1.justification: v3 adds an implementation-release link, baseline construction details, the alternate-source configuration and hardware-specific time/memory measurements. v1 already supplied detailed pseudocode and core settings. Its separate reproducibility statement, including the 128 GB hardware specification, is removed, although Table 4 retains the GPU model.

E1.justification: MaliciousInstruct, AdvBench and HADES remain the evaluated datasets. Appendix H adds a defended-input scenario using uniform and Gaussian noise preprocessing. Alternate source models and frequency restrictions change experimental configurations rather than dataset or task coverage.

E2.justification: v1 empirically compares FORCE with PGD. v3 additionally evaluates textual GCG in Table 7 and ensemble optimization, MI-PGD, DI-PGD and an adapted MLAI selection baseline in Table 8, substantially broadening the comparison methods.

E3.justification: Section 4.1 changes FORCE's reported noise neighbourhood from 8/255 to 4/255 and regularization strength from 1 to 0.75. New designs include InstructBLIP as source with lambda=0.01, frequency-restricted optimization, noise-defence settings and cost measurement. The original benchmark subsets, judges and one-query/100-query settings remain.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained initialization, zero-shot and component analyses, v3 adds early-layer and spectral checks on InstructBLIP, low-frequency versus high-frequency optimization controls, alternate-source transfer analysis, noise robustness and generation-cost analysis. These substantially expand tests of mechanism, generality and practicality.

E5.justification: Table 4 newly specifies averaging cost measurements over 30 optimization iterations. This adds limited statistical aggregation information, not evidence of repeated independent attack runs. Neither version reports ASR confidence intervals, seed variability or significance tests.

E6.justification: Tables 1–3 revise numerous FORCE results: for example, LLaVA's MaliciousInstruct ASR changes from 64.00 to 69.00, while Idefics3's AdvBench ASR changes from 38.46 to 35.96. These accompany revised method/settings, so they are not same-setting gains or losses. Tables 4–9 add substantial results; the original PGD and commercial-model scores remain unchanged.

M1.justification: Equation (7) and Algorithm 3 introduce a multiplicative spectral scaling factor beta, set to 0.95, replacing v1's unscaled weights. This changes the perturbation update while retaining the PGD backbone and layer-aware regularization.

P1.justification: Most existing prose and the main section sequence are retained, with localized rewrites and new cross-references. The appendix structure expands, algorithms and case studies move, acknowledgments are added, and the separate LLM-use, ethics and reproducibility statements are removed.

P2.justification: v3 adopts a two-column layout, rearranges panels in Figures 2, 4 and 7, and adds Tables 4–9 and two mechanism-analysis figures. The three existing case studies are reordered and compressed onto one page rather than constituting new examples.

R1.justification: The related-work taxonomy and central motivation remain. v3 adds references and positioning around MLAI, momentum/input-diversity attacks and textual transfer, plus broader future-work literature. Appendix G also explicitly characterizes the work as among the first studying this transferability setting.

T1.justification: Equation (7)'s spectral-weight definition changes from min(1, loss ratio) to beta times that expression, also reflected in Algorithm 3. Other mathematical formulations remain equivalent, and neither version adds theoretical guarantees or proofs.

improvement.justification: v1's comparative evidence relied on PGD and one attack-source model. v3 substantially strengthens validation through additional comparators, another source model, controlled frequency experiments, defence tests and cost measurements, while explicitly acknowledging practical limitations. These address important evidential gaps. Reporting weaknesses remain: ASR uncertainty is absent, and Table 2 incorrectly calls the Qwen ASR rise from 7% to 15% a 214% improvement rather than approximately 114%.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same FORCE research work. Their text, equations, tables, figures and complete appendices are readable and support reliable comparison, including matching relocated algorithms and case studies.

after.justification: v3 retains original empirical results and adds baseline comparisons, alternate-source experiments, frequency controls, defence tests and computational-cost measurements.

before.justification: v1 reports original transfer experiments on three benchmarks, component ablations, feature analyses and model-response case studies.

results.title: FORCE: Transferable Visual Jailbreaking Attacks via Feature Over-Reliance CorrEction

C1.justification: Both versions claim a universal compressor combining UCM and IAFT, robust compression across diverse densities and distributions, and state-of-the-art results on 15 datasets. The revised coarse/fine-context wording clarifies the contribution without materially changing its scope.

C2.justification: v2 expands the mechanism explanation around coarse- versus fine-grained context and adds data-dependent grouping interpretations, adaptation and weight-overhead trade-offs, and training-mixture explanations. It also explains the restricted lossy evaluation and adds deployment, standardization and scaling discussions in Sections 9–11.

D1.justification: Table 4 newly specifies architectures, optimizers, learning rates, schedules, training steps and IAFT regularization. Tables 5–6 and Section 8 supply sequences, sample counts, quantization, sampling weights and corruption-generation details. The abstract changes the code/data release statement from planned to reportedly completed.

E1.justification: The same 15 benchmark categories and lossless/lossy tasks remain. Section 8.1 additionally names Frog, Head, Egyptian and ULB as training sources, but v1's nonexhaustive training description and absent referenced appendix leave unclear whether these sources were newly used or merely newly documented.

E2.justification: Table 8 substantially expands the reported dense lossless comparison with ECM-OPCC, EHEM, VoxelDNN, MsVoxelDNN, UniPCGC and LINR-PCGC variants. Table 7 supplies RENO-U and SparsePCGC-U results only referenced in v1. The original Table 1 comparator set remains unchanged.

E3.justification: The added studies introduce controlled evaluations of grouping configurations, tunable modules, weight precision and coders, and training mixtures. Table 9 also adds lossy BD-Rate reporting. These expand the documented evaluation design; the PDFs do not establish revisions to the retained main benchmark settings.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained core ablations, v2 supplies grouping-count and uniformity tests, fine-tuning iteration and module sensitivity, quantization/coder comparisons, and training-mixture analyses in Table 10 and Figures 9–12. Figure 8 adds spatial reconstruction-error case studies.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, experimental seeds, confidence intervals, significance tests or uncertainty bars. The added results continue point-estimate reporting; the Gaussian-noise parameters describe dataset construction, not estimation uncertainty.

E6.justification: Table 1 and Figure 5 are unchanged, and v1's Tables 3–4 values survive in v2's merged Table 3. Tables 7–10 and Figures 8–12 nevertheless add substantial results, including GS weight-coding totals of 11.74 bpp with DeepCABAC versus 11.93 with GZIP at q=16. These are additional reported results, not version-to-version performance gains.

M1.justification: The UCM factorization, head-only IAFT with cached features and L1 regularization, weight transmission, and top-k lossy reconstruction remain. v2 presents the single-stage lossy path and weight-quantization specifications as further implementation details; it does not establish a replacement algorithm.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction and substantial method passages are rewritten, with clearer context terminology and separate IAFT adaptation, optimization and coding descriptions. The structured supplement and resolved appendix references substantially expand and reorganize the explanation.

P2.justification: The original figures are retained, while v1 Tables 3–4 are merged into v2 Table 3. New Figures 6–13 add architecture/context diagrams, error heatmaps, sensitivity plots and dataset visualizations; Tables 4–10 add implementation, dataset and experimental displays.

R1.justification: Sections 7.1 and 9.1 substantially expand architectural and practical positioning against RENO, SparsePCGC, UniPCGC and LINR-PCGC. v2 clarifies the use of SparsePCGC-U as a predecessor-based substitute for unavailable Unicorn-U and adds references to a PCC survey, DPCset and VGD.

T1.justification: v1 states two theoretical principles but points to an unavailable appendix. v2 Section 6 supplies formal statements and proofs for occupancy-bit/voxel autoregressive equivalence and receptive-field scaling. This substantially expands the available mathematical argument while retaining the main factorization and optimization objective.

improvement.justification: v2 supplies important support missing from the supplied v1: proofs, reproducibility specifications, broader comparisons and targeted diagnostic evidence. This substantially improves the assessability of the method and its claims without changing headline scores. Supplementary inconsistencies—including GS's OOD classification and the 2.84-second 'upper bound' despite longer tuning experiments—reduce clarity but do not outweigh those gains.

A1.justification: The PDFs clearly describe the same AnyPcc work, with readable, matching main experiments. However, v1 repeatedly references an appendix absent from its supplied PDF; v2 includes supplementary Sections 6–11. This limits distinguishing some newly disclosed details from actual experimental changes.

after.justification: v2 retains those original experiments and supplies additional comparator results, sensitivity studies, timing analyses and reconstruction visualizations.

before.justification: v1 reports original compression experiments across 15 datasets, rate-distortion curves, and component and fine-tuning ablations in Tables 1–4 and Figure 5.

results.title: AnyPcc: Compressing Any Point Cloud with a Single Universal Model

C1.justification: v2 foregrounds large VLMs surpassing specialized methods on most metrics and claims to resolve annotation limitations. v3 qualifies performance as competitive or sometimes superior and describes mitigating annotation problems. Its central findings now emphasize complementary strengths, including HOI-model advantages in multi-action recognition and person attribution.

C2.justification: v3 explicitly limits MCQA to a diagnostic benchmark rather than a replacement for open-set generation. It adds explanations involving global attention, spatial topology, training-data scale and model capacity, while acknowledging unresolved causal contributions. New interpretations address domain shifts, concurrent-action omissions and predictions involving the wrong object.

D1.justification: v3 adds a repository link, screening prompt templates, four-annotator majority-vote procedures, LoRA target layers, five training epochs and batch size 32. It also documents object-pair prompts and licensing/access instructions for the additional datasets. These substantially improve disclosure; the newly specified fine-tuning details do not themselves establish a changed training method.

E1.justification: v3 adds V-COCO-based multi-person evaluation with 647 questions and SWiG-HOI-based human–human evaluation with 1,852 questions. It also adds explicit target human–object-pair tasks, whereas v2's localized evaluations target only the person. These substantially broaden evaluated populations and task requirements.

E2.justification: v3 adds Qwen3-VL-30B-Instruct to retained comparisons and evaluates ADA-CM and CMMP with ground-truth boxes in Setting 2, previously restricted to VLMs. The V-COCO-trained fine-tuning comparator disappears from the main-benchmark comparison but remains in the full-test comparison in Table 24.

E3.justification: New protocols include detecting or providing both human and object boxes, evaluating 9,546 full-test questions, varying Top-K and confidence thresholds, and excluding Qwen screening on a 12% subset. The reported Qwen2/2.5 resizing multiple also changes from 28 to 14. The PDFs do not establish whether retained experiments were rerun; swapping Settings 1 and 3 alone is renumbering.

E4.justification: v3 adds screening-agreement and circular-bias checks, option-position analysis, prediction-selection sensitivity, annotation audits, comparative failure taxonomies, cross-dataset robustness and full-test difficulty comparisons. These investigate substantially more questions than v2's detector and fine-tuning analyses. The earlier 68-class temporal-ambiguity inventory and V-COCO-trained head-bias panel are omitted.

E5.justification: Unlike v2's point estimates, v3 Table 7 reports 95% bootstrap confidence intervals from 1,000 question-level resamples for four methods and two metrics in Setting 1. Appendix A.3 also newly reports inter-annotator agreement. These are limited additions to statistical reporting, without evidence of increased model-run counts.

E6.justification: Extensive new results accompany revisions to retained entries. Detection Macro-F1 changes from 57.25 to 50.71 for Qwen2.5-VL-32B and from 50.98 to 38.04 for InternVL3-38B, while their other columns remain unchanged (v2 Table 4; v3 Table 1). Fine-tuning scores and the main benchmark's multi-person percentage also change, the latter from 38.9% to 31.2%. These are reported revisions, not established performance losses.

M1.justification: The reported negative-screening rule changes: v2 Section 2.2 describes Qwen refinement with GPT-4o cross-checking rejected candidates; v3 Section 3.1 requires both models to judge a candidate incorrect before retaining it. The overall multiple-answer formulation and manual-refinement pipeline remain.

P1.justification: The title introduces CrossHOI-Bench, and the abstract, introduction and conclusions are substantially rewritten. Related work moves before benchmark construction, Settings 1 and 3 exchange numbers, and metric definitions and fine-tuning discussion move into reorganized appendices. These are extensive narrative and structural changes beyond added experiments.

P2.justification: The document changes from single-column to two-column layout. Figure 1 is redesigned with a multiple-choice illustration, and new construction diagrams, distribution plots, comparison charts and diagnostic tables substantially expand the visual presentation. Existing displays are also revised or relocated, including removal of the V-COCO panel from the fine-tuning figure.

R1.justification: The cited literature expands substantially to additional HOI methods, fine-grained VLM recognition, hallucination, scaling, instruction tuning and downstream applications. Appendix A.2 newly distinguishes the benchmark from DAM and COCONut-PanCap and positions MCQA relative to open-set evaluation. This exceeds bibliographic updating or relocation of related work.

T1.justification: The four metric definitions remain mathematically equivalent, moving from v2 Section 2.3 to v3 Appendix C. Neither version provides theoretical propositions or proofs that are substantively revised.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially strengthens v2's limited benchmark validation through screening and selection controls, annotation-agreement reporting, confidence intervals, object-pair evaluation and cross-dataset tests. Added implementation details and explicit MCQA limitations make the work more reproducible and its conclusions better qualified. Reporting defects remain, including stale setting references and inconsistent HOLa Macro-F1 values between Tables 1 and 7, but they do not outweigh these substantial gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same HOI benchmarking work, and their text, figures, tables and appendices are readable. The retained 1,274-image main benchmark and experiments can be matched despite extensive reorganization and the interchange of Settings 1 and 3.

after.justification: v3 retains original empirical evaluations and adds cross-dataset experiments, ablations, annotation audits and statistical analyses.

before.justification: v2 reports original VLM and HOI-model evaluations, detector-assisted experiments and supervised fine-tuning results in Tables 2–4 and 6–7.

results.title: CrossHOI-Bench: A Unified Benchmark for HOI Evaluation across Vision-Language Models and HOI-Specific Methods

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction and conclusion retain the same central contributions: a long-term RVOS benchmark, three description types, temporal/spatiotemporal metrics and the motion-enhanced ReferMo baseline. Updating the benchmarked-method count from six to seven expands supporting evaluation without redefining these contributions.

C2.justification: V2 adds interpretations concerning MLLM data requirements, motion's role in global reasoning, gating against irrelevant motion, and robustness when keyframes miss objects. Section 12 explicitly discusses task boundaries and excluded background classes. Conversely, v1's caveat about inferior tIoU is replaced by an across-all-types-and-metrics improvement statement, although v2 Table 3 still gives ReferDINO higher hybrid tIoU: 73.1 versus 72.9.

D1.justification: V2 Section 8 substantially expands implementation documentation with block matching, motion-extraction throughput and CPU hardware, cosine-based object matching, training loss components, positive/negative sequence assignment, inference query selection and clip-wise propagation. It also explicitly states that all compared models use no external segmentation datasets. These are newly documented details; the principal hyperparameters, GPU training resources and project-page access information remain unchanged.

E1.justification: The same Long-RVOS dataset, source domains, description-based segmentation task and MeViS oracle comparison remain. Additional validation results and subgroup analyses examine existing coverage. Tasks mentioned in v2's future-work discussion are not evaluated.

E2.justification: V2 Table 3 adds RGA3 to the six retained RVOS comparators from v1 Table 2. V2 Table 4c additionally compares XMem++ and Cutie with SAM2 as propagation alternatives. These extend the comparison set without replacing its principal methods.

E3.justification: Section 5.1 changes the validation/test allocation from 113/225 videos and 1,379/2,588 descriptions to 112/226 videos and 1,326/2,641 descriptions. Training allocation, metrics, resolution and stated training budget remain unchanged. New analyses introduce component controls and grouping by occlusion, description length and keyword-derived event count; these are additional protocols rather than evidence that the retained experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: V2 substantially expands component and robustness analysis: propagation alternatives, global interaction with motion, gating mechanisms, occlusion rates, description lengths, event complexity and qualitative comparisons appear in Tables 4–6 and 10–12 and Figure 8. Tables 7–8 also quantify challenging video attributes. The oracle analysis remains and the keyframe ablation is revised, but v1 Table 3c's motion-length sweep is removed.

E5.justification: Neither version reports experimental run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, error bars or significance tests. V2's additional descriptive percentages and result tables do not introduce uncertainty estimation.

E6.justification: The main benchmark scores change extensively between v1 Table 2 and v2 Table 3. ReferMo's overall J&F/tIoU/vIoU changes from 51.3/71.2/42.6 to 52.9/73.6/45.2, while VideoLISA's overall J&F changes from 33.1 to 14.0. SAM2 oracle and keyframe results also change. V2 adds validation results in Table 9 and numerous analytical results. Because the reported held-out allocation changes, these are revised results, not established same-setting performance gains or losses.

M1.justification: Both versions use MPEG-4 keyframe/motion decomposition, spatial and channel gating, aligned global object interactions, keyframe supervision and SAM2 propagation. V2 Section 8 supplies additional training and inference specifications; it does not establish a change to the proposed procedure.

P1.justification: The main six-section narrative remains largely intact, with localized rewriting of the introduction, dataset discussion and experimental interpretations. V2 organizes additional material into supplementary Sections 7–12. This extends the document without extensively rewriting or reordering its existing narrative.

P2.justification: V2 replaces the predominantly single-column layout with a two-column format and substantially reorganizes displays. Dataset statistics are split across figures, the description-type pie chart becomes Table 2, and v1 Figures 5–6 are merged into v2 Figure 7. V2 also expands the example montage and adds analytical tables and qualitative Figure 8. These changes exceed renumbering or numerical updates.

R1.justification: V2 adds references for XMem++, Cutie, RGA3 and Conditional Convolutions for Instance Segmentation, supporting the additional comparisons and implementation description. The related-work categories and central novelty positioning remain stable. ReferDINO's preprint-to-conference citation update represents the same work.

T1.justification: V2 Section 8 adds explicit mathematical definitions for motion-vector block matching, the weighted sequence-matching/training cost and inference query selection in Equations 6–8. This is a limited extension of mathematical specification. The metric and fusion mathematics in Equations 1–5 remain equivalent, and no theorem or proof is introduced.

improvement.justification: V2 addresses important gaps in v1's reproducibility and empirical attribution. Section 8 documents previously unspecified training and inference logic, while propagation, interaction and gating controls help distinguish the contributions of ReferMo's components. Attribute statistics and robustness analyses also substantiate the benchmark's challenges and applicability boundaries. These gains outweigh the removed motion-length sweep and localized reporting problems, including the overstated all-metrics claim and Table 5's inconsistent first-row J&F average. The improvement rests on stronger documentation and diagnostic evidence, not on higher revised scores.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe Long-RVOS and ReferMo. Their text, equations, tables and figures support reliable comparison. All pages were inspected: v1 ends with references, while v2 includes three supplementary pages.

after.justification: Section 5 and the supplementary material report original benchmark and validation results, component ablations, robustness analyses and dataset statistics.

before.justification: Section 5 and Tables 2–3 report original benchmark experiments, SAM2 oracle evaluations and ReferMo ablations.

results.title: Long-RVOS: A Comprehensive Benchmark for Long-term Referring Video Object Segmentation

C1.justification: v1 emphasizes controllable video generation, multiview synthesis, and sim-to-real transfer, presenting downstream learning largely as a prospective benefit. v2's abstract, contributions, and conclusion explicitly claim demonstrated improvements in visual planning and policy learning, substantially extending the claimed contribution beyond video synthesis.

C2.justification: v2 explicitly characterizes ORV as non-interactive and dependent on complete action/occupancy priors, limits demonstrated policy augmentation to appearance changes, and places policy evaluation inside the world model outside scope. Section 12 adds substantive discussion of conditioning robustness, online occupancy forecasting, and long-horizon limitations while retaining the earlier joint-representation and multiview-initialization limitations.

D1.justification: v2 newly documents embedding models, 51 semantic clusters, RAFT filtering, multiview weight initialization, x-flux initialization, VLM prompts/filtering, policy checkpoints, full versus LoRA finetuning, and asset licenses. It also advertises data access alongside code/models. Conversely, v1's batch size 64, learning rate 1e-4, AdamW coefficients, and explicit singleview-module freezing statement are omitted.

E1.justification: The original three video datasets remain; naming their curated occupancy data ORV-Data does not itself expand coverage. Substantial new coverage comprises VP2 visual planning using Robosuite and RoboDesk, policy learning evaluated on four SimplerEnv-WidowX tasks, and mismatched coarse/fine conditioning scenarios.

E2.justification: v2 adds occupancy-conditioned IRASim comparisons and evaluates IRASim on DROID, previously absent. New planning comparisons include MCVD, FitVid, MaskViT, iVideoGPT, and the simulator reference. Policy experiments compare RoboVLM and SpatialVLA training variants, while Table 4 quantitatively evaluates ControlNet-style conditioning.

E3.justification: New protocols include planning training on 5K Robosuite and 35K RoboDesk trajectories, equal-size policy-finetuning datasets with approximately 25% synthetic data, and cross-granularity conditioning tests. Original video preprocessing tables and the 30K-plus-20K training schedule are retained. v2 also explicitly excludes AVID's reported FID from comparison because of an evaluation-mode problem.

E4.justification: Beyond retained depth/semantics and pretraining ablations, v2 tests action-modulation placement, temporal chunking, and ControlNet versus input-noise conditioning in Table 4. It adds quantitative multiview ablation results, coarse/fine transfer tests, and Gaussian-scaling sensitivity examples in Table 6, Table 7, and Figure 12.

E5.justification: v1 reports point estimates without repeated-run information. v2 Table 2 introduces means and standard deviations over three runs for visual planning. Video-generation and policy-learning tables still report point estimates; the PDFs do not establish increased repetition of the retained experiments.

E6.justification: Full-condition ORV scores remain unchanged between v1 Table 2 and v2 Table 1, including BridgeV2 PSNR 28.258 and FVD 16.525. v2 adds comparator, planning, policy, and ablation results. Table 3 reports RoboVLM success increasing from 29.8% to 33.9% and SpatialVLA from 36.2% to 38.5% with augmentation. Table 6's stated with/without ordering conflicts with its claimed improvement, leaving that direction ambiguous.

M1.justification: The backbone, chunked action modulation, visual-conditioning injection, and multiview architecture are retained. The stated Gaussian rendering specification changes normalized depth from (0,1] to [1,2). The new policy-data augmentation workflow also introduces VLM captioning and quality filtering; expanded explanations of existing action conditioning do not constitute a new architecture.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, methodology narrative, and discussion are extensively rewritten. Dataset curation moves after model formulation and architecture; multiview and sim-to-real methods become nested subsections. The appendices are reorganized into numbered sections with a contents guide and expanded structured discussions.

P2.justification: v2 adopts a two-column layout, redraws the overview diagrams, adds an action-modulation diagram, consolidates qualitative results, restructures the main comparison table by conditioning type, and adds experiment tables and figures. Retained material is also relocated: v1 Figures J–L reappear as v2 Figures 24–26 with identical image content.

R1.justification: The related-work discussion is substantially refocused and expanded through Section 12. Added works include VAP, Ctrl-World, WristWorld, and policy-data synthesis research. Comparisons now address interactive versus non-interactive generation, conditioning granularity, appearance augmentation, and the distinct roles of world models in synthesis and policy evaluation.

T1.justification: v2 adds a mathematical state/observation and conditioning formulation in Section 3.1 and a perspective-projection derivation motivating Gaussian scaling in Section 10.1.2. v1 states the scaling rule without this derivation. Existing camera-alignment, condition-fusion, and positional-encoding equations are retained.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially addresses v1's untested downstream-usefulness claims through controlled policy-learning and planning experiments. Matched-conditioning comparisons and new mechanism/robustness tests strengthen validation of the design, while explicit offline-input limitations clarify applicability. These gains outweigh the remaining reporting problems, notably Table 6's contradictory ordering and the removal of useful optimizer and training details.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe ORV and retain identifiable methods, datasets, and results. The complete main papers and appendices are readable, including equations, tables, and figures, supporting reliable comparison despite substantial reorganization.

after.justification: v2 retains original video-generation results and adds visual-planning, policy-learning, conditioning, and robustness experiments in Tables 1–7 and the supplementary material.

before.justification: v1 reports original video-generation experiments on BridgeV2, DROID, and RT-1, conditioning and pretraining ablations, and qualitative analyses in Appendix D.

results.title: ORV: 4D Occupancy-centric Robot Video Generation

C1.justification: The abstract qualifies the LiDAR claim: v1 says OneOcc beats popular LiDAR baselines, whereas v2 says it remains competitive with classical LiDAR baselines. The four-component method, two dataset contributions, and headline H3O performance claims otherwise retain their meaning.

C2.justification: V1's brief calibration limitation becomes a broader discussion of coarse-grid limits for manipulation, restricted real-world coverage, the humanoid sim-to-real gap, and single-frame motion limitations. V2 also interprets calibration robustness versus clean accuracy, temporal fusion versus deployment cost, and semantic failures under rare weather/layout combinations.

D1.justification: Sections 9–11 newly document sensor synchronization, annotation and dynamic-object handling, voxel refinement, simulator capture, metadata, baseline adaptations, optimizers, schedules, normalization, and losses. Sections 6 and 8 add profiling and deployment details. These are substantial disclosures, although some grid-bound descriptions conflict. The repository destination and future-release wording remain unchanged.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate the same QuadOcc and H3O datasets and occupancy tasks. V2 extends test conditions through restricted-field-of-view inputs and controlled calibration perturbations. The KITTI tables document configuration adaptations; they do not establish an additional evaluated benchmark.

E2.justification: Comparator membership in the main benchmark tables is unchanged. Table 12 adds pose-aligned temporal averaging and BEVFormer-style temporal attention as comparative alternatives to single-frame OneOcc. Section 11 primarily documents existing baseline adaptations rather than establishing changes to those retained comparators.

E3.justification: V2 adds substantial experimental protocols: evaluation-only panorama cropping, expert and grid configurations, resolution scaling, deterministic calibration perturbations and noise-augmented retraining, three-frame fusion, and nested spatial evaluation ranges. It also introduces INT8/FP16 Jetson profiling. Newly disclosed settings for retained benchmarks do not establish that those experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: Beyond v1's cumulative component ablation and lighting comparison, v2 adds expert-count/routing, field-of-view, Cartesian/cylindrical-grid, projection-path, resolution, calibration-noise, and temporal-fusion analyses. GDC visualizations, distance-wise comparisons, and a rainy-dusk semantic failure case further examine mechanisms and failure conditions.

E5.justification: V2 newly states that baseline seeds are fixed and calibration perturbations are deterministic by seed and frame ID. Jetson timings are explicitly averaged over 100 runs after five warm-ups. Neither version reports accuracy confidence intervals, error bars, or multi-seed variability; an increase in repeated training runs is not established.

E6.justification: Tables 2–5 retain their scores, but v2 adds extensive results. Table 12 reports temporal-attention mIoU of 21.18/34.25 on QuadOcc/H3O-Heter, versus single-frame 20.56/32.23; Table 15 reports Jetson throughput of 13.64 FPS versus MonoScene's 10.20. Section 4.5 also changes allocated/reserved FP32 memory from 1.86/2.65 GB to 1.82/2.58 GB.

M1.justification: The core DP-ER, BGV, GDC, AMoE-3D architecture and loss remain unchanged. Section 6.7 adds evaluated three-frame extensions using pose-aligned feature averaging or BEVFormer-style temporal attention. The new explanation of bilinear lifting clarifies a procedure already specified in v1's equations.

P1.justification: The main text receives limited clarifications and editorial changes. The supplement substantially expands explanations of retained components, dataset construction, and baseline adaptations, using question/setup/findings/takeaway sections and consistent per-method templates. It also develops the previously brief limitations and outlook into an extensive discussion.

P2.justification: V2 adds Figures 5–19 and Tables 6–26, including projection illustrations, annotation pipelines, dataset statistics, runtime breakdowns, failure cases, and configuration tables. Some displays re-express existing information, such as semantic frequencies from Tables 2–3. Main Tables 2 and 4 are also compressed/reformatted while retaining their results.

R1.justification: V2 adds references supporting implementation and supplementary discussion, including Point-MoE/Point-MoDE, FAST-LIO2, CARLA, open-vocabulary occupancy, and occupancy world models/flow. These broaden supporting context while leaving the main related-work narrative and central research positioning largely unchanged.

T1.justification: The core model equations remain unchanged. V2 adds mathematical specifications for annotation voting and confidence, the empty-vote mask and gated refinement, and density-based label acceptance in Sections 9–10. Section 6.2 also defines AET as mIoU multiplied by FPS. These extend formal specification without adding theoretical guarantees or proofs.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially strengthens validation and transparency: measured Jetson runtime replaces v1's Thor extrapolation, targeted ablations test central design choices, and detailed benchmark-construction and baseline documentation address major reproducibility gaps. Failure analyses and explicit applicability limits also improve the balance of the claims. Conflicting voxel bounds in Sections 9–11 and Figure 7's inconsistent resolution caption still require clarification, but the added evidence and documentation provide a substantial net quality improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe OneOcc, with matching core methods, datasets, and main experiments. The text, equations, tables, and figures support comparison. V1 ends after its references; v2 adds supplementary Sections 6–13.

after.justification: V2 retains those original results and adds experiments on projection choices, calibration robustness, temporal aggregation, resolution, field of view, and embedded-device runtime.

before.justification: V1 reports original QuadOcc and Human360Occ benchmark results, retrained baseline comparisons, component ablations, lighting analyses, and runtime measurements in Sections 4.1–4.5.

results.title: OneOcc: Semantic Occupancy Prediction for Legged Robots with a Single Panoramic Camera

C1.justification: The abstract, contributions, and conclusion broaden the work from demonstrated linear restoration/MRI reconstruction to a unified framework with demonstrated linear and nonlinear applications. Nonlinear implementation was explicitly future work in v1. The proximal-prior interpretation, few-NFE efficiency, and first MRI-trained CM claims remain.

C2.justification: v2 removes the LSUN-only limitation and nonlinear-future-work discussion as coverage expands. It adds interpretations of comparable visual quality to diffusion-PnP methods, robustness to hyperparameter perturbations, and phase-retrieval ambiguity. Its new MRI analysis qualifies momentum as especially useful at low NFEs and not the primary performance driver, replacing v1's emphasis on momentum dominance in its LSUN ablation.

D1.justification: v2 adds a code-repository link, explicit noise/penalty/momentum schedules, coefficient values for CelebA-HQ and MRI in Table 3, nonlinear implementation instructions, additional baseline tuning details, and training losses and budgets. v1 largely described empirical tuning and referenced external implementations. Conversely, v1's explicit [0,1] input-normalization statement is no longer stated.

E1.justification: v2 adds CelebA-HQ training and evaluation and evaluates JPEG restoration, nonlinear deblurring, and coded-mask phase retrieval on both natural-image datasets. LSUN Bedroom's original linear restoration tasks and fastMRI PD/PD-FS reconstruction remain.

E2.justification: Linear natural-image comparisons add DiffPIR, DPnP, and PnP-DM. The new nonlinear comparisons evaluate DPS, ΠGDM, and DPnP. MRI comparisons now include quantitative and visual CM4IR results alongside DPS and DDS; v1 only described CM4IR's failure without corresponding comparative entries.

E3.justification: The reported MRI CM distillation budget changes from 7M iterations in v1 Appendix D.1 to 700k in v2 Supplement C; this establishes a revised stated setting, without establishing retraining. New protocols include CelebA-HQ training/evaluation splits, JPEG quality factor 5, eight-NFE phase retrieval, MRI momentum controls at 4/10/20 NFEs, and randomized hyperparameter perturbations up to 25%.

E4.justification: v2 adds an MRI study testing whether momentum benefits diminish with increasing NFEs and a CelebA-HQ deblurring hyperparameter-sensitivity study (Supplement D.1–D.2). The four-way component ablation and noise/NFE sweep move from LSUN Bedroom experiments to CelebA-HQ experiments, replacing their evidence rather than merely relocating it.

E5.justification: Both versions use averaged reconstruction metrics and retain plus/minus reporting for MRI. Neither introduces seed counts, repeated-run counts, confidence intervals, or significance tests. The new randomized sensitivity study changes experimental design without adding uncertainty estimation.

E6.justification: v2 adds extensive CelebA-HQ, nonlinear-task, baseline, and sensitivity results while revising retained entries. For example, four-NFE LSUN deblurring changes from 28.10/0.237 to 27.49/0.285 PSNR/LPIPS, and MRI PD R=4 PnP-CM mean PSNR changes from 32.69 to 35.57. These are revised reported results, not established controlled performance gains. Original two-NFE comparator entries and LSUN ablation/sweep results are removed or replaced.

M1.justification: v2 implements nonlinear data-fidelity optimization, including a differentiable JPEG surrogate, whereas v1 left nonlinear implementation to future work. Supplement B.1 also adds phase-retrieval output disambiguation and specifies median-filter initialization for inpainting, contrasting with v1's explicit zero-initialization/no-heuristics description. The ADMM-CM core remains; the explicit CM noise-scale parameter mainly formalizes separately tuned noise levels already mentioned in v1.

P1.justification: The abstract, contributions, related-work discussion, acceleration narrative, and results discussion are substantially rewritten. v2 introduces separate Final Algorithm and Ablation Studies subsections, removes the standalone Discussion section, and reorganizes the appendices into experimental details, training details, and further results. These changes extend beyond renaming and renumbering.

P2.justification: v2 adopts a two-column layout, redraws the introductory overview, and merges the original natural-image and MRI tables into an expanded multipart Table 1. It adds nonlinear comparisons, a sensitivity plot, and CelebA-HQ image grids. Retained LSUN and MRI grids are expanded with comparator columns and rearranged; new hyperparameter and momentum tables further change the presentation.

R1.justification: Section 2.3 replaces the Schrödinger-bridge discussion of I2SB/CDDB with substantive positioning against diffusion-based PnP approaches, including newly cited work by Graikos, Park, Wu, and Xu/Chi. v2 also expands nonlinear-imaging references and more explicitly positions noise and momentum as established acceleration techniques, including momentum-ADMM prior work.

T1.justification: Section 2.1 removes v1's specialized empirical ODE, dx/dt = -t sϕ, and instead describes sampling through the general drift/diffusion probability-flow equation. This is a limited mathematical-formulation revision. Theorem 1, its Lipschitz and summable-noise assumptions, and Appendix A's convergence argument remain substantively unchanged.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens validation and reproducibility: it addresses v1's acknowledged narrow natural-image coverage and untested nonlinear extension, adds relevant diffusion-PnP comparisons, and documents tuning with sensitivity evidence and explicit coefficients. These gains outweigh the loss of some original LSUN analyses. Important gaps remain: Table 3 omits LSUN coefficients, and broad superiority wording is not supported uniformly across Table 1's metrics.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same PnP-CM research, with matching authors, core algorithm, and convergence theorem. The main text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices are readable and support reliable comparison.

after.justification: v2 reports original reconstruction experiments on LSUN Bedroom, CelebA-HQ, and fastMRI, including nonlinear tasks and additional ablation and sensitivity results.

before.justification: v1 reports original LSUN Bedroom and fastMRI reconstruction experiments, component ablations, and noise/NFE analyses in Tables 1–4 and the appendices.

results.title: PnP-CM: Consistency Models as Plug-and-Play Priors for Inverse Problems

C1.justification: v2 explicitly frames the abstract around human-centric generation and promotes the already-reported benefit of staged multi-task training into the abstract and introduction. The conclusion drops the explicit claim that FAM adds no significant computational overhead. The principal architectural contributions and overall performance claims remain.

C2.justification: The supplement adds explanations for interleaved and before-self-attention module placement, and identifies an alignment-versus-image-quality tradeoff for unrestricted MA-CFG. It explains restricted guidance as a mitigation. Section 11 newly states concrete limitations: absent video-aligned ambient-sound generation and constrained multi-person audio generation associated with the text encoder.

D1.justification: Sections 6–7 supply previously unavailable details: A2V window size 1/2, handling of one-frame versus four-frame video latents, 50-step Euler sampling, Vocos decoding, guidance scales 3 and 2, interval [0.5, 1], empty-text unconditional sampling, and the full Gemini scoring prompt. Section 10 additionally documents interaction insertion choices. These substantially expand reproducibility information without demonstrating changes to the retained experiments.

E1.justification: Supplement Section 9 adds public-benchmark evaluation on GRID for video-to-audio dubbing with unseen-speaker reference audio and EMTD for audio-driven half-body animation. These conditional tasks already appeared in v1's training framework, but their benchmark evaluation coverage is new. The original training datasets and 100-sample joint-generation test remain unchanged.

E2.justification: Table 5 adds StyleDubber and EmoDubber as evaluated dubbing comparators. Table 9 also explicitly compares MA-CFG against vanilla CFG and no CFG. The main Table 1 comparator set remains unchanged; the EMTD comparison and user study reuse existing baseline models.

E3.justification: v2 adds a 34-participant preference study assessing audio quality, video quality, and audiovisual coherence. New conditional evaluations use GRID Dubbing Setting 3.0 and EMTD, introducing LSE-D, FID, and FVD measurements alongside retained metrics. These are additional evaluation protocols; the original test composition, training budgets, and main evaluation settings remain unchanged.

E4.justification: Supplement Tables 7–8 newly test which layers receive interaction modules and where modules enter each DiT block. Table 9 quantitatively compares four guidance policies, including restricted-interval MA-CFG, extending v1's qualitative guidance analysis. The original interaction, FAM, and training-strategy ablations are retained.

E5.justification: Both versions report averaging three independent Gemini evaluations per sample. The supplement repeats this practice without introducing new seed counts, repeated-training information, confidence intervals, or significance-testing procedures. The 34-participant count describes the new study's sample size rather than an uncertainty-reporting change.

E6.justification: Tables 1–3 retain their numerical results, apart from equivalent decimal formatting. New Table 4 reports UniAVGen preference shares of 68.90%, 62.60%, and 74.30% for AQ, VQ, and AVC. Table 5 reports GRID LSE-C/LSE-D/WER of 7.59/6.11/10.64, leading both dubbing comparators. EMTD results are mixed: UniAVGen has the best reported FID but worse FVD than both comparators. Tables 7–9 add placement and guidance results, not same-setting performance gains over v1.

M1.justification: The dual-branch architecture, asymmetric aligners, FAM, MA-CFG formulation, five task interfaces, and three-stage training remain unchanged. The supplement documents alignment, placement, and inference choices for the existing framework; it does not establish that the underlying method changed from v1.

P1.justification: The main section sequence and most prose are retained. v2 revises the abstract, moves the introduction's task-unification discussion, clarifies the V2A motivation, shortens the conclusion, and adds acknowledgements. The new supplement has dedicated implementation, evaluation, ablation, and limitations sections, but the existing paper is not extensively rewritten.

P2.justification: Figure 1 changes from a compact three-task schematic to a full-width opening display with generated examples for four modes. Existing figures and tables are substantially resized, and Figure 5 is relocated. The supplement adds six tables, Tables 4–9, displaying new evidence rather than merely renumbering existing results.

R1.justification: v2 adds references for dubbing methods, benchmarks, inference components, and related generators, including VoiceCraft-Dub, MOVA, AudioX, and CMMD. However, the three-paradigm related-work organization and substantive positioning against UniVerse-1 and Ovi remain largely unchanged; this is an extension rather than a reframing.

T1.justification: The flow-matching losses, attention and interpolation equations, mask formulation, and guidance equations retain their mathematical substance. Changes to parameter-index notation are equivalent. Neither version supplies formal theorems or proofs, and the supplementary implementation explanations do not introduce new theoretical results.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially improves support for the claimed task unification through GRID and EMTD evaluations and adds human preference evidence. The new placement and guidance ablations expose design choices and an important quality tradeoff, while implementation details and the evaluator prompt address major documentation gaps in the supplied v1. Explicit limitations also clarify applicability. Study-protocol detail and uncertainty reporting remain limited, but the added evidence and reproducibility information provide a substantial net improvement without relying on unchanged headline scores.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe UniAVGen, with matching authors, core methods, and main experiments. Text, equations, tables, and figures support reliable comparison. The supplied v1 ends after the references; v2 additionally includes Supplementary Material, Sections 6–11, which was inspected.

after.justification: v2 retains those original results and adds a user study, conditional-generation benchmark results, and further ablations in supplementary Tables 4–9.

before.justification: v1 reports original quantitative comparisons in Table 1, interaction and modulation ablations in Tables 2–3, and qualitative and training-strategy results in Figures 4–7.

results.title: UniAVGen: Unified Audio and Video Generation with Asymmetric Cross-Modal Interactions

C1.justification: v2 elevates efficiency into a headline contribution, claiming state-of-the-art latency and computational cost and over 40 fps, beyond v1's general efficiency assertions. The abstract's reported MAE/RMSE advantages change from 30.3%/37.2% to 24.9%/33.2% alongside the expanded comparisons. The central polynomial-fitting contribution remains.

C2.justification: Appendix G interprets new controls as evidence of actual radar dependence, attributes regression-baseline shortcomings to radar noise, and discusses possible depth inversions using the new monotonicity analysis. Section 4.2 connects measured efficiency to deployment practicality. The stated limitations concerning degree selection and polynomial oscillation remain.

D1.justification: Appendices C and F newly supply dataset sizes, split descriptions, sensors, image crops, 60 training epochs, a cosine learning-rate schedule starting at 5e-5, and loss weights of 1.0/0.4/0.25. Table 2 identifies an NVIDIA A6000 for training-time measurements. These substantially improve documentation without establishing changes to previously unspecified settings.

E1.justification: The three datasets and radar-camera depth-estimation task remain. Appendix G adds zero-shot nuScenes-to-ZJU/VoD transfer and reduced-radar-input scenarios, extending coverage to domain transfer and degraded sensing conditions within the existing driving domain.

E2.justification: v2 adds TacoDepth to nuScenes/ZJU accuracy comparisons, numerous methods including NLSPN, BPNet and CaFNet in Table 7, and isotonic/spline regression plus LoRA and ViT-Adapter in Table 13. Lin's nuScenes results move to Table 7, while its ZJU/VoD accuracy comparisons disappear.

E3.justification: The main MAE/RMSE evaluations at 50, 70 and 80 meters remain. New protocols measure training time, inference latency and GFLOPs; evaluate source-trained models on target datasets; retain specified radar fractions; introduce learned-point controls; and measure ordinal agreement using Kendall's tau. These extend evaluation design substantially.

E4.justification: v1's backbone, polynomial-degree and component studies largely reappear in Appendix A. v2 adds positional-embedding and learned-point ablations, zero-shot transfer, radar-density robustness, quantitative depth-ordering analysis and VoD qualitative case studies. These test additional questions about spatial information, radar dependence and generalization.

E5.justification: v1 reports no corresponding statistical assessment. Appendix G introduces 30 bootstrap samples for Kendall's tau and a two-sample t-test comparing POLAR with raw MDE, reporting p = 0.012. This is a localized addition; bootstrap samples do not establish repeated training runs.

E6.justification: Table 1 changes the proposed method's nuScenes results: at 80 meters, MAE/RMSE change from 1454.1/3488.9 to 1407.8/3193.5, while its main ZJU/VoD entries remain unchanged. v2 adds extensive efficiency, comparator, transfer and robustness results. Its Table 6 VoD full-model entry conflicts with Table 1, so that entry cannot support a reliable performance interpretation.

M1.justification: Section 3.2 replaces dot-product prototype aggregation with temperature-controlled, distance-based soft clustering. It also introduces sinusoidal 3D radar embeddings and learned 2D positional embeddings in fusion, supported by a new embedding ablation. These change important representation components, while polynomial prediction and the three-term loss remain.

P1.justification: PolyRad becomes POLAR throughout. The abstract, contribution statement and regularization explanations are revised; Section 3.2 gains component-specific organization; and comparative studies move from main Section 4.2 to Appendix A. Computational efficiency replaces them in the main experimental narrative, with additional material organized into eight appendices.

P2.justification: The document changes from two-column to predominantly single-column layout, with extensive reflow and relocation. The original qualitative and polynomial illustrations remain with exchanged figure numbering. v2 adds efficiency and diagnostic tables, shared colorbars, VoD examples, radar-versus-lidar visualizations and a counterexample plot.

R1.justification: v2 updates positioning with TacoDepth, LoRA, ViT-Adapter, BPNet and additional benchmark references, while pruning older discussion and citations such as CSPN/CSPN++ and R4Dyn. Its central distinction between polynomial scene fitting and direct completion or fusion remains.

T1.justification: Appendix H adds a constructive proposition proving that some sets of three or more depth pairs cannot share an affine fit, followed by a polynomial-approximation corollary. Appendix B derives incremental polynomial computation costs. These provide limited formal extensions to v1's existing mathematical motivation.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens assessment of the method through stronger comparators, explicit radar-dependence and robustness controls, measured computational efficiency, and previously missing training details. These address important evidential and reproducibility weaknesses in v1. The gains outweigh localized reporting problems, including Table 6's inconsistent VoD entry and Appendix A percentage improvements that are not supported by Table 4.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same work, and their text, equations, tables and figures are readable and matchable. v1 ends after the references despite mentioning supplementary material; v2 includes Appendices A–H. The comparison covers the material actually supplied.

after.justification: v2 retains original benchmark experiments and additionally reports computational efficiency, cross-dataset transfer, radar sparsity, regression comparisons and monotonicity analysis.

before.justification: v1 reports original depth-estimation results on nuScenes, ZJU-4DRadarCam and View-of-Delft, with backbone comparisons, polynomial-degree experiments and component ablations.

results.title: Radar-Guided Polynomial Fitting for Metric Depth Estimation

C1.justification: Both versions claim the first direct reconstruction of sharp, animatable Gaussian avatars from blurry videos through joint motion/avatar optimization, introduce synthetic and captured benchmarks, and claim superiority over the evaluated baselines. The expanded experiments support these retained core contributions.

C2.justification: v2 adds interpretations concerning tolerance to inaccurate initialization, mask estimation, and limited training views. It replaces v1's foreground/background blending and mask-dependence limitations discussion with geometry/BRDF recovery, nonlinear-sRGB blur formation, and failures involving handheld objects or loose garments.

D1.justification: v2 adds camera trigger-delay details, identifies deformation networks as CNNs, and specifies iPhone/TRAM processing. It omits details including 6,890-Gaussian initialization, 50 synthetic frames per camera, the Camera 03 exclusion, and the 15 FPS capture rate. Code/data wording changes from publicly available to a future release.

E1.justification: The synthetic and captured multi-camera benchmarks remain. v2 adds out-of-domain AMASS motions for novel-pose animation and monocular iPhone 16 Pro footage (Figures 13–14), substantially extending evaluation beyond the original multi-view reconstruction scenarios.

E2.justification: GauHuman and the ShiftNet, RVRT, VRT, and BSST plus GauHuman baselines remain unchanged. v2 Table 5 adds Slerp as an explicitly evaluated trajectory alternative to the proposed B-spline representation, expanding comparison methods within the interpolation analysis.

E3.justification: Synthetic blur preprocessing changes from eight RIFE intermediate frames to 16. New evaluation designs vary training views between two, three, and four, perturb SMPL initialization using uniform noise, and compare alternative mask constructions. These are substantial protocol additions; the PDFs do not establish that retained benchmark scores were rerun.

E4.justification: v2 adds trajectory-representation comparisons, initialization perturbations, freezing all SMPL parameters, mask-quality controls, and view-count ablations. It also extends control-knot and virtual-frame sensitivity analyses to real data. Existing component, regularization, and blur-magnitude ablations are retained.
