E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, significance tests, or uncertainty estimates. v2's random initialization perturbations constitute robustness testing rather than uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: Main benchmark and existing component-ablation numbers remain unchanged, but v2 adds substantial quantitative robustness results and qualitative animation and smartphone results. Its high-blur comparison also revises the Ours entries: at Kblur=7, PSNR changes from 25.113 to 25.155, now matching the existing full-model ablation result. This is not evidence of a newly established same-setting performance gain.

M1.justification: The reported inter-frame regularizer changes from L2 distance in v1 Equation 15 to geodesic distance in v2 Equation 9. The B-spline motion model, pose displacements, LBS refinement, Gaussian rendering, and image-averaging pipeline otherwise remain.

P1.justification: The title changes, much of the prose is condensed or rewritten, duplicated deblurring-related-work text is removed, and the standalone SMPL/3DGS preliminaries disappear. Experiments are reorganized around ablation, robustness, and further-discussion sections.

P2.justification: The pipeline diagram is redrawn, dataset-specific comparison and ablation tables are merged, and the combined hyperparameter table is split and expanded. New timing, initialization, mask, animation, and smartphone displays are added; the former limitations figure is removed. Existing qualitative comparisons are relocated and resized.

R1.justification: v2 adds citations including BARD-GS, AMASS, TRAM, and recent Gaussian/avatar research, while removing works including SelfRecon and the time-lapse examples. The central positioning against 2D deblurring and sharp-input avatar methods remains.

T1.justification: The regularizer's mathematical distance changes from L2 to geodesic distance. The continuous blur equation also drops v1's normalization factor, although normalized discrete averaging remains. The B-spline formulation is retained, and no new theorem or proof is introduced.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens evidence for central assumptions that v1 left insufficiently tested: tolerance to coarse SMPL initialization and imperfect masks, plus actual novel-pose animation. The smartphone demonstration extends practical validation, and rewritten limitations clarify important failure conditions. These gains outweigh the loss of some implementation details and the weaker resource-release statement, although the changed loss and preprocessing descriptions leave reproducibility questions.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same avatar-deblurring work despite a changed title and substantial reorganization. Text, equations, tables, and figures support reliable comparison. Neither supplied PDF contains a separate appendix.

after.justification: v2 retains these original experiments and adds robustness tests, AMASS-driven animation results, and an iPhone capture demonstration.

before.justification: v1 reports original reconstruction experiments on synthetic ZJU-MoCap data and a captured multi-camera dataset, including baseline comparisons and ablations in Tables 2–9.

results.title: Motion-Aware Animatable Gaussian Avatars Deblurring

C1.justification: The central efficiency claim is substantially reduced: approximately 150-fold overall savings in v1 becomes approximately 40-fold in v2. Claimed sampling savings change from about 30-fold to 13–15-fold, and aggregation savings from about five-fold to three-fold. The contributions remain efficient full-distribution crowdsourced evaluation and comparison of explanation methods, with Linear Explanations still ranked best overall.

C2.justification: V2 develops budget-dependent applicability boundaries: automated-only evaluation for very small budgets, hybrid evaluation for intermediate budgets, and purely human evaluation for sufficiently large budgets (B.5). It also discusses ambiguous dataset labels, insufficient evidence for estimating individual error rates, and task ambiguity as a source of annotator disagreement. These substantially qualify practical interpretation, although the existing limitations in A.1 remain largely unchanged.

D1.justification: V2 adds OpenCLIP/model identifiers and specifies the alternative error model's fitted parameters and 100-bin integration approximation. The promised code repository destination changes, while hardware, runtime, worker eligibility, and payment details are retained. Reproducibility remains locally ambiguous: B.7 specifies SigLIP ViT-L-16-384 for sampling/aggregation, whereas C.3 retains the statement that all guidance uses SO400M.

E1.justification: The visual datasets, neuron-explanation tasks, and evaluated ResNet-50/ViT layers remain unchanged. V2 Appendix C.7 adds an author-annotator cohort for comparison with MTurk workers, providing limited additional population coverage.

E2.justification: The explanation-method sets in the automated and large-scale human comparisons are retained. However, the MTurk aggregation comparison adds SigLIP-only evaluation and no longer displays averaging alongside the other aggregators (v1 Figure 3b versus v2 Figure 11). V2 Table 4 also adds majority-vote aggregation to the large-scale study, previously reported only with Bayesian aggregation.

E3.justification: Validation changes from five selected neurons with 300 inputs each to ten randomly selected, non-vague neurons with 600 inputs each; nine raters per input are retained. The large study changes from 90 inputs with two raters to 180 with three. Simulated noise rises from 13% to 23%, beta changes from 0.01 to 0.05, and RCE changes from mean per-neuron relative error to summed absolute errors normalized by summed ground-truth correlations. V2 also adds full-dataset aggregation-only and author-rating controls.

E4.justification: V2 adds explicit joint-versus-separate sampling/aggregation controls, mixture-weight sensitivity, heterogeneous error-model testing, automated-only evaluation comparisons, CLIP/SigLIP/SigLIP2 ablations, and author-versus-worker agreement analysis. Existing beta sensitivity and activation-only sampling analyses are revised, rather than wholly new. Appendix examples are also replaced and expanded to include ViT cases.

E5.justification: V1 reports standard errors and repeated sampling but no significance tests or agreement statistics. V2 adds two-sample Student's t-tests for explanation comparisons in Table 5 and Fleiss's kappa in Appendix C.7. Appendix B.2 newly specifies averaging its beta ablation over 30 random seeds; this does not establish an increase from v1's unspecified count for that analysis.

E6.justification: Automated Tables 1 and 2 retain their numerical results, but crowdsourced scores are extensively revised. For example, LE(SigLIP) with the SigLIP Bayesian prior changes from 0.2107 to 0.1803 on ResNet-50 and from 0.2382 to 0.2450 on ViT; the ResNet runner-up changes from CLIP-Dissect to INVERT. These are results under revised protocols, not same-setting gains or losses. V2 additionally reports substantial new ablation, significance, and agreement results.

M1.justification: The importance-sampling and Bayesian-aggregation pipeline is retained with procedural refinements. V2 replaces epsilon-based sampling regularization with an explicit 80% model-guided/20% uniform mixture and changes the stated activation normalization from sample to full-dataset statistics. Appendix B.4 also introduces an optional per-input/concept error-rate model, while retaining constant error rates for the main method.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction, related work, and method exposition are substantially rewritten, and MG-IS/BRAgg terminology is introduced throughout. Individual simulation studies are integrated into the method sections, Section 4 becomes combined validation, and the appendices are reorganized into discussion, ablations, and technical details with a new overview.

P2.justification: The main paper changes from single-column to two-column layout, Figure 1 is redrawn, and the principal human results gain a bar-chart presentation with detailed tables moved to the appendix. Numerous analysis plots and a significance table are added; example-neuron panels and their color thresholds are revised. The unchanged complex-explanation table is relocated rather than removed.

R1.justification: V2 adds citations to Borowski et al.'s feature-visualization evaluation, OpenCLIP, and SigLIP2. Section 2.2 expands the distinction from activation-prediction/AUC-based human studies and clarifies the relationship to NeuronEval. The overall related-work coverage and positioning remain recognizable.

T1.justification: The optimal-importance-sampling theorem and reproduced proof are retained, moving from B.3 to C.5. V2 explicitly states the proposal-support condition, revises the mathematical definition of RCE, corrects normalization expressions, and derives a posterior marginalizing per-input/concept error rates in B.4. These are substantive but bounded mathematical changes.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially strengthens validation of the central evaluation pipeline. Joint component controls, guiding-model and error-model ablations, automated-only comparisons, and annotator-agreement measurements address important gaps in v1's evidence about reliability and dependence on modeling choices. Significance tests also make the explanation-ranking evidence more assessable, including nonsignificant comparisons. Conflicting SigLIP specifications remain a reproducibility weakness, but the added validation and clearer applicability boundaries outweigh that limitation.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same neuron-explanation evaluation research despite the changed title and substantial revision. Their text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices support reliable comparison.

after.justification: V2 reports original simulations and crowdsourced results, including additional component ablations, model comparisons, and annotator-agreement measurements.

before.justification: V1 reports original sampling and label-noise simulations, MTurk validation, automated explanation comparisons, and a crowdsourced study of two vision models.

results.title: Beyond Top Activations: Efficient and Reliable Crowdsourced Evaluation of Automated Interpretability

C1.justification: The benchmark and two principal methodological contributions remain the same. However, the conclusion removes 'in specialized domains' from its assertion that multi-dataset RL requires reward balancing and domain-adapted evaluation, modestly broadening the stated scope of that claim.

C2.justification: v2 adds interpretations concerning inadequate transfer from the new baselines, generalization across model architectures and sizes, clinical validity of the judge, and relative insensitivity to normalization slope. The existing explanations of task synergy and CVS calibration failures remain unchanged.

D1.justification: Appendix D newly explains averaging six OSATS scores and thresholding them into three skill classes, although numerical thresholds are unspecified. The project-site address changes. Removing the main-text 'frozen vision encoder' statement resolves a conflict with the all-component fine-tuning already documented in v1's appendix; it does not establish an actual training change.

E1.justification: The eight medical datasets, eight benchmark tasks and four domains remain unchanged. v2 adds a distinct human-evaluation population and task: board-certified clinicians score captions on five dimensions to validate the judge, supplementing the retained medical-data-expert study of caption preferences.

E2.justification: Table 2 adds VideoChat-R1.5-7B and NVIDIA's Qwen2.5-VL-7B-Surg-CholecT50, introducing evaluated general-video RL and specialized surgical comparators alongside all original baselines. New Table 5 also compares off-the-shelf, SFT and MedGRPO versions of Qwen3-VL-4B, substantially broadening the comparison evidence.

E3.justification: v2 adds evaluation with a 4B backbone and a protocol in which 10 clinicians score 30 samples across five dimensions. Appendix D additionally reports skill-assessment macro-accuracy and MAE. Existing benchmark splits, sampling settings and training budgets remain unchanged; the PDFs do not establish that the original tables were recomputed using the newly described skill metrics.

E4.justification: v2 adds direct validation of the medical judge against clinician ratings, a second-backbone generalization analysis, and STG reward-distribution comparisons for normalization slopes k=2, 3 and 4. These address judge validity, model generalization and parameter sensitivity. The original component ablations, scaling analysis and qualitative failure cases are retained.

E5.justification: Appendix E.1 introduces Pearson correlation and Cohen's kappa for judge–clinician agreement, with per-dimension and inter-clinician correlations in Figure 8. The original preference-study error bars remain unchanged. No additional training-seed, repeated-run or confidence-interval reporting is introduced.

E6.justification: Tables 2–3 revise full-model CVS from 0.914 to 0.896, NAP from 0.427 to 0.405, SA from 0.244 to 0.254 and DVC F1 from 0.210 to 0.214. v2 also adds baseline scores, skill-assessment MAE/macro-accuracy, and Table 5 results: Qwen3-VL-4B TAG@0.3 rises from 0.465 with SFT to 0.504 with MedGRPO. New judge validation reports Pearson r=0.977 and kappa=0.817.

M1.justification: Sections 3.2–3.4 retain the same GRPO objective, dataset-task logistic normalization, grounding rewards and hybrid semantic/medical-judge caption rewards. Qwen3-VL-4B is evaluated using the same pipeline; no new algorithmic component or architectural modification is introduced.

P1.justification: The abstract, related work and results receive targeted rewrites and terminology corrections. A new quantitative-results appendix shifts subsequent appendix labels, and the judge appendix gains validation and rubric subsections. Most prose and the main section sequence remain intact.

P2.justification: v2 expands Table 2 and adds Table 5, the clinician-correlation heatmap in Figure 8 and reward-distribution plots in Figure 10. Existing displays are resized, repositioned or renumbered, including the qualitative examples. The overall visual design and retained scaling curves remain unchanged.

R1.justification: v2 adds references and discussion covering Qwen3-VL, VideoChat-R1.5, NVIDIA's surgical model, clinical LLM judges and concurrent medical reasoning, foundation-model and distillation work. It narrows the evaluation gap from medical-domain evaluation generally to medical-video evaluation, while retaining the main positioning around heterogeneous multi-task learning.

T1.justification: The GRPO equations, logistic normalization definition, derivative and stated normalization properties are unchanged. The new empirical validation and sensitivity plots introduce no theorem, proof or revised mathematical derivation.

improvement.justification: v1's human study validated annotation prompting, leaving its central medical judge without direct clinician validation. v2 substantially strengthens that foundation through clinician agreement measurements, while the second-backbone experiment and relevant RL/surgical baselines strengthen generalization and comparison evidence. The 30-sample validation remains limited, and Appendix D's skill macro-accuracy values differ from Table 2's accuracy values without explaining their relationship, but these reporting weaknesses do not outweigh the substantial validation gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe MedGRPO and MedVidBench. Their complete main texts and appendices, including equations, tables and figures, support reliable comparison after matching relocated and renumbered content.

after.justification: v2 retains original empirical results and adds evaluated baselines, Qwen3-VL-4B experiments, clinician validation of the LLM judge and reward-normalization sensitivity analysis.

before.justification: v1 reports original benchmark evaluations, training ablations, scaling experiments, qualitative analyses and a 12-participant caption-preference study.

results.title: MedGRPO: Multi-Task Reinforcement Learning for Heterogeneous Medical Video Understanding

C1.justification: The three central architectural contributions remain unchanged. The introduction narrows the wide-coverage claim from outperforming optimization-based 3D-GS in reconstruction quality to achieving comparable performance in approximately 0.5 seconds versus approximately eight minutes.

C2.justification: v3 clarifies refinement under fixed image evidence and interprets attention visualizations as progressive correspondence formation. It adds static-scene and geometry-supervision limitations, explicitly qualifies pseudo-depth agreement as indirect evidence, and attributes faster post-prediction optimization partly to geometric quality. The original scalability and camera-pose limitations remain.

D1.justification: v3 newly specifies 50,000 high-resolution fine-tuning iterations, post-prediction optimization learning rates, and Long-LRM checkpoint provenance, while correcting the reported AdamW beta2. It removes v2's explicit training disclosure of FlashAttention-2, BFloat16, and gradient-checkpointing use. The project-page destination is unchanged.

E1.justification: v3 adds Tanks&Temples and Mip-NeRF360 evaluations for novel-view synthesis and depth, plus NRGBD and ETH3D pointmap evaluations. It also introduces corrupted-camera-input scenarios. This substantially extends the original RE10K, ACID, and DL3DV coverage beyond image synthesis into geometric accuracy and imperfect inputs.

E2.justification: Mip-Splatting is removed from the 16-view and 32-view wide-coverage comparisons in Table 5. The other principal reconstruction comparators remain. MoGe-2 supplies pseudo-depth reference targets rather than serving as a newly evaluated reconstruction baseline.

E3.justification: v3 introduces a 51-scene DL3DV evaluation split, tests 32-view-trained models with unseen view counts, and adds depth, pointmap, and translation-noise protocols. Geometry evaluation specifies an F1 threshold of 0.1 and downsampling ground-truth pointmaps for iLRM. Long-LRM is explicitly re-evaluated using released checkpoints except for 16-view metrics. Reported AdamW beta2 changes from 0.095 to 0.95, without establishing that training was rerun.

E4.justification: v3 adds layerwise attention-correspondence analysis, camera-translation perturbation tests, generalization beyond the training view count, and latency scaling through 256 views. It extends post-prediction optimization analysis to additional datasets. These investigate mechanisms and robustness beyond the retained architectural, overlap, and representation-density ablations.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, experimental seeds, confidence intervals, or significance tests. The new Gaussian-noise standard deviations specify input perturbations, not uncertainty in estimated results.

E6.justification: Numerous new results accompany the added evaluations. Retained eight-view MC results also change: Table 1 RE10K PSNR increases numerically from 30.96 to 31.24, and Table 2 ACID/DL3DV PSNR changes from 30.47/29.03 to 30.72/29.33. Table 5 revises baseline results: 32-view 3D-GS PSNR changes from 23.60 to 24.43, while iLRM remains 24.30. Its timings and Long-LRM results are revised, and the 50-epoch iLRM row is removed; these should not be interpreted as demonstrated same-setting performance gains.

M1.justification: The viewpoint tokenization, per-view cross-attention, global self-attention, token uplifting, mini-batch attention, Gaussian decoder, and training loss remain unchanged. The added optimization interpretation and implementation disclosures do not establish a revised algorithm.

P1.justification: Related work moves into the main text, experimental-setup subsections become condensed run-in paragraphs, and several method explanations are shortened. Affiliation and acknowledgement text also changes. The existing introduction, method narrative, ablation explanations, and conclusion largely retain their structure and wording.

P2.justification: v3 replaces the single-column presentation with a two-column layout and substantially reorganizes tables and illustrations. It adds attention, depth, geometry, and optimization visualizations plus new evaluation tables. Existing displays are also resized, reordered, or relocated; for example, v2 Figure 7's high-resolution comparison becomes v3 Figure 15.

R1.justification: v3 adds references including Perceiver, sparse transformers, state-space alternatives, MoGe-2, DUSt3R, Rayzer, FLARE, and newly evaluated benchmarks. Mip-Splatting and several implementation references disappear. The principal related-work discussion is substantially retained from v2 Appendix A, now in main Section 2.

T1.justification: The model equations, training objective, and FLOPs calculation are retained. v3's added approximate-gradient expressions illustrate the existing optimization analogy; they introduce no defined energy function, formal guarantee, proof, or substantive derivation.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially strengthens evidence for reconstruction quality and scalability by testing previously unmeasured geometry, pose-error sensitivity, and behavior beyond the training view count. The revised 3D-GS comparison and narrower introduction claim improve calibration. Proxy-depth dependence, method-specific pointmap downsampling, and removal of Mip-Splatting limit some comparisons, but the broader validation and clearer applicability boundaries provide a substantial net improvement over v2.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same iLRM research and contain readable main text, equations, tables, figures, and appendices. Content can be matched despite substantial reformatting and section renumbering.

after.justification: v3 retains original empirical results and adds depth, geometry, camera-pose robustness, attention visualization, and scalability evaluations.

before.justification: v2 reports original reconstruction, efficiency, generalization, and ablation results on RE10K, ACID, and DL3DV, including appendix experiments.

results.title: iLRM: An Iterative Large 3D Reconstruction Model

C1.justification: The central claims of greater expressivity, efficient conditioning and easy integration remain. v3 adds probabilistic justification as an explicit contribution and broadens the abstract and conclusion to both pipelines and 29 subjects across six datasets. Multi-view applicability itself was already claimed and illustrated in v1's appendix.

C2.justification: v3 adds an implicit-prior regularization explanation, interprets uncertainty caused by unstable foreground masks, and suggests a memory-locality explanation for the 1D FPS anomaly. It removes v1's explicit caveats about inheriting the host method's limitations and unresolved scaling to thousands of dimensions. The existing local-context explanation is retained.

D1.justification: v3 substantially documents the previously brief GaussianHeadAvatar case study: attribute-specific latents, preprocessing, ten NeRSemble subject IDs, sequence selection, 16 cameras, 2048 × 2048 images and 600k iterations. It also states that an implementation is publicly released. Reported multi-view training time changes from 9–9.5 hours to over two days with 30 minutes of overhead, without explaining the cross-version difference.

E1.justification: v3 lists five rather than four monocular source datasets, newly including NerFACE, but retains 19 subjects and identical aggregate scores. NeRSemble multi-view reconstruction already appears in v1 Appendix A.2.3. Without a corresponding v1 subject inventory, the PDFs do not establish whether represented data changed or dataset attribution was corrected.

E2.justification: v1 compares NDGS within FlashAvatar, while its GaussianHeadAvatar comparison contains only the baseline and HyperGaussians. v3 adds NDGS to the GaussianHeadAvatar comparison in Table 3 and Figure 10. The monocular comparator set remains unchanged; newly discussed feed-forward and diffusion methods are not experimentally evaluated.

E3.justification: The stated monocular resolution, frame split, metrics and 30k training iterations are unchanged. For GaussianHeadAvatar, v3 specifies 600k iterations and a detailed multi-view protocol, whereas v1 lacks corresponding settings and reports 9–9.5 hours instead of over two days. Whether the underlying protocol changed or was newly documented cannot be reliably determined.

E4.justification: v3 extends NDGS failure analysis to GaussianHeadAvatar, examining displaced glasses, weak reflections and disappearing wrinkles. Table 4 also extends the latent-dimension analysis with rendering FPS. The accuracy, MLP-size, convergence and uncertainty analyses largely already exist in v1, although their placement changes.

E5.justification: Both versions average the conditioning benchmark over 1000 runs after warm-up and retain the same covariance-based uncertainty measure and visualization. v3 adds no reported seed counts, confidence intervals or significance tests for reconstruction quality.

E6.justification: v3 adds aggregate multi-view results: Table 1 reports PSNR 24.10 for GaussianHeadAvatar and 24.38 for HyperGaussians, with equal reported SSIM; Table 3 adds NDGS at 24.22 PSNR. These are not directly comparable with v1 Figure 10's individual-example scores. v3 also adds multi-view qualitative results and FPS entries across latent dimensions. Monocular reconstruction and accuracy-ablation values remain unchanged.

M1.justification: Gaussian conditioning, the inverse covariance trick and the FlashAvatar integration are retained. GaussianHeadAvatar integration already appears in v1 Appendix A.2.3; v3 Section 3.3 and Appendix C document its implementation more fully without establishing a changed procedure. The Bayesian treatment adds interpretation rather than a new training objective.

P1.justification: v3 extensively rewrites the introduction, related work and method exposition, divides the case studies and experiments into monocular and multi-view settings, and reorganizes the supplement into Appendices A–E. Model-scaling discussion moves into the main text, while uncertainty and latent-dimensionality discussion move into the supplement.

P2.justification: v3 replaces the teaser with GaussianHeadAvatar examples, expands multi-view comparison displays, adds aggregate comparison tables, and enlarges the related-work table with resource categories. It consolidates ablation displays and adds an FPS column. Conditioning, uncertainty and convergence figures are retained but relocated, producing substantial visual reorganization.

R1.justification: Section 2 and Appendix A substantially expand positioning through 6DGS/7DGS and recent feed-forward and diffusion-based avatars. The enlarged related-work table distinguishes optimization, feed-forward and pseudo-ground-truth approaches and their resource requirements. v3 also claims a unified probabilistic interpretation of earlier high-dimensional Gaussian methods.

T1.justification: v3 adds the MAP equality in Equation 4, a conditional-support argument distinguishing HyperGaussians from NDGS, and explicit computational and parameter-complexity bounds. The Gaussian-conditioning, Cholesky and uncertainty derivations are substantially retained from v1.

improvement.justification: v1 supports its second integration mainly through two illustrated multi-view examples with little implementation or evaluation detail. v3 supplies aggregate ten-subject results, an NDGS control and detailed integration and data protocols, substantially strengthening the assessability and reproducibility of the broader applicability claim. The unchanged monocular evidence is preserved. Dropped limitations and unexplained dataset-count and training-time differences remain weaknesses, but the gains in empirical support and documentation outweigh them.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe HyperGaussians with the same authors and core formulation. All 16 pages of v1 and 19 pages of v3, including appendices, equations, tables and figures, support comparison.

after.justification: v3 retains original monocular results and reports aggregate multi-view reconstruction results, NDGS comparisons, ablations and computational measurements.

before.justification: v1 reports original avatar reconstruction results, quantitative ablations, computational benchmarks, and appendix comparisons involving GaussianHeadAvatar and NDGS.

results.title: HyperGaussians: High-Dimensional Gaussian Splatting for High-Fidelity Animatable Face Avatars

C1.justification: The central contribution shifts from object-contrastive image-pair construction and local/global self-VQA scoring to hard preference pairs involving both texts and images, coupled with conditional preference optimization. V2's abstract and conclusion also explicitly claim superiority to specialized diffusion models. The central aim of improving object-level alignment without external training resources remains.

C2.justification: The explanation for modest Non-spatial gains shifts from weak semantic contrast in v1 to limited CLIP-T sensitivity in v2. V2 adds interpretations about weak textual grounding, loss-dependent precision/recall and over-generation tradeoffs, and confirmation bias in self-rewarding. These substantially change the proposed mechanisms and qualifications beyond the numerical findings.

D1.justification: V2 Table 7 adds per-backbone optimizer parameters, clipping, weight decay, accumulation, precision, attention implementation, and loss weights, and specifies four A100 80GB GPUs. V1's approximately 26-hour runtime on eight A100s and explicit language-model-only training disclosure disappear. Appendix F also removes most category-specific prompt templates and detailed keyword-pool construction, retaining a smaller template selection.

E1.justification: The three generation benchmarks and four training-prompt categories remain. However, v2 replaces the preliminary synthetic Best-of-N scenario with fine-grained image and text discrimination using AnyEdit and SugarCrepe, respectively. These introduce external evaluation data and distinct discrimination tasks, rather than merely additional generation scores; they are not used as external training data.

E2.justification: V2 adds DSR and T2I-R1 to Tables 1–2 and UniRL to the Janus-1.3B comparison in Table 3. It also adds Show-o, Janus, Emu3, UniTok, FLUX.1, and SD3 in the relevant benchmark tables, while removing older diffusion comparators including SD-v1.5, PixArt-alpha, and DALL-E 2. SILMM remains quantitatively evaluated but disappears from the qualitative comparison panels.

E3.justification: Reported initial training prompts increase from 16,000 to 19,000, while the stated T2I-CompBench++ prompt count changes from 8,000 to 2,400. Janus-Pro training changes from a 4e-5 learning rate and one epoch to 1e-5 and 330 steps, with revised loss hyperparameters. V2 adds backbone configurations, 1,000-example discrimination datasets, and explicit test-time sampling protocols. The benchmark-count revision alone does not establish that evaluations were rerun.

E4.justification: V2 adds loss-component and filtering/selection ablations, discrimination analyses, iterative-training and data-size studies, inference-time comparisons, and self-versus-Qwen reward controls. The densification ablation is retained with revised results and supporting analysis. V1's local/global gap-distribution study and SILMM-specific VQA-scoring experiment are removed, rather than relocated.

E5.justification: V1 explicitly reports generating ten images with varying random seeds per prompt and illustrates seed variability in its preliminary experiment; this reporting disappears with that experiment in v2. Neither version reports training-run variability, confidence intervals, or significance tests. V2's model-uncertainty measure is a selection criterion, not statistical uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: Tables 1–2 substantially revise OSPO and SILMM scores. For example, OSPO's reported T2I color score changes from 0.8868 to 0.8438, DPGBench total from 85.94 to 85.34, and GenEval total from 0.80 to 0.82. These are revised results under changed methods/settings, not controlled performance gains or losses. V2 additionally reports backbone, discrimination, loss, scaling, and reward-control results absent from v1.

M1.justification: V1 selects image pairs using a normalized local/global VQA-gap ratio and trains with SimPO. V2 replaces this with threshold-based VQA filtering and selection by minimal log-probability gaps, including negative text candidates. Its objective combines SimPO, conditional preference loss, and supervised loss. Appendix D.2 also introduces VQA-based inference-time image selection. Prompt perturbation and pairwise densification remain.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, method, and experimental narrative are extensively rewritten. The preliminary experiment becomes a standalone section, related work moves to Appendix A, and implementation details and additional analyses are reorganized. Prompt documentation is heavily condensed, while the dedicated Discussion and Broader Impacts sections disappear. These are substantial structural and language changes.

P2.justification: V2 adopts a two-column layout, redraws the framework diagram, replaces the preliminary figures, adds an algorithm display, and substantially expands and restructures tables and analytical plots. Qualitative galleries are consolidated: several Janus-Pro examples are retained and rearranged, SILMM columns are removed, and comparisons for additional backbones are added. The earlier local/global density plot disappears.

R1.justification: V2 substantially repositions OSPO against newer self-improving methods, including DSR and UniRL, and discusses T2I-R1's external supervision. It adds compositional-reasoning motivation through SugarCrepe and Winoground and emphasizes discrete unified MLLMs. Much of v1's general vision-language, RLHF, and compositional-diffusion background is removed. This exceeds the accompanying relocation of related work to the appendix.

T1.justification: V1's mathematical definition of the normalized local/global preference-strength score is removed. V2 introduces the thresholded discrimination ratio, formal positive/negative filtering sets, and conditional and combined OSPO objectives in Equations 1 and 3–7. These substantially revise the formal definitions underlying evaluation and optimization. Neither version supplies theorems or proofs.

improvement.justification: V1's empirical support is concentrated on one backbone and data-construction ablations. V2 substantially strengthens validation through additional backbones and competitive baselines, targeted loss and selection controls in Tables 3–6, and iterative-training, scaling, and self-reward analyses in Appendix D. These address important gaps in evidence for generality and mechanism. Reduced category-specific prompt documentation and omitted runtime information weaken reproducibility, and statistical uncertainty remains unreported, but the expanded, targeted validation provides a substantial overall quality improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same authors' OSPO research on object-centric text-to-image preference optimization. Their complete main texts and appendices, including equations, tables, and figures, are readable and support comparison despite substantial methodological and presentational revision.

after.justification: V2 reports original generation and discrimination results, experiments with three backbones, loss and selection ablations, and additional scaling and reward-model analyses.

before.justification: V1 reports original Janus-Pro training results, a preliminary Best-of-N experiment, and component ablations in Tables 1–4 and the appendices.

results.title: OSPO: Object-Centric Self-Improving Preference Optimization for Text-to-Image Generation

C1.justification: Both versions retain the same central contributions: progressive correspondence filtering, anchor-based geometric proxies and joint feature/geometric optimization. The headline claim of approximately 32-fold CPU speedup over MAC on KITTI with comparable accuracy is also retained. Rewriting does not materially redefine these claims.

C2.justification: Supplement B adds substantive interpretations of parameter stability, normal-estimation robustness, computational tradeoffs and overlap-dependent parameter choices. The conclusion explains very-low-inlier failures through the assumption that the inlier set exceeds competing outlier clusters. V1's discussion of nonadaptive proxy radii and unused color information is removed.

D1.justification: V2 adds a project-page pointer, demo-video references, RTX 3090 hardware information and the default normal-estimation neighborhood K = 20. Most existing implementation and hyperparameter details move to Supplement A. Conversely, v1's explicit eight-scene 3DMatch and 555-pair KITTI test descriptions are omitted.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate rigid registration on 3DMatch, 3DLoMatch and KITTI using FPFH and FCGF features. V2's additional analyses stratify existing data or vary processing and parameters; they do not establish additional dataset, domain or task coverage.

E2.justification: V2 Table 1 adds PointDSC and VBReg across all three datasets and both feature types, substantially broadening the comparison to learning-based registration methods. Supplementary Table 5 also adds angular-difference filtering as a comparator. TurboReg was already evaluated in v1 and is retained.

E3.justification: V2 adds systematic parameter sweeps, normal-estimation controls using K = 10, 20 and 30 and Open3D versus PyMeshLab, and evaluation stratified by inlier ratio. It specifies GPU execution for PointDSC, VBReg and TurboReg and separates their timings from CPU rankings. The reported filtering cutoff also changes, while benchmark success criteria remain unchanged.

E4.justification: The existing component ablations are retained, with v1 Tables IV–V corresponding to v2 Tables 3 and 2. Supplement B adds stage-wise runtime analysis, recall/error and iteration-count curves across inlier ratios, angular-filter and normal-estimator comparisons, and sensitivity analyses for five parameters (Tables 4–6 and Figures 8–9).

E5.justification: Neither version reports experimental seed or repeated-run counts, confidence intervals, error bars or significance tests. V2's additional curves and average runtimes do not introduce uncertainty estimation.

E6.justification: V2 adds substantial baseline, runtime and robustness results. Existing values also change: DualReg's 3DLoMatch/FCGF recall changes from 60.47% to 60.86% and RMSE from 7.76 to 7.81 cm; TurboReg's 3DMatch/FPFH RMSE changes from 5.03 to 4.99 cm (v1 Tables I–II; v2 Table 1). Given the filtering-cutoff revision, the DualReg changes are revised reported results rather than established same-setting improvements.

M1.justification: Equations (1) and (5) tighten the length-consistency condition from DL < 2τ to DL < τ, while both versions specify τ as three times the point-cloud resolution. This is a limited reported filtering change. The one-point filtering, weighted three-point refinement, geometric proxies and dual-space optimization otherwise remain.

P1.justification: Substantial editing and compression accompany a reorganization into main text and supplementary sections. Detailed symmetry mathematics, pseudocode, refinement procedures, settings and extended benchmark discussion move to the supplement. Related-work and conclusion passages are rewritten, and section organization and terminology are revised.

P2.justification: V2 adopts a different document layout, merges the three benchmark tables into Table 1, reformats the ablation tables and relocates expanded qualitative comparison grids to the supplement. V1's tangential-distance schematic is removed. New runtime and robustness displays appear in Tables 4–6 and Figures 8–9.

R1.justification: V2 adds six references covering robust loss, iteratively reweighted least squares, Anderson acceleration, non-rigid registration and Open3D, with a limited expansion of the robust-estimation discussion. The central positioning against TCF and maximal-clique methods remains. Publication updates for existing citations are not new works.

T1.justification: The formal consensus-set definitions in Equations (1) and (5) change through the stricter length threshold. Beyond this limited mathematical revision, the reflection/SVD derivation and optimization formulation are retained, partly relocated to Supplement A; no new theorem or proof is introduced.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially strengthens empirical support by addressing validation gaps in v1: it evaluates learning-based comparators and directly examines normal-estimation choices and parameter dependence (Table 1, Tables 5–6 and Figure 9). Runtime breakdowns and hardware annotations also make efficiency claims easier to assess. These gains outweigh the loss of some limitations detail, although the unexplained cutoff revision prevents treating changed scores as clean performance improvements.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same DualReg research. Their text, equations, figures and tables are readable, including v2's supplementary material. Material relocated from v1's main text can be matched reliably to v2.

after.justification: V2 retains original benchmark experiments and ablations, and adds runtime, normal-estimation and parameter-sensitivity results in its supplement.

before.justification: V1 reports original registration experiments on 3DMatch, 3DLoMatch and KITTI, including quantitative comparisons and component ablations in Tables I–V.

results.title: DualReg: Dual-Space Filtering and Reinforcement for Rigid Registration

C1.justification: v1 presents improved camera-pose estimation as a headline contribution and emphasizes implications for annotation-free training of 3D foundation models. v2 removes that headline contribution and narrows the conclusion to marginal improvement of VGGT geometry. The central placement, compactness, and novel-view synthesis claims remain.

C2.justification: v2 adds limitations concerning view-dependent color, lighting variations, human subjects, and very thin geometry. It attributes DA3 rendering defects to transparency and focal-length inaccuracies and discusses compatibility with view-aggregation compression. The existing missing-surface limitation and supplementary depth-failure explanations largely remain.

D1.justification: v2 specifies grayscale histograms for entropy calculation and identifies the DA3 checkpoint version and parameter count. The median-depth rendering qualifier is omitted without a stated replacement procedure. Supplementary architecture details, softmax temperature, interpolation instructions, hardware disclosure, and project-page destination remain unchanged.

E1.justification: Training expands from six datasets to ten by adding WildRGBD, BlendedMVS, DTU, and KITTI360. Evaluation adds 7Scenes, SCRREAM, Tanks and Temples, and MipNeRF360 to DL3DV and Charge. SCRREAM also extends quantitative geometry evaluation, while the separate DL3DV focal-length evaluation disappears.

E2.justification: The main NVS comparison changes from AnySplat, FLARE, and VGGT+DepthSplat to AnySplat and DA3-GIANT-1.1. DA3 also joins the geometry comparison. Placement ablations add a SplatterImage-style pixel-plus-offset comparator and AnySplat. DepthSplat remains in the supplementary qualitative depth comparison.

E3.justification: v2 reports target-pose scale correction, which v1 explicitly omitted for its own model. DL3DV sampling changes from fixed frame spacing to uniform sequence sampling; image sizing changes from training-resolution inputs and 518×518 renders to maximum-dimension-518 resizing. Geometry reporting drops AUC@15, depth-threshold accuracy, focal-length MAE, and the angular-error threshold metric.

E4.justification: v2 Table 3 adds no-self-rendering and pixel-plus-offset controls, testing self-rendering and detection against alternative placement flexibility. Placement experiments now cover Tanks and Temples and MipNeRF360; the explicit two-resolution pixel-aligned comparison is removed. Existing adaptive-density/confidence results are retained in Table 4, and supplementary depth case studies remain.

E5.justification: Neither version reports experimental seeds, repeated-run counts, uncertainty intervals, or significance tests. Learned per-Gaussian confidence and averaging across view configurations do not constitute statistical uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: Tables 1–3 contain substantially revised and additional results. For Charge, v1 reports worse AbsRel than VGGT at every tested view count; v2 Table 2 reports 0.1609 versus 0.178. Changed training and evaluation prevent interpreting this as a same-setting gain. Focal-length results are partly removed, while v2 Table 4 exactly retains the earlier adaptive-density/confidence scores.

M1.justification: The VGGT backbone, U-Net decoder, DSNT-based placement, adaptive densities, confidence pruning, and training losses are retained. The added entropy formula explains an existing calculation. Pixel-plus-offset and no-self-rendering variants are experimental controls, not changes to the proposed full model.

P1.justification: v2 edits the abstract, introduction, and conclusion and reorganizes the experimental discussion: geometry evaluation moves inside the comparison subsection, and ablations separate placement from density/confidence. The focal-length appendix section is removed. Overall section progression and most method, related-work, and implementation prose remain recognizable.

P2.justification: Figure 1 becomes full-width. The main comparison and ablation image grids are replaced and expanded, while v1 Figure 7 moves to v2 Figure 6. Tables are substantially redesigned around dataset averages and separate ablation questions; the focal-length appendix tables disappear. The core architecture diagrams and supplementary Figure 9 are retained.

R1.justification: Targeted citations add the new datasets, DA3, ICO3D, Chroma, and Zpressor. Previously cited SplatterImage becomes an explicit alternative placement design. The related-work organization and central positioning against rigid primitive grids remain largely unchanged; the Charge publication update is bibliographic.

T1.justification: The DSNT expectation equation and mathematical loss definitions are retained. Writing out standard Shannon entropy elaborates the existing patch-entropy criterion; no new theorem, proof, formal assumption, or substantive derivation is introduced.

improvement.justification: The new learned-offset and no-self-rendering controls address important gaps in isolating the proposed placement mechanism and training design. Broader held-out evaluation and the DA3 comparison strengthen evidence for generality and competitiveness, while narrower geometry claims and concrete limitations improve calibration. Losing per-view and focal-length breakdowns and making tables much denser reduces reporting clarity, but the added experimental controls provide a substantial net improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Off-The-Grid research work. Their complete main texts, figures, tables, equations, and supplementary sections are readable, allowing retained, relocated, revised, and removed material to be matched.

after.justification: v2 reports original novel-view synthesis, geometry, and ablation results in Tables 1–4, including experiments on additional datasets and new component controls.

before.justification: v1 reports original novel-view synthesis, geometry, and ablation results in Tables 1–3, plus focal-length experiments in supplementary Tables 4–5.

results.title: Off The Grid: Detection of Primitives for Feed-Forward 3D Gaussian Splatting

C1.justification: The central contributions remain MeasureBench, controllable synthesis, evidence of fine-grained perception failures, and preliminary synthetic-data training gains with limited real-world transfer. Although v2's abstract describes transfer more positively, its introduction and conclusion retain the qualification. The expanded experiments principally strengthen evidence for the existing contribution scope.

C2.justification: v2 adds interpretations concerning SFT overfitting, limited benefits from procedural instructions, stronger RFT gains on simpler instruments, and mitigation of clock-time priors. The electricity-meter case changes from faulting left-to-right reading to accepting the procedure and attributing failure to pointer localization (v1 Appendix A.1 versus v2 D.1). It also removes v1's inference that similar model ordering establishes strong synthetic-to-real transferability.

D1.justification: v2 identifies FlagEvalMM for evaluation and verl for training, specifies GPT-5.2-generated SFT rationales, and discloses avoidance of real clock images showing 10:10 and uniform synthetic clock-time sampling. It also mentions code releases while retaining the project-page address. These disclosures do not establish changes to the existing dataset or implementation; the main GRPO hyperparameters remain unchanged.

E1.justification: v2 adds actual evaluations on MMMU, MMMU-Pro, MathVista, and TextVQA to test retention of broader capabilities (Table 5), substantially extending task coverage beyond instrument reading. MeasureBench itself retains the same 2,442 examples and instrument coverage; the synthetic-type count of 17 in v1 Section 2.4 becomes 16, consistent with Table 1 in both versions.

E2.justification: v2 introduces answer-only and rationale-based SFT as substantive training comparators to GRPO (Table 6). It also adds Qwen3-VL-8B to the main and thinking comparisons and GPT-4.1-Mini to prompt experiments. The traditional systems were already evaluated in v1 Appendix A.7; v2 Table 7 retains them and adds Qwen3-VL-8B to that comparison.

E3.justification: New protocols compare general versus instrument-specific prompts, with and without a precision suffix, excluding 10.53% of prompts deemed immutable. v2 also tests detailed instructions, two SFT response formats, and GRPO on Qwen2.5-VL-3B. The existing GRPO training budget remains 3,900 synthetic examples and 15 epochs. These additions do not establish that retained experiments used changed settings.

E4.justification: v2 adds prompt-sensitivity and instructional-guidance analyses, SFT-versus-GRPO transfer comparisons, checks for degradation on general benchmarks, per-instrument training gains, and a before/after analysis of the clock-time bias. Integer-output diagnostics expand across model families, while v1's [0,1] distribution panels are removed. The soft-margin ablation is retained in the appendix.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, or significance tests. The expanded numerical-output distributions describe model behavior rather than introducing uncertainty estimation for performance results.

E6.justification: New prompt, SFT, general-benchmark, and 3B-model results substantially expand the evidence. Retained scores also change: Gemini-2.5-Pro's real/synthetic overall accuracy becomes 30.2/26.3 instead of 30.3/26.1, and Qwen2.5-VL-7B becomes 14.6/10.9 instead of 15.5/11.0. Its GRPO real-world score changes from 20.1 to 19.7. Clock-bias and traditional-system results also change; the PDFs do not explain all revisions to retained scores.

M1.justification: The registry-based 2D/3D synthesis pipeline, GRPO procedure, correctness-plus-format reward, and soft-margin alternative remain substantively unchanged. Moving the soft-margin reward to Appendix A.2 and applying GRPO to another model size do not introduce a new proposed method.

P1.justification: The document undergoes substantial reorganization: the traditional-system comparison moves into Section 3.8, reward design and training results receive separate subsections, and the former Appendix A.1–A.7 is reorganized into Appendices A–F. The introduction and synthesis description are condensed and rewritten, and distribution analysis is redistributed between the main text and appendices.

P2.justification: v1 Tables 2 and 3 are merged into v2 Table 2, and the synthesis schematic and example figures are combined. v2 adds experimental tables and an instrument-gain bar chart, redraws distribution plots, reorders the category heatmap, and revises electricity-meter annotations. These are substantial display changes beyond renumbering and numerical updates.

R1.justification: v2 adds references for FlagEvalMM and HybridFlow, plus formal citations for previously discussed benchmarks including MMBench, MM-Vet, SEED-Bench, MathVision, and MathVerse. The central positioning against fragmented, instrument-specific evaluations remains substantially unchanged.

T1.justification: v2 rewrites the existing reward using indicator notation and alpha = 0.9, while retaining the same interval-distance, margin, and partial-credit definitions. Relocating the soft-margin equations does not change their mathematics. No new theorem, proof, or substantive derivation is introduced.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens empirical support by testing alternative explanations that v1 left largely unexamined: prompt wording, procedural guidance, and whether synthetic-data gains depend on GRPO rather than SFT (Tables 3, 4, and 6). General-benchmark checks and another trained model size further strengthen the training analysis. These gains outweigh localized reporting weaknesses: Table 7 repeats full-benchmark VLM scores despite describing a dial-meter subset, leaving comparison scope unclear, and Section 3.6 claims no degradation although Table 5 shows small MathVista and TextVQA declines.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same MeasureBench study. Their text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices are readable and support matching retained, relocated, and revised content.

after.justification: v2 retains original empirical evaluations and adds prompt experiments, supervised fine-tuning comparisons, general-benchmark evaluations, and GRPO results for a 3B model.

before.justification: v1 reports original evaluations of 17 VLMs, thinking-mode comparisons, GRPO training experiments, numerical-output analyses, and tests of traditional gauge-reading systems.

results.title: Do Vision-Language Models Measure Up? Benchmarking Visual Measurement Reading with MeasureBench

C1.justification: Both versions claim unsupervised monocular 3D keypoint discovery using multi-view diffusion priors, explicit volumetric features, broad generalization, and manipulation of generated objects. The added bird experiments support these existing contributions rather than redefine their scope.

C2.justification: v1's diffusion-quality and computational-cost limitations are expanded into specific failure cases and measured tradeoffs. v2 adds left-right ambiguity, qualifications about CUB preprocessing comparability, and explanations concerning affine-training shortcuts, visibility errors, and accuracy versus keypoint interpretability. v1's limitation about masking discarding scene context is omitted.

D1.justification: Appendix D supplies layer structures, channels, activations, resolutions, reconstruction conditioning, loss weighting, dataset-specific masking and cropping, and inverse coordinate mapping beyond v1's brief implementation paragraph. Appendix A identifies the preprocessing source and controlled baseline reproduction setup, while Table 6 specifies measurement hardware. v2 omits v1's promise of a future code release.

E1.justification: v2 adds training and evaluation on CUB-200-2011 birds, including aligned and unaligned images and projected 2D keypoint assessment. Human3.6M, Stanford Dogs, DAVIS, GSO, and AP-10K remain. The bird experiments substantially broaden the represented morphology and quantitative evaluation coverage.

E2.justification: v2 adds nine 2D comparison methods to the CUB evaluation, including SCOPS, GANSeg, AutoLink, and StableKeypoints (Table 2). It also adds CLIP and DINOv2 feature comparisons and BKinD-3D qualitative comparisons. The Human3.6M comparator membership in Table 1 remains unchanged.

E3.justification: v2 introduces image-size-normalized 2D evaluation on CUB-align and CUB-all, matched-preprocessing baseline retraining, controlled sensitivity protocols, and A6000 timing comparisons. Appendix D.3 reports SAM prompted by provided Human3.6M keypoints and Grounded-SAM2 for animals, revising v1's general Grounded SAM description, although v2's main text retains that older description. These disclosures do not establish rerunning the retained experiments.

E4.justification: Beyond v1's feature-extractor and view-count ablations, v2 examines triangulation versus volumetric prediction, additional backbones, keypoint counts, diffusion timesteps, training-set sizes, affine augmentation, camera perturbations, and visibility-based aggregation. Appendices B-C also add concrete failure cases and computational-cost analysis (Tables 3, 5-6; Figures 8-9).

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run or seed counts, confidence intervals, error bars, or significance tests. The Gaussian camera-noise levels in v2 are robustness-test settings, not estimates of result uncertainty.

E6.justification: Human3.6M Table 1 errors remain unchanged, but v2 adds substantial results: CUB-align error 5.16, CUB-all errors 7.7 with four keypoints and 5.5 with ten, plus new ablation, timing, and qualitative findings. The three-view P-MPJPE changes from 86.95 in v1 Table 2 to 86.59 in v2 Table 3. The ResNet-linear ablation row is omitted.

M1.justification: The core diffusion-feature, volumetric keypoint, and animation pipelines remain. Appendix D.1 adds a rotation-based view-invariant consistency loss, weighted 0.1, for Stanford Dogs and CUB. This extends the stated training objective beyond v1's VGG reconstruction and mask losses without replacing the central method.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and related-work discussion are extensively reworded, especially the distinction between generated supervision and intermediate feature extraction. Experiments are reorganized into separate 3D, animal, and generalization sections, and the limitations discussion is redistributed into expanded appendix analyses. Author and acknowledgment text also changes.

P2.justification: v2 adopts a two-column layout, moves Figure 1 to the first page, redraws the pipeline, replaces the Human3.6M qualitative display with baseline comparisons, and reorganizes animal/generalization panels. It restructures the ablation table and adds CUB, failure-case, sensitivity, computational, and appendix-gallery displays.

R1.justification: v2 adds targeted references for bird-keypoint comparisons, ResNet, CLIP, DINOv2, V2V-PoseNet, and preprocessing resources, and removes the Xinyu Yu et al. temporal-consistency reference. The central positioning as extending diffusion-based keypoint discovery to 3D without calibrated multi-view training remains.

T1.justification: Appendix D.1 newly defines the consistency objective as the average squared discrepancy between original and rotated-volume keypoint projections. The existing projection, aggregation, integral-regression, and skinning mathematics is retained. No theorem, proof, or substantial theoretical analysis is added.

improvement.justification: v1 provides mainly qualitative evidence beyond Human3.6M and limited diagnostic and reproducibility detail. v2 substantially strengthens the empirical basis through controlled CUB baseline reproductions, targeted robustness analyses, concrete failure cases, measured computational costs, and detailed implementation instructions. These gains improve evaluation and auditability despite unchanged main Human3.6M scores. An important unresolved qualification remains: Appendix D.3's use of provided Human3.6M keypoints needs reconciliation with the annotation-free claims and main-text preprocessing description.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same KeyDiff3D work, with matching core methods and experiments. Their text, equations, tables, and figures support reliable comparison. The supplied v1 ends after its references; v2 includes Appendices A-E and additional qualitative figures, all inspected.

after.justification: v2 reports original Human3.6M and CUB experiments, baseline reproductions, robustness tests, computational measurements, and qualitative results throughout the main text and appendices.

before.justification: v1 reports original Human3.6M measurements and ablations in Tables 1-2, alongside qualitative keypoint, generalization, and object-manipulation results.

results.title: Unsupervised Monocular 3D Keypoint Discovery from Multi-View Diffusion Priors

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the same core contributions: POMDP-inspired recurrent conditioning, active visual attention, strong benchmark performance, and transfer to real-world manipulation. The new supporting experiments do not redefine these claims or their scope.

C2.justification: v3 adds substantive interpretations concerning architectural benefits versus additional training, complementary component roles across task horizons, and the regularizer's role in suppressing distracting attention. New Appendix E attributes precision-sensitive failures to accumulated perception errors and belief drift, connects this limitation to long-horizon pruning sensitivity, and discusses possible remedies. v1 lacks this explicit limitations analysis.

D1.justification: v3 supplies a project-page link, reports that the added modules contain fewer than 50 million parameters and under 1% of the full model, and documents the new matched-training settings. The existing architecture descriptions, hardware, principal hyperparameters, and real-robot implementation details are retained.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate the same four LIBERO suites, CALVIN ABC-to-D setting, seven LIBERO+ perturbation dimensions, and four Mobile ALOHA tasks. The new ablations and failure cases use this existing coverage rather than introducing another dataset, domain, or test scenario.

E2.justification: v3 adds VLA-Adapter to the CALVIN comparison in Table 2, reporting an average completed length of 4.42. The existing benchmark and real-robot comparator sets otherwise remain intact. Newly discussed methods such as MemoryVLA are not added as evaluated baselines.

E3.justification: New Table 7 introduces a controlled LIBERO comparison: both methods start from the same pretrained OpenVLA checkpoint and train for 100,000 steps with batch size 256. This supplements the retained main recipe, which initializes AVA-VLA from trained OpenVLA-OFT and fine-tunes for 40,000 steps with batch size 64. Existing task splits, metrics, and real-robot trial counts remain unchanged.

E4.justification: v3 adds analyses of the extra-training confound (Table 7), the attention regularizer (Table 8 and Figure 12), component contributions on CALVIN (Table 9), and manipulation failures (Figure 13). These substantially expand the questions investigated. The LIBERO+ robustness study and earlier attention visualizations are retained and relocated, not newly introduced.

E5.justification: Neither version reports training-seed counts, repeated-run variability, confidence intervals, or significance tests. Both use point estimates, and the stated real-robot trial counts are unchanged. The added experiments do not introduce uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: Table 1 revises AVA-VLA's per-suite-policy Goal score from 98.2% to 97.9% and its average from 98.3% to 98.2%. Table 2 revises OpenVLA-OFT's CALVIN average from 4.10 to 4.28; AVA-VLA remains at 4.65. New results include 98.3% versus 96.8% under matched training, 97.5% without the regularizer versus 98.0% with it, and CALVIN component-only averages of 4.63 and 4.61. These additions substantially expand the findings; the matched-training result is not a same-setting improvement over the earlier main experiment.

M1.justification: Sections 3.1–3.4 and Appendix A retain the recurrent-state construction, state-based action initialization, AVA architecture, attention reweighting, training losses, and inference procedure. The additional experiments test existing components and alternative training conditions without revising the proposed method.

P1.justification: The abstract and conclusion are rewritten, introductory and technical prose is polished, and explanations of component roles are expanded. The supplement gains dedicated discussion and limitations sections, while execution trajectories move into Appendix B. The main five-section narrative and most technical exposition remain recognizable.

P2.justification: The manuscript changes from a predominantly single-column preprint layout to a two-column layout, with extensive table and figure resizing and relocation. v1 Figure 4 becomes supplementary Figure 6, and the existing attention figures are redistributed. v3 also adds Tables 7–9, a robot-platform image, regularizer visualization, and failure-case panels, and expands several captions.

R1.justification: New Appendix C substantially expands positioning beyond v1's general VLA and sequential-VLM discussion. It distinguishes AVA-VLA from MemoryVLA's explicit memory retrieval and discusses its relationship to VLN-BERT, SafeVLA, NaVid, and recurrent reinforcement-learning approaches. These are substantive comparisons concerning memory representation and visual processing, alongside additional citations such as VLA-Adapter.

T1.justification: The POMDP formulation, recurrent-state definition, attention equations, and loss definitions in Equations 1–14 remain substantively unchanged. Notational corrections and expanded explanations introduce no new assumptions, derivations, theorems, or proofs.

improvement.justification: v1's main training recipe leaves additional training as a plausible explanation for AVA-VLA's advantage. v3 substantially strengthens attribution through the common-initialization, matched-budget comparison in Table 7. The regularizer and CALVIN ablations test previously underexamined design choices, while failure cases and explicit limitations provide a more balanced account of applicability. These gains materially improve empirical support and transparency despite unchanged uncertainty reporting and unexplained revisions to some existing scores.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same AVA-VLA work. All 18 pages of v1 and 19 pages of v3, including appendices, support comparison. Text, equations, tables, and figures can be matched despite substantial reformatting and relocation.

after.justification: v3 retains original simulation and real-robot results and adds matched-training comparisons, regularizer and CALVIN component ablations, and qualitative failure cases.

before.justification: v1 reports original AVA-VLA experiments on LIBERO, CALVIN, LIBERO+, and Mobile ALOHA, including benchmark results, component ablations, and token-pruning analyses.

results.title: AVA-VLA: Improving Vision-Language-Action models with Active Visual Attention

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction and conclusion shift the central model contribution from sequence-length guidance to fine-detail/local-context encoding and accelerated decoding. Accuracy–speed tradeoffs and configurable model sizes become central claims, while the UniMER dataset contribution and broad real-world recognition claims remain.

C2.justification: v1 explains improvements through length guidance; v2 emphasizes local/global features, redundant shifted windows and decoder computational bottlenecks. New interpretations address depth saturation, Squeeze Attention's accuracy–speed tradeoff, and weaker handwriting benefits from predominantly printed-text pretraining.

D1.justification: The new appendix documents collection-source proportions, perceptual-hash deduplication, fonts, 80–350 DPI rendering, a XeLaTeX template, normalization and augmentation implementation. v2 also specifies model configurations, pretraining-data construction and an additional dataset-access link. Much of the dataset documentation elaborates the existing pipeline rather than establishing changed data.

E1.justification: The UniMER formula-training sources and four evaluation categories remain. However, v2 newly reports training with 16 million text-image pairs extracted from arXiv papers, extending training coverage from formula recognition to general text-block recognition through pretraining (Table 6).

E2.justification: v2 adds Texify* trained on UniMER-1M with matching augmentation, plus controlled Texify pretraining comparisons. It removes v1 Table 6's comparison against DWAP, DWAP-MSA, BTTR, CoMER, CAN-DWAP, CAN-ABM and SAN. Original Pix2tex/Texify comparisons and qualitative Nougat examples remain.

E3.justification: Reported defaults change from 1024 to 1536 maximum sequence length, 180,000 to 300,000 iterations, and four to eight training GPUs. v2 adds model-size/depth configurations, pretraining controls and throughput testing on an A100 with batch size 128. The separate handwriting evaluation using ExpRate and one-/two-edit tolerances disappears.

E4.justification: The LAM ablation is replaced by component ablations for the revised architecture. v2 adds pretraining ablations, encoder/decoder depth sweeps and dataset symbol-frequency/image-size analyses. Training-source and augmentation ablations remain, with the latter relocated to the appendix and reporting revised results.

E5.justification: Neither version reports random seeds, repeated-run counts, standard deviations, confidence intervals or significance tests. Experimental results remain point estimates.

E6.justification: Table 5 replaces v1 UniMERNet's CPE/HWE BLEU scores of 0.916/0.921 with UniMERNet-B scores of 0.925/0.895 under revised architecture and training; these are not same-setting gains or losses. v2 adds model-scale, throughput, pretraining and depth results, and removes dedicated handwriting results. Original Pix2tex/Texify scores remain unchanged.

M1.justification: v1's Length-Aware Module, length embeddings and auxiliary length-prediction loss disappear. v2 introduces Fine-Grained Embedding, convolutional enhancement, removal of shifted-window operations and Squeeze Attention in the decoder, substantially revising the architecture and objective.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, dataset description, methods and experimental narrative undergo extensive rewriting. CNN and Transformer related-work subsections are merged, and augmentation material moves into a new appendix alongside expanded dataset documentation and architecture analyses.

P2.justification: The document changes from single-column to two-column layout, replaces the architecture diagram, restyles retained figures and expands comparison tables with parameter counts and throughput. New dataset-distribution plots, an augmentation gallery, a rendering listing and additional ablation tables substantially change the presentation.

R1.justification: Most MER related-work coverage remains. v2 adds convolution/Transformer references such as CMT and ConViT, and newer resources including DocGenome, MMSci and OpenDataLab. The LAM comparison with counting-aware recognition and several backbone/handwriting references disappear, but the overall research framing remains recognizable.

T1.justification: v1's joint language/length objective and piecewise SmoothL1 length-loss definitions disappear (Equations 1 and 3), while cross-entropy is retained as v2 Equation 1. This is a limited revision of formal loss definitions; neither version contains theoretical proofs.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens the evidence separating architecture benefits from training-data effects through matched-data Texify comparisons and shared-pretraining controls (Tables 5–6). Component/depth studies and throughput measurements support its revised claims, while the appendix resolves important gaps in dataset-construction documentation. Removing the specialist handwriting comparison weakens that aspect of evaluation, but the improvements in experimental attribution and reproducibility outweigh this loss.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same UniMER dataset and UniMERNet research work. Their text, equations, figures and tables support comparison, including v2's appendix. v1 has no separate appendix.

after.justification: v2 reports original recognition experiments, architecture and pretraining ablations, throughput measurements, and appendix studies of encoder and decoder depth.

before.justification: v1 reports original dataset, augmentation and Length-Aware Module ablations, UniMER-Test results, and CROHME/HME100K evaluations in Tables 2–6.

results.title: UniMERNet: A Universal Network for Real-World Mathematical Expression Recognition

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction and conclusion retain the same central claims: retrieval adaptation degrades native compositional reasoning, the model-agnostic ReCALL pipeline recalibrates it, and ReCALL achieves state-of-the-art CIRR/FashionIQ performance. Additional evidence does not redefine these contributions.

C2.justification: v2 adds explanations concerning shared versus model-specific blind spots, semantic correction versus negative repulsion, capacity-related overfitting and distribution preservation. Unlike v1's success-focused discussion, Section 8.3 examines sparse annotations, ambiguous instructions and residual spatial-rotation failures, including possible inherited backbone weaknesses.

D1.justification: v2 supplies full retrieval, verification and generation prompts, structured output requirements, a filtering confidence threshold, and stage-specific runtime and generated/retained sample counts. Its abstract also replaces the promised future code release with a stated repository address. These substantially extend v1's implementation documentation.

E1.justification: Both versions use CIRR and FashionIQ for composed image retrieval. The supplementary studies examine the same benchmark data and generated triplets; additional backbones, parameter settings and quality checks do not introduce a new retrieval domain or test scenario.

E2.justification: The main benchmark comparator sets in Tables 1–2 are unchanged. v2 adds CIRR comparisons against Random Mining and Hard Neg. Mining (No Edit) in Table 7; v1's mining comparison covered Random Mining on FashionIQ only.

E3.justification: Primary benchmark protocols remain stable, but the supplement adds substantial experimental designs: K=1–5 scaling without VQA filtering and using InfoNCE, a loss-weight/margin grid, LLaVA-NeXT transfer settings, larger LoRA ranks and full fine-tuning, and three human evaluators checking 300 filtered triplets.

E4.justification: Beyond v1's mining/component ablations and Qwen backbone comparison, v2 adds data-scale and hyperparameter sensitivity studies, computational analysis, cross-family transfer, direct hard-negative and capacity controls, and human validation of filtering. Sections 8.1–8.3 also add retrieval, synthesis and failure-case analyses.

E5.justification: Both versions report four-seed means and standard deviations for Random Mining in Table 3. The new studies provide point estimates without additional repeated-run reporting, confidence intervals, significance tests or inter-rater agreement statistics.

E6.justification: Main-table results remain unchanged, including ReCALL's CIRR R@1 of 55.52% and FashionIQ average R@10 of 57.04%. Substantial new results include LLaVA R@1 of 51.93% baseline, 53.08% with transferred data and 54.65% with the full pipeline, plus scaling, sensitivity, capacity, runtime and 92% human-validated triplet accuracy results.

M1.justification: The adaptation, failure mining, CoT-based minimal editing, VQA filtering and grouped refinement pipeline remains unchanged, including the InfoNCE-plus-triplet objective. The supplement documents prompts and evaluates variants without establishing a revision to the proposed method.

P1.justification: The retained narrative receives grammar edits, more consistent informative-instance terminology and a shortened conclusion, while Sections 1–5 preserve their organization. Author/affiliation details and acknowledgments change. New supplementary sections organize added material rather than substantially restructuring the original argument.

P2.justification: v2 adds Tables 5–8 and Figures 5–15, including scaling plots, a sensitivity heatmap, prompt panels, retrieval failures and synthesis walkthroughs. The original backbone and qualitative figures are retained but renumbered and relocated from the references area into the experimental presentation.

R1.justification: v2 adds citations including TRACE, TiGER and WISER, and removes Anwaar et al.'s compositional-learning reference. The relationship to prior MLLM retrieval and self-improvement work remains substantially unchanged; many other reference edits concern metadata or duplicate consolidation.

T1.justification: The task formulation and loss equations (1)–(3) retain their mathematical content. The supplement adds empirical analyses and qualitative reasoning, without new formal assumptions, propositions, proofs or derivations.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially improves evidential support and reproducibility through direct mining/capacity controls, cross-family transfer, human validation, full prompts, cost reporting and explicit failure analysis. These address important omissions in v1 without relying on higher headline scores. Some causal explanations remain inferential, and the new FashionIQ filtering count is inconsistent: Section 6.3 reports 5,947 removals, whereas Table 5 implies 5,970. These limitations do not outweigh the gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same ReCALL framework and retain matching core experiments. Text, equations, tables and figures support comparison. v1 ends with references; v2 additionally contains readable supplementary Sections 6–8.

after.justification: v2 retains those original results and adds scaling, transfer, model-capacity and human triplet-validation results in its supplement.

before.justification: v1 reports original CIRR and FashionIQ retrieval results, mining and component ablations, backbone comparisons and qualitative retrieval examples.

results.title: ReCALL: Recalibrating Capability Degradation for MLLM-based Composed Image Retrieval

C1.justification: The abstract narrows the novelty statement from AR watermarking being unexplored to underexplored. The contributions and conclusion now include token prediction alongside cluster prediction and explicitly claim superiority to concurrent AR methods, including WMAR. The central claim that clustering improves robustness while preserving image quality remains.
