C2.justification: V2 attributes unfavorable-prefix false positives to repetitive token transitions in uniform image regions. It develops v1's geometric limitation into an explanation involving spatial synchronization and recoverability. New Appendix D introduces private-model/API deployment assumptions and discusses prefix-search security and larger key spaces, substantially expanding applicability boundaries and security qualifications.

D1.justification: V2 supplies a ClusterMark source-code link instead of v1's future-release promise. Appendices A–B clarify tuning/test sample separation and image reuse, add baseline implementation details such as TrustMark configuration Q, and specify the CLIP text template. These are documentation and access-information additions; they do not establish that previously unspecified settings changed. The existing classifier training budget remains.

E1.justification: The ImageNet class-conditioned image coverage remains unchanged, but v2 adds a substantial family of geometric test scenarios: translation, cropping, flipping, perspective, rotation, scaling and combined scaling/blur (Tables 8–10). V1 discussed geometric vulnerability without reporting these evaluations.

E2.justification: Table 1 adds TrustMark and SSL for all three models and WMAR (FT+AUGS) for RAR-XL, while removing DWT-DCT. IndexMark (+IE), DWT-DCT-SVD and RivaGAN remain in the main comparison. Appendix Table 7 separately removes all its post-hoc comparator rows, including DWT-DCT-SVD and RivaGAN.

E3.justification: Figure 3 switches from weak perturbation Set A to stronger Set B. Figure 5 changes the model, prefixes, green fraction and perturbations used for the prefix analysis. New protocols include CLIP evaluation on 50,000 images and inverse-transformation/SyncSeal controls. TrustMark uses its built-in detection procedure rather than the empirical ROC procedure used for other methods.

E4.justification: V2 adds token-classifier comparisons with and without clustering, geometric failure and recovery controls, sensitivity to cluster initialization, and CLIP-based analysis of semantic fidelity. The revised prefix case study includes an image and token-pattern example to investigate false positives. These substantially extend v1's cluster-count, watermark-strength, green-fraction and prefix ablations.

E5.justification: V2 reports variation across six cluster initializations in Table 6 and newly discloses consistent generation seeds across experiments. Eight-prefix averages and standard-deviation bands already existed in v1 and remain for training-free plots. However, v1's detailed Tables 8–9 of prefix-wise AUC/TPR means and standard deviations, including cluster-classifier variability, are removed.

E6.justification: V2 adds extensive classifier, baseline, geometric, CLIP and runtime results and revises multiple Table 1 estimates. For example, RAR-XL's training-free 64-cluster blur TPR is 0.163 in v1 and 0.100 in v2; the revised test-sample documentation prevents treating this as an established controlled performance decline. Own-method Set A values in Table 7 remain unchanged, while its baseline rows and the old prefix-summary tables disappear.

M1.justification: Section 3.3 adds a token classifier trained with token-label cross-entropy, whose predictions can subsequently be mapped to clusters. V1 trained only a direct cluster classifier. This extends the reconstruction component while retaining the core k-means clustering, green-set construction and biased sampling procedure.

P1.justification: V2 extensively revises prose across the abstract, method explanation, evaluation discussion and conclusion, adopts ClusterMark/KGW terminology, and reorganizes the experimental setup and appendix explanations. The title, author information and acknowledgements also change. The broad main-section order remains, but the editorial revision extends well beyond isolated corrections.

P2.justification: The pipeline diagram is redrawn, the prefix figure gains image/token illustrations, and a main-text sample montage is introduced. Main comparison tables expand, runtime presentation changes to milliseconds, and perturbation-setting tables are merged. New CLIP and robustness displays accompany removal of the old prefix-summary tables and substantial appendix reformatting; retained sample galleries are largely relocated and renumbered.

R1.justification: V2 adds references and context for TrustMark, SSL, SyncSeal, CLIPScore, BitMark, Safe-VAR and watermark attacks. Section 5 refines comparisons with IndexMark and WMAR, including the distinction concerning decoder fine-tuning. WMAR was already discussed in v1; its new experimental participation is separate from these positioning changes.

T1.justification: Section 2.2 corrects the formal rejection condition from rejecting when the p-value exceeds the threshold to rejecting when it is below the threshold, explicitly identifying the right-tailed probability. V1's algorithm already computed a right-tailed p-value, so this establishes a correction to the stated mathematics rather than an implemented detector change. No new theorem or proof is introduced.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially strengthens the evidence by comparing against WMAR and additional post-hoc methods, isolating clustering's contribution with a trained-token control, and testing the geometric failure conditions that v1 only discussed. Clearer tuning/test documentation and code-access information further improve assessability. These gains outweigh the loss of detailed prefix statistics and some overgeneralized summaries: notably, the claimed 99+% SyncSeal recovery has a 95.1% GPT-L scaling result in Table 10.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same cluster-based watermarking research for autoregressive image generators. Their complete text, equations, tables, figures and appendices support comparison despite the ClusterMark renaming and substantial revision.

after.justification: Original experiments remain and are extended with token-classifier comparisons, additional baselines, CLIP scores, geometric-transformation tests and cluster-initialization analyses.

before.justification: Section 4 and the appendices report original watermark-detection, image-quality, runtime and ablation results for LlamaGen GPT-B, GPT-L and RAR-XL.

results.title: ClusterMark: Towards Robust Watermarking for Autoregressive Image Generators with Visual Token Clustering

C1.justification: The central contributions remain a semantically aligned MLLM-generated misinformation benchmark and an efficient AMD framework for detection, grounding and generalization. v2 adds numerical highlights to the abstract and contribution list, but these substantiate retained claims rather than introduce a different core contribution.

C2.justification: v2 qualifies dataset difficulty through size-controlled comparisons, explains limited transfer to untampered but mismatched COSMOS pairs, and discusses persistent FA&TF/TF failures and possible retrieval-based remedies (Appendices C, H and M). This substantially expands the interpretation beyond v1's brief celebrity-face scope limitation and general performance discussion.

D1.justification: Appendices D–E add full prompts, coordinate conventions, baseline adaptations, hardware, image preprocessing, batch size, optimizer, learning-rate schedule and training duration. Appendix L documents head-shot sourcing and filtering. v1 supplied mainly the backbone, frozen encoder and token count. Both versions still promise future code release.

E1.justification: Evaluation expands beyond MDSM and DGM4 to COSMOS, MiRAGe, DiFF and DiffFace, plus diffusion-based face editing, background modification and full-image generation (Appendices H–I). v2 also evaluates missing-modality and non-aligned inputs and introduces a human participant study.

E2.justification: Table 9 adds fine-tuned Qwen2.5-VL-3B and -7B comparisons on MDSM; v1 evaluated Qwen2.5-VL only zero-shot. This is a focused comparator addition. The original ViLT, HAMMER, HAMMER++, FKA-Owl and zero-shot comparator rows remain.

E3.justification: New designs include a 100-pair study with 15 volunteers, size-matched dataset comparisons including a 103k-sample Guardian subset, cross-dataset transfer, and two-epoch LoRA fine-tuning of Qwen models (Appendices A, C, G–J). Newly disclosed settings for the retained AMD experiments do not establish that their protocols changed.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained component and cross-MLLM analyses, v2 tests token length, knowledge-preservation strategies, TRP placement, modality removal and semantic alignment. It adds corpus analysis, diffusion robustness tests, token visualizations and concrete failure cases (Tables 5–8 and 11–15; Figures 5 and 11–14).

E5.justification: Appendix K.2 newly specifies averaging token representations over 100 samples per group, with three independent groups per manipulation class, to reduce sampling randomness. This is limited statistical aggregation for visualizations. Neither version reports training seeds, repeated-training variability, confidence intervals or significance tests.

E6.justification: Tables 2–4 retain their numerical results, but v2 adds extensive outcomes in Tables 5–15 and new figures. For example, Table 9 reports 72.00 average ACC for NYT-trained Qwen2.5-VL-7B, and Table 10 reports AMD's 54.08 average cross-dataset ACC. These are newly reported experiments, not improvements to the original scores.

M1.justification: AMD retains artifact tokens, frozen pre-perception encoding, manipulation-oriented reasoning, auxiliary losses, TRP and textual inference. The fuller prompts and dataset-construction descriptions document existing procedures rather than establish a changed method. Diffusion and non-alignment variants serve as experimental conditions.

P1.justification: v2 substantially reorganizes the explanatory material: dataset construction is rewritten by manipulation category, related work is expanded, quantitative discussion is condensed, and experimental setup moves into a structured A–M appendix with a contents list. The method and conclusion remain largely verbatim.

P2.justification: Figure 1 is revised and placed before the abstract, Figure 2 is extensively redrawn, and Table 1 gains a dataset row and training-support column. New Figures 5–14 and Tables 5–15 add visualizations, comparisons and cases, substantially expanding the presentation beyond relocation or numerical edits.

R1.justification: Related work adds a focused comparison with MMFakeBench and elaborates FKA-Owl's task and computational limitations. Supporting references expand to diffusion benchmarks, corpus tools, visualization and celebrity resources. The principal positioning around semantically aligned, MLLM-driven misinformation remains intact.

T1.justification: The mathematical formulation and Equations 1–10 are retained, including attention pooling, auxiliary objectives and TRP. The appendices add empirical analyses and metric explanations, without new formal assumptions, theorems, proofs or substantive derivations.

improvement.justification: v1 lacked human validation, evaluation beyond MDSM/DGM4 and substantial reproduction details. v2 addresses these gaps with human evaluation, size and alignment controls, fine-tuned comparators, transfer tests, failure analysis and detailed prompts/settings. These additions substantially strengthen empirical scrutiny and reproducibility. Some new reporting is imprecise—for example, Appendix G calls Table 9's domain-average accuracies in-domain—and performance uncertainty remains unquantified, but these limitations do not outweigh the gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same MDSM dataset and AMD framework. Their text, equations, tables and figures support reliable comparison. v1 ends with references and has no separate appendix; v2 includes readable appendices A–M.

after.justification: v2 retains those experiments and adds original human evaluation, controlled comparisons, transfer experiments, ablations and failure analyses.

before.justification: Tables 2–4 report original MDSM/DGM4 experiments, component ablations and evaluations across narrative-generating MLLMs.

results.title: The Coherence Trap: When MLLM-Crafted Narratives Exploit Manipulated Visual Contexts

C1.justification: V1 foregrounds VGBench as the first dedicated visual-geometry benchmark, the 28K SpatialScore collection and Hard subset, and SpatialAgent. V2 redefines the central contributions around a curated 30-task benchmark, the 331K SpatialCorpus training resource, and complementary fine-tuning and expanded agent approaches. VGBench and SpatialScore-Hard cease to be separately claimed contributions.

C2.justification: V2 attributes larger fine-tuning gains on Repurpose to training-distribution alignment, discusses potential forgetting and uneven task improvements, and adds limitations concerning SpatialCorpus diversity. It also interprets measured failure rates as evidence of ReAct's greater stability. The RGB-input and rudimentary-toolbox limitations already existed in v1; their relocation to Section 7 is not a new limitation.

D1.justification: V2 documents the new fine-tuning recipe: one epoch, batch size 512, learning rate 1e-5, 3% warm-up, and a frozen visual encoder. It expands construction templates, distractor rules, scoring prompts, and tool specifications, and reports eight rather than four A100 GPUs. Explicit code and dataset links are added, although the PDFs do not establish actual resource availability.

E1.justification: Coverage expands from 11 integrated datasets to 23, adding tasks such as maze navigation, paper folding, mental rotation, velocity estimation, and size compatibility. V2 also introduces real-world and simulated training coverage through SpatialCorpus. Geometry tasks persist within the repurposed data; that component adds Omni3D and PointOdyssey and stops sourcing ScanNet.

E2.justification: V2 adds evaluated comparators including Qwen3-VL, InternVL3.5, SpaceThinker, and SpaceR, while Cambrian-8B and SpatialBot-Phi2 disappear from the quantitative comparisons. Proprietary comparisons shift from GPT-4o, Claude-3.5-Haiku, and Gemini-2.0-Flash to newer systems. Human, random, and text-only baselines are also added.

E3.justification: V1's 28,093 samples and 1,400-sample Hard subset give way to 5,025 samples selected using text-only filtering and manual verification. SpatialScore numerical scoring changes from factor-two tolerance to MRA with parser/LLM score averaging; MRA already appeared in v1's separate VSI-Bench evaluation. Video sampling changes from eight frames by default to 32 for open models and 16/8 for proprietary models. The agent token limit increases from 2,048 to 4,096.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained Figure 4 cases, v2 adds annotation-error examples (Figure 5), analyses of fine-tuning versus agent generalization across OpenSource and Repurpose subsets (Appendix C.1), quantitative reasoning-failure analysis (Appendix B.3), and new qualitative cases (Figures 9–10). These provide substantial new evidence about data quality, distribution dependence, and agent reliability.

E5.justification: Both versions specify a fixed random seed and deterministic decoding. Neither reports repeated-run variability, confidence intervals, or significance tests. V2's human-participant count and agent failure percentages do not introduce uncertainty estimation.

E6.justification: The original benchmark and source-dataset result tables are replaced by results for the redesigned benchmark and new training/agent comparisons. For example, v2 Table 3 reports Qwen3-VL-8B scores of 45.48 zero-shot, 54.71 after fine-tuning, and 53.81 with ReAct; Table 2 adds human performance of 86.60. These are newly reported results under revised conditions, not direct gains over v1's scores.

M1.justification: V2 adds supervised fine-tuning on SpatialCorpus using cross-entropy, absent from v1. SpatialAgent retains Plan-Execute and ReAct but substantially changes its toolbox: Rex-Omni replaces OWLv2 localization and supports counting, while DetAny3D and MapAnything add 3D detection and metric-distance capabilities (Sections 3.2–3.4).

P1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction, contribution narrative, and substantial portions of the main text are rewritten. Baseline evaluation moves into the benchmark section, methodology is reorganized around two improvement approaches, limitations move into the main text, and six appendix sections are reorganized into three. This exceeds renaming or routine editing.

P2.justification: V2 redraws the overview, construction pipeline, toolbox diagram, and dataset-flow visualization. Result tables adopt new task columns, grouping, rankings, and highlighting; benchmark-comparison, annotation-error, and additional qualitative displays are added. Figure 4 is substantially retained and relocated, while the document typography, prompt boxes, and page layout are extensively reformatted.

R1.justification: V2 substantially expands engagement with recent spatial benchmarks, training approaches, and perception tools, including SpatialEval, OmniSpatial, SPAR-Bench, MMSI-Bench, Rex-Omni, and MapAnything. The new benchmark-comparison Table 1 and revised related work position the contribution as a comprehensive evaluation and improvement framework, replacing the earlier emphasis on VGBench's visual-geometry novelty.

T1.justification: The Plan-Execute and ReAct mathematical formulations remain equivalent apart from notation and explicit backbone bookkeeping. Neither version develops theorems or proofs. V2's standard fine-tuning description and MRA scoring instructions add method and evaluation documentation rather than substantive mathematical reasoning.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially strengthens evaluation validity through annotation-error auditing, visual-dependence filtering, full-set manual verification, and explicit human/text-only controls, addressing weaknesses left open in v1. Detailed fine-tuning experiments, source-dependent generalization analysis, and quantified agent failures also deepen the evidence beyond headline accuracy. These gains outweigh the loss of source-by-source result tables. Some reporting inconsistencies remain: Appendix C.1 uses 48.72 as the starting point for an agent improvement, although Table 6 identifies that as the fine-tuned score and gives 42.97 for zero-shot.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same SpatialScore/SpatialAgent research project, and their main text, figures, tables, equations, and appendices support reliable comparison. The redesigned benchmark and protocols limit direct score comparisons, rather than document comparability.

after.justification: V2 reports original benchmark evaluations, human and text-only controls, supervised fine-tuning results, SpatialAgent comparisons, and additional subset and failure analyses.

before.justification: V1 reports original evaluations of MLLMs and SpatialAgent on VGBench, SpatialScore, and SpatialScore-Hard, with additional source-dataset results in Appendix F.

results.title: SpatialScore: Towards Comprehensive Evaluation for Spatial Intelligence

C1.justification: The central adaptive-width and Token Recycling contributions, including the headline 2.0/2.9 percentage-point ImageNet claims, remain unchanged. v2 adds explicit main-text claims of demonstrated segmentation and Swin transfer and superiority to depth-adaptive methods. These refine and extend applicability claims whose broader architectural motivation already appeared in v1.

C2.justification: v1 Section 4.5 presents uniformly hard inputs as an efficiency limitation; v2 Section 4.8 recasts the retained evidence as successful routing and continued superiority, dropping the explicit efficiency warning. The discussion of hierarchical token-alignment difficulties is also removed. v2 adds interpretations of segmentation refinement and demonstrated pruning complementarity, while retaining training-overhead and excessive-expansion limitations in Appendix I.

D1.justification: v2 newly specifies inference batch size 512, validation-set throughput aggregation, GMAC accounting, and filtering/rebatching pseudocode in Appendix J. It also documents Swin stage allocation and the pruning ratio. Reported training hardware changes from A100 to H100, without establishing reruns of retained results. Code access is unchanged, and detailed training settings for the new applications remain sparse.

E1.justification: v2 adds semantic segmentation on ADE20K and Cityscapes, extending evaluation beyond ImageNet-family classification to dense prediction and urban scenes. The existing ImageNet variants remain covered. Swin is an architectural extension, while DETR remains future work rather than evaluated coverage.

E2.justification: v2 Figure 8 adds Swin-T/S/B comparisons and six early-exit comparators: SDN, PABEE, BERxiT, ViT-EE, PCEE, and LGViT. Figure 14 adds A-ViT and AdaViT; Figure 9 compares Segmenter backbones. The depth-expanded controls in v1 Table 1 disappear. The earlier appendix Early Exit baseline is retained under the name BranchyNet, with unchanged results.

E3.justification: New segmentation evaluations introduce mIoU under single-scale and multi-scale inference with a linear Segmenter decoder, while the new early-exit comparison uses Swin backbones. The DynamicViT combination specifies a 0.8 pruning ratio. v2 also exempts the new KV-cache experiment from the retained ablations' stochastic-training setup. These are added experimental settings, not evidence that retained ImageNet experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: v2 adds targeted tests of KV-cache reuse and compatibility with DynamicViT, plus qualitative segmentation examples comparing inference rounds. It removes the depth-expansion control in Table 1. Existing head-expansion, loss-weighting, fusion, entropy, and prediction-dynamics analyses largely remain; moving the head-expansion analyses to Appendix K does not make them new.

E5.justification: Neither version reports seeds, repeated-run uncertainty, confidence intervals, or significance tests for the results. The statement about roughly 100 prototyping runs remains unchanged. Prediction entropy is a routing signal, not newly added statistical uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: v2 adds segmentation, Swin, early-exit, and pruning-combination results. Section 4.6 reports 83.5% accuracy at 9.5 GMACs for the Swin adaptation, and Table 4 adds KV-cache accuracies of 73.872% and 75.674% across rounds. Table 1 changes the one-extra-iteration cost from 3.45 to 2.5 GMACs and removes depth-expanded results. Most retained ImageNet results, including the entropy-threshold table, are unchanged.

M1.justification: The core nested subnetworks, Token Recycling, joint losses, and entropy-based stopping remain unchanged. v2 adds a Swin-S adaptation that keeps the first architectural stage intact while initially halving the other stages, and an optional DynamicViT pruning component in the second inference round. The batching pseudocode documents inference rather than establishing a changed core algorithm.

P1.justification: v2 rewrites the abstract, method overview, hard-input discussion, and conclusion around a broader application narrative. It removes the isomorphic-architecture subsection, reorganizes evaluation and appendices, and moves head-expansion/loss-weighting explanations into Appendix K. These are substantial structural and narrative revisions alongside the added scientific content.

P2.justification: The paper changes from a predominantly single-column layout to two columns, swaps the opening performance and architecture figures, merges ImageNet comparison panels, and splits other appendix panels. Ablation tables move into the supplement. New Swin, segmentation, and qualitative figures, expanded pruning plots, and batching pseudocode substantially change the visual presentation.

R1.justification: v2 adds a substantial early-exit discussion distinguishing adaptive depth from ThinkingViT's progressive width, covering methods such as MSDNet, SDN, PABEE, BERxiT, LGViT, and JEI-DNN. It adds references supporting segmentation, Swin, A-ViT, and AdaViT, while removing works including Once-for-All, LLaMaFlex, MatMamba, and Sliced Recursive Transformer. This expands research positioning beyond bibliographic reformatting.

T1.justification: The mathematical formulation of nesting, token fusion, joint training, and entropy stopping is retained, with equation splitting and renumbering. v2's weighted-average GMACs formula explains the existing compute metric; it does not introduce a new theoretical result. Neither version supplies substantive theorems or proofs.

improvement.justification: The segmentation and Swin experiments provide substantial empirical support for portability claims that v1 largely left untested. Broader early-exit comparisons address an important alternative to progressive width, while pruning integration and inference-measurement details strengthen practical validation. These gains outweigh sparse settings for the new experiments and the less explicit treatment of the hard-input efficiency limitation; the improvement comes from stronger validation, not higher retained ImageNet scores.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe ThinkingViT and contain readable main text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices. Retained experiments can be matched across substantial reformatting, renumbering, and relocation.

after.justification: v2 retains original classification experiments and reports additional segmentation, Swin, early-exit comparison, and token-reuse/pruning results.

before.justification: v1 reports original ImageNet classification, throughput, robustness, routing, and ablation results in the main text and appendices.

results.title: ThinkingViT: Matryoshka Thinking Vision Transformer for Elastic Inference

C1.justification: The central single-stage, dual-level PixelDiT contribution is retained. The abstract extends its performance claim to ImageNet-512, while the conclusion strengthens the description from closing much of the latent-space gap to image quality 'on par' with latent diffusion on class- and text-conditioned generation.

C2.justification: v2 adds interpretations of REPA's regularizing role, conditioning trade-offs, and unsuccessful architectural choices. Appendix G explicitly qualifies its observations as not fully controlled; Appendix I adds loss-spike risks for deeper models and long training runs. The conclusion additionally attributes pixel-space difficulty to data/noise complexity and immature training recipes, expanding v1's architecture-centered explanation.

D1.justification: v2 newly supplies code, pretrained-model, and project links. It also documents additional preprocessing, fine-tuning initialization and schedules, SAM3-based evaluation processing, and implementation choices such as fixed sinusoidal pixel embeddings and the x-prediction stability threshold. These substantially expand access and reproducibility information; the linked resources themselves were not accessed.

E1.justification: v2 reports evaluation on the 281-pair FlowEdit editing corpus, broadening coverage beyond v1's illustrated bicycle-to-motorcycle edit (Figure 1b; v2 Appendix D.2). This extends an existing editing task; the underlying ImageNet and text-to-image dataset coverage is retained.

E2.justification: FLUX-schnell is added alongside FLUX-dev in the 1024-resolution text-to-image comparison (v1 Table 3; v2 Table 4). The new ImageNet-512 comparison also includes Bao et al.'s U-ViT-H, absent from v1's comparisons. Most existing comparator families are retained.

E3.justification: New protocols include ImageNet-512 fine-tuning for 530 epochs from a 320-epoch checkpoint, guidance 3.5 over [0.1, 1.0], and extended ImageNet-256 training to 800 epochs. Editing evaluation introduces SAM3 bounding boxes and background MSE/SSIM on 281 pairs. Table 1 also changes the reported EPG configuration from 583M parameters/800 epochs to 789M/600 epochs.

E4.justification: v2 adds REPA removal experiments, ImageNet-512 patch-size ablations, resolution/patch-size compute analysis, and training-duration studies (Tables 11, 13, 16-18). Appendix G adds qualitative experiments on conditioning, transforms, prediction targets, and architectural alternatives. Existing solver, guidance, depth-allocation, and compaction analyses are retained.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run or seed counts, confidence intervals, error bars, or formal significance tests. Added results continue the same point-estimate reporting practice; longer training and additional evaluation samples do not introduce uncertainty estimation.

E6.justification: Retained 320-epoch ImageNet-256 gFID 1.61 and text-to-image scores are unchanged. New entries include ImageNet-512 gFID 1.81, 800-epoch ImageNet-256 gFID 1.54, and editing background MSE 0.001522/SSIM 0.8628, alongside new ablation and negative findings. EPG's Table 1 gFID changes from 2.04 to 1.81 under a different configuration, not a matched-setting improvement.

M1.justification: The proposed dual-level architecture, pixel-wise AdaLN, token compaction, text conditioning, and velocity-plus-REPA objective remain unchanged in Section 3 and Appendix A. Appendix G reports alternative designs and prediction targets as unsuccessful experiments, without replacing components of the final method.

P1.justification: The abstract and introduction receive localized edits, the conclusion is rewritten, and an ablation summary is added. The appendix gains extended-training and failed-attempt sections, with corresponding subsection renumbering. Most existing method, related-work, and experimental prose and the main section order are retained.

P2.justification: v2 substantially expands the displays with an ImageNet-512 sample grid (Figure 6) and tables covering its benchmark, REPA, patch size, editing preservation, compute scaling, and training duration (Tables 2, 11, 13-14, 16-18). The text-to-image table gains a FLUX-schnell row. Existing diagrams, plots, and appendix image galleries are retained, with relocation and renumbering.

R1.justification: v2 adds 'All Are Worth Words: A ViT Backbone for Diffusion Models' and 'Analyzing and Improving the Training Dynamics of Diffusion Models.' Section 2 otherwise retains its research positioning, while the introduction drops its explicit description of 1024-resolution training as a breakthrough over prior pixel-space models.

T1.justification: The main mathematical formulation remains unchanged. Appendix G adds mathematical specifications for experimental variants: DCT-basis modulation with an O(KC) versus O(P²C) parameter-count argument, and a stabilized clean-image-to-velocity mapping. These are limited additions; no theorems or proofs are introduced.

improvement.justification: v2 addresses important validation gaps: the previously illustrated editing advantage receives a 281-pair quantitative evaluation, and REPA ablations and ImageNet-512 experiments strengthen component and scalability evidence. Failed-attempt reporting, explicit training-instability limitations, and access links improve transparency and reproducibility information. The stronger parity conclusion remains broader than the mixed benchmark results, and Appendix G is not fully controlled, but these qualifications do not outweigh the substantial gains in empirical support.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same PixelDiT work. Their readable main texts, equations, tables, figures, and appendices support reliable comparison, including matching material moved or renumbered in v2.

after.justification: v2 retains those original results and adds ImageNet-512 evaluation, quantitative editing results, additional ablations, extended training, and negative experimental findings.

before.justification: v1 reports original ImageNet and text-to-image experiments, architectural ablations, sampling analyses, and qualitative editing results.

results.title: PixelDiT: Pixel Diffusion Transformers for Image Generation

C1.justification: Some headline performance claims now use audio scores already reported in v1: abstract MMMU accuracy changes from 75.53% to 69.2%, and introductory MATH accuracy from 94% to 92%. The eyeballing advantage is specified against GPT-5. The central paradigm, benchmark, few-shot learning, and self-consistency contributions remain.

C2.justification: V2 introduces a five-ability hierarchy and a rationale connecting visual text learning with language reasoning. Its visual-puzzle interpretation emphasizes competitiveness with Claude on symmetry rather than shape-drawing tasks. The strong characterization of temporal consistency as a confidence proxy is removed, while the prompt-rewriter hypothesis and closed-model limitation remain.

D1.justification: V2 documents the mini-set composition and changes the benchmark access link from the fnlp namespace to OpenMOSS-Team. Conversely, it omits the exact ARC-AGI-2 prompt and detailed palette-based grid extraction procedure, and removes the official-result markers for AIME25 and GPQA comparators. Most other prompts and generation parameters are retained or relocated.

E1.justification: Both versions retain the same eyeballing puzzles, visual puzzles, ARC-AGI-2, three maze geometries, and text-centric benchmarks. V2's 750-sample mini set draws from the existing 4,149-sample benchmark. Renamed task groupings and additional model evaluations do not introduce new dataset or task coverage.

E2.justification: V2 Tables 7–8 substantially expand comparisons with Veo 3.1, MiniMax Hailuo 2.3, Seedance 1.0 Pro, MOVA, Wan2.2-TI2V-5B, five image generators, and Qwen3-VL variants. Image comparators include Nano Banana Pro, Seedream 4.5, GPT Image 1.5, BAGEL, and Qwen-Image-Edit-2511. V2 also adds Grok 4 to the ARC-AGI-2 comparison and VLM comparisons on mazes.

E3.justification: V2 introduces a separate 750-sample evaluation subset comprising 500 vision-centric and 250 text-centric samples. Table 1 switches text-centric summaries from last-frame to audio accuracy, and visual-puzzle aggregation changes from color/shape groups to symmetry/gradient/compositionality. Joint video/audio correctness metrics are dropped. The stated Perpendicular VLM prompt is corrected; unchanged scores do not establish that the original experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: Appendix D adds qualitative multimodal-question cases from MathVista, MMMU, and MMBench. Visual-puzzle subgroup analysis shifts from output type to reasoning type. The principal few-shot, self-consistency, numerical-perturbation, prompt-rewriting, and reasoning-error analyses remain substantially unchanged.

E5.justification: The stated Avg@4 AIME reporting and five-attempt self-consistency voting are retained. V2 adds no seed reporting, confidence intervals, error bars, or statistical significance tests; its new comparison tables continue reporting point accuracies.

E6.justification: Tables 7–8 add extensive mini-set results, including vision-centric averages of 31.6% for Sora-2, 27.7% for Veo 3.1, and 29.8% for Nano Banana Pro. All 13 retained text-benchmark rows are unchanged, but reported overall last-frame/audio averages change from 56.3/73.6 to 57.0/67.8. V2 also corrects the ARC summary to match v1 Table 4, reports new subgroup aggregates, and removes joint-modality result entries. These changes do not establish same-setting Sora-2 performance gains.

M1.justification: The proposed video-generation reasoning approach, inputs and outputs, and existing few-shot and self-consistency procedures remain unchanged. Additional evaluated models are comparators; no new architecture, training objective, or proposed algorithmic component is introduced.

P1.justification: The main evaluation and analysis sections are extensively condensed and rewritten around reasoning capabilities. Detailed protocols and results move into reorganized appendices, and prompts are consolidated into Appendix F. Terminology, affiliations, and correspondence information are also revised.

P2.justification: V2 adds bar-chart presentations of retained eyeballing and visual-puzzle results while moving their detailed tables to the appendix. Numerous overview and case figures are redrawn or rearranged; new mini-set tables and multimodal examples are added. Reasoning examples move into the main text, the category-distribution chart moves to the appendix, and joint-modality table columns disappear.

R1.justification: V2 adds references for new comparators and visual text learning, including DeepSeek-OCR and See the Text. Section 4 now explicitly acknowledges quantitative evaluations in earlier video-reasoning work and presents this benchmark as complementary, while adding a first-systematic-comparison claim concerning Thinking with Images. The overall research positioning remains similar.

T1.justification: The visual-puzzle deviation definitions and equations remain equivalent, including RGB distance and binarized shape mismatch. Neither version introduces theoretical propositions or proofs; the new reasoning hierarchy is conceptual rather than mathematical.

improvement.justification: V1's broad paradigm claims relied chiefly on Sora-2 versus three VLMs. V2 Tables 7–8 add comparisons with other video generators and direct image-generation alternatives on a common mini set, substantially strengthening assessment of where video reasoning is competitive. Corrected summary inconsistencies and clearer organization also help. Removed joint-modality statistics and ARC implementation details reduce transparency, but the expanded comparative evidence addresses a substantial weakness and supports a clear overall improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe Thinking with Video and VideoThinkBench, with directly matchable tasks, experiments, and analyses. The complete main texts and appendices, including figures, tables, and equations, support a reliable comparison.

after.justification: V2 retains those empirical studies and adds comparisons involving additional video generators, image generators, and vision-language models in Appendix B.

before.justification: V1 reports original Sora-2 benchmark results, few-shot and self-consistency experiments, reasoning-process analyses, and a Wan2.5 prompt-rewriting ablation.

results.title: Thinking with Video: Video Generation as a Promising Multimodal Reasoning Paradigm

C1.justification: The central claims about multi-subject generation, hierarchical attention, VLM guidance and superior generation quality remain. v4 additionally claims to pioneer online RL for multi-subject video generation and frames its contribution explicitly around balancing identity preservation and motion quality.

C2.justification: v4 adds substantive explanations involving credit assignment, online exploration, reward hacking, worst-subject identity collapse and mitigation of copy-paste artifacts. It also changes the computational-cost framing: v1 identifies high cost as a limitation, whereas v4 Appendix E argues that attention overhead is marginal and RL adds a one-time cost. Misuse and dataset-curation safeguards are newly discussed.

D1.justification: v1's reward-calculation appendix is empty. v4 supplies reward weights, noise and normalization settings, and an RL hyperparameter table including learning rate, AdamW settings, batch size and gradient clipping. It revises architectural specifications, states that evaluation data are disjoint from training, reports approximately one-minute inference, and adds a project address. The PDFs still describe model/data release prospectively.

E1.justification: The same training sources, subject categories, 180 subject-text evaluation pairs and video-editing task are retained. v4 Table S.8 tabulates dataset quantities already reported in v1 Appendix C. New ablations and human judgments do not establish additional data domains or task coverage.

E2.justification: v4 Table 3 newly evaluates offline DPO against online GRPO and the existing SFT/base model. The generator comparators in Table 1 and Figure 4 remain unchanged. The new human study uses existing comparators: VACE-14B, Vidu, Phantom and Kling.

E3.justification: v4 replaces Table 2's Text-Video Alignment metric with Q-Align and changes the reported GmeScore encoder from Qwen2-VL to Qwen2.5-VL. It introduces a five-model, four-criterion human evaluation using 200 questionnaires from 30 participants. The architecture table also revises DiT depth from 60 to 30/40 layers. These are reported setting changes; they do not establish that all retained experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: v1 provides whole-component ablations and qualitative RL examples. v4 adds quantitative online-versus-offline optimization and reward-component ablations in Table 3, individual attention-stage ablations in Table S.5, mean-versus-minimum identity-reward sensitivity in Table S.7, and training dynamics in Figure S.7.

E5.justification: Neither version reports experimental seed counts, repeated-run variability, confidence intervals or formal significance tests. v4's moving-average training curves and human preference percentages add results without introducing uncertainty estimates.

E6.justification: v4 newly reports online-RL results of 55.16% Total Score and 66.10% FaceSim, extensive ablation results, and human preference rates of 54%, 60%, 43% and 65% across four criteria. Existing values also change: VACE-14B GmeScore changes from 67.27% to 73.27%, and Ours-14B FaceSim from 60.50% to 60.71%. Revised metrics and configurations prevent treating every difference as a same-setting performance gain.

M1.justification: The reported attention procedure changes substantively. v1 Section 3.2.1 uses concatenated inter-subject self-attention followed by self-attention over subjects, text and video. v4 Appendix A.1 specifies gated inter-subject cross-attention and residual cross-modal attention, with these blocks inserted in the first 20 DiT layers. This goes beyond renaming or disclosing reward settings.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction and method motivations are extensively rewritten around VLM-grounded online RL. The model and title are renamed, author information changes, editing is folded into the analysis section, and the supplement is reorganized with an overview and additional subsections. The earlier LLM-writing declaration is removed.

P2.justification: The document changes from a single-column preprint to a two-column layout. The teaser and several pipeline, dataset and prompt illustrations are redesigned; existing qualitative figures are resized or relocated. New displays include RL and sensitivity tables, training curves and preference charts. v1 Figures 7–10 survive as v4 Figures S.9–S.12 rather than constituting new analyses.

R1.justification: v4 adds targeted references including Identity-GRPO, RAFT, CustomVideo, Vimi, Seedance, Waver and DPO, while removing the earlier VGGT/PartCrafter inspiration citations. It adds a specific novelty claim about integrating VLM reasoning into open-source Wan. The broad related-work organization and principal competing approaches remain.

T1.justification: v4 adds explicit mathematical definitions for mean/minimum facial fidelity, holistic fidelity, aesthetic/naturalness rewards and gated attention. v1 specifies only a generic quality-plus-identity reward. The underlying rectified-flow and GRPO formulations remain, and neither version presents theoretical guarantees or proofs.

improvement.justification: v4 substantially addresses v1's underdocumented and weakly tested RL component: the empty reward appendix becomes a concrete specification, supported by DPO comparisons, reward/stage ablations, sensitivity analysis and human evaluation. This materially improves reproducibility and empirical support. Remaining weaknesses temper the gains: uncertainty is still unreported, and broad improvement claims overlook Table 1's lower motion, GmeScore and NaturalScore after RL.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same multi-subject video-generation work, renamed from ID-Composer to ID-Crafter. Their main text, equations, tables, figures and appendices are readable and support comparison despite substantial revisions.

after.justification: v4 retains original experiments and adds quantitative RL comparisons, reward and attention ablations, training curves and a human preference study.

before.justification: v1 reports original benchmark results and component ablations in Tables 1–2, plus qualitative generation, RL and editing results.

results.title: ID-Crafter: VLM-Grounded Online RL for Compositional Multi-Subject Video Generation

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the same three scientific contributions and claims about geometric fidelity, synthetic-to-real generalization, and partial-sketch performance. The new experiments support these claims without redefining their headline scope.

C2.justification: Section A-1 qualifies the ordering explanation: consistent sequential structure helps, without establishing that synthetic ordering models human drawing behavior. Section A-5 discusses furniture-prior failures on unseen objects, while A-6 proposes abstraction as an explanation for experts' lower reconstruction scores. These substantially expand mechanism interpretations and applicability boundaries.

D1.justification: The abstract changes data/model availability from a promised release to a stated completed release at the same project site. Table A-2 additionally specifies batch size 1 for timing. The core architecture, optimizer, training schedule, hardware, and training-time disclosures remain unchanged; external availability was not independently checked.

E1.justification: The original training coverage remains unchanged, but v3 adds reference-free sketches, explicit unsnapped-input evaluations, unseen ShapeNet categories, ModelNet objects, and expert-versus-beginner sketches. These substantially extend the evaluated input conditions, object categories, data sources, and sketcher populations.

E2.justification: Table 2 retains Luo et al. and LAS-Diffusion as its external baselines. However, Figure A-6 extends the real-test-set qualitative comparison to include LAS-Diffusion, whereas v1's Figure 4 compares only against Luo et al. This changes comparator participation within that qualitative evaluation.

E3.justification: Existing benchmark splits, geometric metrics, and training budgets remain unchanged. New protocols include a 40-sketch study with 38 participants providing 1,900 Likert ratings, comparison of expert and beginner drawings of 100 shapes, and evaluation at 10, 25, 50, and 100 DDIM steps.

E4.justification: v3 adds Fourier-feature ablations, DFS/BFS and ordering-perturbation tests, an order-aware versus order-agnostic partial-input comparison, snapping and unseen-class robustness analyses, expertise effects, and sampling tradeoffs. The original ablation table is retained, and the earlier completion-performance curve moves from Figure 7 to Figure A-1.

E5.justification: v1 reports a plus/minus quantity for generation time; v3 extends such reporting to human correspondence ratings in Table 3 and expertise-specific F-scores in Section A-6. The new quantities are not clearly identified as standard deviations, standard errors, or confidence intervals. No seed counts or formal significance tests are added.

E6.justification: The main benchmark scores and original ablation results are unchanged, but substantial new results appear. Free-hand ratings are 3.60±1.01 for the proposed method versus 2.02±0.89 for Luo et al.; BFS obtains 47.8 F-score versus 56.8 for the full model. New DDIM settings, expertise comparisons, and qualitative generalization successes and failures further expand the findings.

M1.justification: Sections 3–4 retain the same synthetic-sketch pipeline, Fourier/BERT encoder, augmentations, frozen VQ-VAE, and SDFusion training objective. The additional ordering variants and reduced DDIM budgets are experimental comparisons, not replacements of the proposed method.

P1.justification: Most introductory, methodological, and concluding prose is retained. Changes include locally expanded related work, moving partial-sketch discussion into the supplement, introducing the free-hand study in the main text, and expanding acknowledgments. This is a localized reorganization rather than extensive rewriting of the existing narrative.

P2.justification: v3 adds user-study, additional-ablation, and sampling-tradeoff tables, together with substantial free-hand, unsnapped, unseen-class, and baseline-comparison image grids. Completion illustrations are reorganized and expanded, while the original completion curve is relocated. Table 1 moves and Table 2 receives a side-caption layout.

R1.justification: Section 2.3 adds focused discussion of classical sketch rendering and structured CAD/B-rep work, including CAD2Sketch, Text2CAD, and BrepGen. v3 also credits StrokeAggregator as inspiration for culling and adds dataset references. The central positioning against unordered point-cloud sketch encoders remains intact.

T1.justification: Equations 1–7 retain the same sketch tokenization, Fourier encodings, projections, and embedding combination. Neither version develops additional theorems or proofs; the supplement's ordering discussion provides empirical interpretation rather than new formal reasoning.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially addresses v1's limited validation of reference-free use and its incomplete explanation of why ordering helps. The user study, ordering perturbations, and explicit unseen-class failures strengthen both practical evidence and the boundaries of the central interpretation. Undefined plus/minus quantities and inconsistencies between Table A-2's timing units and claimed speedup weaken parts of the new reporting, but do not outweigh these substantive gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same work, with matching authors, dataset, model, and principal experiments. Text, equations, tables, and figures support reliable comparison. v1 ends after its references; v3 additionally contains readable supplementary Sections A-1–A-8.

after.justification: v3 retains those original results and adds a user study, further ablations, robustness evaluations, an expertise comparison, and sampling-speed experiments.

before.justification: v1 reports original benchmark results, model ablations, synthetic-to-real adaptation experiments, and partial-sketch evaluations in Tables 2–3 and Figures 5–7.

results.title: Order Matters: 3D Shape Generation from Sequential VR Sketches

C1.justification: The central arbitrary-target grounding attack claim remains. However, v3 removes existence/convergence guarantees and a new attack dataset from the headline contributions, emphasizing superiority over input-aware competitors and broader transferability instead. Its abstract newly claims transferability across models, although the reported experiments do not clearly specify a source-to-target-model transfer test.

C2.justification: v3 adds explanations involving text-conditioned feature alignment, limitations of competing generators, and attention shifting toward attack targets. It interprets JPEG defense through its attack-success/benign-accuracy tradeoff and discusses preservation of other benign tasks. The no-language-loss ablation is now interpreted as failed target alignment despite preserved benign grounding, unlike v2's all-zero results.

D1.justification: v3 newly documents generator channels and attention heads, baseline adaptations, attack-data examples, image-subset counts, semantic-matching implementation, and defense parameters. It specifies 50-token ShowUI targets and reports four RTX6000 GPUs instead of one; Table 7's core training hyperparameters remain unchanged. Conversely, v2 Appendix I's commitment to release code and datasets upon acceptance disappears.

E1.justification: v3 adds Flickr30k Entities and systematic ShowUI-Web evaluation, attacker-targeted VQA on OKVQA and VQA-v2 using Hate-Speech-18 sentences, and benign-task evaluation on RealWorldQA and MMBench. These substantially broaden the evaluated data and tasks. COCO-2017 remains in Table 8; real-world GUI examples were already present in v2.

E2.justification: v3 Table 1 introduces evaluated One-to-N, Random, Imperio and Marksman comparisons across the victim models. The static-attack comparison changes from BadEncoder and TrojVLM in v2 Table 2 to BadVLMDriver, TrojVLM and VLOOD in v3 Table 10. BadEncoder is removed, while TrojVLM is retained under a revised protocol.

E3.justification: The static-baseline evaluation changes from v2's restricted 100-target setting to v3's per-target triggers with Sentence-BERT semantic matching at inference. Added experiments introduce ShowUI center-point correctness, L1/LPIPS/PSNR measurements, and a 1,000-target-sentence VQA poisoning protocol. Table 6 changes from original-dataset expression statistics to attack-image counts; this alone does not establish that retained RefCOCO splits were changed.

E4.justification: v3 adds quantitative reconstruction-loss ablations, a beta sweep measuring attack success versus image quality, and defenses using mean/median filtering, JPEG compression, clean retraining and INT8 quantization. It also adds attention-map analysis and expands the webpage case study to multiple targets within one image. These investigate perceptual tradeoffs, practical robustness and attack mechanisms beyond v2's analyses.

E5.justification: Both versions describe timing measurements over 10 sampled questions and report means and standard deviations. Neither reports attack-training seed counts, repeated-run uncertainty, confidence intervals or significance tests. v3's probabilistic theorem is theoretical analysis, not new empirical uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: Numerous baseline, defense, perceptual and VQA results are added. Retained rows also change: InternVL RefCOCO-val ASR is 65.9% in v2 versus 66.9% in v3, and LLaVA RefCOCOg-val ASR/BA changes from 41.3/77.3 to 47.3/77.6. The no-language-loss ablation's benign accuracies change from zero to 90.2/85.3/86.6. v3 also reports Imperio outperforming IAG on InternVL/RefCOCOg, 52.4% versus 50.2%. These are reported revisions and additions, not established same-setting gains across versions.

M1.justification: The text-conditioned U-Net, additive triggers, poisoning pipeline and joint language-model training remain. v3 Section 3.3 replaces v2's smoothed pixel-only reconstruction loss with weighted L1 and LPIPS terms, using weights 1 and 0.05. Appendix N adapts the same mechanism to sentence targets for VQA. Newly specified U-Net layer sizes establish additional documentation, not an architectural change.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, background, methodology and experimental discussion are extensively rewritten. Eight main sections become five, with threat modeling integrated into Backgrounds and theory incorporated into Methodology. The separate Discussion is dissolved, appendices are substantially reorganized, and the title and author information change.

P2.justification: Figures 1 and 2 are substantially redrawn, Figure 3 replaces some cases, and plots are restyled. Table 1 becomes a large baseline comparison while the fuller IAG results move to appendix Table 8. New architecture, perceptual, hyperparameter and VQA tables and an attention visualization substantially change the displays. Cross-dataset results and retained real-world illustrations are relocated within a reformatted supplement.

R1.justification: v3 substantially repositions IAG against arbitrary-target and input-aware attacks, especially Imperio, Marksman and One-to-N, explaining alleged architectural limitations. It adds GUI-grounding and VisualTrap context, perceptual-metric literature, and references supporting the new tasks. Much of the approximation/convergence literature supporting v2's removed proofs is dropped.

T1.justification: v2 Section 5 and Appendix A's existence and convergence propositions, including universal-approximation and Polyak-Lojasiewicz arguments, are removed. v3 Section 3.6 and Appendix B replace them with log-likelihood margins, perceptual-subspace and local-linearization assumptions, a probabilistic margin lower bound, and identifiability/perceptual-tradeoff corollaries.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially addresses two important weaknesses in v2: comparison only against static attacks in a restricted target setting, and largely qualitative evidence of imperceptibility. Relevant input-aware competitors, quantitative perceptual tests, practical defenses and benign-task checks provide much stronger validation, while architecture and baseline details improve reproducibility. These gains outweigh the removed release commitment and remaining inconsistencies, including Algorithm 1 omitting the stated LPIPS weight and the abstract asserting cross-model transfer without a clearly documented corresponding experiment.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe IAG. Their complete main texts, equations, tables, figures and appendices are readable and support reliable comparison despite extensive rewriting and reorganization.

after.justification: v3 retains original grounding experiments and adds baseline comparisons, perceptual measurements, defense tests and VQA experiments, including results in its appendices.

before.justification: v2 reports original grounding-attack experiments, baseline comparisons, ablations, defense evaluations, timing measurements and real-world examples.

results.title: IAG: Input-aware Backdoor Attack on VLM-based Visual Grounding

C1.justification: The broad claim of prior-free extrapolation from videos remains. However, v2 makes generalized higher-order dynamics beyond velocity-field models a central contribution and explicitly claims independence from geometric priors. It drops v1's categorical claim to be the first end-to-end general extrapolation method without manually defined physical priors.

C2.justification: v2 interprets performance through higher-order dynamics, shared-field efficiency, latent-state coherence, and the new training ablations. It replaces v1's emphasis on new-scene generalization and possible large-scale pretraining with a limitation concerning unseen changes in motion, such as breakage. v1's caution that rendering metrics can confound reconstruction quality with dynamics accuracy is also omitted.

D1.justification: Supplementary Section 7 specifies the 14-dimensional input, 2,048/4,096 sampled keypoints, 32 neighbors, latent dimensions, GELU activations, Adam optimizer, and detailed training stages. Network depths and widths are revised relative to v1 Appendix A.1. Conversely, v1's explicit code-availability statement and repository URL are removed; this establishes a disclosure loss, not that the repository became unavailable.

E1.justification: The Dynamic Object and Dynamic Indoor Scene datasets are retained. PanopticSports human-motion evaluation is removed, while Dynamic Multipart and FreeGave-GoPro add articulated-object motion and real-world human-object interactions. The appendix also adds a noisy 2D damped-oscillator experiment, extending coverage beyond video rendering.

E2.justification: On the retained synthetic benchmarks, v2 adds TRACE and FreeGave and removes 4D-GS from the quantitative comparisons. HexPlane, TiNeuVox, DeformGS, Grid4D, NVFi, and GaussianPrediction remain. These changes materially strengthen the velocity-field comparison and alter the comparator set independently of the added datasets.

E3.justification: Reported training budgets on the retained Object and Indoor datasets change from 50,000 and 60,000 iterations to 40,000, with a new dynamics warm-up between iterations 3,000 and 7,000. Their 75/25 temporal split is retained. v2 adds FPS evaluation and new ablation settings, including field-count sweeps and an A6000 exception to the otherwise RTX 4090 setup.

E4.justification: v1 Table 4 ablates latent space, Neural ODEs, and affine deformation. v2 substantially redesigns this analysis around factorized encoding, field count, ODE versus parameter-matched MLP, Rodrigues decoding, progressive training, and neighborhood rebuilding. Figure 3 adds latent-state analysis, and supplementary Section 6 adds a toy comparison of time-conditioned fitting against ODE extrapolation.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run or seed counts, confidence intervals, standard deviations, or statistical significance tests. Both primarily provide point estimates; the toy experiment's noisy inputs do not constitute uncertainty estimation.

E6.justification: ParticleGS extrapolation PSNR changes from 27.558 to 38.067 for Falling Ball and from 33.568 to 32.679 for Factory (v1 Tables 1–2; v2 Tables 5–6). These are revised-model and training-setting results, not controlled version-to-version gains. The six retained baselines keep their shared-dataset scene scores. New benchmark, speed, and ablation results are added, while PanopticSports results disappear.

M1.justification: v2 replaces position-hash features and a max-pooled global state with Gaussian-attribute features and learnable-query attention over multiple dynamic fields. It revises the ODE architecture, replaces general affine/additive rotation updates with Rodrigues-based and quaternion updates, changes the stated loss weighting, and adds a separate dynamics warm-up. Periodic neighborhood rebuilding already existed in v1.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, related work, methodology, and experimental discussion are extensively rewritten. The separate preliminaries are folded into the method formulation, and the appendix is reorganized into dedicated experimental, implementation, rotation-formula, visualization, and quantitative-results sections. The title and author information also change.

P2.justification: v2 switches to a two-column layout, redraws the introductory and architecture figures, and reorganizes qualitative comparisons with marked locations and enlarged details. It adds latent-state and spiral plots. Main-text NVFi scene tables become dataset summaries, with scene-level results relocated to the appendix; table highlighting changes from colored cells to bold and underlining.

R1.justification: v2 substantially expands positioning against velocity-field methods and approaches requiring structured geometry, adding discussion and citations for TRACE, FreeGave, NeuMA, VisionLaw, and neural constitutive-law learning. v1 mainly contrasts reconstruction methods, imposed physical constraints, and GaussianPrediction. This revises the novelty argument beyond reference renumbering or publication updates.

T1.justification: v2 Section 3.2 adds the standard reduction of higher-order differential equations to an augmented first-order system, together with an explicit O(NG)-to-O(FG) evolution-complexity argument. These are bounded mathematical additions to v1's ODE formulation; no formal extrapolation or stability guarantee is established.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens assessment of the central extrapolation claim: TRACE/FreeGave comparisons, targeted factorization and training ablations, and speed measurements address important gaps in v1's comparative and component evidence. More explicit architecture and implementation descriptions improve transparency. These gains outweigh the loss of PanopticSports coverage, code-access disclosure, and some qualifications. The improvement rests on stronger validation and documentation, not on treating revised scores as controlled gains or accepting physical-law identification as proven.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe ParticleGS and contain readable text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices. The substantial architectural and experimental revisions can be reliably compared.

after.justification: v2 reports original benchmark results, component ablations, rendering-speed measurements, latent-state visualizations, and a spiral-dynamics toy experiment.

before.justification: v1 reports original reconstruction and extrapolation experiments on synthetic datasets and PanopticSports, together with component ablations.

results.title: ParticleGS: Learning Neural Gaussian Particle Dynamics from Videos for Prior-free Physical Motion Extrapolation

C1.justification: The abstract and contributions redefine the work as an audit of three geospatial datasets rather than primarily a CrowdAI investigation. The conclusion newly recommends INRIA and SpaceNet as more suitable benchmarks. The central CrowdAI contamination and overfitting claims remain, while the explicit cleaned-dataset release contribution disappears.

C2.justification: v2 explains low-contrast and no-data false positives, discusses hash sensitivity to structural differences, and interprets pHash as less prone to false positives than aHash. Its new limitations discussion acknowledges lack of inherent rotation/flip invariance and dependence on prior dataset inspection when choosing augmentations.

D1.justification: v2 substantially expands reproducibility information through explicit hash settings, AMD EPYC 7313 hardware, eight allocated cores, 32 GB memory, runtimes, dataset preparation, benchmark construction, and identification of the pretrained HiSup checkpoint. The code address changes from CrowdAI_Hash_and_search to Hash_and_search, while v1's explicit cleaned-dataset download statement is omitted; actual external availability cannot be established from the PDFs.

E1.justification: v2 actually evaluates INRIA Aerial Image Labelling and SpaceNet 2, which v1 only mentions as background datasets. This substantially expands the audit beyond CrowdAI. CrowdAI and AICrowd refer to the same retained dataset.

E2.justification: v2 adds average hashing as a comparator to perceptual hashing on official AICrowd splits (Table 4) and the constructed benchmark (Table 6). PolyWorld and HiSup remain in the qualitative comparison; other cited hashing methods are not evaluated.

E3.justification: New protocols include INRIA tiling into 250×250 patches, evaluation of AICrowd's separate test split, HiSup testing on seen/unseen subsets with AP and AR metrics, and a 10,000-image benchmark measuring duplicate-detection precision, recall, F1, and errors. v1's stated merging and 90%/10% repartitioning of the cleaned dataset is no longer reported.

E4.justification: Beyond v1's qualitative examples, v2 adds a quantitative seen/unseen HiSup analysis of leakage effects, controlled comparison of hashing reliability on known duplicates, and false-positive case studies for INRIA and SpaceNet. These substantially extend analysis of both downstream consequences and detector failure modes.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, significance tests, or uncertainty estimates. v2's new benchmark metrics and average runtimes do not introduce uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: v2 adds extensive audit and comparison results, including HiSup AP of 79.7 on seen versus 65.4 on unseen images (Table 5), and pHash/aHash F1 scores of 0.9999/0.9429 (Table 6). The methodology's augmented-overlap count changes from 107,913 to 108,707. Exact validation-to-training leakage remains 56,368 images, or 93.45%; the new model scores are not version-to-version performance gains.

M1.justification: The DCT-based perceptual hash, exact hash matching, rotation/flip augmentation, arbitrary retention of duplicate representatives, and removal of cross-split leakage remain unchanged. v2's explicit 64-bit hash and zero Hamming-distance threshold clarify the existing procedure.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, contribution list, and related-work narrative are substantially rewritten. Methodology and experiments gain explicit subsections, the conclusion expands into discussion and limitations, and supplementary sections are introduced. The title, author list, and dataset terminology also change.

P2.justification: v2 replaces the hashing pseudocode with a pipeline diagram, removes the related-work catalogue table, expands the audit tables, and adds comparison and supplementary displays. The original leakage examples are reformatted, and the PolyWorld/HiSup figure is transposed from method columns to method rows. Figures and tables are integrated more closely with the text.

R1.justification: v2 adds a focused dataset-quality discussion with references to visual-data leakage, scale-dependent duplication, and large datasets including ImageNet, Cityscapes, VOC, and LAION-5B. The existing building-extraction and deduplication literature remains, with its detailed review condensed.

T1.justification: The DCT-and-threshold construction in v1 Algorithm 1 and Equation 1 is restated through v2 Figure 1 and its caption. No substantive mathematical definition, assumption, derivation, theorem, or proof is introduced or revised.

improvement.justification: v1 relies on a single-dataset audit and illustrative overfitting examples. v2 addresses important validation gaps through additional dataset audits, an explicit hashing comparator and labeled benchmark, and quantitative HiSup seen/unseen evaluation, supported by implementation details and concrete limitations. Section 7's duplicate-group arithmetic is inconsistent, and the HiSup comparison does not isolate leakage as the sole cause of the performance gap. Nevertheless, the added validation substantially strengthens the paper's overall evidential quality.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same perceptual-hashing deduplication and leakage-detection study, despite changes to the title, authorship, and scope. All substantive text, equations, tables, figures, and v2 supplementary material support comparison; v1 contains no separate appendix.

after.justification: v2 reports dataset audits and hashing comparisons in Tables 1–4, plus original HiSup subset evaluations and duplicate-detection benchmark results in supplementary Tables 5–6.

before.justification: v1 reports original CrowdAI duplication and leakage measurements in Table 2 and qualitative analyses of PolyWorld and HiSup predictions in Figure 2.

results.title: Data Leakage Detection and De-duplication in Large Scale Geospatial Image Datasets

C1.justification: v4 adds an explicit claim to be the first learning-based approach scheduling the hard/false-negative trade-off in contrastive learning and extends the abstract's named framework coverage to SigLIP-2. The central contribution remains adaptive, anchor-specific negative sampling through learned mini-batch construction.

C2.justification: v4 interprets its learned schedule as initially favoring harder negatives and subsequently reducing hardness, attributes the larger DataComp advantage to MAFA's dependence on its filtering model's pretraining distribution, and introduces an applicability limitation concerning proxies that do not involve both encoders. The earlier noisy-caption limitation remains discussed in Sections 4.1 and 8.3.

D1.justification: v4 documents SigLIP-2 checkpoint initialization and loss modifications, DataComp subset filtering, and the larger corpus composition. Core pseudocode, hardware, and hyperparameters are retained. Conversely, v1's direct BLIP dataset-download footnote and separate 567K Conceptual Captions counts are omitted.

E1.justification: v4 adds standard 4M pretraining incorporating SBU and Visual Genome captions, DataComp pretraining with its 38-task classification/retrieval evaluation suite, and BLIP-2 evaluations on OKVQA, GQA, and captioning. The original COCO/Flickr retrieval, VQA, NLVR2, and clean/noisy Conceptual Captions coverage is retained.

E2.justification: The new comparison in v4 Table 2 includes ImageBERT, UNITER, ViLT, TCL, and ALIGN, none of which had reported comparison rows in v1. Table 4 also compares SigLIP-2 with and without FALCON. The original Table 1 comparator set remains unchanged.

E3.justification: New protocols include zero-shot and fine-tuned MSCOCO retrieval under 4M pretraining, evaluation after training on a 1M CLIP/English-filtered DataComp subset, and BLIP-2 Stage-2 evaluations including CIDEr and SPICE. SigLIP-2 uses continued pretraining from an official checkpoint with modified losses. The original COCO 5K evaluation and core hyperparameters are retained.

E4.justification: v4 adds the learned quantile trajectory in Figure 6 and compares Conceptual Captions versus DataComp at approximately matched data budgets to examine sensitivity to the filtering model's training distribution (Section 8.4). Existing search-space, objective, and instance-level ablations, baseline sweeps, and qualitative examples remain unchanged.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, error bars, or significance tests. v4 continues the same point-estimate reporting practice; its additional task averages do not establish uncertainty estimation.

E6.justification: Original result entries are retained, but v4 adds substantial results in Tables 2–4 and 10–12. New 4M experiments report FALCON zero-shot text/image retrieval R@1 of 74.1/54.8. Findings are mixed: within the new SigLIP-2 comparison, FALCON changes text R@1 from 69.96 to 72.96 but image R@1 from 54.21 to 54.15; BLIP-2 captioning CIDEr is 106.0 with FALCON versus 107.2 without it.

M1.justification: The quantile-based batch construction, Beta-distribution scheduler, and policy-gradient training remain unchanged. v4 introduces a SigLIP-2 adaptation using its generative losses as the proxy; this adaptation also replaces sigmoid contrastive loss with softmax and excludes SILC/TIPS (Sections 4.3 and 7.4).

P1.justification: The title changes from Vision-Language Pretraining to Vision-Language Alignment. v4 adds an explicit contribution summary, shortens the conclusion, consolidates experimental setup in the supplement, and reorders appendix material. Most existing methodological and explanatory prose remains closely matched.

P2.justification: The document changes from predominantly single-column to two-column layout, with widespread resizing and relocation of displays. v4 adds benchmark tables and the quantile-trajectory figure, reorganizes BLIP-2 results into Stage-1/Stage-2 columns with abbreviated and full tables, and moves the clean/noisy-caption comparison from main Table 2 to supplementary Table 9.

R1.justification: v4 adds references and discussion concerning SigLIP-2, DataComp, GeoMM, additional comparison models, and large vision-language models. GeoMM is positioned as compatible but unevaluated. References supporting the deleted inevitability discussion disappear, while the principal positioning against heuristic sampling and pretrained false-negative filters remains.

T1.justification: v4 removes v1 Section 2's Proposition 1 and Appendix B's entire proof, including the semantic-compatibility relation, label-coverage definitions, and derivation of positive false-negative sampling probability. This eliminates the paper's formal proposition and proof; the scheduler objective and gradient-update mathematics remain unchanged.

improvement.justification: v4 substantially strengthens evidence for generality beyond v1's COCO-centered pretraining through standard 4M comparisons and DataComp's diverse evaluation suite. The SigLIP-2 and expanded BLIP-2 experiments also reveal mixed outcomes and motivate a concrete applicability boundary, improving the assessment of where FALCON helps. These gains outweigh removal of the elementary false-negative proposition, although statistical uncertainty and detailed protocols for some new evaluations remain insufficiently documented.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe FALCON, with matching authors, core algorithms, and original experiments. Their text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices support reliable comparison despite substantial additions and reformatting.

after.justification: v4 retains those original experiments and adds results for standard 4M pretraining, DataComp, SigLIP-2, and BLIP-2 Stage-2 tasks.

before.justification: v1 reports original FALCON experiments on retrieval, VQA, and NLVR2, including ALBEF/BLIP-2 comparisons, ablations, and appendix analyses.

results.title: FALCON: False-Negative Aware Learning of Contrastive Negatives in Vision-Language Alignment

C1.justification: v3 makes improved semantic consistency and solvability central contributions, including claimed average improvements of 20% and 17% over baseline generation. v1 primarily emphasizes scalable generation and discrimination among agents. Its explicit claim to be the first framework automatically generating interactive web tasks is removed.

C2.justification: New Appendix D identifies dependence on accurate, complete KGs and restricted coverage beyond predefined relationships. Section 4.3 attributes KG-free multi-page failures to missing inter-page relations. The web-agent performance gap is newly interpreted as showing that the benchmark emphasizes multi-step reasoning rather than simple visual grounding.

D1.justification: Appendix A adds privacy/compliance filtering, prohibited task operations and BUSINESS_DATA placeholder details. The template difficulty list omits Expert, and single-agent error handling is relabeled partially supported. Conversely, v1's numerical coverage proportions disappear. Generation model, temperature, embeddings, evaluation prompts and project access information remain unchanged.

E1.justification: Both retain the same 16 document sources, eight websites, 1,002 document tasks and 317 web tasks, with identical source and task-type distributions. The ablation uses the same source coverage; OSWorld and MMBench receive descriptive comparisons, not reported evaluations on additional datasets.

E2.justification: v3 introduces a directly evaluated KG-free task-generation baseline in Table 4, adding a central comparison absent from v1. Table 3 also adds UI-TARS-1.5-7B under both web-agent configurations. Tables 5–6 compare OSWorld, MMBench and TaskCraft descriptively rather than reporting numerical baseline runs.

E3.justification: Section 4.3 introduces 1,000 generated tasks per method, divided equally between document and web tasks, with GPT-4o generation and two human annotators assessing consistency and solvability. v3 also adds a 100-node-pair graph check and a 50-trajectory evaluator audit. The ablation's agent configuration is ambiguous: its prose names Gemini 2.5 Flash, whereas Table 4 lists Qwen models.

E4.justification: v3 adds a central ablation testing whether KG structure improves generated-task quality, plus graph-edge verification and human validation of web-task judgments. Conversely, v1's document task-type performance analyses in Figures 6–7 disappear. The execution case study and exploratory safety-generation discussion are retained.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals or significance tests for performance. The new graph-precision and human–judge agreement percentages are point-estimate validation results, not uncertainty estimates for the reported scores.
