E6.justification: New Table 4 reports document/web consistency of 0.95/0.78 versus 0.74/0.62 without KG, and solvability of 0.93/0.72 versus 0.73/0.60. v3 also reports 88% graph-edge precision, 88% human–judge agreement, and UI-TARS overall success rates of 0.0491 and 0.0719. Existing Table 2 and retained Table 3 scores are unchanged, while document task-type results are removed.

M1.justification: KG construction, Algorithm 1's sampling rules, template and meta-path task generation, MMR selection and agent architectures remain substantively unchanged. Appendix A newly documents filtering and content constraints without establishing that the underlying procedure was changed.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction and contribution narrative are extensively rewritten around task quality. Existing experimental discussions are consolidated into Main Results, appendices are reordered, and duplicate task-template sections are merged. Terminology is standardized around document understanding and RAG/Web Agents.

P2.justification: The document changes from single-column to two-column layout. v1's overview diagram, coverage chart and document performance plots are removed; v3 adds Tables 4–6 and expands Figure 1 and Table 3 for UI-TARS. Retained figures are resized or relocated, and the source-distribution display and captions are corrected.

R1.justification: v3 substantially revises positioning around semantic consistency and executability, adds discussion of Learn-by-Interact, and contrasts Graph2Eval's graph-based generation with TaskCraft's task composition. New comparative tables cover TaskCraft, OSWorld and MMBench, additional benchmark literature is cited, and the first-automatic-web-task-generation novelty claim is withdrawn.

T1.justification: The graph representation, sampling mathematics and existing metric formulas are retained. Carrying the relation set R consistently through Algorithm 1 and explaining the task-objective embedding clarify notation rather than introduce new theory. No new theorem, proof or substantive derivation appears.

improvement.justification: v1 demonstrates benchmark use without directly testing the benefit of KG-based generation. v3 substantially addresses this deficiency through the KG-free ablation, graph-quality audit and human validation of web judging, while adding concrete limitations. These gains outweigh the lost task-type analyses and coverage proportions. Reporting remains imperfect: the ablation's Gemini/Qwen descriptions conflict, and Table 4 implies average human-score gains of 18.5 and 16 percentage points, not exactly the headline 20% and 17%.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe Graph2Eval and Graph2Eval-Bench. All 20 pages of v1 and 17 pages of v3, including appendices, equations, tables and figures, support comparison despite substantial reorganization.

after.justification: v3 retains original agent evaluations and adds a KG-free ablation, UI-TARS results, graph-quality checking and human validation of the web-task evaluator.

before.justification: v1 reports original document and web-agent evaluations in Tables 2–3, task-generation timings, and an execution case study.

results.title: Graph2Eval: Automatic Multimodal Task Generation for Agents via Knowledge Graphs

C1.justification: The introduction and conclusion narrow the priority claim from first addressing and benchmarking multi-period 3D reconstruction to first reconstructing it within a unified, differentiable Gaussian-splatting framework. V2 also removes the assertion that ChronoScene is the only available benchmark coupling geometric and appearance evolution.

C2.justification: V2 explicitly assumes within-period changes are small. Appendix C attributes performance differences to incremental-change versus fixed-geometry appearance settings and acknowledges lower performance than NeuSC. Section 3.2 removes the earlier empirical assertion that opacity gating stabilizes training.

D1.justification: The introduction newly discloses that periods are manually defined using metadata or prior knowledge. Hardware, software versions, learning rates, densification schedules, feature dimensions, and code/data access information otherwise remain unchanged; an actual preprocessing change is not established.

E1.justification: V1 evaluates exclusively on ChronoScene. V2 adds WAT, the CL-Splats real-world benchmark, and NeuSC's 5Pointz scene, extending coverage to other continual-rendering and appearance-evolution settings. ChronoScene's 12 scenes and 8,891 images are retained.

E2.justification: Table 1 adds NeuSC and CLNeRF alongside all five retained baselines. New Tables 9–11 introduce further comparisons including NeRF, MEIL-NeRF, GsEditor, CL-NeRF, CL-Splats, NeRFW, HaNeRF, and time-conditioned variants. CLNeRF and CL-NeRF are distinct cited methods.

E3.justification: The added WAT comparison reports PSNR and SSIM, while the added CL-Splats and 5Pointz comparisons also report LPIPS. Existing ChronoScene evaluation, period averaging, and the stated 40k-iteration budget remain unchanged. Benchmark-specific splits and training procedures for the new comparisons are not detailed.

E4.justification: The component ablations, feature-dimension sweeps, initialization study, per-period training comparison, and temporal-interpolation examples are retained. Appendix C adds benchmark comparisons, without a distinct new ablation, robustness test, or error analysis.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, error bars, or significance tests. V2's use of 'significantly' in discussing performance is not accompanied by statistical testing.

E6.justification: V2 adds NeuSC/CLNeRF scores throughout Table 1 and three external-benchmark result tables. ChronoGS reports PSNR 28.31 on WAT, 32.03 on CL-Splats, and 19.35 on 5Pointz, where NeuSC reports 21.32. Table 1 also revises Overstreet PSNR from 22.46 to 22.66, matching unchanged Table 2.

M1.justification: The unified anchor scaffold, invariant/local/global features, temporal interpolation, opacity activation, Gaussian decoding, and optimization remain unchanged. Expanded descriptions of voxelization and visibility filtering repeat details already present in v1's supplement.

P1.justification: V2 locally rewrites related work and the method introduction, standardizes period terminology, and corrects wording. It reorganizes supplementary sections as A–E, adds separate supplementary references and acknowledgments, and updates affiliation/corresponding-author information. Most narrative structure is retained.

P2.justification: Table 1 is expanded and reformatted, and Tables 9–11 are added. Diagram labels and several captions receive limited edits, while appendix figures move with the added material. Existing qualitative panels and point-cloud visualizations are retained.

R1.justification: Section 2.3 becomes 'Long-Term Scene Evolution Modeling' and substantially expands positioning around historical scene chronology, temporal ordering, time-lapse reconstruction, and continual adaptation. Added literature includes CLNeRF and CL-Splats, supporting a more specific distinction between ChronoGS and prior temporal-scene research.

T1.justification: Equations 1–5 and the supplementary grid-occupancy definition retain the same mathematical content. No theorem, proof, derivation, or substantive formal assumption is introduced or revised.

improvement.justification: V2 addresses important gaps in v1's empirical coverage and positioning: evaluation expands beyond the authors' benchmark, directly relevant chronological and continual methods enter the comparisons, and the novelty claim becomes more precise. Reporting the NeuSC shortfall also clarifies performance boundaries. These changes substantially strengthen the paper's evidential basis, although sparse protocol details for the new benchmarks still limit reproducibility.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same ChronoGS method and ChronoScene dataset. Their main text, equations, tables, figures, and complete supplementary material support reliable comparison, including matching renumbered and relocated content.

after.justification: V2 retains these original experiments and adds baseline comparisons and ChronoGS results on WAT, CL-Splats, and NeuSC's 5Pointz scene.

before.justification: V1 reports original reconstruction experiments on real and synthetic ChronoScene scenes, comparisons with baselines, and component, feature-dimension, and initialization ablations.

results.title: ChronoGS: Disentangling Invariants and Changes in Multi-Period Scenes

C1.justification: v2 adds effective, data-efficient active view selection as a principal contribution in the abstract, introduction, and conclusion, including a state-of-the-art AVS claim. The RGB/depth uncertainty and cross-scene generalization claims remain, while v1's explicit claim to the first uncertainty models providing out-of-scene generalization is removed.

C2.justification: v2 adds hypotheses connecting LF transfer difficulties to inconsistent depth scales and directional benefits to view-dependent color effects, while removing detailed per-scene failure discussion. Some revised interpretations overstate retained evidence: the universal claim of single-view object-centric correlations above 0.8 conflicts with Table 3's TUM PRIMU values of 0.756 for rendering and 0.745 for depth.

D1.justification: v2 documents AVS initialization and training schedules and clarifies the existing CNN learning-rate decay from 0.001 to 0.00001. Most original feature and CNN settings remain. It omits the named TUM ablation subset and removes v1's code-availability sentence containing a placeholder URL; this does not establish a change in actual code availability.

E1.justification: v1 evaluates uncertainty estimation on four LF and eleven TUM scenes. v2 retains these and adds nine MipNeRF360 scenes and eight front-facing LLFF scenes for rendering uncertainty, substantially broadening scene coverage. It also introduces the active-view-selection task on MipNeRF360.

E2.justification: v1 compares against FisherRF and regression-FisherRF. v2 additionally evaluates manifold and var3DGS for rendering uncertainty, and BayesRays and manifold for depth uncertainty. Its new AVS comparison includes FisherRF, manifold, and a controlled manifold variant using the selected views with vanilla GS. The original scene-separation comparator set is retained.

E3.justification: v2 introduces an AVS protocol reserving every eighth view for evaluation, starting from four views, and selecting up to twenty with specified iteration intervals and a 5000-iteration spherical-harmonics schedule. It also reports PSNR, SSIM, and LPIPS alongside uncertainty metrics. The feature-selection removal criterion is worded oppositely to v1, although retained plots and scores do not establish that this experiment was rerun.

E4.justification: The feature-selection, scene-separation, and CNN receptive-field studies are retained; the CNN study moves to Appendix E. v2 extends cross-scene analysis to background regions, adds qualitative comparisons against additional baselines, and introduces the manifold AVS control to distinguish view-selection effects from rendering-pipeline effects. These extend the existing analytical suite.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-seed counts, confidence intervals, or formal significance tests. The averaged feature-selection curves and shaded variability bands are retained from v1 Figure 2 in v2 Figure 4; additional result tables do not introduce a new statistical reporting practice.

E6.justification: v2 adds substantial benchmark, reconstruction-quality, AVS, AUSE, and background-transfer results. For example, its new AVS Table 6 reports PSNR 20.721 for PRIMU-AVS, 20.392 for FisherRF, and 20.102 for manifold with vanilla GS. Matched LF/TUM scene-separation and full-scene/object-centric transfer Pearson scores remain unchanged. Detailed per-scene results in v1 Tables 5–14 are removed, with dataset-level summaries retained.

M1.justification: The original feature construction and regression framework remain essentially unchanged. However, v2 adds PRIMU-AVS: it renders a direction-dependent coverage map with max aggregation and omitted opacity, selects the candidate view with lowest mean coverage, and iteratively adds training views without an uncertainty regressor. This substantially extends the proposed procedure.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, method explanations, results discussion, and conclusion are extensively rewritten. The method is named PRIMU, visibility terminology becomes coverage, and the experiments are reorganized around general uncertainty comparisons, scene separation, and AVS. Cross-scene generalization and spatial-interaction material move into reorganized appendices; author and affiliation information also changes.

P2.justification: v2 adds comparative image grids and benchmark/AVS tables, consolidates earlier tables into different summary structures, and removes detailed per-scene tables. The workflow diagram gains an explicit regression block, and existing qualitative panels are reordered. The introductory example reuses earlier Teddy2 outputs, while the unchanged CNN plots move from v1 Figure 3 to v2 Figure 5.

R1.justification: v2 substantially expands positioning around Bayesian and stochastic radiance-field uncertainty, adding discussion of BayesRays, ProvNeRF, var3DGS, and manifold. A new AVS subsection contrasts coverage-based selection with uncertainty and information-gain approaches, including ActiveNeRF and progressive camera placement. Conversely, v1's cited lineage of prediction-quality regression in detection and segmentation is removed.

T1.justification: The mathematical constructions in Equations 1–9 and the CNN kernel-family specification in Equation 10 remain equivalent. Renaming visibility as coverage and rewriting explanations do not establish a theoretical change. Neither version contains a theorem or proof, and the AVS addition is procedural rather than a new theoretical analysis.

improvement.justification: v1's state-of-the-art claim was evaluated only against FisherRF and its regression variant on LF/TUM. v2 substantially strengthens comparative validation with additional GS/NeRF baselines, broader scene coverage, reconstruction-quality context, and an AVS experiment controlling for manifold's different rendering pipeline. Removing per-scene tables and introducing misleading single-view claims and ambiguous feature-selection wording reduce transparency and precision, but the stronger comparative evidence provides a substantial net improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Gaussian-splatting uncertainty framework, renamed PRIMU in v2. The text, equations, tables, figures, and supplied appendices are readable and support reliable comparison despite substantial reorganization.

after.justification: v2 retains original LF/TUM experiments and reports additional uncertainty comparisons on MipNeRF360 and LLFF, plus active-view-selection results in Table 6.

before.justification: v1 reports original LF/TUM uncertainty-estimation experiments, feature-selection ablations, cross-scene generalization results, and CNN spatial-interaction experiments in Section 4 and the appendices.

results.title: PRIMU: Uncertainty Estimation for Novel Views in Gaussian Splatting from Primitive-Based Representations of Error and Coverage

C1.justification: The first contribution changes from introducing the 'first framework' to introducing 'a framework,' narrowing the novelty claim. v3 emphasizes SDF-domain Poisson fusion while retaining the central claims of high-fidelity editing, structural consistency, and versatility.

C2.justification: v3 newly explains that repetitive textures disrupt gradient-domain color propagation, motivating distribution alignment. It also interprets backend comparisons as attributing gains to fusion rather than a particular generator. The stated limitations concerning generative-model dependence and complex/open/noisy meshes remain unchanged.

D1.justification: v3 adds a project-page address, an alignment-method citation, and explicit edited-image conditioning for texture generation. It removes the post-acceptance implementation-release promise and the explicit description of supervision viewpoints as random. The PDFs do not establish actual code availability.

E1.justification: Section 4.1 broadens the evaluation collection beyond v2's six illustrated sculpture/fantasy objects to assets selected from Objaverse-XL, Google Scanned Objects, and internet sources, including scanned household objects. The underlying mesh-editing tasks and drag-based demonstrations remain.

E2.justification: VoxHammer joins FocalDreamer, MagicClay, and Instant3dit in Table 1 and Figure 4. Trellis and Hunyuan3D 2.5 are alternative CraftMesh generation backends, rather than additional competing editing methods.

E3.justification: The stated evaluation expands from six objects to 100 models with three editing prompts per model. Section 4.5 also introduces alternative-generator configurations. The four evaluation metrics and reported GPU, iteration budgets, and optimization times remain unchanged.

E4.justification: Section 4.5 adds a backend sensitivity analysis comparing MeshyAI, Trellis, and Hunyuan3D 2.5. Existing geometry/texture component ablations and qualitative distribution-, gradient-, and boundary-loss removal tests remain.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, significance tests, or comparable uncertainty estimates for the experimental results.

E6.justification: Both tables replace the retained methods' numerical scores and add results. CraftMesh's Table 1 scores change from 22.768/13.594/3.203/5.071 to 20.801/18.479/4.710/5.928 for CLIPsim/CLIPdir/NIQE/NIMA. These concern different evaluation collections, not same-setting performance changes. CraftMesh still leads the main comparison on all four metrics; VoxHammer and alternative-backend results are newly reported.

M1.justification: The image-editing, mesh-generation, Boolean/SDF fusion pipeline and its geometry and texture losses remain unchanged. Added alignment and texture-conditioning descriptions clarify implementation without establishing a changed procedure; the fusion block is also renamed.

P1.justification: The abstract and selected introduction, related-work, and method paragraphs are rewritten. The fusion terminology changes, texture-loss explanations are reordered, and affiliations, contact information, and acknowledgments are revised. The overall section organization remains intact.

P2.justification: Figure 2 adds explicit texture-generation conditioning inputs, Figure 4 gains a VoxHammer column, and Tables 1–2 gain comparison rows. Front matter and surrounding text are reflowed, while the six-figure, two-table organization and retained demonstrations remain recognizable.

R1.justification: v3 adds references to Google Scanned Objects, VoxHammer, and Imaginarium, and removes Deep Image Analogy. It refines positioning against classical Poisson mesh editing through connectivity and gradient-incompatibility arguments; most related-work coverage remains.

T1.justification: v3 adds an asymptotic complexity comparison asserting O(kn^2) for image-space Poisson processing versus O(n^3) for volumetric processing in Sections 1 and 3.2.1, without a derivation or proof. The existing mathematical definitions and equations remain, with texture-loss equations reordered.

improvement.justification: v2's quantitative claims rested on six objects and one mesh-generation backend. v3's 100-model evaluation with three prompts per model, VoxHammer comparison, and alternative-backend analysis substantially strengthen the empirical foundation and address that narrow evaluation. Run-to-run uncertainty remains absent, and the new complexity and causal-attribution explanations are less firmly supported, but the overall evidential gain is substantial.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe CraftMesh and provide readable text, equations, figures, tables, and references across 11 pages. Neither supplied PDF contains an appendix; no material reading gaps prevent comparison.

after.justification: v3 reports original results on an expanded evaluation collection, including an additional competing method and mesh-generation-backend comparisons, alongside the retained editing demonstrations and ablations.

before.justification: v2 reports original quantitative comparisons, qualitative editing results, drag-based demonstrations, and component ablations in Section 4, Tables 1–2, and Figures 4–6.

results.title: CraftMesh: High-Fidelity Generative Mesh Manipulation via Poisson Seamless Fusion

C1.justification: The central contribution of global annual pixel embeddings and evaluation on five applications remains. The abstract qualifies broad outperformance as closely matching or outperforming baselines. The introduction adds an explicit combined-property novelty claim and distinguishes the reported 2024 release from the intended 2017-2024 coverage.

C2.justification: Appendices B-C add substantive interpretations concerning scaling, the importance of shuffling and mixup, modest Sentinel-1 benefits, and the accuracy/storage tradeoff of quantization. New discussion addresses compute limits and assumes short-term canopy stability despite reference-date mismatches. The stocking-index section also newly attributes its superior performance specifically to embedding efficiency.

D1.justification: v2 adds parameter and hyperparameter tables and detailed canopy, fire, biomass, and stocking-index procedures in Appendices F-I. Reported pretraining resources change from 3,000 GPU-hours on eight MI300X GPUs to 6,200 on sixteen. Previously intended releases gain concrete GEOTESSERA retrieval and integrity-checking instructions, model/code access information, and disclosure that Brazilian plot data require a Data Transfer Agreement.

E1.justification: The reported global pretraining corpus and five evaluated settings remain: Austrian crops, Borneo canopy heights, Finnish biomass, two California burn regions, and Brazilian agroforestry plots. Scaling and ablation experiments reuse Austrian crops. Newly documented land-cover aids support existing tasks; Appendix J presents a Cambridge tool demonstration without an additional habitat-classification evaluation.

E2.justification: Google Satellite Embedding is added to crop pixel classification, few-shot learning, segmentation, canopy-height, and biomass comparisons. A Sentinel-2 annual-median-composite UNet baseline is also added for canopy height. These additions substantially expand the evaluated comparator set across several principal applications.

E3.justification: Reported settings change substantially: pretraining batch size increases from 8,192 to 32,768; canopy-height patches change from 64x64 to 32x32; and patch-based comparator encoders change from frozen to fine-tuned. BioMassters label subsets are now selected before the 80:20 training/validation split. New scaling and ablation protocols introduce architecture sweeps and RankMe evaluation. These reported revisions do not establish that every retained result was rerun.

E4.justification: New Appendices B-C add projector-depth/width and compute-scaling experiments, plus ablations of shuffling, mixup, Sentinel-1 inputs, and quantization. Figure 11 adds qualitative crop-segmentation comparisons. The earlier shuffling-stability analysis remains, while Figure 3 removes the canopy-height binned-bias analysis and example prediction maps.

E5.justification: v2 Figure 2c newly specifies few-shot repetition counts, from 2,000 for one-shot to 100 for twenty-shot; v1 only stated multiple runs. Biomass Figure 4 newly reports averages over five random splits and minimum-maximum ranges. The canopy-height twelve-run evaluation and its uncertainty reporting already appeared in v1.

E6.justification: v2 adds results for the new comparators, scaling experiments, and ablations; Table 4 reports F1 of 0.773 for the full model versus 0.626 without shuffling and mixup. Existing values also change: PRESTO's crop-embedding Davies-Bouldin index changes from 11.656 to 14.136, and ETH global canopy RMSE from 20.17 to 20.28 m. Biomass curves are replaced under revised protocols, so their lower errors are not established same-setting gains.

M1.justification: Figure 1 and Appendix A.5 revise the reported encoder depth from eight Transformer blocks to four. The dual Sentinel-1/2 encoders, MLP fusion, 128-dimensional embeddings, quantization, and Barlow Twins plus mixup objective remain. This is a limited architectural revision; the PDFs do not establish whether it reflects retraining or correction of the earlier description.

P1.justification: The abstract and introduction are extensively rewritten, encoder/projector explanations are consolidated, duplicate crop subsections are merged, and biomass precedes wildfire analysis. Existing methods are reorganized into dedicated appendices, while acknowledgments and availability information move before them. Terminology shifts broadly from representations and Model-as-Data to embeddings and Embeddings-as-Data.

P2.justification: Figures 1-3 are redrawn or substantially reorganized, and the biomass figure gains additional comparison panels and uncertainty displays. New figures show scaling, crop predictions, and the interactive tool; new tables cover architecture, hyperparameters, ablations, and research positioning. Fire maps, stocking-index plots, and training/shuffling graphics are retained despite relocation or renumbering.

R1.justification: Table 5 adds an extensive model-by-feature survey supporting a new explicit positioning claim about TESSERA's combination of openness, ready-to-use outputs, scale, and temporal pixel features. Numerous works are newly cited, including GSE, AnySat, Galileo, and RankMe. This substantially expands research positioning beyond v1's introductory literature discussion.

T1.justification: Appendix C introduces a formal definition of the new RankMe diagnostic using normalized entropy of normalized embedding singular values, Equation 12. The existing Barlow Twins/mixup mathematics and clustering-metric definitions remain substantively unchanged. No new theorem or proof is introduced.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens support for the method through controlled component/scaling experiments and additional baselines, addressing important evidential gaps in v1. Dedicated application appendices, access instructions, and biomass uncertainty reporting also materially improve reproducibility and assessment. These gains outweigh the removed canopy diagnostics, although conflicting fire years and RH95 versus RH90 stocking-index targets leave unresolved reproducibility problems.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe TESSERA and retain matching methods, application datasets, and figures. The main texts, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices are readable and support a reliable comparison.

after.justification: v2 retains original application results and adds baseline comparisons, model-scaling experiments, and component ablations.

before.justification: v1 reports original crop-classification, canopy-height, biomass, wildfire-embedding, and stocking-index results, alongside a training-stability comparison.

results.title: TESSERA: Temporal Embeddings of Surface Spectra for Earth Representation and Analysis

C1.justification: The central efficiency claim changes from a subquadratic-space speed/memory trade-off to linear time and space with memory comparable to on-demand sampling. Abstract maxima change from 90%/95%/50% to 92%/99%/63% for sampling runtime, memory, and end-to-end savings. V2 drops the first reference-based ultra-high-resolution evaluation claim and emphasizes the accuracy/runtime Pareto frontier.

C2.justification: V2 adds specific qualifications: only the forward pass is optimized, and the default sampler can remain faster at some small sizes on particular GPUs. Section 9.4 attributes Kubric's preference for lower-resolution inference to less-detailed objects. V1's discussion of cache overhead and future kernel fusion is replaced by interpretation of the fused implementation.

D1.justification: V2 adds actual CuTe DSL implementation listings, including GEMM helpers, sampling functions, and the fused kernel. It documents Ampere targeting, bfloat16 inputs, float32 accumulation, MMA instruction sizes, and shared-memory/register handling beyond v1's pseudocode and implementation outline. The Blender setup script is retained, but the explicit Spring subvalidation-split disclosure disappears.

E1.justification: V2 adds evaluated Kubric-8K scenes with generated moving objects, including accuracy and resource measurements in Tables 6-7. V1's ultra-high-resolution evaluation used only Charge's movie scenes. This substantially broadens the central high-resolution evaluation to another scene distribution; Charge, Spring, Sintel, and KITTI remain represented.

E2.justification: The Charge comparisons add DPFlow, ReCoVEr-CX, and WAFT and remove CCMR+ (v1 Tables 2/7 versus v2 Tables 1/11). The Spring/Sintel/KITTI comparison set is narrowed to RAFT, MS-RAFT+, SEA-RAFT, and newly added DPFlow. V2 Table 9 also evaluates a mixed default/on-demand sampler against the proposed sampler.

E3.justification: The main Charge comparison selects each method's lowest-1px-error resolution instead of its highest feasible resolution. V2 also introduces alternative low/high-resolution iteration budgets and changes the iteration/channel sweeps from 256 x 112 to 512 x 224 feature maps. The latter is supported by Section 9.1 and Table 10, although Section 5.1 inconsistently retains the earlier default.

E4.justification: V2 Table 9 adds tests of whether reallocating iterations toward lower resolutions or mixing existing samplers can reproduce the proposed efficiency benefits. The original caching ablation is removed, and the component analysis is replaced by measurements of fused-kernel stages using early exits (Section 8.4, Table 4). Resolution, iteration, feature-dimension, and hardware sensitivity analyses are retained.

E5.justification: Both versions specify one run per image for isolated benchmarking and report means and standard deviations across image samples, including shaded standard deviations in plots. V2 adds no repeated-run, seed, confidence-interval, or significance-testing procedure; changed uncertainty values retain the existing reporting practice.

E6.justification: Sampler timings and memory measurements are extensively replaced: at corresponding GH200 8K-input/1024-feature width, reported values change from 1004 ms and 15384 MB to 347 ms and 2829 MB. Charge results also change, including full-resolution RAFT EPE from 45.56 to 59.94 pixels, while cascaded SEA-RAFT retains 13.3% 1px error and 2.70-pixel EPE. Kubric and inference-strategy results are added; auxiliary-dataset accuracy entries are removed. Main-table changes also reflect the revised resolution-selection rule.

M1.justification: V2 Section 4.3 introduces a fused sampler using per-thread block lists, inter-thread minimum voting, and immediate computation and sampling of correlation tiles. This avoids the explicit mask, globally stored blocks, and cross-iteration cache used by v1's implementation. The mathematical sampling target and main cascaded SEA-RAFT procedure remain unchanged.

P1.justification: The introduction and conclusion are substantially rewritten around operator efficiency, and Section 4 is reorganized from separate mask/computation/sampling/cache subsections into high-level and fused implementations. Component analysis moves from the main evaluation to the method supplement, whose explanatory structure is expanded and reorganized. These changes exceed the title and terminology edits.

P2.justification: Figure 1 replaces the qualitative teaser with an accuracy/runtime comparison, and Figure 4 gains a fused-execution diagram. V2 adds a block-mask illustration and resolution-dependent comparison plots, changes plot axes and scales, and restructures several tables. The same three appendix image examples are retained with revised comparator rows, rather than constituting new case studies.

R1.justification: Related work receives a targeted update with DPFlow, ReCoVEr, and WAFT. V2 acknowledges DPFlow's concurrent synthetic 8K evaluation and discusses cost-volume-free approaches, qualifying the earlier evaluation-novelty positioning. The broader positioning as an exact, RAFT-compatible correlation operator remains.

T1.justification: V1 Section 8.3 derives O(P^1.5) memory with block size B=P^(1/8). V2 Section 8.5 replaces this with separate time and memory derivations that are linear in pixel count for fixed sampling parameters. It also revises the requested-block bound to account for the bilinear sampling footprint, obtaining at most nine blocks per pixel for r=4 and B=8.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially addresses v1's acknowledged mask/cache overhead bottleneck through a documented fused design and supporting measurements. A second 8K scene distribution, contemporary comparators, alternative-strategy controls, and best-resolution comparisons strengthen the empirical case, while kernel listings materially improve reproducibility. Conflicting default-size descriptions and omitted Spring split information reduce clarity, but these limitations do not outweigh the substantial gains in technical completeness and validation.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same correlation-sampling and cascaded optical-flow research despite the title change. Their complete main texts, appendices, equations, tables, figures, and code listings support reliable comparison.

after.justification: V2 reports original experiments with the revised sampler, Charge and Kubric-8K evaluations, and additional inference-strategy analyses.

before.justification: V1 reports original sampling-pattern measurements, runtime and memory benchmarks, component ablations, and optical-flow evaluations on Charge, Spring, Sintel, and KITTI.

results.title: Efficient All-Pairs Correlation Volume Sampling for Optical Flow Estimation

C1.justification: The benchmark, MRFS, and retrieval/fusion bottleneck contributions remain. The introduction and conclusion replace the claim that HERBench far exceeds the previous 2.6–4.2 MRFS range with the narrower claim that it has the highest MRFS among benchmarks tested under the canonical protocol.

C2.justification: v2 adds explanations of track selection and counting bins as noise controls, interprets human performance as supporting oracle-evidence sufficiency, and identifies compositional question complexity as a possible explanation for AGQA’s departure from the MRFS–accuracy trend. The central retrieval-versus-fusion interpretation is retained.

D1.justification: v2 specifies RF-DETR-L, discloses that existing counting bins span approximately ±40% around the true count on average, and documents correction or removal of human-flagged items. It also changes the embedded project-site destination. Existing prompts, TrackRank weights, and tracking thresholds are retained.

E1.justification: Table 1 and Figure 9 expand MRFS evaluation from four benchmarks to ten, adding TemporalBench, MMBench-Video, Video-MME, AGQA, CVRR-ES, and MINERVA. A curated DanceTrack subset is also newly evaluated for tracking quality. HERBench retains its twelve tasks and original video sources.

E2.justification: The original 13-model and five-selector comparisons are retained. New comparisons add human reference performance, six detector/tracker combinations involving RF-DETR-L, YOLO-v11-x, Grounding-DINO, DeepSORT, and ByteTrack, and the T* selector. Table 8 also extends MRFS comparisons to additional backbones.

E3.justification: New protocols include separate six-annotator groups evaluating 240 full-video questions and 2,160 oracle questions, tracking evaluation using HOTA/IDF1, a 30-video shot-boundary audit, and 50% stratified samples for MRFS robustness. The original 16-frame model evaluations and their stated sampling arrangements remain unchanged.

E4.justification: v2 adds tests of human answerability and oracle-evidence sufficiency, audits of annotation and segmentation errors, tracking-pipeline comparisons, and MRFS sensitivity across four backbones and three selectors. Figure 9 extends the MRFS–accuracy analysis with more benchmarks and a fitted relationship. Existing frame-selection and attribution analyses remain.

E5.justification: v2 introduces inter-annotator agreement reporting using Fleiss’ kappa (0.74) and a regression fit statistic for Figure 9 (reported R-squared 0.82). It does not introduce model repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, or significance tests.

E6.justification: The original model accuracies, selector-ablation scores, and per-task MRFS values are retained. Added results include Video-MME MRFS 5.31, MINERVA MRFS 5.14, human accuracies of 88.8% and 95.7% in separate studies, tracking scores, shot-boundary F1 of 0.97, and Table 8 robustness measurements. These are additional results, not demonstrated improvements to existing model scores.

M1.justification: The construction pipeline, MRFS definition and search, TrackRank, descriptor generation, and frame-attribution procedure remain unchanged. Both appendices retain selection of 6–10 tracks; v2 explains the approximately top-20% confidence observation as post-hoc analysis. The detector variant and counting-bin width are additional specifications, not demonstrated algorithm changes.

P1.justification: The abstract, related-work discussion, conclusion, benchmark-statistics section, and several captions are rewritten or condensed. New appendix subsections organize human validation and MRFS robustness, but the overall narrative and section order remain largely intact.

P2.justification: Table 1 is substantially redesigned with additional benchmarks and design-property columns. New Tables 4, 5, and 8 display tracking, human, and robustness results; Figure 9 becomes a ten-benchmark plot with a fitted line. Existing displays are also resized or relocated, while the appendix task-example images remain identical.

R1.justification: Sections 2 and 3.4 add focused positioning against MINERVA and distinguish MRFS from Temporal Indispensability and Certificate Length. References are added for the new tracking comparisons and T*, while RF-DETR and Qwen3-VL receive more directly relevant citations. The central positioning around required temporal evidence integration remains.

T1.justification: The MRFS definition, tracking merge-cost and TrackRank equations, spatial predicates, and frame-contribution formulas are unchanged. No new theorem, proof, formal assumption, or substantive mathematical derivation is introduced.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens benchmark validation by addressing v1’s lack of measured human answerability and untested MRFS configuration dependence. Human studies, quantified quality audits, reported dataset cleanup, and backbone/selector sensitivity tests provide important additional support, while broader comparisons better calibrate the MRFS claim. A reporting inconsistency remains: Section 5.2 associates the human study with oracle-only inputs, whereas Section 7.8 includes distractor frames. This limits precise human–model alignment but does not outweigh the substantial validation gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same HERBench research. Their main text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices are readable and support reliable matching across revisions.

after.justification: v2 retains these empirical results and adds human studies, tracking and segmentation validation, broader benchmark measurements, and MRFS robustness experiments.

before.justification: v1 reports original evaluations of 13 Video-LLMs, cross-benchmark MRFS measurements, frame-selection experiments, and oracle-frame attribution analyses.

results.title: HERBench: A Benchmark for Multi-Evidence Integration in Video Question Answering

C1.justification: The three stated contributions and central claims about delay-conditioned remote prediction, local fusion, and real-time applicability remain the same. The abstract retains the reported 100-ms improvements of 6.4 and 9.8 mIoU points; its added resource-release statement primarily changes reproducibility information.

C2.justification: V3 adds interpretations of delay-mismatch robustness, explaining why underestimating delay can produce overconfident localization and recommending conservative delay inputs under jitter. It also discusses abrupt scene changes and specific pseudolabel ambiguities and boundary errors, while retaining the original interpretation of stale predictions and local fallback.

D1.justification: V2 provides an inline code sketch; v3 additionally announces training-code, pretrained-model, and library release with an access address. Its appendix clarifies tensor handling, delay-embedding layer sizes, and 3D block internals, and supplies codec settings, additional training details, and hardware/precision information for runtime measurements. Resource availability is asserted by the PDF, not externally verified.

E1.justification: V3 adds Nymeria egocentric semantic segmentation using the ADE20K taxonomy, including evaluation on unseen environments and actions, beyond the retained driving-scene coverage. It also explicitly evaluates mismatched delays and delays beyond the training range in Appendix 8.3.

E2.justification: The main comparison configurations in Figure 7 and Table 3 are retained. V3 Table 4 adds a delay-unconditioned variant as a controlled comparator against the full fused model; no new external competing method is evaluated.

E3.justification: The main experimental settings remain unchanged, but v3 documents substantial protocols for added experiments: a 0–10-frame delay-mismatch sweep, ten-epoch finetuning at 224/320/480-pixel local resolutions, and H.264/H.265 tests at 1/3/5 Mbps. Nymeria introduces training on 35k clips from 229 sequences and evaluation on 2k clips from 25 disjoint sequences.

E4.justification: V3 supplies the delay-mismatch heatmap absent behind v2's unresolved jitter reference. Appendices 8.4–8.10 additionally test local resolution, removal of delay conditioning, compression robustness, component costs, an unocclusion example, and validation pseudolabel quality.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, or significance tests. The additional appendix results do not introduce statistical uncertainty estimation; averaging the delay-ablation effect across conditions is not repeated-run uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: The existing Figure 7 and Table 3 results are unchanged, but v3 adds substantial numerical and qualitative evidence. Table 4 reports an average 0.015 mIoU decrease without delay conditioning; Table 7 reports Nymeria scores of 0.2450 at zero delay and 0.2443 at five frames versus 0.2034 locally. Compression, runtime, resolution, and mismatch results are newly reported under their respective settings.

M1.justification: The architecture, fusion operation, and training objective remain unchanged. Appendix 8.3 newly proposes an optional inference rule that selects received remote features using a precomputed accuracy matrix indexed by observed and conditioning delays; the PDFs do not establish that reported experiments use this rule.

P1.justification: V3 standardizes the name to DeDelayed, makes localized wording edits, reorders the local and remote implementation descriptions, and places the expanded appendix after the references. The main narrative and section organization remain largely intact.

P2.justification: V3 adds Figures 8–12 and Tables 4–7, including a heatmap, resolution curves, quantitative summaries, and qualitative examples. It also revises labels and styling in existing diagrams, particularly Figures 2, 3, 5, and 6, and reformats the full-page code listing into an appendix column.

R1.justification: V3 adds the Nymeria dataset paper as reference 28 for its new evaluation. The existing related-work categories, cited competing approaches, and positioning relative to prior research otherwise remain unchanged after matching renumbered references.

T1.justification: The framework equations, notation, and task-loss formulation are retained. V3 adds implementation descriptions and empirical analyses, without new formal assumptions, theorems, proofs, or substantive mathematical derivations.

improvement.justification: V2's practical robustness evidence centered on fixed-delay BDD100K results and included an unresolved reference to missing jitter evidence. V3 supplies that evidence, directly tests delay conditioning and compression, and adds a distinct evaluation domain, component runtimes, and substantial reproducibility information. These additions materially strengthen validation of the central deployment claims, although statistical uncertainty remains unreported.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same DeDelayed framework and retain corresponding main experiments, equations, and figures. All supplied pages, including both appendices, are readable and support a reliable comparison.

after.justification: V3 retains those experiments and reports additional original ablation, robustness, runtime, and Nymeria evaluation results in its appendix.

before.justification: V2 reports original BDD100K segmentation experiments, including comparisons across inference configurations and delays in Figure 7 and Table 3.

results.title: DeDelayed: Deleting Remote Inference Delay via On-Device Correction

C1.justification: V1 presents Fixed and Balanced coreset construction and claims state-of-the-art compression with approximately preserved performance. V2 redefines the contribution around gradient-based SSTP, explicitly claims one-time selection with substantial training-time savings, and emphasizes improvements over full-data training in dense scenes. The central half-data and scenario-balancing goals remain, but the proposed contribution and claimed benefits expand materially.

C2.justification: V2 adds substantive explanations of why balancing and informativeness must work jointly, why moderate pretraining can outperform a converged selector, and how partition intervals should adapt to dataset characteristics. It also explicitly identifies selection overhead and performance at very low retention as limitations. These extend v1's predominantly distribution-imbalance and coreset-transfer interpretation.

D1.justification: V1 provides a detailed training recipe, including AdamW, 64 epochs, batch size 32, learning rate, weight decay, dropout and scheduling. V2 largely replaces this with references to official protocols, reducing self-contained reproducibility information. It adds a code-availability statement and repository pointer, baseline-selection descriptions, and RTX 4090 selection/training timings. The repository's availability was not externally verified.

E1.justification: V1 evaluates only Argoverse 1. V2 adds actual Argoverse 2 evaluations, extending coverage to different driving scenarios and a five-second observation window with six-second forecasting, versus Argoverse 1's two-second observation and three-second forecast. Other datasets mentioned in background discussions do not establish additional SSTP evaluations.

E2.justification: V1's external selection comparator is random sampling. V2 Table 2 adds K-means Clustering and Herding against SSTP on Argoverse 1 across all three retained prediction models. Table 3 evaluates Random and Clustering on Argoverse 2. The nonrandom comparators substantially strengthen the competitive comparison.

E3.justification: V2 substantially expands the evaluation design: QCNet/DeMo configurations for Argoverse 2, alternative selection backbones, pretraining budgets of 0/5/8/10/15/64 epochs and partition intervals of 5/10/20 agents. It adds 60% retention and no longer displays v1's 1%, 2% and 5% tests. The six prediction modes and minADE/minFDE/MR metrics remain.

E4.justification: Beyond v1's retention, density and transfer analyses, v2 adds explicit partition-only and submodular-only controls (Table 5), pretraining sensitivity (Table 6), selection-backbone comparisons (Table 7), partition sensitivity (Table 8) and measured efficiency analysis. V1's detailed low-retention dense-scene curves and distribution-variance analysis are replaced by more limited density summaries.

E5.justification: Neither supplied PDF reports repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, performance error bars or significance tests. V1's variance across scenario-category proportions describes dataset balance; it is not an estimate of uncertainty in model performance.

E6.justification: Numerous results are revised or newly reported. Full-data HiVT-64 changes from 0.692/1.047/0.104 for minADE/minFDE/MR in v1 Figure 2 to 0.695/1.037/0.109 in v2 Table 2, although v2 Table 5 retains the earlier values. V2 adds Argoverse 2, comparator, ablation and timing results. Changed methods and incompletely specified settings prevent interpreting cross-version score differences as controlled performance gains.

M1.justification: V1 scores squared differences between HiVT objective values and selects by maximizing gain. V2 instead constructs output-gradient/decoder-embedding features, scores their cosine similarities and minimizes the selection score (Equations 2–6). Algorithm 1 also revises dynamic budget allocation and replaces the separate Fixed/Balanced formulations with a balanced SSTP pipeline. These change the selection procedure substantially.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction and substantial portions of the remaining prose are rewritten around SSTP. Problem formulation moves inside Method; the experimental narrative is reorganized into main results, ablations, efficiency and generalizability, with explicit limitations. Terminology, contribution organization and author information also change.

P2.justification: V1's opening scene examples reappear in v2 Figure 2 with revised distribution plots, rather than being wholly new illustrations. V2 adds an opening performance/timing graphic and substantially restructures result displays: v1's twelve-panel density/retention figure and embedded tables give way to larger comparison tables, four retention plots and separate ablation tables. Typography and page layout also change extensively.

R1.justification: V2 adds a dedicated long-tail trajectory-prediction discussion, positioning scenario-level selection against feature-learning approaches including FEND, Hi-SCL and TRACT. It also expands coverage of recent forecasting and condensation methods while removing earlier references such as Dataset Quantization and the federated submodular-selection work. This materially revises research positioning, beyond reference renumbering.

T1.justification: The central mathematical formulation changes substantially: v1 Equation 1's squared objective-value differences become explicitly defined gradient features and a cosine-kernel criterion in v2 Equations 2–6, with a different optimization direction. The budget-allocation rule is also mathematically revised. Neither version provides a theorem or proof establishing the claimed submodular properties.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially addresses v1's weak comparative and diagnostic evidence: nonrandom selection baselines, a second benchmark and component controls test whether the method offers benefits beyond random sampling and density balancing alone. Sensitivity studies and measured selection costs further strengthen its practical assessment. These gains outweigh reduced implementation detail and reporting inconsistencies, including differing full-data HiVT values and HPNet training times of 268.8 hours in Figure 1 versus 307.2 hours in Section 4.4. Those issues still limit reproducibility and confidence in precise efficiency claims.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same work despite the SSTP retitling, and their text, equations, tables and figures are readable. Neither contains an appendix. However, v2 Section 4.5 references additional backbone results in Supplementary Material that is absent from the supplied PDFs. The main papers support reliable comparison; those supplementary results cannot be assessed.

after.justification: V2 reports original Argoverse 1 and Argoverse 2 experiments, component ablations, sensitivity studies and timing measurements. These are distinct from the prior-work training times compiled in Table 1.

before.justification: V1 reports original Argoverse 1 experiments with HiVT-64, HiVT-128 and HPNet, including retention-rate comparisons, dense-scene evaluations and dataset-distribution analysis.

results.title: Den-TP: A Density-Balanced Data Curation and Evaluation Framework for Trajectory Prediction

C1.justification: The central RefAV benchmark and program-synthesis contributions remain. The abstract and introduction replace the prospective challenge contribution with analysis of completed community results. The nuPrompt discussion additionally claims cross-dataset generalization and state-of-the-art zero-shot accuracy.

C2.justification: v3 adds explanations involving vehicle-class dominance, CLIP sensitivity to predicted boxes, ReferGPT's missing temporal context, and token efficiency from code scaffolding. Its case studies distinguish expressivity, semantic and logical failures. It also argues for cross-dataset applicability while removing v1's explicit runtime/scalability limitation and shortening the dataset-annotation limitations.

D1.justification: v3 supplies detailed ReferGPT and GPT-5 prompts, model identifiers, reasoning/tool settings, cropping and scoring rules, and synthesized-program examples. It newly documents annotation effort and generation success rate. Challenge-report access is added, while v1's direct tracker-output download link is removed; the main code and dataset links remain.

E1.justification: v1 evaluates tracking methods on RefAV; v3 additionally evaluates RefProg on nuPrompt, introducing nuScenes data and its referential expressions. Appendix C also analyzes sampled expressions from nuPrompt, Refer-KITTI and nuScenes-QA. The underlying RefAV coverage remains 1,000 driving logs and 10,000 log-prompt pairs.

E2.justification: Table 2 removes RefInflate/GroundingDINO and adds caption-based ReferGPT, GPT-5 black-box inference and three challenge submissions. Table 4 adds nuPrompt comparisons with CenterPoint Tracker, DQTrack, ADA-Track and PromptTrack. RefBlind and RefClassify are retained as Filter by Referred Class and Image-Embedding Similarity, respectively.

E3.justification: New protocols include nuPrompt evaluation with StreamPETR and AMOTA, AMOTP, recall and MOTA; GPT-5-based cost comparisons; and embedding-based farthest-point sampling of 30 expressions per dataset. Existing RefAV HOTA/balanced-accuracy metrics and 2 Hz evaluation are retained. These additions do not establish reruns of the retained experiments.

E4.justification: v3 adds token/cost analysis in Appendix B, systematic qualitative dataset comparison in C, per-scenario occurrence analysis in G, and three successful plus three unsuccessful synthesized-program case studies in I. The earlier LLM, related/other-object and sampling-rate analyses remain.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, significance tests or comparable uncertainty estimates. Added dataset frequencies and token measurements do not introduce uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: Shared RefProg/Le3DE2E performance remains 50.1 HOTA-Temporal. v3 adds ReferGPT at 20.2, GPT-5 black-box inference at 37.2 and the leading challenge entry at 53.4 in Table 2, and RefProg/StreamPETR at 0.321 AMOTA on nuPrompt in Table 4. RefInflate's 4.0 result disappears. New cost results use different LLM configurations. Table 1 also changes RefAV frames from 15,500 to 155k and nuPrompt expressions from 40,776 to 407k; these are not equivalent rounding.

M1.justification: The central program-synthesis-and-track-filtering procedure remains. v3 adds SigLIP2 visual-attribute access and an is_color function absent from v1's API. Its nuPrompt adaptation changes the category list and excludes map-dependent functions while retaining the remaining atomic definitions.

P1.justification: Baseline and empirical-analysis explanations are substantially rewritten, including replacement of RefBlind/RefClassify terminology. Section 4 consolidates formerly separate metrics, ablation, challenge and limitations subsections. The supplement is reorganized from Appendices A–F into A–J, although much of the introduction, related work and conclusion remains.

P2.justification: v3 adopts two-column layout throughout, redraws the problem-setup and dataset-creation figures, relocates and reformats retained illustrations and tables, and adds nuPrompt and cost tables plus a scenario-occurrence chart. Existing distribution plots and supplementary performance tables are mostly reformatted or moved rather than replaced.

R1.justification: The main related-work discussion is largely retained. v3 adds citations for ADA-Track, DQTrack, SigLIP2, StreamPETR and CenterPoint, and removes GroundingDINO. Appendix C elaborates RefAV's planning-oriented positioning through sampled comparisons with existing driving-language datasets.

T1.justification: v3 Appendix A adds explicit mathematical definitions for ReferGPT's motion-feature vector and weighted matching score, s = s_cosine + 0.1 s_fuzzy. This is a limited formal specification addition; neither version develops theoretical guarantees or proofs.

improvement.justification: The nuPrompt evaluation tests portability beyond RefAV's shared generation/mining API, while actual ReferGPT and GPT-5 comparisons strengthen baseline validation. Detailed implementation, cost and failure analyses substantially improve assessability and reproducibility. Drawbacks include removal of the runtime caveat, different decoders in the nuPrompt comparison, and unexplained ReferGPT scores of 20.2 versus 20.7 across Tables 2 and 5. These limit particular conclusions but do not outweigh the substantial validation and documentation gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe RefAV and RefProg. Their text, tables, figures and complete appendices are readable and matchable despite substantial restructuring.

after.justification: v3 retains original experiments and adds baseline evaluations, nuPrompt results, token-cost measurements and qualitative analyses.

before.justification: v1 reports original baseline evaluations, LLM ablations, sampling-rate experiments and dataset analyses in the main text and appendices.

results.title: RefAV: Towards Planning-Centric Scenario Mining

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction's contribution statements, and Discussion retain the same central claims about encoder-dependent spatial circuits, attention analysis, and differing prompt robustness. The added methods and experiments expand their support without changing these headline claims.

C2.justification: v2 explains how T5 heads produce spatial gradients from relation factors in object tokens and connects perturbations to distorted gradients and biased placement. It also adds substantive qualifications: zero-sum factorization can bias feature discovery, screened heads require causal validation, CLIP ablations also harm object attributes, and pretrained transfer remains limited (Appendices A.8–A.10 and B.6–B.7).

D1.justification: v1 promises code and data release after acceptance; v2 supplies a repository address and states that code, configurations, and datasets are available. It also documents the CLIP checkpoint, precision and embedding dimensions, provides screening pseudocode, and newly identifies Table 2's 4000-epoch EMA checkpoint.

E1.justification: Beyond the retained synthetic two-object task and filler-word variations, v2 evaluates locative inversion and color synonyms (Appendix A.8). It also introduces natural-object prompts covering 30 object pairs for pretrained PixArt-Sigma, extending actual evaluation beyond synthetic shapes (Appendix A.10).

E2.justification: Table 2 retains the existing RTE and T5 comparison configurations and adds one encoder family, CLIP, at DiT-B and DiT-mini sizes under the same prompt templates. Renamed random-embedding configurations match the earlier comparators.

E3.justification: The new PixArt-Sigma evaluation introduces object-order and relation-reversal controls, SAM detection plus annotation, and relation accuracy conditioned on correct objects (Figure 30). The embedding-intervention multiplier changes from 2 to 3, and Appendix B.5 revises the stated attention-synopsis sweep from 168 to 96 prompts; this reporting revision does not establish reruns.

E4.justification: Appendices A.7–A.10 add screening across model configurations, analyses connecting prompt perturbations to embeddings and spatial gradients, CLIP token and head ablations, and a pretrained-model case study. These substantially extend the mechanistic and robustness evidence. The original RTE ablations remain, despite being merged into different figures.

E5.justification: Figure 30A newly specifies 100 generation seeds for the pretrained-model evaluation. This is additional seed-count information, not evidence of increased repetitions for existing experiments. The original Table 2 sampling description and Appendix B.6 permutation-testing procedure are retained.

E6.justification: Existing Table 2 results are unchanged, but CLIP results are added: DiT-mini loose spatial accuracy is 0.814 on the original template and 0.819 with 'the' before object 2. New findings identify T5 L3H7 and CLIP L0H2/L0H5, show substantial effects of CLIP head ablation, and report nontrivial pretrained performance for 8 of 30 object pairs. The vector-intervention illustration is also replaced under different scaling.

M1.justification: v2 adds a weight-space head-screening algorithm that combines positional queries with relation-feature keys and ranks heads through directional-ramp alignment (Section 5, Appendix B.7). This substantially extends v1's attention-synopsis and targeted QK inspection procedures, allowing systematic screening without generating images.

P1.justification: Section 5 receives localized rewriting, Appendix B.6 gains intuitive exposition, and the earlier robustness discussion moves into Appendix A.8. Terminology is revised toward RTE naming. The abstract, introduction, Discussion, and main section organization remain largely unchanged.

P2.justification: Figures 3–5 and 7 are substantially recomposed with additional panels. v1's Figure 6 ablations become panels in v2's Figures 4–5, while its Figure 9 moves to Figure 26. New screening, robustness, CLIP, and pretrained-model figures and an expanded Table 2 substantially extend the visual presentation.

R1.justification: v2 adds Fel et al.'s 'Into the rabbit hull' citation when discussing alternative spatial query representations. Appendices B.6–B.7 also briefly position variance partitioning as supervised feature discovery relative to sparse autoencoders. The existing background and principal novelty positioning remain stable.

T1.justification: Appendix B.7 adds a substantial mathematical formulation of head screening (Equations 27–38), including the positional-embedding approximation for queries, spatial QK maps, directional ramp templates, and aggregate head scores. The earlier variance-partition derivation remains unchanged.

improvement.justification: v1 left the specific T5 relation-head mechanism unresolved. v2 substantially closes that gap through weight-space localization and perturbation analysis, strengthens generality with causal CLIP experiments, and adds an initial pretrained-model check. Detailed screening instructions and reported code/data availability also improve reproducibility. Pretrained head causality remains unvalidated, and localized reporting inconsistencies remain, including the alignment sign in Appendix A.8 versus Figure 27, but the mechanistic and evidential gains are substantial.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same study. Their complete main texts and appendices, including equations, tables, and figures, support reliable comparison after matching relocated and renumbered material.

after.justification: v2 retains these original results and adds weight-space screening, CLIP-DiT experiments, further robustness analyses, and a pretrained PixArt-Sigma evaluation.

before.justification: v1 reports original DiT training results, attention analyses, head ablations, embedding interventions, and prompt-robustness experiments.

results.title: Circuit Mechanisms for Spatial Relation Generation in Diffusion Transformers

C1.justification: PCD and the controlled SensorRainFall benchmark remain the central contributions. The abstract, introduction, and conclusion broaden the explicitly claimed dataset and validation scope to illumination variation and segmentation, while retaining the central claim of distance-dependent reliability beyond static metrics.

C2.justification: v2 adds safety-envelope interpretations, application-specific threshold guidance, and variance/failure-tail explanations for disagreements with conventional metrics. It also changes the threshold interpretation: v1 Section 5.2.3 describes abrupt rainy-daylight behavior, whereas v2 Section 5.2 describes both daylight surfaces as smooth and emphasizes nighttime instability.

D1.justification: Supplement Sections 7 and 9 substantially expand documentation of sensor synchronization, DGPS distances, lighting, target placement, pedestrian coverings, checkpoints, preprocessing, optimization, and model configurations. Most are newly disclosed details rather than demonstrated changes to existing experiments. The code/data links and computing environment remain unchanged.

E1.justification: Coverage expands from vehicle detection under clear and rainy daylight to vehicle and pedestrian detection and instance segmentation across four conditions, adding rainy night with and without streetlights. These are substantive changes in targets, task requirements, and illumination conditions.

E2.justification: The five original object detectors remain. v2 additionally evaluates Mask R-CNN, ConvNeXt-V2, SOLOv2, Mask2Former, and RTMDet in the segmentation comparisons, as documented in Tables 9–10.

E3.justification: v2 adds AR and F150 evaluation and controlled simulation protocols varying sample sizes, change-point counts, and variance contrasts. Supplement Section 9 also reports YOLOX depth/width factors of 1.33/1.25 versus v1's 0.33/0.5, although v2's main text retains the old factors. This establishes conflicting reported settings, not verified rerunning.

E4.justification: New Section 5.3 tests change-point detection sensitivity to sample size and effect size. Figures 5–6 add model-pair case studies explaining metric disagreements, and Figure 7 extends threshold-sensitivity analysis to nighttime conditions. These substantially expand the analytical support beyond v1's daylight analyses.

E5.justification: Section 5.3 newly specifies 1,000 replications per sample-size/change-point-count combination, with means and standard deviations in Figure 8. This uncertainty reporting is confined to the simulation; benchmark tables still lack reported repeated-run uncertainty, and the existing alpha = 0.05 change-point criterion remains.

E6.justification: v2 adds extensive nighttime, pedestrian, segmentation, and simulation results. Retained clear-daylight scores also change: Deformable DETR's aggregate PCD is 106.275 versus 104.855 m, and AP50 is 0.953 versus 0.947 in v1 Table 3 and v2 Table 7. Original rainy-daylight scores and change-point locations are retained. The PDFs do not explain all numerical revisions.

M1.justification: Both versions use IoU × confidence, spline mean estimation, recursive variance-change testing, Gaussian exceedance probabilities, and the same maximum-distance rule. Renaming mPCD to aPCD preserves the threshold-aggregation construction; segmentation experiments do not introduce a new PCD procedure.

P1.justification: The method section is reordered to present PCD computation first, and experiments are reorganized around representative comparisons, insights, and estimator validation. Full results and configurations move into supplementary sections. The abstract and explanatory passages are extensively rewritten, with mPCD renamed aPCD throughout.

P2.justification: v2 adopts a two-column layout, redraws the conceptual PCD figure, expands dataset and threshold panels, and adds model-comparison, simulation, and annotation figures. Dataset and benchmark tables are relocated, restructured, and expanded in the supplement, with a new representative-results table in the main text.

R1.justification: Section 2 substantially broadens the evaluation-metric context by discussing LRP/oLRP, PDQ, JIoU, and GIoU, extending positioning beyond conventional and temporal metrics to localization and uncertainty-aware evaluation. Additional segmentation and statistical references support the expanded scope; these citations alone are not experimental comparisons.

T1.justification: The formal PCD definition, Gaussian assumptions, spline objective, and variance-change test remain mathematically equivalent. Section 5.3 restates the existing rejection rule in equivalent probability form and adds empirical simulations, rather than new theory or proofs.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially addresses v1's narrow vehicle-only daylight validation and absence of empirical testing of the change-point estimator through broader experiments and replicated simulations. Expanded related work and implementation documentation further strengthen the paper. Unreconciled rainfall descriptions (64 versus 20/40 mm/h), conflicting YOLOX configurations, and unexplained score revisions weaken reproducibility, but the new evidence substantially improves support for the central evaluation framework.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same PCD metric and SensorRainFall research. Their text, equations, figures, and tables are readable, including v2's supplementary Sections 7–9. Retained material can be matched across restructuring and renumbering.

after.justification: v2 reports expanded detection and segmentation experiments in Tables 1 and 3–10, plus original synthetic change-point simulations in Section 5.3.

before.justification: v1 reports original detector evaluations, estimated variance change points, and threshold-sensitivity results on SensorRainFall in Tables 2–3 and Figures 4–6.

results.title: Perception Characteristics Distance: Measuring Stability and Robustness of Perception System in Dynamic Conditions under a Certain Decision Rule

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, contribution list, and conclusion retain the same claims about intrinsic-space weather editing, IMAA, the two datasets, and downstream perception benefits. The headline ACDC improvements and claimed advantages over existing approaches are unchanged; the supplement chiefly supplies supporting evidence and details.

C2.justification: The existing temporal-consistency limitation is supplemented by a specific qualification: severe occlusion can cause hallucinated backgrounds and unreliable re-rendered details (supplement I and Figure 25). Sections C.4 and E also explain IMAA collapse without heuristic pretraining and connect distillation to more natural intermediate weather states.

D1.justification: Supplement C–D and G supply substantial previously unavailable implementation information: latent channels, guidance and dropout settings, losses, training stages, learning rates, batch sizes, resolutions, LoRA rank, hardware and runtimes, captioning/filtering procedures, and downstream checkpoints. Dataset release remains promised upon acceptance. The supplement's 35K WeatherSynthetic count conflicts with the retained 38K main-text count, leaving the actual size unresolved.

E1.justification: Reported coverage expands beyond driving scenes to indoor training and evaluation using InteriorVerse and Hypersim, which v2 only discusses as existing datasets. Supplement H.3 and Figure 23 also demonstrate non-driving outdoor scenes with people. These extend the represented domains beyond merely adding examples from retained benchmarks.

E2.justification: TurboEdit is newly included as an evaluated weather-removal comparator in supplement F.1 and Figure 9. The original main-table comparator sets remain unchanged, and the indoor evaluation largely reuses the existing inverse-rendering baselines.

E3.justification: The supplementary evaluations add controls crossing IMAA use with additional fine-tuning, plus a control without progressive training. Indoor evaluation assigns four intrinsic maps to InteriorVerse and irradiance to Hypersim. The retained main experiments, metrics, ACDC validation setting, and 61-participant/eight-case study are unchanged; newly specified training settings are implementation disclosures.

E4.justification: Beyond v2's main IMAA and forward-renderer data ablations, v5 supplies stage-specific IMAA controls, heuristic-pretraining analysis, indoor-only training and inverse-renderer WeatherReal ablations, and comparisons of interpolation and feature distillation. It also provides out-of-distribution examples and explicit dense-fog failure cases, substantially expanding the evidence about component necessity and robustness.

E5.justification: Neither PDF reports repeated-run counts, experimental seeds, confidence intervals, error bars, or significance tests. The supplementary tables continue point-estimate reporting, and the user-study participant count is unchanged.

E6.justification: Main Tables 1–3 retain their numerical results. v5 adds indoor results in supplementary Table 4, including 23.58 dB albedo PSNR and 3.11 normal MAE, additional ablation rows, cross-weather consistency values, and user preferences of 77.07% for removal and 86.28% for synthesis. These are newly reported results, not improvements over v2 under matched settings.

M1.justification: The two-renderer framework, intrinsic map-aware attention, CLIP weather-direction interpolation, heuristic training, and feature distillation are already described in v2 and retained in v5. Supplement C specifies their implementation and training; it does not establish a redesign of the proposed method.

P1.justification: The main narrative, terminology, and section sequence remain essentially verbatim. v5 condenses the author and affiliation block, removes email addresses, and adds separately organized supplementary explanations. The existing argument is not extensively rewritten or reorganized.

P2.justification: The main figure images and table contents are retained but reflowed, with several displays relocated between pages. The supplement adds an architecture diagram, dataset comparison table, expanded ablation and indoor-result tables, and extensive qualitative and failure-case panels. Some material is redisplayed, such as retained ablation rows and Waymo examples, but substantial new visual evidence is supplied.

R1.justification: Supplement A adds historical context on Retinex, prior-based decomposition, and learned inverse rendering. Additional references support implementation choices, datasets, and TurboEdit. The central positioning against pixel-space weather editing and indoor/object-focused rendering methods remains unchanged.

T1.justification: The five main-method equations are unchanged. Supplement C.4 and C.6 add explicit mathematical definitions of IMAA supervision and the feature-distillation objective, including its normalized-feature MSE and cosine terms. This is limited formalization of previously described components; no new theorem, proof, or theoretical guarantee is introduced.

improvement.justification: v5 resolves substantial documentation and evidential gaps in the supplied v2 by providing implementation details and supporting analyses previously deferred to an absent supplement. Training specifications, component controls, indoor evaluations, and the explicit hallucination failure case make the work substantially easier to reproduce and assess. The unresolved 35K/38K dataset discrepancy detracts from consistency, but does not outweigh these gains; the headline performance results themselves are unchanged.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe WeatherDiffusion, and their text, equations, tables, and figures are readable. v2 ends after the references despite referring to supplementary material; v5 includes that material. Added documentation can therefore be identified, without assuming that the underlying experiments or procedures were newly performed.

after.justification: v5 retains those original results and supplies additional indoor evaluations, ablation results, user-preference breakdowns, and qualitative analyses in its supplement.

before.justification: v2 reports original weather-editing comparisons, inverse-rendering measurements, ACDC detection and segmentation results, ablations, and a 61-participant user study.

results.title: IntrinsicWeather: Controllable Weather Editing in Intrinsic Space

C1.justification: v3 presents PriorDiffusion as a novel model and claims state-of-the-art zero-shot performance. v4 presents Iris as an investigation of text integration across Marigold, Lotus and E2E-FT, claiming generally improved baseline-relative accuracy. It also explicitly claims occasional benefits from text used at only one stage and promotes the existing iterative-refinement observation into a central finding.

C2.justification: v4 adds distinct explanations for training-only benefits through learned disambiguation and inference-only benefits through pretrained text associations. It interprets caption-count saturation as redundancy in geometric information. The discussion emphasizes conditioning that reduces possible 3D solutions and proposes consistency filtering or uncertainty estimation for inaccurate descriptions, extending the earlier geometric-prior and attention-based interpretation.

D1.justification: Appendix B.2 adds detailed Lotus and E2E-FT configurations, including GPU counts, batch accumulation, optimizers, schedules, precision, preprocessing, dataset mixing and InternVL3 captions with a 77-token limit. Existing Marigold details largely remain. The release promise expands from code to code and generated text data, but neither PDF establishes an available release. Caption-count documentation remains inconsistent.

E1.justification: v4 adds DIODE as a fifth real-world zero-shot depth benchmark. Hypersim and Virtual KITTI training coverage and the NYUv2, KITTI, ETH3D and ScanNet evaluations remain. This extends dataset coverage within the existing monocular depth task.

E2.justification: Table 1 adds evaluated Lotus-D, Lotus-G and E2E-FT baselines, including reported and retrained results; these methods were only discussed in v3. HDN, DiverseDepth, LeReS and MiDaS disappear from the quantitative comparison. Appendix Table 3 also adds a Marigold comparator to the prompt ablation.
