E3.justification: The new Lotus and E2E-FT experiments introduce 20,000-iteration training and one-step inference configurations, with backbone-specific sample counts, resolutions, normalization and caption generators. Text-stage and caption-count controls expand the evaluation design. v4's main text changes the reported default from ten sampled training captions to one, although Appendix B.2 still describes ten for Marigold, leaving that default inconsistently documented.

E4.justification: Table 1 expands text-availability analysis to training-only, inference-only and joint conditioning across several backbones; v3 already tested missing inference text for its own model. New Table 6 evaluates one, two, five and ten training captions. Figure 9 adds the correct-text prediction beside the incorrect-text failure. Existing small-area, prompt, denoising-step and iterative-refinement analyses are retained.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, standard deviations or significance tests for its experimental results. v4's proposed future uncertainty-based language filtering is not implemented statistical reporting.

E6.justification: v4 adds extensive Lotus/E2E-FT, text-stage and DIODE results, including DIODE δ1/AbsRel of 78.9/29.8 for Marigold with text. Table 6 adds two- and five-caption outcomes. Many Marigold scores are retained or redistributed: v4's default matches v3's one-caption prompt-ablation results, while the earlier ten-caption scores remain in Table 6. The small-area and denoising-step tables retain their numerical results.

M1.justification: Section 3 retains the same text-integration mechanism: frozen CLIP text embeddings and VAE image/depth representations condition the diffusion model, with unchanged diffusion equations, loss and inference recurrence. The additional backbone experiments apply this conditioning strategy without introducing a new integration component.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction, contribution statements and conclusion are extensively rewritten around Iris and an empirical investigation. 'Our contributions' becomes 'Our findings,' Method becomes Formulation, implementation detail shifts toward the appendix, and appendix training and caption sections are expanded and reorganized. These changes substantially alter the narrative beyond renaming.

P2.justification: Table 1 is redesigned into backbone-specific comparison blocks with DIODE columns, text-stage variants, highlighting and gray styling for results the authors could not reproduce. Table 6 is added, Figure 9 gains a correct-text comparison panel, and several figures and appendix tables move. Most qualitative image panels are retained. Figure 7's former NYUv2 panel is incorrectly relabeled KITTI in v4.

R1.justification: The work shifts from claiming the first language-prior approach for diffusion-based 3D perception to investigating an insufficiently studied capability of existing depth estimators. This substantially changes its novelty positioning. References add Jasmine, InternVL3, DIODE, ETA, ProtoDepth and HOMER, while removing the LLaVA-generated-prompts paper, ExpansionNet v2 and the MaskDINO reference.

T1.justification: The diffusion formulation, conditioning variables, training loss, inference update and appendix alignment/metric definitions remain unchanged. Neither version supplies theoretical propositions or proofs. The expanded conditional-distribution explanation is qualitative rather than a new derivation or formal result.

improvement.justification: v3's broad language-benefit claims rely chiefly on one Marigold-based system. v4 substantially strengthens their empirical foundation through paired baseline/text-enabled evaluations across several estimators, text-stage controls and caption-count analysis, while replacing broad state-of-the-art framing with more measured claims. Caption-count inconsistencies, missing DIODE protocol details and the Figure 7 labeling error limit reproducibility and presentation, but the stronger evidence for generality and clearer contribution scope provide a substantial net improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same language-conditioned depth-estimation research, renamed from PriorDiffusion to Iris. Their complete main texts and appendices are readable, and corresponding methods, experiments, tables and figures can be matched despite substantial restructuring.

after.justification: v4 retains original experiments and reports additional backbone comparisons, DIODE evaluations, text-stage controls and caption-count ablations.

before.justification: v3 reports original depth-estimation experiments, convergence comparisons, small-region evaluations, prompt ablations and qualitative analyses in the main text and appendix.

results.title: Iris: Integrating Language into Diffusion-based Monocular Depth Estimation

C1.justification: The central claims of training-free mask/palette control, local fidelity, global harmony and efficient consumer-GPU inference remain. v2's conclusion adds explicit compatibility with more advanced foundational models. Its stronger emphasis on latent composition largely restates the composition formulation already present in v1.

C2.justification: v2 adds substantive interpretations concerning pixel-space interaction, CSS3 compatibility with pretrained models, colour naming versus LLMs, palette-size ambiguity and domain-specific performance. Existing small-region and colour-vocabulary limitations remain. The new claim that local results achieve best FID and DCCW across all datasets overstates Table 1, which contains counterexamples.

D1.justification: v2 identifies official/HuggingFace implementations, TF-ICON and Prompt-to-Prompt implementation sources, local CFG=2.5, and metric feature extractors. It removes the approximate 30-second runtime and detailed component/comparator timings, while replacing exact AFHQ sample counts with approximate counts. The stated GPU and project-access link remain.

E1.justification: v2 adds indoor/outdoor Place365-small scenes, Danbooru2023 anime and PascalVOC2012 multi-object scenes, substantially broadening evaluated domains. AFHQ-cat/dog and the 15 internet sketches remain. AFHQ-wildlife, evaluated in v1 supplementary Table S2, is absent from v2.

E2.justification: v2 adds T2I-Adapter plus IDeepColor to global comparisons and ColorizeDiffusion, ColorFlow, MangaNinja and Cobra to local benchmarks. Supplementary comparisons also introduce IDeepColor, SDEdit and standalone Scribble ControlNet. DiffBlender and T2I-Adapter remain, and DiSS is retained in Figure S6. Anime-Painter/CounterfeitXL appear as proposed-method variants, not independent baseline rows.

E3.justification: Sketch extraction changes from PiDiNet alone to PiDiNet plus LineartDetector, and the reported local backbone changes from SD2.1 to SD1.5. New local benchmarks use two random masks and shared reference patches. v2 adds DCCW, drops MSE, tests palette sizes 1–5 and evaluates an Anime-Painter/CounterfeitXL variant. PSNR and SSIM already appeared in v1's supplement.

E4.justification: v2 adds palette-size sensitivity analysis and tests local composition against IDeepColor, refinement against SDEdit, and spatial control against text-guided ControlNet. Original prompt, attention-injection, scaling-factor, VQA and solver analyses remain. The SD2.1-versus-SD1.5 ablation and component/runtime analysis from v1's supplement are removed.

E5.justification: Neither version reports evaluation-run counts, explicit evaluation seeds, error bars, confidence intervals or significance tests. v2 mentions changing random seeds for interactive previews, but introduces no statistical replication or uncertainty-reporting practice.

E6.justification: v2 adds extensive local/global benchmark and ablation results. Existing AFHQ global scores also change: proposed-method cat/dog FID values are 56.51/60.90 in v1 Table 1 and 50.31/89.70 in v2 Table 2. Changed preprocessing prevents interpreting these as established same-setting gains or losses. Wildlife, MSE, timing and the SD1.5 substitution result are removed.

M1.justification: The global-to-local pipeline, BLIP-2, colour-name retrieval, inversion, exceptional prompts and self-attention schedule remain. However, v2 specifies Stable Diffusion v1.5 for the local stage where v1 specifies v2.1, and revises the transition-mask expression used for noise injection. These are limited changes within the retained method.

P1.justification: The title, abstract and introduction are substantially rewritten around latent composition, replacing the childhood-colouring narrative. Background and ControlNet explanations are condensed, sketch-to-image generation is integrated into the global-stage section, experiments are reorganized around local/global evaluation, and the supplement is extensively restructured.

P2.justification: v2 adopts a two-column layout and replaces the original architecture presentation with an overview and detailed stage diagrams, adding colour-search, interactive-refinement and noise-injection illustrations. Benchmark displays expand substantially. Original attention/scaling ablations are retained, the DiffBlender/DiSS comparison moves to Figure S6 with additional examples, and six supplementary sketch-gallery figures are consolidated into three.

R1.justification: The broad training-free, user-guided positioning remains. v2 explicitly acknowledges Automatic Controllable Colorization via Imagination as an antecedent and updates discussion with MangaNinja, ColorFlow, Cobra and other line-art work. Some earlier editing/composition references disappear, including DiffEdit and Applying a Color Palette with Local Control using Diffusion Models; supplementary Section K elaborates the novelty positioning.

T1.justification: The transition-mask definition changes from max(sum of rectangular-mask XOR terms, 1) in v1 Section 3.4 to the plain sum in v2 Section 3.3. This is a non-equivalent mathematical revision, although the PDFs do not establish whether implementation changed accordingly. The principal diffusion, guidance and attention equations remain; no new theorem or proof is introduced.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially addresses v1's central validation gap: local colourisation previously had mainly qualitative evidence, while systematic comparisons focused on the global stage. Multi-domain local benchmarks, explicit palette-fidelity measurement and targeted refinement ablations now test the main contribution directly. These gains outweigh the removed timing evidence and inaccurate superiority wording. Those errors remain material: Table 1 gives ColorFlow better Danbooru FID than SketchDeco (94.87 versus 134.54), and ColorizeDiffusion better indoor DCCW (9.73 versus 11.85).

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe SketchDeco, with matching authors, core methodology and retained experiments. Their main text, equations, tables, figures and complete supplementary material are readable and support comparison despite retitling and substantial reformatting.

after.justification: v2 reports original global and local colourisation benchmarks, palette-size experiments and qualitative component comparisons in Tables 1–3 and the supplement.

before.justification: v1 reports original quantitative colourisation results, qualitative outputs, component ablations and computational timings in Table 1 and supplementary Tables S1–S2.

results.title: SketchDeco: Training-Free Latent Composition for Precise Sketch Colourisation

C1.justification: The central claims remain action-space reasoning through complementary EAR/IAR modules and strong simulation and real-world performance. V2 removes benchmark percentages from the abstract and contribution summary, but retains the underlying claims and corresponding results elsewhere.

C2.justification: Appendix C newly attributes simulation-to-real performance retention to kinematically grounded action priors that remain invariant to visual perturbations. Section 4.2 distinguishes generalization findings by evaluation regime. The computational and action-representation limitations in Appendix D are unchanged.

D1.justification: V2 adds a code-availability statement and repository link, identifies frozen LLM backbones in existing result tables, and clarifies checkpoint provenance and training regimes. These annotations disclose previously unstated details rather than establishing changes to retained experiments. Existing hardware, hyperparameters, and Appendix B training details remain available.

E1.justification: Appendix C adds Genie Sim 3.0 coverage: color-, size-, and category-based object selection and tabletop organization, with simulation-trained policies evaluated in simulation and reality. This introduces a distinct transfer scenario beyond the retained simulation benchmarks and experiments trained on real-world demonstrations.

E2.justification: Table 1 adds GO-1 and VLA-Adapter to the LIBERO comparison. Table 2 removes OpenVLA-OFT+, while retaining OpenVLA-OFT. Most comparator membership remains unchanged; the new Genie Sim comparison uses the existing π0.5 baseline.

E3.justification: V2 adds LIBERO-trained zero-shot evaluation on LIBERO-Plus alongside the retained supervised setting, reports configurations with and without LLM freezing, and introduces simulation-trained real-world deployment on Genie Sim. Section 4.2 also corrects LIBERO's stated total from 500 to 2,000 rollouts while retaining 40 tasks and 50 trials per task; this does not establish additional runs.

E4.justification: The robustness analysis expands to test LIBERO-Plus generalization without training on that benchmark and simulation-to-real performance retention in Appendix C. Existing EAR/IAR, reference-horizon, KV-cache, model-scaling, denoising, and latency analyses remain unchanged.

E5.justification: Neither version reports training-seed variability, confidence intervals, error bars, or significance tests. Per-task repetition practices remain unchanged, and the new transfer experiment introduces no uncertainty estimation. The corrected LIBERO evaluation total is a sample-count reporting change covered under E3.

E6.justification: Tables 1–2 add baseline and training-configuration results. V2 retains the original LIBERO mean of 98.5% and LIBERO-Plus supervised mean of 84.1%, adding zero-shot means of 83.6% and 86.6% and a non-frozen supervised result of 88.0%. New Table 11 reports Genie Sim averages of 84.2% in simulation and 82.9% in reality, versus π0.5's 75.7% and 77.5%. These are additional settings, not same-setting improvements over v1.

M1.justification: The EAR, IAR, action-guided prediction, flow-matching objectives, teacher-forcing procedure, and inference mechanism remain unchanged in Section 3. Additional backbone-training configurations do not introduce a new method component.

P1.justification: V2 condenses benchmark descriptions and headline summaries, edits the conclusion and terminology, and adds a transfer-evaluation paragraph in Appendix C. The overall narrative, section order, and most prose remain intact.

P2.justification: Table 2 is reorganized into zero-shot and supervised blocks; Table 1 gains rows, and several captions gain configuration annotations. A new Genie Sim table becomes Table 11, moving the unchanged efficiency table to Table 12. Figures 1–4 retain their content, with limited layout reflow elsewhere.

R1.justification: V2 adds references to VLA-Adapter and Genie Sim 3.0. GO-1 uses the already-cited AgiBot World work. The related-work organization and positioning of action-space reasoning against linguistic and visual intermediaries remain substantially unchanged.

T1.justification: The problem formulation and Equations 1–12 retain the same mathematical content. Neither version contains additional theorems or proofs, and v2 adds no formal derivation.

improvement.justification: V1 combined zero-shot baselines and models trained on LIBERO-Plus in one comparison. V2 separates these regimes, supplies its own zero-shot results, and identifies backbone freezing, resolving a material comparability problem in the central robustness evidence. Direct simulation-to-real evaluation further strengthens generalization support. Its missing trial counts and uncertainty estimates, and the untested invariance explanation, limit that additional evidence but do not outweigh the improved evaluation validity.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe ACoT-VLA and contain readable main text, equations, figures, tables, and Appendices A–E. Retained material can be matched reliably across pagination and table renumbering.

after.justification: V2 retains those original experiments and adds training variants, zero-shot evaluations, and Genie Sim 3.0 simulation-to-real results.

before.justification: V1 reports original simulation benchmarks, component ablations, efficiency measurements, and real-world robot experiments.

results.title: ACoT-VLA: Action Chain-of-Thought for Vision-Language-Action Models

C1.justification: The title, abstract, contributions and conclusion broaden the work from efficient 3D layout estimation to 3D scene understanding encompassing layout and object detection on synthetic and real-world data. The introduction adds a 5.14-fold detection-speedup claim alongside the retained 5.09-fold layout claim. The central MTP, filtering and parameter-efficiency contributions remain.

C2.justification: v2 adds explanations involving MTP regularization, inter-head agreement as a confidence-learning signal, and layout-token redundancy versus detection-token structure. It also discusses limited SceneCAD training data and explicitly identifies incomplete point clouds and non-Manhattan layouts as failure conditions. These substantially extend v1's discussion of softmax reliability and decoding tradeoffs.

D1.justification: v2 discloses the default CGD threshold of 0.90, teacher-forcing confidence-label construction, residual projection-block diagrams, detection annotation generation, task-specific training schedules and ASE split-file names. Existing optimizer, learning-rate, batch-size and layout-training details move to Appendix B largely unchanged. The split-file references do not themselves supply their contents.

E1.justification: v1 evaluates layout estimation on synthetic ASE and Structured3D. v2 adds real-world SceneCAD and evaluates 3D object detection on both ASE and SceneCAD. ASE detection covers cabinet, chair, table, sofa and bed, substantially broadening both task and domain coverage.

E2.justification: The existing SceneScript, SceneScript+MTP, RoomFormer, ProductThre and SoftmaxThre comparisons are retained. Table S4 adds the ground-truth-supervised confidence variant CGD, GT as a comparator. Extending existing baselines to detection and SceneCAD does not itself change their membership; TR3D supplies annotations rather than serving as an evaluated baseline.

E3.justification: Existing layout protocols are retained. New detection experiments introduce an ASE 19k/1k train/test split, generated bounding-box annotations, and F1 evaluation at 0.25 and 0.50 IoU. Appendix B specifies detection training budgets and SceneCAD fine-tuning. Additional experiments vary head counts and thresholds and compare 60- versus 90-epoch SceneScript training.

E4.justification: The original ablations remain as Table 4. Tables S1-S5 add 12/16-head tests, scoring-threshold sweeps, confidence-supervision tolerance tests, ground-truth versus first-head supervision, and a longer-training baseline control. New analyses examine classwise and detection token-score distributions and show failures on incomplete point clouds and non-Manhattan scenes. The Structured3D visualization is relocated, not newly added.

E5.justification: Neither version reports experimental seed counts, repeated-run variability, confidence intervals or significance tests. The new confidence-score distributions and discussion of model uncertainty concern token predictions, not uncertainty estimation for experimental performance.

E6.justification: Original Tables 1-2 and v1 Table 3, now Table 4, retain their numbers. New results include SceneCAD layout SSD at 0.556 F1 and 42 ms versus SceneScript at 0.556 and 108 ms, and ASE detection SSD at 0.829 F1@0.50 and 104 ms versus 0.823 and 535 ms. Supplementary tables add sensitivity and control outcomes. Table S2 inconsistently reports 16.10 M parameters for ProductThre/SoftmaxThre versus 15.05 M in retained Table 4.

M1.justification: Section 3.3 changes the reported projection sub-block architecture from two ReLU activations to one, consistent with v2 Figure S7. This is a limited architecture-description revision; the PDFs do not establish whether implementation changed or the description was corrected. MTP, SSD, CGD, their losses and head sharing otherwise remain unchanged.

P1.justification: The title and selected introductory and concluding passages are revised around scene understanding. Experiments are separated into layout and detection sections, while layout-related work and training details move to the supplement. Most existing method and results prose remains closely matched, so the editorial reworking is limited despite substantial new scientific content.

P2.justification: v2 substantially expands the visual presentation with new benchmark and ablation tables, distribution plots, failure examples, and training and architecture diagrams. v1 Figure 6 moves to Figure S1, and Figures 7-8 become Figures 6-7. Existing displays also undergo placement, caption and styling adjustments; these relocations are distinct from the new visual content.

R1.justification: v2 adds references for MMDetection3D, TR3D and AdamW to support annotation generation and training details. The existing literature and first-use-of-MTP positioning are retained. The layout-estimation related-work subsection moves from Section 2.2 to Appendix C without a substantive change in its research positioning.

T1.justification: Equations (1)-(5), the numerical-token consistency criterion and the training objectives remain unchanged. Appendix B.1 and Figure S6 explain the existing confidence-label construction with explicit head indices. No new theorem, proof or substantive mathematical derivation is introduced.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially addresses v1's limited evidence for applicability beyond synthetic layout estimation through real-world SceneCAD and object-detection experiments. Sensitivity tests, confidence-supervision comparisons, a longer-training control, failure cases and implementation details make the method better supported and more assessable. Limitations remain: ASE detection uses generated annotations, Table S2 conflicts with Table 4 on parameter counts, and Section 4.4 combines a CGD speedup with an SSD accuracy gain for SceneCAD. These reporting problems qualify some claims but do not outweigh the substantial validation and transparency gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe Fast SceneScript by the same authors, with matching core methods and experiments. All supplied text, equations, tables and figures support comparison. v1 ends with references; v2 includes supplementary Sections A-D.

after.justification: v2 retains the original experiments and adds SceneCAD evaluation, object-detection results, and original supplementary sensitivity analyses and training controls.

before.justification: Tables 1-3 report original layout-estimation experiments on ASE and Structured3D, including models trained by this work and component ablations.

results.title: Fast SceneScript: Fast and Accurate Language-Based 3D Scene Understanding via Multi-Token Prediction

C1.justification: The central contribution shifts from three travel-lifecycle agents emphasizing disruption management to IMAIA's Maps Plus/PAISA framework emphasizing conversational maps, camera-aware grounding, and efficient spatial reasoning. V2 drops v1's 34% navigation-error reduction, 93% navigation-success, and 85% disruption-handling claims, while introducing distilled-model accuracy and speed claims.

C2.justification: V1 explains retrieval deterioration through reduced spatial locality and increasing candidate counts; this limitation discussion disappears. V2 instead interprets ranking gains as improved relevant-candidate coverage and spatial gains as benefits of task-aligned distillation over parameter scaling. It also connects richer object coverage and lower latency to scene understanding and practical deployment.

D1.justification: V2 documents CLIP feature construction, teacher and annotation models, five mining prompts per image, top-ten entity selection, over fifteen query variants, and full-parameter Florence-2-large training in Dense Region Captioning format. It also identifies NVIDIA V100 32GB evaluation hardware. Conversely, v1's proprietary/Yelp review-data provenance statement is removed. Full training hyperparameters remain unspecified.

E1.justification: V2 adds street-view object identification and spatial-relationship understanding, using 40,000 images for training-data generation and 400 test images. These tasks were absent from v1. The ten-city map-query coverage and Caffe Nero navigation example remain; geographic overlap between the versions' venue-evaluation data is unspecified.

E2.justification: The three POI-detection baselines remain unchanged. V2 adds distance-sorting and similarity-sorting comparisons for venue ranking in Table II. Section IV.D additionally evaluates Florence-VL 8B for accuracy, ASM v2 for object coverage, and an external-model agentic pipeline for latency.

E3.justification: V1's filtering-radius sweep measuring matching accuracy and runtime is replaced by venue-ranking evaluation with 500 training queries, 50 held-out queries, and precision/recall at ranks 1 and 3. New spatial evaluation uses 400 images, OpenAI o1 judgments, object counts, and latency measurements. The 4,300-query POI protocol is retained.

E4.justification: V2 removes the entire 100–1,000-meter filtering-radius sensitivity analysis, eliminating v1's evidence about retrieval degradation and runtime growth. It adds a worked nearest-boba reasoning case with agent traces in Figures 8–9 and a qualitative spatial-relation comparison in Figure 12. The existing navigation case is retained.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated evaluation runs, seeds, confidence intervals, error bars, or significance tests. V2's five prompts per training image describe data generation, not statistical uncertainty estimation.

E6.justification: Table I preserves all four POI accuracies from v1 Table 1: 39.30%, 41.46%, 42.74%, and 89.83%. The distance-sweep results disappear. New results include XGBoost precision@1 of 80.4%, spatial accuracy of 84% versus Florence-VL's 27%, approximately seven versus four objects for ASM v2, and 1.7 versus 12.4 seconds against the agentic pipeline. These are new comparisons, not same-setting improvements over v1.

M1.justification: The grid-based planning and bearing-based navigation procedures are retained under new names. However, v2 replaces image-to-image threshold matching with CLIP image/text place representations and XGBoost ranking using distance, heading, and popularity features. It also introduces a distilled Florence-2 spatial-understanding module and explicit orchestrator-mediated agent coordination.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, substantial introduction passages, and conclusion are rewritten. The three-agent narrative is reorganized around Maps Plus and PAISA, with dedicated related work and expanded architectural subsections. Navigation discussion is substantially condensed, and author/header information changes. This is extensive restructuring beyond the added scientific content.

P2.justification: V2 reworks the system overview, adds grid-analysis, PAISA architecture, agent-trace, and spatial-answer displays, and replaces the distance-sweep table with a differently structured ranking table. Existing map and navigation examples are redisplayed with revised sizing, legends, and captions. The document adopts a different two-column template and removes v1's overlapping placeholder running headers.

R1.justification: V2 introduces a substantive Related Work section positioning the system against geospatial language models and spatial-reasoning approaches including ASMv2, SpatialVLM, and SpatialRGPT. It adds extensive component-model references and arguments about latency and task alignment. V1's Yelp-analysis and human-walking-path references are removed; most earlier geospatial references are retained.

T1.justification: V1's explicit radius-filtered and similarity-thresholded candidate-set definitions in Section 2.3 are removed with the replacement retrieval procedure. The bearing and relative-orientation equations remain unchanged. Neither version supplies theoretical guarantees or proofs.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially improves methodological specificity and empirical assessability through a documented ranking model, held-out baseline comparisons, and a detailed spatial-model training recipe with accuracy and latency evaluation. It also removes numerical navigation/disruption claims that v1 did not substantiate with corresponding experimental descriptions. The lost radius-sensitivity analysis and incomplete training, judging, and uncertainty details remain limitations, but the stronger connection between specified methods, reported protocols, and central claims constitutes a substantial overall improvement.

A1.justification: The PDFs describe successive versions of the same geospatial assistant, despite substantial renaming and expansion. All eight v1 pages and nine v2 pages, including equations, figures, tables, and references, support comparison. Neither supplied PDF contains a separate appendix.

after.justification: V2 retains the POI experiment and reports original venue-ranking results in Table II and spatial-understanding accuracy, object coverage, and latency results in Section IV.D.

before.justification: V1 reports original POI-detection results on 4,300 queries in Table 1 and image-matching accuracy/runtime measurements across filtering distances in Table 2.

results.title: IMAIA: Interactive Maps AI Assistant for Travel Planning and Geo-Spatial Intelligence

C1.justification: The principal dataset, curation-pipeline, and foundation-model contributions remain unchanged. The abstract strengthens the stated segmentation advantage from +8.3 to +10.3 percentage points, reflecting revised baseline values rather than a changed LemonFM score.

C2.justification: v4 adds substantive explanations linking ConvNeXt's local structure to segmentation performance, image-based modeling to computational efficiency, and augmentation thresholds to diversity-versus-noise tradeoffs. It also expands the generic discussion of difficult procedure classification into specific failure patterns involving adjacent anatomy or shared instruments.

D1.justification: The appendices newly disclose five-model curation ensembles, 70% confidence thresholds, voting/NMS rules, masking-coordinate JSON availability, and a detailed 106-person-hour annotation breakdown. They also document annotation validation and computational measurements. These substantially expand reproducibility information without establishing that the existing curation pipeline was changed.

E1.justification: LEMON, ImageNet-1K, the six surgical benchmarks, and the task coverage are retained. The new Cholec80 pretraining control, annotation subset, and validation experiments reuse already represented data and tasks rather than introducing new coverage.

E2.justification: VideoMAEv2 is added as an evaluated comparator in Tables 2–4. Existing foundation-model, specialist, and video-classification comparators are retained. SurgeNetXL already appeared in v3's comparisons; its addition to Figure 1 is a display change.

E3.justification: v4 substantially expands evaluation design with five-fold downstream linear probing, video-level linear probing, and a stratified 500-video annotation-agreement study. It also introduces 20-neighbor evaluation, ConvNeXt-S threshold experiments, and an A100/FP16 timing protocol with training batch size eight. Original benchmark splits and principal training budgets remain unchanged.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained ablations, v4 adds a Cholec80-pretraining control, cosine-versus-L2 nearest-neighbor evaluation, and sensitivity to 1.5×, 3×, and 6× augmentation thresholds. New analyses examine split robustness, annotation reliability, computational efficiency, and qualitative confusions between related surgical procedures.

E5.justification: v3 already reports curation-model fold statistics and mentions cross-validation for half-data fine-tuning. v4 extends statistical reporting to LemonFM's four downstream tasks with five-fold means and standard deviations in Table 5, and adds Cohen's kappa for annotation agreement. No increased random-seed count or formal significance test is reported.

E6.justification: v4 adds substantial results for VideoMAEv2, cross-validation, sensitivity, annotation quality, video-level probing, and runtime. Table 3 changes SurgeNetXL's AutoLaparo accuracy from 80.0 to 85.0. Table 4 replaces four baseline segmentation scores with prior-study values, including EndoViT's 73.0 to 71.0 mDice, while LemonFM remains at 81.3. These replacements do not establish same-setting performance improvements.

M1.justification: Section 4 replaces the stated argmax-based d-minus-n training objective with cross-entropy using the teacher's full probability distribution. This is a localized, non-equivalent loss revision; the architecture, augmentation-selection procedure, and LemonFM-Vid aggregation remain unchanged. The PDFs do not establish whether the implementation changed.

P1.justification: There are localized prose revisions, an updated affiliation, corrected multi-label terminology, and a renamed Section 5.2. Ethics, validation, design-choice, and cost discussions extend the existing organization; the overall narrative and main section order remain stable.

P2.justification: v4 adds Tables 5, 11, and 12, expands comparison and ablation tables, and updates Figure 1 with SurgeNetXL and rearranged axes. Existing supplementary displays are retained and renumbered, including appendix Tables 1–3 becoming Tables 8–10. The basic two-column presentation remains.

R1.justification: v4 adds references and short discussions covering surgical vision-language resources, other surgical modalities, newer self-supervised/video methods, and nearest-neighbor learning. The central positioning against existing surgical datasets and foundation models remains. Publication and bibliographic updates to retained references are not new works.

T1.justification: Equation 1 receives a substantive mathematical correction: the argmax/log-sum-exp expression becomes a sum of teacher probabilities times student log-probabilities. This exceeds equivalent notation or typesetting changes. Equation 2 is retained, and no new theorem or proof is introduced.

improvement.justification: v4 substantially strengthens evidence for its central dataset and model claims through annotation-agreement checks, downstream variability estimates, and targeted design and efficiency analyses. The corrected loss formulation and fuller curation documentation address important clarity and reproducibility gaps in v3. Baseline substitutions enlarge the headline segmentation margin without improving LemonFM's score; the overall quality gain rests on stronger validation and documentation.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same LEMON dataset and LemonFM models. Their text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices are readable and support comparison, including matching relocated and renumbered material.

after.justification: v4 retains original empirical results and adds downstream cross-validation, annotation-reliability measurements, sensitivity experiments, and computational-cost results.

before.justification: v3 reports original downstream evaluations, ablations, video-classification experiments, and performance measurements for its data-curation models.

results.title: LEMON: A Large Endoscopic MONocular Dataset and Foundation Model for Perception in Surgical Settings

C1.justification: The central MP-Bench and three-module MMLM contributions remain. However, the abstract changes 'first large-scale temporal multimodal dataset' to 'first large-scale multimodal dataset,' removing the temporal restriction and broadening the asserted novelty. The introduction's contribution list and conclusion otherwise retain their main scope.

C2.justification: v2 substantially revises the physical interpretation of TGCA and DTGF weights, adding synoptic explanations for different pressure-level peaks and category-specific CMA warning-time arguments. It also introduces a claimed performance–computation justification for the 12-hour window, discusses geographical performance decline, and explains rainstorm-to-gale errors through competing signals in compound weather.

D1.justification: v2 newly documents the two-hour warning-merging rule, tensor shapes, DTGF first-step padding, nearest-grid coordinate mapping, and the 20-rainstorm sample count for the retained case study. Most hyperparameters remain unchanged, while the explicit LLaMA-Factory/default-settings disclosure disappears. Both versions still promise future code and dataset release.

E1.justification: v2 adds evaluation on 1,000 U.S. NOAA Storm Events samples, extending the China-only evaluation to a distinct geographical and climatic domain through MC-main classification. The original MP-Bench coverage, weather categories, and four QA tasks remain.

E2.justification: v1 Table 2 compares GPT-4o with module-enhanced open models. v2 adds explicitly evaluated, fine-tuned three-channel baseline versions of LLaVA-NeXT-Video-7B, Video-LLaVA-7B, InternVL3-8B, and Qwen2.5-VL-7B-Instruct. These are additional comparator configurations in the main comparison, not new backbone names.

E3.justification: v2 introduces Macro-F1 for MC-main and MC-sub, controlled 1-, 6-, and 12-hour window experiments on the 5,000-sample subset, and direct China-trained model testing on U.S. samples matched to MP-Bench test-category proportions across seasons. Existing training hyperparameters largely remain unchanged; newly explained cleaning and implementation details do not establish revised procedures.

E4.justification: v2 adds temporal-context sensitivity experiments and cross-geographical robustness testing. It removes v1's weather-type accuracy radar and normal-weather temporal-stability example, while retaining the module-combination ablation and existing COE error-distribution plots. Thus the analytical coverage changes substantially rather than merely moving into the supplement.

E5.justification: v2's supplementary Experiment Settings first states that results are averaged over three independent runs, and Tables 8–9 disclose seed 42. v1 provides neither disclosure. This does not establish an increase in runs; confidence intervals, dispersion estimates, and statistical tests remain absent.

E6.justification: Table 2 revises reported MMLM scores, including InternVL3 RSW from 39.10 to 70.03 and Qwen RSW from 67.46 to 71.23. Table 3 changes full-module MC-sub accuracy from 36.01 to 47.37. v2 adds baseline, Macro-F1, window-length, and U.S. results, including 64.20 accuracy and 35.18 Macro-F1, and replaces attention findings such as the V-wind peak at 125 versus 500 hPa. These are reported revisions and additions, not established same-setting performance gains.

M1.justification: Both versions use parallel DTGF, TGS, and TGCA modules, concatenation, 3D-convolution fusion, and an MLP mapping to the language-model input. Expanded tensor descriptions, zero-padding details, and corrected spatial-mask equations document the existing procedure rather than establish a new architecture or algorithm.

P1.justification: v2 rewrites the abstract and substantial experimental discussion, separates baseline and MMLM comparisons into dedicated subsections, and reorganizes the appendix into dataset details, settings, supplementary experiments, physical interpretations, scoring, and case-study sections. QA terminology is expanded and corrected throughout. These changes extend beyond adding scientific content.

P2.justification: v2 redraws the conceptual figure, expands comparison tables with baseline rows and Macro-F1 columns, adds temporal-window tables, and replaces temporal-weight line plots with signed-difference bars. It removes the weather-type radar, relocates the China map alongside a new U.S. map, and substantially rearranges supplementary figures, prompts, and training/evaluation tables.

R1.justification: v2 adds the NOAA dataset reference and four references supporting LLM-based evaluation, removes three appendix references supporting physical interpretations, and expands Table 1 with temporal-alignment comparisons. The broader dataset novelty wording also changes positioning slightly, but the related-work taxonomy and principal comparisons remain.

T1.justification: v2 corrects the TGS mathematical definition in Equations 4–6: the inconsistent indices and mask summation in v1 become an explicit nearest-grid mapping and a position-dependent sum of Gaussian masks over textual locations. This is a limited mathematical correction; neither version supplies theoretical propositions or proofs.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens empirical support: Table 2 adds relevant fine-tuned counterparts and imbalance-sensitive Macro-F1, while temporal-window and U.S. transfer experiments test assumptions left unexamined in v1. Clearer mathematical definitions and run disclosure further improve assessability. These gains outweigh the loss of weather-type breakdowns and the training-framework disclosure, although unexplained score revisions, absent uncertainty estimates, and missing U.S. baseline scores still limit the conclusions.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same MeteorPred study, MP-Bench dataset, and MMLM framework. Their main text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices are readable and support reliable comparison despite substantial reorganization.

after.justification: v2 retains original empirical evaluations and adds fine-tuned baseline results, temporal-window experiments, and testing on U.S. NOAA events.

before.justification: v1 reports original MP-Bench evaluations, module ablations, attention analyses, and error-distribution results in Tables 2–3 and the appendix.

results.title: MeteorPred: A Meteorological Multimodal Large Model and Dataset for Severe Weather Event Prediction

C1.justification: The introduction promotes the already-described content-style decoupling pipeline and its 100K image pairs to an explicit fourth contribution. The central claims about reference-guided font control, simultaneous regional editing, zero-shot transfer and state-of-the-art performance remain substantially unchanged.

C2.justification: v2 adds explanations for background mixing and random cropping, and argues that content divergence matters more than semantic alignment in style references. Appendix C explicitly identifies dense artistic paragraph generation as difficult because suitable training data are scarce. The original ablation interpretations remain intact.

D1.justification: Appendices A-B substantially expand reproducibility information: OCR data sources, expert annotation, filtering thresholds, Nano Banana editing, SAM2 segmentation, background blending, random cropping, and NED/DINO acceptance thresholds of 0.9/0.8. v2 also identifies benchmark OCR evaluators, reports approximately eight-second inference on an A800, and supplies a code/model access link. Much of this is newly disclosed detail, not demonstrated procedural change.

E1.justification: The existing editing and handwriting benchmarks remain. v2 adds reported OCR detection/recognition evaluation on regular and non-regular fonts, small-text and garbled-text editing scenarios, and paragraph-level training and evaluation. These substantially broaden the evaluated task requirements.

E2.justification: Calligrapher is added to both existing editing comparisons in Tables 1 and 2. The new OCR comparison in Table 6 evaluates PP-OCRv4, PP-OCRv5, PaddleOCR-VL, Qwen2.5-VL-7B-Instruct and Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct against the proposed OCR model, substantially expanding evaluated comparators.

E3.justification: New designs include a randomly held-out 200-image OCR benchmark with regular/non-regular evaluations, a win/tie/loss preference study, and paragraph adaptation using 5K curated plus 5K synthetic samples. Section 3.2 also changes the stated filtering rule from small or overlapping regions to overlapping regions. These additions do not establish reruns of the retained benchmarks.

E4.justification: The original font-reference and loss-weight ablations remain unchanged. v2 adds dataset validation through style-feature t-SNE, NED/DINO distributions, text-length and character-overlap analyses, plus targeted small-text and paragraph-editing case studies. These directly examine data quality, decoupling and applicability beyond the original analyses.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, significance tests or experimental uncertainty estimates. v2's dataset histograms and preference percentages describe observations rather than uncertainty in estimated performance.

E6.justification: All pre-existing numerical rows in Tables 1-4 are unchanged. Substantial new results include Calligrapher scores, OCR performance such as 0.9276 non-regular-font sentence accuracy, and preference wins such as 84.5% against FLUX-Kontext-Pro. Dataset diagnostics and additional qualitative editing results further expand the evidence; these are newly reported outcomes, not improvements to retained benchmark scores.

M1.justification: Appendix C adds a paragraph-editing adaptation through continued LoRA training on 10K paragraph samples. The core dual-stream conditioning, weighted loss and eight-step distillation remain unchanged. Newly specified Nano Banana and SAM2 usage documents implementation details without establishing replacements to the original method.

P1.justification: The main section order and narrative are retained. v2 polishes grammar and terminology, revises portions of the experimental discussion and conclusion, expands the contribution list, and organizes additional explanations into supplementary Sections A-C.

P2.justification: v2 adds a data-pipeline diagram, preference chart, OCR and dataset displays, editing galleries, and Tables 5-8. Tables 1-2 gain comparator rows and several existing displays move. v1 Figure 2 reappears as v2 Figure 14, while the architecture diagram and original qualitative comparisons are retained with presentation refinements.

R1.justification: v2 adds citations for Calligrapher, Qwen3-VL, SAM2, DuGuangOCR, MUSIQ, NRQM and Q-Align, mainly supporting comparisons and implementation documentation. The related-work argument remains largely unchanged. Consolidating duplicate Seedream references and updating publication metadata do not represent removal or addition of distinct research.

T1.justification: Appendix B introduces a limited quantitative definition of Effective Text: replacements with less than 20% character overlap with the original. The latent-concatenation and weighted-loss equations remain equivalent, and no new theorems or proofs are introduced.

improvement.justification: Appendices A-B substantially address an important weakness of v1: its OCR contribution and data-quality claims lacked direct evaluation and detailed curation documentation. v2 adds comparative OCR evidence, dataset diagnostics and concrete reproduction details, while broader comparisons and an explicit paragraph-editing limitation strengthen assessment of applicability. The user study lacks participant counts, sample counts and uncertainty estimates, limiting that addition's evidential value, but the overall gains in validation and transparency are substantial.

A1.justification: Both PDFs clearly describe the same work, with readable text, equations, tables and figures. The supplied v1 ends after the references despite mentioning an appendix; v2 includes supplementary Sections A-C. The comparison covers all material actually supplied.

after.justification: v2 retains those original experiments and additionally reports OCR evaluations, user preferences, dataset analyses and further editing demonstrations.

before.justification: v1 reports original SkyReels-Text results on poster editing, AnyText, IAM and CVL, together with font-reference and loss-weight ablations.

results.title: SkyReels-Text: Fine-Grained Font-Controllable Text Editing for Poster Design

C1.justification: v1's central claim concerns the existence and effectiveness of spatially consistent universal attacks. v3 adds a central explanatory claim that these attacks expose over-reliance on contextual object-co-occurrence priors and significant dataset deficiencies, prominently stated in the abstract and introduction. Its conclusion also explicitly claims validation through physical experiments.

C2.justification: v3 expands contextual-prior and dataset-bias explanations and adds a physical-to-digital limitation attributed to RGB/CMYK printing differences. It removes v1's explicit limitations concerning BEVDet4D and random placement. The unchanged random-placement results, v1 Table 5 and v3 Table 6, are now presented as robustness evidence with a deployment-cost tradeoff.

D1.justification: v3 newly specifies model-specific training times, 48GB GPU memory, 15 meshes at test time and a 7–27-meter random-placement range. It documents physical camera acquisition and calibration, lighting parameters, adaptation stages and PGD settings, and adds a project-page pointer. These disclosures substantially expand reproducibility information; the newly stated test counts and placement range do not establish changes to earlier experiments.

E1.justification: Both versions use nuScenes, but v3 adds captured physical scenes containing fabricated adversarial objects and nearby vehicles, including different viewpoints and partial occlusions (Sections 4.5 and 11). This extends evaluation from digitally inserted meshes to actual physical inputs.

E2.justification: v1 evaluates Adv3D as its competing attack method. v3 retains Adv3D and adds an explicit UAP comparison in Table 3, covering an invasive patch attack already cited in v1. This is a limited expansion of the comparator set.

E3.justification: The reported loss weights alpha and beta change from 1 to 10, and Table 1 drops the ASR threshold of 0.2. New protocols include sequential six-view physical capture, 10-plus-5-epoch physical adaptation, GeoBEV evaluation, and testing BEVDet fine-tuned for two epochs with PGD examples replacing 10% of training data. The nuScenes split remains unchanged.

E4.justification: v3 adds loss-component and geometry-versus-color ablations (Tables 7–8), digital validation of the physical adaptation (Table 11), target-to-ego distance analysis (Table 13), defense robustness testing (Table 15), and physical cross-view and occlusion case studies (Figure 9). Earlier shape, random-placement and mesh-to-target distance analyses are retained.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, error bars or significance tests for its experimental results. The additional experiments retain point-estimate reporting.

E6.justification: Many matched white-box, shape, distance and transfer results are revised. For example, Table 1's BEVDet4D ASR0.3 without Real Occ changes from 0.321 to 0.530 while its NDS/mAP entries remain unchanged. v3 adds UAP, ablation, physical, GeoBEV and defense results; Table 2 replaces pedestrian/barrier AP entries with bicycle AP. Given the method and setting revisions, these are not uniformly comparable performance gains.

M1.justification: Section 3.3 replaces v1's minimum-distance occlusion check with a combined image-overlap and BEV convex-hull visibility test. Section 11 also introduces a physical-deployment variant using texture-only optimization, an additional lighting-perturbed training stage and masked total-variation regularization. These substantially extend the retained placement and three-loss optimization framework.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, related work and results discussion are extensively rewritten, with an explicit contribution list and new SABER terminology. Implementation and shape details move into a reorganized supplement containing Sections 7–15, replacing the earlier Appendix A–C organization. These changes substantially alter the narrative and document structure.

P2.justification: v3 adopts a two-column layout, redraws the pipeline diagram, merges and rearranges v1 Figures 4 and 6 into Figure 4, and adds physical-experiment, acquisition and occlusion illustrations. Tables gain clean-baseline and percentage-drop columns alongside new experimental tables. Earlier appendix visualizations are retained as Figures 10–11.

R1.justification: The same three related-work themes and central distinction from Adv3D remain. v3 adds supporting references for newer BEV models, physical acquisition, rendering and defense methods, including GeoBEV, VGGT and PGD, while removing BEVFusion and BEV-DG citations. It also elaborates its positioning relative to invasive UAP attacks.

T1.justification: v3 adds mathematical definitions for the BEV visibility cone and combined occlusion criterion, replacing the scalar depth comparison, and defines masked, normalized total-variation regularization in Equation 10. These are limited formal extensions; neither version develops theorems or proofs.

improvement.justification: v3 addresses important gaps in v1's feasibility and component evidence through documented physical demonstrations, loss/geometry ablations and defense testing. The revised occlusion reasoning and expanded implementation details further strengthen the work. These substantial gains are tempered by qualitative-only physical validation, stronger causal claims and removal of earlier robustness caveats. A new reporting error also remains: Table 2 claims a 55.6% mAP drop, whereas its displayed initial and adversarial values imply about 50.6%.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same universal, non-invasive mesh attack on BEV detectors, renamed from Meeseeks Mesh to SABER. Their text, equations, tables, figures and complete appendices are readable and support reliable matching despite substantial revision.

after.justification: v3 reports original digital attack experiments, expanded ablations and robustness evaluations, and physical experiments with fabricated adversarial objects.

before.justification: v1 reports original nuScenes attack experiments, shape and placement ablations, and cross-model transfer and distance-robustness results in its appendices.

results.title: SABER: Spatially Consistent 3D Universal Adversarial Objects for BEV Detectors

C1.justification: Both versions present MultiBanana as a challenging benchmark covering up to eight references and heterogeneous reference conditions. The central findings about omitted subjects versus compositional distortion remain. v2 foregrounds findings already present in v1 and adds supporting validation without redefining the central contribution.

C2.justification: v2 adds substantive discussion of synthetic-source favoritism, compatibility between reference fidelity and scene coherence, and practical advertising applications. Appendix I newly identifies the exclusion of temporal generation and ambiguity of natural-language spatial instructions. Appendix F.2 also revises and qualifies the explanation of Qwen’s failure threshold.

D1.justification: Appendix G adds a dataset-access link, exact judge API identifiers, and generator-version dates. Appendix E.4 reports evaluation costs of approximately $44 for GPT-5 and $29 for Gemini 2.5. Existing construction thresholds, agent settings, and complete evaluation prompts are retained.

E1.justification: The core benchmark, languages, reference counts, and external benchmark coverage are retained. Appendix F.5 adds cross-domain scenarios explicitly prioritizing reference consistency or background–subject matching. The 48-to-24 multi-reference task-count revision does not establish removal of evaluated coverage: both versions report the same 24-task grid.

E2.justification: v2 adds Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct as an evaluated alternative to GPT-5 and Gemini 2.5 in the judge comparison against human ratings (Table 4). The image-generation comparator set and the IPR, CAFG, and SRA comparisons remain unchanged.

E3.justification: New evaluation designs include three human evaluators rating 32 samples, Qwen3-VL-only benchmark scoring, partitioning by synthetic-reference source, and priority-instruction tests on 20 prompts. The new Qwen-judged results explicitly use January 2026 versions of the closed generators. The original five scoring criteria and their weights remain unchanged.

E4.justification: v2 substantially expands benchmark validation through direct human agreement, judge self-consistency, synthetic-source bias analysis, and tests of competing cross-domain criteria (Section 4.4 and Appendices E and F.4–F.5). Existing reference-count, difficulty, model-sensitivity, and agent-step analyses are retained rather than newly introduced.

E5.justification: v1 already reports cross-VLM correlations with 95% confidence intervals over ten subsets. v2 additionally reports standard errors across three random seeds, 99% confidence intervals for reference-source comparisons, and Pearson, Spearman, and Cohen’s kappa statistics against human ratings. These are new reporting practices, not an established increase in runs for the original experiments.

E6.justification: Original benchmark tables and matched plots retain their numerical results. v2 adds extensive Qwen-judged scores, human agreement coefficients, seed errors, source-bias results, and prompt-priority outcomes. It also changes the background-task weakness attribution from Qwen-Image-Edit-2509 to Nano Banana. The new Qwen-judged scores involve different judge and generator settings and therefore do not establish same-setting performance gains.

M1.justification: The benchmark construction pipeline and IPR, CAFG, and SRA algorithms retain their procedures, equations, planner/generator pairings, and prompts. The additional Qwen3-VL judge extends evaluation rather than changing the generation algorithms.

P1.justification: The introduction, task rationale, and supplementary prose undergo extensive editing and condensation. Duplicative extended related work is rewritten, the reliability discussion is reorganized, and appendix ordering and prompt documentation are consolidated. Task-count and category-count inconsistencies are also corrected.

P2.justification: v2 adds displays for human agreement, Qwen-judged results, seed consistency, synthetic-source bias, and prompt priorities, alongside new qualitative examples. Retained quantitative and qualitative figures are extensively regrouped, the IPR example is relocated, and Figures 6 and 7 exchange order. Example prompt labels and the construction diagram are also revised.

R1.justification: v2 substantially broadens research positioning through comparisons with MultiRef-Bench, RealEdit, and SpotEdit, plus a dedicated discussion connecting multi-reference generation to LLM instruction following. Additional literature supports applications, video-conditioning limitations, and structured-layout alternatives; these works are not newly evaluated baselines.

T1.justification: The agentic-framework equations and scoring weights are unchanged. Neither version introduces theoretical propositions or proofs; the added validation statistics and conceptual discussion do not change the mathematical framework.

improvement.justification: v1 relied on proprietary judges supported mainly by prior work and inter-judge agreement. v2 substantially strengthens this central benchmark dependency through direct human validation, an open-weight evaluation option, consistency checks, and bias analyses, supported by clearer reproducibility information and limitations. The human study remains small, and Table 15 shows declines in unprioritized scores despite claims of maintaining them, but these weaknesses do not outweigh the substantial gains in validation and accessibility.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same MultiBanana study and provide readable main text, figures, tables, equations, and appendices. Retained experiments and supplementary material can be matched despite substantial reordering.

after.justification: v2 retains those experiments and adds original human–VLM agreement, judge consistency, synthetic-reference bias, and prompt-priority results.

before.justification: v1 reports original evaluations of five image-generation models, reference-count and difficulty analyses, and experiments with three agentic frameworks.

results.title: MultiBanana: A Challenging Benchmark for Multi-Reference Text-to-Image Generation

C1.justification: The central contributions remain monocular-video spatial reasoning, Spatial-Visual-View Fusion, scalable instruction data, and a temporal benchmark. V3 softens v1's explicit 'first 3D vision-language framework' contribution claim and extends the introduction's claims to OST-Bench generalization and competitiveness with ground-truth-depth models.

C2.justification: V3 adds explanations connecting encoder choice to metric scale and temporal ordering, and discusses spatial gains versus non-spatial losses on OpenEQA and recovery through data mixing. Existing static-scene and reconstruction-quality limitations remain. Some new interpretations overreach: Table 7's caption claims improvement across all OST categories although counting and agent-information scores decline.

D1.justification: V3 newly specifies adherence to source-dataset train/test splits and explains mixed 2-, 3-, and 4-choice camera-direction questions and their chance baseline. It documents the 200k-plus-30k data-mixing recipe. Most implementation details, hardware, hyperparameters, preprocessing instructions, and the project link are retained; v1's explicit VSTI fine-tuning statement is omitted.

E1.justification: V3 expands beyond VSI-Bench and VSTI-Bench to ScanQA and SQA3D scene QA, OST-Bench online embodied reasoning, Video-MME, VQAv2, and OpenEQA. Training also includes ScanQA/SQA3D splits for their evaluations and an experiment incorporating general LLaVA-Video data. The original temporal benchmark remains based on static scenes.

E2.justification: V3 Table 1 adds Qwen2.5-VL-7B, Spatial-MLLM-4B, VG-LLM-4B, and a fine-tuned LLaVA-OneVision comparison. Gemini-2.5 Pro replaces Gemini-1.5 entries in Tables 1–2, while several smaller-model comparisons and VSI tiny-set/human rows are removed. New experiments introduce substantial additional comparator groups, including Video-3D LLM and GPT-4V.

E3.justification: New protocols include combined ScanQA/SQA3D training, evaluation on 4,675 validation and 3,519 test questions with language-generation and EM/EM-R metrics, zero-shot OpenEQA evaluation, and a controlled addition of 30k general videos. These expand the evaluation design; the original one-epoch recipe and VSTI train/test counts remain unchanged.

E4.justification: V3 adds 2D–2D and explicit-point fusion ablations, a CUT3R-versus-VGGT comparison, general-data mixing, and spatial/non-spatial transfer analysis on OpenEQA. These test architectural choices and capability tradeoffs absent from v1. Token-removal ablations remain, but most of their task-specific scores are omitted from the condensed Table 6.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, error bars, or statistical significance tests. The added experiments retain point-estimate reporting.

E6.justification: The headline VLM-3R averages remain 60.9 on VSI-Bench and 58.8 on VSTI-Bench. V3 adds extensive results, including ScanQA CIDEr 101.9, SQA3D EM 60.7, OST-Bench 42.9, and Video-MME 59.9 versus 62.1 with data mixing. Some old comparison and ablation entries disappear. V3 also introduces a prose/table inconsistency: 50.09 versus Table 6's retained 59.09 for removing view tokens.

M1.justification: The proposed model retains CUT3R spatial and camera tokens, cross-attention fusion with visual tokens, a two-layer projector, frozen encoders, and LoRA fine-tuning. The residual connection explicitly formulated in v3 Section 4.1 was already documented in v1 Appendix A.1. Alternative fusion and encoder configurations are evaluated as ablations.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, related work, dataset explanations, and architecture narrative are extensively rewritten and condensed. Contributions are reorganized, experiments gain a broader benchmark structure, and Appendix C becomes three named analyses. Much of Appendices A–B remains substantially unchanged.

P2.justification: V3 changes the document to two columns, redraws Figure 3, adds numerous comparison tables, and replaces the detailed component-ablation table with an average-only summary. Figure 2 loses its donut chart although its caption still refers to rings. The existing trajectory illustration and dataset-distribution tables are retained and relocated.

R1.justification: V3 substantially updates positioning around Spatial-MLLM, VG-LLM, SpatialStack, and newer dynamic-scene work such as VLM4D and DynamicVerse. It develops a specific distinction between CUT3R's metric-scale representations and VGGT-based approaches, extending v1's emphasis on avoiding depth sensors and prebuilt maps.

T1.justification: The recurrent tokenization, cross-attention, residual fusion, and MRA definitions are unchanged in substance. V3's explicit residual equation restates v1 Appendix A.1. Neither version supplies theoretical propositions or proofs, and the new encoder discussion is qualitative interpretation.

improvement.justification: V3 substantially addresses v1's limited evidence for transfer, general-purpose capability retention, and the choice of fusion and geometry encoder through Tables 3–7 and D–F. Reporting non-spatial losses alongside spatial gains makes the applicability assessment more informative. These gains outweigh the loss of detailed token-ablation scores and localized reporting errors, including the view-token score inconsistency and overstated OST caption. The improvement comes from stronger validation and clearer tradeoffs, not higher retained headline scores.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe VLM-3R and contain readable main text, equations, figures, tables, and Appendices A–C. The retained architecture, datasets, and results can be matched despite substantial rewriting and layout changes.

after.justification: V3 retains these original results and adds evaluations on additional benchmarks, fusion and geometry-encoder ablations, and a data-mixing experiment.

before.justification: V1 reports original VLM-3R evaluations on VSI-Bench and VSTI-Bench, together with component ablations in Tables 1–3.

results.title: VLM-3R: Vision-Language Models Augmented with Instruction-Aligned 3D Reconstruction

C1.justification: v2 adds an explicit contribution claim of negligible or minimal additional inference overhead in the abstract and introduction. The central claims concerning reward optimization, generalization, composability and mitigation of reward hacking remain unchanged.

C2.justification: v2 adds substantive explanations attributing prompt-length differences to generator capability, intent preservation to original-prompt conditioning and episodic rewards, and training stability to initialization, LoRA and a fixed environment. It also explains early denoised-state usefulness and argues that relative policy overhead decreases with larger generators.

D1.justification: v2 newly discloses approximately three days per training run, the GPT-5 model snapshot, DanceGRPO training and code information, and the models used for semantic-recall evaluation. Existing GRPO, LoRA, hardware, resizing and prompting details remain substantially unchanged.

E1.justification: The named prompt datasets and alignment tasks remain Pick-a-Pic v2, RePrompt prompts and GenEval; the new generator configurations do not establish new data coverage. However, v2 Appendix C.4 introduces DanceGRPO training on its unspecified 'official' dataset, so the PDFs cannot establish whether this adds different represented data.

E2.justification: v2 adds GPT-5 to the single- and composite-reward comparisons and DanceGRPO to the SD1.5 composability experiment (Tables 1–2). DanceGRPO was only discussed as prior work in v1. Existing comparators are retained.

E3.justification: Existing benchmark protocols are retained, but substantial new evaluation settings are introduced: inference timing on one A100 with batch size 8, BERTScore and LLM-based intent recall, FLUX.1-dev and SD3.5-large configurations, and a Qwen3-VL-4B policy ablation. DanceGRPO additionally uses 50 training epochs with HPSv2 reward.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained component and refinement-step ablations, v2 tests prompt-length growth, semantic drift, interpretability of early denoised feedback, training stability and stronger policy initialization (Appendices D.2–D.3 and E.2–E.3). Runtime profiling also directly examines the cost of additional refinement steps.

E5.justification: v2 Figure 11 explicitly reports average token counts with standard-deviation bands. v1 already contains shaded bands in Figure 6, which are retained, but lacks this explicitly identified variability statistic. No additional repeated-run counts, seeds or significance tests are specified.

E6.justification: All original score rows in v1 Tables 2–4 are retained in v2 Tables 1–3. Added results include GPT-5 and DanceGRPO comparisons, flow-matching transfer scores, runtime measurements and new diagnostic curves. Table 7 reports ImageReward 0.6922 with Qwen3-VL-4B versus 0.6320 with Qwen2.5-VL-3B, explicitly comparing different policy configurations.

M1.justification: v2 Appendix E.1 introduces an inference adaptation that converts flow-matching timesteps into diffusion timesteps with equivalent SNR before supplying them to the policy. The core MDP, GRPO training, sparse refinement and Algorithms 1–2 remain unchanged.

P1.justification: Most existing prose and section order are preserved. Changes include adding PromptLoop to the title, terminology and grammar corrections, an acknowledgment, and reorganizing the former additional-results appendix into prompt-evolution and additional-results sections.

P2.justification: The main text changes from a single-column preprint layout to two columns. The original MDP comparison table is incorporated into Figure 3, Figure 2 gains a preference/runtime panel, and GPT-5 columns expand comparison grids. New runtime, transfer and initialization tables and Figures 11–14 substantially expand the visual presentation.

R1.justification: v2 adds Idea2Img to related work and references supporting denoised-state evaluation, flow-matching backbones and semantic scoring, including Free2Guide and BERTScore. Its central positioning relative to weight-level alignment and existing prompt-refinement approaches is retained.

T1.justification: The substantive diffusion equations, MDP definitions, GRPO objective and denoised-estimate formulation are retained. Correcting the sampled-action index in prose makes it consistent with the existing definition; no substantive theorem, proof or derivation is added.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens empirical support for practicality and reliability: v1 lacks direct runtime and semantic-drift measurements, while v2 adds these alongside training diagnostics and transfer to flow-matching models. These address important validation gaps while retaining the original results. The 'negligible overhead' wording is overstated relative to Table 4's approximately 23% increase at five refinements, but the overall gain in evidence is substantial.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe PromptLoop, with matching core methods and experiments. Text, equations, tables, figures and appendices are readable and support comparison despite substantial reformatting and renumbering.

after.justification: v2 retains those experiments and adds original baseline comparisons, runtime measurements, transfer experiments and prompt-behavior analyses.

before.justification: v1 reports original reward-alignment experiments, component ablations and qualitative analyses in Tables 2–4, Figure 6 and Appendix D.

results.title: PromptLoop: Plug-and-Play Prompt Refinement via Latent Feedback for Diffusion Model Alignment

C1.justification: The three methodological contributions remain unchanged. The abstract broadens the empirical claim from outperforming one voxel baseline with up to threefold memory savings to state-of-the-art generation with lower memory, faster inference, and greater editability than voxel-based methods. The conclusion similarly extends the comparison to multiple baselines.

C2.justification: v2 adds explanations involving SemCity's query-sampling mismatch and triplane consistency, and PDD's refinement and split-scene generation. Appendix G newly identifies fixed semantic categories, absent hard geometric constraints, and outpainting seams as limitations. The explicit single-dataset limitation is replaced by discussion of dataset availability and potential applicability elsewhere.

D1.justification: v2 Appendix D and Table 7 document baseline hierarchies, resolutions, training durations, and GPU counts; Section 4.2 newly specifies balanced vegetation conditioning. The abstract explicitly reports public code and models, whereas v1 only supplies a project link. Earlier dataset/software license disclosures and the 300-versus-18-epoch comparison are removed.

E1.justification: Both versions use KITTI-360 and synthetic vehicle primitives for the same reconstruction, generation, editing, outpainting, and street-view synthesis tasks. Iterative extrapolation already appears in v1. Other datasets mentioned in v2 describe prior work, not additional datasets evaluated by this work.

E2.justification: v1 evaluates SemCity as its external baseline. v2 adds XCube to reconstruction and both PDD and XCube to generation and sampling-sensitivity comparisons, plus PDD to large-scale extrapolation. SemCity 'Base' in v1 matches 'SemCity-1M' in v2; that rename is not a new comparator.

E3.justification: The main generation evaluation switches from a 10 m reference-pose threshold, yielding 3,855 samples, to 1,000 farthest-pose samples, a setting previously explored in v1's appendix. Added hierarchical comparisons introduce level-specific resolutions, upsampling controls, training budgets, and cumulative generation timing. The KITTI-360 train/test split remains unchanged.

E4.justification: The original architecture ablations and sampling-sensitivity study remain, with the latter extended to PDD and XCube. v2 adds substantial analyses of hierarchical refinement, good and poor BEV generations, and extrapolation coherence against PDD, including Figures 13, 16–19, and 24–25.

E5.justification: Both appendices report five random seeds for synthetic dataset generation and average the parameterization ablation results across seeds. The corresponding shaded plot is retained. Neither version adds repeated-run uncertainty estimates or significance tests for the main generation comparisons.

E6.justification: v2 adds XCube reconstruction results and per-level PDD/XCube generation, memory, and timing entries. Main-table generation values also change: DiT-B FID is 55.041 in v1 Table 1 and 73.952 in v2 Table 3, under different reference sampling, so this is not a same-setting deterioration. Existing reconstruction and architecture-ablation table values are retained.

M1.justification: The hybrid representation, separate ground/object VAE branches, Cholesky encoding, matching losses, diffusion transformer, and RePaint-based editing procedures remain unchanged. Expanded reconstruction and outpainting explanations document the existing method rather than introduce new components.

P1.justification: The introduction is extensively rewritten around urban simulation needs, and the abstract, method descriptions, and experimental discussion are substantially revised. The appendix gains separate baseline and precision/recall sections and reorganizes implementation details. These narrative changes extend well beyond inserting new results; the title also adds 'Urban'.

P2.justification: The document changes from single-column to two-column layout. Former combined reconstruction and ablation figures are separated into tables and figures, with revised highlighting and expanded comparisons. New extrusion and latent-outpainting diagrams accompany extensive generation and editing galleries; several earlier qualitative panels are retained or rearranged.

R1.justification: v2 adds SPAGHETTI and SALAD to distinguish object-part generation from instance-based scene layouts, and introduces a substantial 3D Scene Generation discussion covering geometry, appearance, and panoramic approaches. It also acknowledges sparse-voxel memory efficiency and more explicitly positions PrITTI around semantic control rather than appearance fidelity.

T1.justification: The scatter-matrix construction, symmetry and positive-definiteness reasoning, Cholesky recovery, loss formulations, diffusion equations, and precision/recall definitions are mathematically unchanged. Separately displaying the Cholesky factorization and expanding explanatory prose do not introduce new theory.

improvement.justification: The documented PDD and sparse-XCube comparisons substantially address v1's reliance on SemCity when arguing for primitives over voxel representations. Hierarchical analyses, good and poor examples, clearer implementation explanations, and additional limitations make the evidence more assessable. The stronger abstract claims still rest on KITTI-360, and changed reference sampling prevents interpreting headline score differences as performance gains, but these limits do not outweigh the substantial improvement in empirical support.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe PrITTI with the same authors and core framework. All 26 pages of v1 and 40 pages of v2, including their appendices, equations, tables, and figures, support reliable comparison.

after.justification: v2 retains these original experiments and reports additional evaluations of PDD and XCube, including hierarchical generation and qualitative extrapolation comparisons.

before.justification: v1 reports original KITTI-360 reconstruction and generation experiments, synthetic parameterization ablations, and qualitative editing results in the main text and appendix.

results.title: PrITTI: Primitive-based Generation of Controllable and Editable 3D Semantic Urban Scenes
