C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, contribution list, and concluding discussion retain the same central claims about active viewpoint planning, TaskMoE, manipulation performance, and generalization. Naming TaskMoE explicitly in the abstract does not introduce a new contribution.

C2.justification: v2 interprets the new robustness results as improved adaptability and identifies heavy occlusion as a principal failure condition. It also attributes data-efficiency gains to architectural improvements. The latency and reflective/transparent-object limitations are moved from Appendix D into Section 5 without substantive revision.

D1.justification: Real-world documentation specifies right-arm use and revises camera models and placements, accompanied by an updated setup image. Core GPU specifications, model hyperparameters, preprocessing descriptions, and the appendix hyperparameter table remain unchanged. The code/project link is also unchanged.

E1.justification: v2 adds real-world Collect Fruits and Put Item In Drawer evaluations and Pick Grape scenarios involving unseen instances, backgrounds, objects, heavy occlusion, and lighting variation. The 18 RLBench tasks remain unchanged. Older kettle-placement and lid-covering executions remain in appendix Figure 6, so those examples were not wholly removed.

E2.justification: Table 1 adds C2F-ARM-BC, PerAct, HiveFormer, PolarNet, RVT, Act3D, and 3D Diffuser Actor to the retained RVT2, ARP, and ARP+ comparisons. Diffusion Policy becomes a quantitative real-world comparator in Tables 4 and 7; the qualitative ARP+ comparison remains.

E3.justification: The reported real-world training budget changes from 100 to 50 demonstrations per task, and the three-D405 camera arrangement changes to D435i, D455, and wrist-mounted D405 cameras. New real-world evaluations specify ten trials per task or condition. Table 8 introduces 20/40/80/100-demonstration training budgets, and Table 2 adds a fixed-view control.

E4.justification: v2 adds a fixed-view ablation alongside the existing random-view ablation, tests five real-world distribution shifts, and examines performance across demonstration budgets. These address view-planning benefits, robustness, and data efficiency. Existing viewpoint-count, radial-range, latency, and zero-shot analyses are retained.

E5.justification: Table 1 changes from point estimates to mean-and-standard-deviation reporting for TAVP and several baselines, including the retained RVT2. Table 8 also reports mean ± standard deviation. Neither version specifies the corresponding run counts or seeds, so this establishes expanded uncertainty reporting without establishing an increase in runs.

E6.justification: Table 1 revises TAVP's reported average from 86.7% to 86.6%, with changes such as Place Cups 44% to 54% and Put in Safe 92% to 78%. v2 also adds comparator scores, an 83.33% fixed-view ablation, real-world averages of 88% versus Diffusion Policy's 68%, and robustness and data-efficiency results. The real-world additions use v2's revised setting.

M1.justification: The overview changes TaskMoE's stated placement from 'before MVT' to 'within the MVT'. The PDFs do not explain whether this reflects an architectural change or a corrected description. Expert routing, viewpoint prediction, losses, and three-stage training otherwise remain unchanged.

P1.justification: Most existing prose is retained. v2 introduces numbered sections, standardizes some MVEP terminology, removes a repetitive sampling explanation, moves real-world setup into the main text, and incorporates appendix limitations into the concluding section. Author affiliations and several local wording errors are also revised.

P2.justification: v2 substantially expands Table 1, adds three result tables, and extends Table 2. Figure 2 is redrawn with clearer aggregation and position labels; the real-robot setup image is replaced and moved into the main text. The standalone real-world demonstration panel is removed, while execution sequences and other appendix figures are retained and relocated.

R1.justification: v2 adds distinct references for HiveFormer, Act3D, and PolarNet to support broader comparisons. Its additional 3D Diffuser Actor entry refers to work already cited in v1. The related-work narrative and positioning of TaskMoE and viewpoint planning remain substantially unchanged.

T1.justification: Equations 1–11 and Algorithm 1 retain the same mathematical content. The added main-text statement that cameras face the origin restates the camera parameterization already present in v1 Appendix B. No new theorem, proof, or derivation appears.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens the empirical support for the paper's practical and view-planning claims. It supplements v1's qualitative real-world evidence with ten-trial baseline comparisons and stress tests, and adds a relevant fixed-view control beyond the random-view ablation. Broader comparisons and uncertainty reporting further improve assessment of the results. Run counts remain unspecified, and some commentary is unreconciled with updated results, notably the claimed Meat off Grill gains despite Table 1's lower score.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same TAVP research. Their text, equations, tables, figures, and appendices are readable and support comparison, including matching material moved between the appendix and main text.

after.justification: v2 retains original simulation results and adds quantitative real-world comparisons, robustness tests, and a demonstration-budget study.

before.justification: v1 reports original TAVP results on RLBench, component ablations, sensitivity and generalization experiments, and qualitative real-robot executions.

results.title: Learning to See and Act: Task-Aware Virtual View Exploration for Robotic Manipulation

C1.justification: The central claims about PAG, the solver, and improved spatial reasoning and scene generation remain unchanged. The conclusion makes a limited change to the dataset contribution claim: v1 says PARSE-10K was released, whereas v2 says it is constructed, withdrawing the explicit release assertion.

C2.justification: v2 removes the conclusion's specific warning that directional-face contact modeling may deviate on highly oblique contacts, while retaining the manual-construction and canonical-pose limitations. Appendix A.2 additionally describes placement failures caused by empty feasible spaces or exhausted sampling attempts.

D1.justification: Appendices A–D substantially expand reproducibility information: solver pseudocode, surface extraction, asset annotation, simulation and contact extraction, task prompts, scene-disjoint test sets, and detailed model training configurations. Examples include Qwen3-VL-235B-A22B-Instruct with LoRA rank 8/scaling 32, Sapien's timestep and duration, and diffusion optimization and hardware details. These are disclosures, not evidence of reruns.

E1.justification: Both versions use the same PARSE-10K coverage, COCO real-image examples, three VLM tasks, and scene-generation evaluation. The appendix names the existing 17 room types and characterizes existing assets without establishing additional training or evaluation coverage.

E2.justification: Table 2 retains GPT-5, Gemini-2.5-Pro, Claude-Opus-4, Robobrain2.0, and Qwen3-VL. The scene-generation comparison retains InstructScene and the conditioned and unconditioned variants. Newly cited implementation tools are not added baselines.

E3.justification: The supplementary dataset analyses introduce measurements of object density per square metre, parts per asset, and contacts per scene. Existing MCQ/SGG scoring and the 20-participant, 12-scene user-study design remain unchanged. Appendix D's training configurations and scene-level test separation are newly disclosed settings, not demonstrated revisions to existing experiments.

E4.justification: Appendices B and C.2 add descriptive analyses of category composition, part counts, room types, object density, and contact counts, addressing dataset diversity and interaction complexity. The existing conditioning comparison and grounding-agnostic analysis are retained; no new robustness or sensitivity experiments are reported.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, evaluation seeds, confidence intervals, significance tests, or uncertainty estimates. The new dataset histograms describe composition rather than experimental uncertainty, and the disclosed diffusion noise sampling is a training detail.

E6.justification: Tables 1–3 retain their numerical values and rankings. New supplementary findings include an average of 17.4 parts per object, over 55% of scenes exceeding 1.35 objects per square metre, and over 57% containing more than 50 part-level contacts, alongside distributions in Figures 9–13.

M1.justification: Sections 3.2 and 4.1 narrow the documented handling of underspecified relations: v1 describes inferring an asset's lowest part and its surface, whereas v2 describes inferring surfaces within the connected part nodes. The overall PAG, solver, and downstream model procedures remain intact; the appendix's architecture and training details are additional disclosure.

P1.justification: v2 substantially expands the explanatory structure through Appendices A–D, including procedural walkthroughs and task prompts. It also rewrites several PAG and solver passages and captions, edits language, and adds author contact roles and acknowledgments, while preserving the main section order.

P2.justification: v2 adds Figures 7–14, the spatial-relation dictionary in Table 4, and Algorithm 1. It also revises the overview and PAG/solver diagrams and relocates Figure 5. The existing experimental tables and scene-generation examples retain their substantive content.

R1.justification: v2 adds CAST to related work and six implementation references covering LayerNorm, Graph Transformers, DDPM, LoRA, P3-SAM, and CoACD. The existing references and positioning against object-level scene representations are otherwise retained.

T1.justification: Table 4 adds explicit mathematical conditions for spatial relations, including centre-of-mass projection for support, enclosure thresholds, and normal and angle constraints. These extend the formal specification beyond v1's prose descriptions, without adding theorems or proofs.

improvement.justification: v1 refers to supplementary training details absent from the supplied PDF. v2 addresses this important reproducibility gap with solver pseudocode, explicit constraints, asset/contact-processing procedures, and concrete VLM and diffusion training configurations. Its dataset analyses also provide additional evidence for scene complexity. These substantial gains outweigh the loss of the oblique-contact limitation, although that omission reduces transparency. The improvement concerns documentation and assessability; benchmark performance remains unchanged.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe PARSE and PARSE-10K, and their text, figures, tables, and mathematical content are readable. The supplied v1 ends after the references; v2 additionally includes supplementary Appendices A–D.

after.justification: v2 retains those original empirical results and adds analyses of asset composition, scene density, and part-level contacts in its supplement.

before.justification: v1 reports original VLM evaluations, scene-generation comparisons, a 20-participant user study, and statistics for the constructed PARSE-10K dataset.

results.title: PARSE: Part-Aware Relational Spatial Modeling

C1.justification: V1 emphasizes training-free transductive fusion and approximately ten-point improvements over CLIP. V2 broadens the contribution to adaptive, prior-free integration across model families, domains and inference settings, and explicitly claims applicability to black-box models accessed through APIs. Its novelty claim expands from VFM/VLM complementarity in transductive ZSL to foundation-model integration in zero-shot classification generally.

C2.justification: V2 adds explanations linking adaptive weights to model agreement, interpreting modest gains among strong models and larger gains under model-quality disparities. It introduces modality-gap, model-subset and efficiency interpretations. V1's explicit limitation concerning fixed/equal weighting is replaced by claims of adaptive weighting, while future-work discussion shifts toward semantic ensemble learning and multi-view clustering.

D1.justification: V2 replaces the deferred code-release promise with a repository link and adds model-variant, weight-initialization and inductive-inference details in Appendix 7.2, directing readers to code for dataset templates. Most basic implementation information is retained: 224×224 center crops, fixed prompts, epsilon 0.01 and a 24GB RTX 4090. Repository availability is stated in the PDF but was not externally verified.

E1.justification: V2 retains the original 11 datasets, expands remote-sensing coverage from EuroSAT to ten datasets, and adds five medical-pathology datasets. It also evaluates inductive generalization to unseen instances alongside transduction. The claimed 26 benchmarks comprise overlapping domain groups: EuroSAT appears in both the natural-image and remote-sensing groups.

E2.justification: V2 substantially revises the evaluated comparator set. Table 1 adds GDA, ZLaP, Stat.A, ADAPT and GTA-CLIP; Table 4 adds Zero, MTA, TIPPLE, DPE and COSMIC. TransCLIP and ECALP remain, while TDA and DMN appear in the inductive comparison. V1's evaluated CoCoOp, TPT, DiffTPT, CuPL, Sus-X, VisDesc and CALIP comparisons disappear. Domain-specific individual models and simple ensemble comparators are also added.

E3.justification: V2 introduces a protocol that learns GMM parameters and weights on unlabeled training data and applies them to unseen test instances, whereas v1 evaluates transduction. It adds DINOv3 and additional model combinations, clustering-accuracy evaluations, and time/memory measurements. Appendix Table 6 specifies adaptation before ensembling. Exact inductive split sizes are not supplied, limiting reproduction of the new protocol.

E4.justification: V2 adds fixed-versus-adaptive weighting controls, a CLIP/MUSK disparity experiment, model-subset tests, clustering analyses and computational comparisons. Visual-source and joint-learning ablations extend questions already tested in v1. V1's feature-concatenation comparison, explicit single-visual-source ablations, epsilon/lambda sensitivity sweeps and convergence-loss plot disappear. The Pets visualization is replaced by EuroSAT/Food101 visualizations.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, standard deviations, error bars or significance tests. V2's additional dataset averages and runtime measurements do not introduce uncertainty estimation.

E6.justification: V1 Table 1 reports OTFusion averages of 74.95% and 70.45% for its two backbone settings. V2 Table 1 reports revised configurations, including 75.7% for CLIP-1+DINOv2 and 77.8% for CLIP-1+DINO(v2+v3), plus extensive new inductive and domain-specific results. These are not controlled same-setting improvements. Table 5 newly reports 71.8% fixed-weight versus 73.1% adaptive-weight accuracy.

M1.justification: V1 uses a linear OT objective with fixed model weights. V2 introduces squared agreement terms and MM-based adaptive weights, substantially changing optimization (Section 3.2.2 and Appendix 6). It also adds inductive inference using learned GMM parameters and fusion weights. Multi-model probability fusion and joint GMM/transport updates already existed in v1.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction, contribution statements and substantial portions of the method and experimental narrative are rewritten. V2 introduces numbered subsections and a supplementary-material structure, moving optimization and implementation material there while expanding the main narrative around adaptive integration and inductive inference. This exceeds a method-name or terminology edit.

P2.justification: V2 adds a pipeline diagram, radial performance/clustering charts, grouped ablation bars and domain-specific comparison tables. The original backbone comparison and ablation tables are substantially reorganized, including separate transductive and inductive displays. Sensitivity and loss plots are removed, and the qualitative visualization becomes a two-dataset figure. Table styling and document layout also change extensively.

R1.justification: The related-work framing changes from inductive/transductive ZSL and Mixture of Experts to foundation models, VLM classification and optimal transport. V2 adds domain-specific foundation models, newer adaptation methods and MM-related literature, and explicitly acknowledges inspiration from TransCLIP. V1's discussion of DINO-assisted prompt learning and its MoE positioning are removed.

T1.justification: Beyond v1's linear OT formulation and alternating updates, v2 derives a quadratic objective, a tangent minorizer in Theorem 1, adaptive coefficients and an MM optimization scheme. It adds a stationary-point convergence claim and computational-complexity analysis. The convergence argument does not establish that the stated GMM update increases the surrogate, so the added guarantee remains insufficiently justified.

improvement.justification: V2 addresses v1's stated fixed-weight limitation and substantially strengthens the previously limited evidence for heterogeneous-model fusion through adaptive-weight controls, domain-specific ensembles, inductive evaluation and measured computational costs. These gains outweigh the loss of sensitivity analyses and reporting weaknesses. Nevertheless, the convergence justification is incomplete, Table 7 swaps the MUSK/PLIP baseline values relative to Table 3, and the claimed 6.9-point lead conflicts with Table 1: CLIP-1+DINOv3 exceeds GTA-CLIP by 2.9 points.

A1.justification: Both PDFs are complete and readable, including equations, figures and tables. Despite renaming OTFusion to SOTA, they share the GMM-based optimal-transport fusion framework and original benchmarks. V1 has no appendix; v2 includes supplementary optimization, implementation and experimental material in Sections 6–8.

after.justification: V2 reports original SOTA results under transductive and inductive settings, with adaptive-weighting ablations, model-subset experiments and computational measurements. Some comparator results are explicitly attributed to earlier work.

before.justification: V1 reports original OTFusion benchmark results, component ablations, parameter-sensitivity experiments and convergence analyses.

results.title: SOTA: Self-adaptive Optimal Transport for Zero-Shot Classification with Multiple Foundation Models

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the central claims of model-agnostic, AP-aligned online curation, complementarity with augmentation and distillation, and robustness to noisy labels. Added experiments strengthen support without redefining the main contribution or novelty claim.

C2.justification: Appendix 3 adds explanations involving cancellation of approximation bias in teacher–student differences and post-NMS handling of within-image interactions. Appendix 8 interprets longer-schedule results as evidence of reduced overfitting rather than merely extra computation. Section 4.5 removes the assertion that joint KD and curation share one teacher pass without additional computational cost.

D1.justification: Appendix 8 expands polynomial-weight implementation details, including optional class weights, post-NMS top-K predictions, and highest-score TP deduplication, and reports timing and memory measurements. The Python-style Listing 1 is removed, but Algorithm 1 and detailed augmentation settings remain. These are limited documentation changes around the retained implementation.

E1.justification: v1 evaluates COCO, including corrupted annotations and additional pseudo-labeled COCO images. v2 Appendix 7 adds Pascal VOC2007/2012 and BDD100K, with evaluation on VOC2007 test and BDD100K validation. This substantially broadens coverage to smaller generic-detection data and a driving domain.

E2.justification: The sampling comparators in v1 Table 5 and v2 Table 4 are unchanged: uniform sampling, GradNorm, hard mining, classification entropy, entropy/information/diversity, Image-AP, and loss-learnability. PKD and CrossKD comparisons also remain unchanged. The additional benchmarks compare DetGain with the same baseline strategy.

E3.justification: v2 adds prior-ranking simulations using 64-image batches and 100 predictions per image, batch-additivity tests varying base-set size, a 0.5×–3× FCOS schedule sweep, and dynamic-versus-fixed sampling evaluation. Appendix 7 specifies splits, ResNet-50, 1× schedules, and COCO-style mAP for the additional datasets. The earlier fixed-batch sampling-ratio sweep is removed; principal COCO training recipes remain unchanged.

E4.justification: New analyses test uniform-versus-fitted-prior ranking agreement (Figure 4), additive batch-score accuracy and ranking stability (Figure 6), runtime and memory costs, longer training, and dynamic sampling (Appendix 8). Conversely, v1 Table 4's sampling-ratio sensitivity study is removed. Earlier noise, teacher, pseudo-label, prior-performance, and Monte Carlo analyses are retained.

E5.justification: Table 1 newly reports means and standard deviations over three different seeds across the six detectors; v1 provides point estimates without a run count. New Figure 4 includes a 95% confidence band, and Figure 6 reports mean±standard deviation. Additional-dataset results explicitly use single runs. The PDFs establish expanded reporting, not an increase from a known v1 run count.

E6.justification: New results include VOC mAP 51.3 versus 54.3 and BDD100K 30.3 versus 32.1 (Table 11), prior-ranking correlation around 0.94, and FCOS 3× results of 37.1 versus 43.8 (Table 13). Dynamic sampling reports 42.5 versus static sampling's 43.0 mAP with approximately 30% less training time. Table 1 replaces point estimates with three-run summaries, including ATSS DetGain AP 41.6→41.5 and FCOS 40.9→41.0. Earlier sampling-ratio results disappear; retained sampler and KD comparison tables keep their values.

M1.justification: Appendix 8 adds a dynamic sampling policy: retain 40% of candidates for the first 60% of iterations, then 20% for the remainder. v1 evaluates fixed ratios. The core teacher–student DetGain scoring, augmentation pipeline, and Algorithm 1 remain unchanged; polynomial approximation was already described in v1.

P1.justification: Revisions are localized to the ablation discussion, expanded Appendix 3 explanations, shortened KD and conclusion passages, and new Appendices 7–8. The title, abstract, introduction, related work, and main method narrative are substantially unchanged. The Python listing is removed and appendix headings receive minor editing.

P2.justification: v2 adds ranking and additivity plots and tables for additional datasets, runtime, and training schedules, while removing the earlier sampling-ratio table. Table 1 drops the Learning Proxy column and incorporates uncertainty values. Several retained figures, tables, and Algorithm 1 move, producing substantial changes to experimental displays despite retaining the two-column style.

R1.justification: v2 adds the Pascal VOC and BDD100K references and removes the TeachAugment reference associated with shortened future-work discussion. Positioning relative to online curation, active learning, coreset selection, and knowledge distillation remains unchanged.

T1.justification: The AP definitions, single-insertion derivations, and uniform-prior closed forms remain unchanged. v2 Eq. (27) numbers the same first-order additivity expression already present in v1. New simulations provide empirical support rather than a new proof; polynomial formulas elaborate the previously described approximation.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens empirical credibility: three-seed reporting addresses uncertainty in the main results, additional datasets test applicability beyond COCO, and ranking/additivity checks directly examine central approximations. Runtime breakdowns and longer-training controls also improve assessment of practical value. Removing the sampling-ratio ablation weakens support for the default ratio, and the new benchmarks remain single-run, but these drawbacks do not outweigh the stronger validation of the paper's central claims.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same DetGain study. Their complete main texts, figures, tables, equations, and appendices support comparison, including matching retained material across renumbering and relocation.

after.justification: v2 retains those original results and adds VOC and BDD100K evaluations, ranking and additivity simulations, and computational analyses.

before.justification: v1 reports original COCO detection experiments, noise and pseudo-label evaluations, ablations, and Monte Carlo simulations.

results.title: Online Data Curation for Object Detection via Marginal Contributions to Dataset-level Average Precision

C1.justification: The introduction's quantitative empirical contribution shifts from standalone superiority on ten-task ImageNet-R to average integration gains across three datasets and both task splits. The central claims of geometry-aware exemplar-free regularization, quadratic Sylvester computation, and compatibility with existing CL methods remain.

C2.justification: v2 adds qualifications about averaging losing fine-grained variation and the computational cost of non-diagonal A. It removes v1's explicit warning that Inf-SSM+ violates orbit invariance and drops the CKD-based discussion of data-dependent need to regularize B. Section 5.1 newly interprets results as supporting sufficiency of regularizing (A,C), although the cited theorem establishes invariance.

D1.justification: Appendix J substantially expands baseline-instantiation explanations and hyperparameters for CLFD and integrations on CIFAR-100 and Caltech-256. Algorithm 1 clarifies frozen previous-model parameters and updates. Conversely, v2 removes CUB-200 hyperparameter columns, L2P pool-size/prompt-length/top-k values, and the reservoir-sampling description. These documentation changes do not establish corresponding implementation changes.

E1.justification: Both versions use ImageNet-R, CIFAR-100, Caltech-256, and CUB-200-2011, with class-incremental learning under exemplar-free and replay settings. Additional integrations use already represented datasets and tasks; Vim-tiny changes model configuration rather than dataset or task coverage.

E2.justification: v2 adds CLFD to the integration comparisons in Table 1 and UCL to the EFCIL comparisons in Table 11, substantially extending comparison across method families. ER, LUCIR, X-DER, EWC, SI, MAS, and the LwF variants remain. L2P-R is not new: it already appears in v1 Table 6.

E3.justification: v2 adds evaluation with 7M-parameter Vim-tiny alongside 26M-parameter Vim-small, plus averaging-axis and batch/task latency protocols. For existing ImageNet-R LUCIR integrations, Appendix J changes the reported Inf-SSM coefficient from 10 to 500 for five tasks and from 1500 to 1000 for ten tasks. These are reported setting revisions, without establishing that experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: v2 adds evidence about information retained by different averaging axes (Table 5), practical CL latency (Table 3), and sensitivity to model size (Appendix H.5). It removes v1's CKD-over-tasks analysis and Figure 3, while retaining layerwise CKD, block-count ablations, and distance-computation simulations. The Inf-SSM+ comparison is retained and regrouped.

E5.justification: Both versions specify seeds 0, 10, and 100 and report classification results with standard deviations. The 10,000-iteration Monte Carlo studies and their correlation, p-value, and variability reporting are retained. Additional tables follow existing reporting practices; no new confidence-interval or significance-testing procedure is documented.

E6.justification: v2 adds integration results on CIFAR-100 and Caltech-256, CLFD/UCL results, Vim-tiny scores, variance measurements, and CL latency measurements. Five-task ImageNet-R LUCIR baseline/augmented AA changes from 48.67/49.73 to 31.18/35.35, alongside revised reported regularization settings. Most existing Inf-SSM and Inf-SSM+ scores are retained. The new 8.31% AA and 9.36% FM integration averages agree with the expanded Table 1.

M1.justification: Appendix D.5 corrects the computation for nearly identical states from cos(theta)=0 to cos(theta)=1. The core observability regularizer, channel averaging, and Gram-matrix computation remain unchanged. Inf-SSM+ is retained in Appendix H.4 rather than removed. The PDFs do not establish whether the computational correction changed the implementation.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, SSM preliminaries, method motivation, related work, and experimental narrative undergo extensive rewriting. Integration results lead the revised evaluation; Inf-SSM+ moves to the appendix, limitations and conclusions are combined, and Appendix J gains structured subsections. These changes substantially reorganize the narrative beyond adding experiments.

P2.justification: Figure 1 is redesigned into a multi-panel summary, Figure 2 moves from the appendix to the main text, and a new orbit illustration becomes Figure 3. The taskwise CKD figure is removed. Results tables are expanded, merged, relocated, and reformatted, including moving v1 Table 1 to v2 Table 6 and separating Inf-SSM+ results into Table 9.

R1.justification: v2 expands coverage of CL families and SSM applications, adding citations including UCL and CLFD. Appendix J.1 develops a substantial baseline-selection and exclusion rationale, positioning other Mamba CL approaches as scenario-specific future integration targets rather than direct comparators. Much of the earlier Mamba discussion is retained in Appendix F.2.

T1.justification: Appendix I replaces proofs restricted to equal principal angles with general multivariate expansions establishing local equivalence of three Grassmannian distances. Appendix C.2 corrects equality of observability matrices to equality of their spanned subspaces. Appendix D.5 also corrects the normalization denominator and the cosine value for matching states.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens the integration claim by extending its evidence beyond ImageNet-R to all three main datasets and additional methods. It also repairs the restricted proofs in Appendix I, corrects the invariance statement, and replaces overstated integration averages with table-supported summaries. Lost tuning details and an overstrong interpretation of (A,C) sufficiency remain drawbacks, but the stronger validation and mathematical corrections provide a substantial overall quality improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Inf-SSM work. Their main texts, appendices A–J, equations, figures, and tables are readable and support a reliable comparison, including content moved between sections.

after.justification: v2 retains original experimental results and adds CLFD and UCL comparisons, Vim-tiny experiments, averaging-axis analysis, and latency measurements.

before.justification: v1 reports original continual-learning experiments, block-count ablations, CKD analyses, and Monte Carlo simulations, including results in its appendices.

results.title: Exemplar-Free Continual Learning for State Space Models

C1.justification: The abstract and introduction broaden demonstrated applicability from VGGT and π3 to include MapAnything. The headline acceleration changes from up to 4× to more than 3×, explicitly described as end-to-end in the introduction. The central contributions of attention analysis, training-free sparsification, and preserving task performance remain.

C2.justification: V2 introduces architecture-dependent explanations: MapAnything's reliance on later layers is linked to predicting poses from patch tokens, and its attention statistics are linked to its single special token. It also attributes apparent ETH3D improvements to randomness, discusses degradation on harder full trajectories, and qualifies MapAnything timing measurements because of preprocessing and postprocessing. These substantially expand mechanisms and limitations beyond v1.

D1.justification: V2 adds a project-page link, documents the existing TUM/ScanNet 90-frame, stride-3 sampling, and specifies sampling and controls for new experiments. It removes v1's explicit ten-random-frame pointmap sampling statement and the Tanks timing table's resolution disclosure. The learned-projection training hyperparameters, block sizes, hardware, and training time are retained.

E1.justification: The named datasets and core pose-estimation and pointmap tasks are retained; 7Scenes, NRGBD, TUM, and ScanNet already had results in v1. V2 Appendix B adds a distinct scenario spanning complete, longer and more complex ScanNet trajectories, providing a bounded expansion of test coverage.

E2.justification: V2 Figure 10 adds evaluated SpargeAttention variants, random masking, and CDF-only controls. Figure 7 also adds MapAnything and explicit dense-model reference comparisons. The SeerAttention-style learned-projection experiment already existed in v1 and is retained, rather than newly introduced.

E3.justification: The new ScanNet experiment evaluates 50 sequences with 100, 300, 500, and 1000 frames evenly sampled across complete trajectories. V2 also introduces MapAnything configurations and masking controls explicitly excluding Hilbert permutation. Tanks & Temples retains only 50/100/200-frame configurations, dropping 25-frame and full-length evaluations, and revises its reported sparsity-parameter grid. These are substantial evaluation-design changes.

E4.justification: V2 adds comparisons testing combined thresholding against CDF-only and random selection, MapAnything layer-skipping experiments, and analyses of its attention statistics. Additional reconstruction and trajectory examples examine behavior under high sparsity. V1's special-token, learned-projection, and VGGT layer-skipping ablations remain, with renumbering and expanded discussion.

E5.justification: V2 Figure 4 explicitly identifies the existing shaded bands as standard deviations and the solid curves as means over tokens; v1 displayed these bands without that explanation. Neither version reports repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, or significance tests for the benchmark results.

E6.justification: V2 adds extensive MapAnything and full-trajectory ScanNet results, revises DTU and Tanks & Temples values, and updates effective sparsity values in retained tables. For example, the nominal 10%, CDF 0.970 VGGT DTU row changes Acc from 1.196 to 1.075 and N.C. from 0.679 to 0.613. Identical underlying settings are not established, so these are reported revisions rather than demonstrated same-setting gains. V1's absolute-runtime table and 25-frame/full-length Tanks results are removed.

M1.justification: Both versions use pooled query/key similarities, combined top-k and CDF block selection, and dense interactions involving special tokens. V2 applies this procedure to MapAnything and clarifies differences from SpargeAttention without documenting a changed algorithm or training objective.

P1.justification: V2 retitles the paper, rewrites the abstract, polishes terminology and grammar, expands related-work explanations, and adds an explicit ablation subsection. The appendices are reorganized around new theory and long-sequence sections. Most existing method and attention-analysis prose retains its original structure and narrative.

P2.justification: V2 substantially revises the visual presentation: Figure 2 becomes compact, Figure 7 gains model series and reference lines, Figure 8 replaces examples and sparsity levels, and Figure 9 changes its panels and displayed metric from RRA@5 to AUC@30, already tabulated in v1. Table 1 is removed, Figure 10 is added, and appendix plots and table structures expand for the new analyses and model.

R1.justification: Section 2.3 substantially expands positioning against sparse attention, low-rank approximations, spatial/temporal attention, and weight pruning. Added works include Scatterbrain, MInference, FlexPrefill, MoBA, and SparseGPT, alongside MapAnything elsewhere. V2 more precisely distinguishes its kernel reuse and block selection from SpargeAttention and learned approaches such as SeerAttention.

T1.justification: V2 Appendix A adds model-level FLOP derivations, equations (3)–(7), counting assumptions and exclusions, and theoretical speed-up estimates in Table A-1. V1 contained only the simpler asymptotic speed-up argument. The addition is substantial, although its dense-attention sparsity convention is inconsistent and equation (6) omits the stated global-layer multiplicity.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially strengthens evidence for the method's design, generality, and scalability through direct sparse-attention controls, an architecturally different model, and complete-trajectory ScanNet evaluation. These address important validation gaps in v1, while the ETH3D randomness qualification improves interpretation. The gains are tempered by removal of the absolute-runtime table and inconsistencies in the new FLOP derivation, which weaken timing transparency and theoretical rigor. Nevertheless, the central empirical case is substantially better supported.

A1.justification: Despite the changed title, both PDFs describe the same block-sparse attention work. Their main text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices are readable and support comparison.

after.justification: V2 retains original empirical results and adds MapAnything evaluations, sparse-attention comparisons, and long-trajectory ScanNet experiments.

before.justification: V1 reports original reconstruction, pose-estimation, runtime, and ablation results for sparse VGGT and π3 in Section 5 and the appendices.

results.title: Block-Sparse Global Attention for Efficient Multi-View Geometry Transformers

C1.justification: v2 presents the headline contribution as pre-training a unified, factorizable model, replacing v1's emphasis on the first joint size- and task-adaptive initializer. It drops the first-multitasking and 5x storage-saving claims and explicitly extends its claimed generality to classification and alternative architectures. The central factorization and initialization-performance claims remain.

C2.justification: v2 adds substantive interpretations: pruning/distillation failures are attributed to disrupted denoising hierarchy and temporal coherence; long-horizon curves are used to argue that initialization affects the entire training trajectory; and PCA alignment is interpreted as cross-scale structural coherence. It also qualifies domain independence as holding 'to a certain extent.' These explanations extend v1's discussion of adaptive transfer.

D1.justification: Appendix A adds factorization pseudocode, dataset counts, a VAE identifier and detailed optimizer, dropout and dataset-specific training settings; the main text identifies RTX 4090 hardware. However, v1's explicit EMA decay of 0.9999, guidance scale of 1.0 and 50K-image evaluation sample count are no longer disclosed. Their omission does not establish that those settings changed.

E1.justification: v2 retains ImageNet-1K, CelebA-HQ and LSUN generation experiments, adds Hubble, MRI and Pokemon generation domains, and introduces ImageNet-1K classification with DeiT (Table 3). These substantially extend the represented domains and task requirements.

E2.justification: BK-SDM and Laptop-diff are added to both corresponding diffusion comparisons in Tables 1–2, introducing pruning/distillation comparators. GHN-3, previously only discussed, is evaluated in the new classification comparison. Direct pre-training remains a comparator, presented in Figure 3 rather than v1 Table 1.

E3.justification: Reported factorization training changes from 30K steps with batch size 256 to 300K with batch size 64; ImageNet downstream training changes from 10K to 100K steps. v2 adds DiT-L and DeiT configurations, 800K-step trajectories and controlled ablation protocols. Sigma-sharing settings also change. Table 2 replaces downstream FID/sFID reporting with FID for natural-image datasets and FDD for the new domains.

E4.justification: v1 has no component ablations. v2 tests shared factorization against independent layer-wise SVD with matched transferred components (Table 4), and trainable Sigma against random, identical and linear initialization (Table 5). Figures 3–5 add long-horizon convergence, qualitative training trajectories and PCA analysis of Sigma across depths.

E5.justification: Neither version reports independent repeated-run counts, seeds, uncertainty intervals, error bars or significance tests. The n=5 in v1 Table 1 describes the five model configurations, not documented independent repetitions.

E6.justification: Main-table results are extensively replaced under revised conditions: FINE's DiT-B L6 FID is 83.79 after 10K steps in v1 Table 1 and 51.58 after 100K in v2, not a same-setting gain. v2 adds DiT-L, new-domain, classification and ablation results, convergence curves and Appendix B samples. Earlier downstream sFID entries are no longer reported.

M1.justification: v2 Section 3.2 expands the stated factorized weight types from qkv, o, in and out to include adaLN. The central procedure remains joint training of shared U/V and layer-specific Sigma, followed by Sigma-only initialization and ordinary downstream training. v1 already trained a factorized auxiliary model, so the new pre-training framing does not establish an entirely new algorithm.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, related work, method explanation and results discussion are extensively rewritten around factorizable pre-training and adaptive initialization. Method preliminaries are reorganized, the results section expands from two principal subsections to six, and detailed settings and baseline descriptions are organized in Appendix A.

P2.justification: v2 adopts a two-column layout, redraws Figures 1–2, substantially restructures Tables 1–2, and adds classification, ablation and implementation tables. New Figures 3–5 display comparisons, convergence and PCA; Appendix B adds eight generated-image figures. Direct-pretraining results are presented graphically rather than as v1's table row.

R1.justification: The main PEFT, initialization and Learngene context, including the KIND/SVDiff contrast, remains. v2 updates its relationship to WAVE toward constrained pre-training, adds pruning/distillation and newer learngene references, and removes the Weight Selection discussion. Publication updates to retained WAVE and KIND references are not new works.

T1.justification: v2 corrects v1's malformed attention-normalization expression and restores the omitted GELU in the feedforward equation (Section 3.1). Section 5.2 adds explicit amortized training-cost expressions. The central factorization and denoising objectives remain substantively equivalent, and neither version provides theoretical propositions or proofs.

improvement.justification: v2 addresses important validation gaps in v1: Tables 4–5 directly test the two central design choices, and Figure 3 examines sustained convergence beyond short-budget results. Appendix A substantially improves implementation transparency. These gains outweigh the loss of some evaluation details. The retained 3n speedup claim remains problematic: v2's stated costs imply 3n/(n+3), not 3n. Overall, the paper provides substantially stronger evidence for its central method.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe FINE, and their text, equations, tables and figures support reliable comparison. v1 ends with references and contains no appendix; v2 includes readable Appendices A–B. Revised experimental settings limit direct score comparisons but do not prevent comparison of the work.

after.justification: v2 reports original generation and classification experiments, component ablations, convergence analyses and generated samples in the main text and Appendix B.

before.justification: v1 Tables 1–2 report original diffusion-model initialization experiments on ImageNet-1K and three downstream datasets.

results.title: FINE: Factorizing Knowledge for Initialization of Variable-sized Diffusion Models

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction's contribution list and conclusion retain the same central claims: a compression-oriented diffusion foundation model, inexpensive reproducible training, strong ultra-low-bitrate performance and favorable pixel-space distortion–perception trade-offs. The revised appendix substantially develops supporting applications without redefining these central contributions.

C2.justification: v3 qualifies the earlier favorable X-prediction conclusion by explaining its likelihood-estimation problems and degraded DiffC results. New discussion connects poor higher-bitrate multi-step fine-tuning to score-norm bias and explains downstream speed–quality trade-offs. The appendix now claims real-time one-step operation, although the conclusion retains the earlier general real-time limitation.

D1.justification: v1 promises future code release; v3 reports release and supplies a repository link. New details specify adaptation stages, LoRA rank, learning rates and inference simplification. Table 3 corrects aggregate training cost from 116 to 464 A100 GPU-hours for the retained four-GPU schedule, while the redesigned complexity table includes conditioning in overall totals.

E1.justification: Training still uses ImageNet-21K, OpenImages and SA-1B; image-compression evaluation still uses Kodak, CLIC2020 and Div2K. The additional human and semantic scores evaluate retained Kodak reconstructions rather than introducing a new image domain or compression task.

E2.justification: The external codec baselines are retained. Comparator membership changes locally: the one-step comparison retains OSCAR, OneDC and StableCodec but omits the standalone multi-step CoD reference shown in v1 Figure 14. v3 Figure 16 additionally compares directly fine-tuned multi-step CoD against other downstream approaches.

E3.justification: Distillation increases from 50K total steps and 5K generator updates to 100K and 10K. The X-prediction comparison changes from 256×256 at 0.0156 bpp to 512×512 at 0.0039 bpp. Figure 4 replaces FID with LPIPS. New protocols include higher-bitrate fine-tuning and Kodak evaluation using 20 human raters, semantic similarities and ten VQA questions per image.

E4.justification: v3 adds comparisons of downstream adaptation strategies, separates prediction-target effects from the JiT backbone choice, tests X-prediction within DiffC, and analyzes post-training loss-weight sensitivity (Figures 16–18). The original unified-training and auxiliary-loss ablation is retained, moving from Table 4 to Table 5.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals or statistical significance tests. The new mean opinion scores are point estimates; no uncertainty reporting accompanies them.

E6.justification: v3 replaces and extends one-step and perceptual-supervision results, adds downstream and sensitivity curves, and reports 25.2 ms one-step processing and a 4.2 human rating. Table 1's fine-tuned MS-ILLM row changes from 21.10/0.402/0.255/80.1 to 21.08/0.376/0.248/80.92 for PSNR/LPIPS/DISTS/FID. Revised training and evaluation settings prevent interpreting all replacements as controlled performance gains.

M1.justification: Appendix B substantially revises one-step CoD: its objective adds patch-GAN and codebook-commitment terms, higher-bitrate adaptation uses staged LoRA and joint fine-tuning, and inference removes redundant AdaLN-Zero modules. Appendix F also specifies weighted one-step and multi-step losses on every post-training sample instead of subset sampling. The main foundation architecture remains stable.

P1.justification: The main narrative is largely retained. v3 adds a change log and appendix summary, divides Appendix B into numbered subsections, inserts a downstream-analysis section and renumbers subsequent appendices. Author-footnote and wording edits are limited; much of the expanded prose documents scientific additions.

P2.justification: Figure 4 changes its plotted metric and axis, and the one-step comparison is redrawn over a wider bitrate range. The appendix adds perceptual-supervision, downstream, prediction-target and sensitivity plots, expands qualitative examples, redesigns the complexity table and adds a human/semantic-results table. Several original displays are retained and relocated.

R1.justification: v3 adds citations to LoRA and Xu's analysis of score-norm bias, using them to support adaptation and interpret downstream failures. The main related-work discussion and positioning against existing compression methods remain substantially unchanged.

T1.justification: v3 revises the mathematical definition of the one-step objective in Equation 10 and introduces an explicit weighted post-training objective. It also specifies the clamped X-to-velocity conversion used to explain downstream failures. The existing rectified-flow and DMD derivations remain; no new theorem or proof is added.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially strengthens the foundation-model argument by extending v1's limited one-step and single-rate perceptual-supervision demonstrations into specified multi-rate applications with measured fast inference. New architectural controls and downstream failure analyses clarify when the proposed choices help or hurt. Corrected resource accounting and code-release information improve reproducibility. The stale real-time limitation and limited user-study reporting remain weaknesses, but do not outweigh these substantial gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe CoD and are readable, including all figures, tables, equations and appendices. Corresponding material can be matched across the appendix reorganization.

after.justification: v3 retains original experiments and adds downstream comparisons, sensitivity analyses, human ratings and semantic evaluation results.

before.justification: v1 reports original compression benchmarks, scaling experiments, training ablations, distillation results and perceptual-supervision experiments.

results.title: CoD: A Diffusion Foundation Model for Image Compression

C1.justification: The central contribution expands from metric human shape, pose and position recovery to joint human/scene reconstruction and pseudo-ground-truth annotation. Human MoE, human-guided depth refinement and SynFocal become explicit contributions. v1's claim of requiring no 3D training supervision disappears. v2's conclusion qualifies its overall superiority claim to online single-frame methods.

C2.justification: v2 introduces substantive mechanism explanations based on semantic expert specialization, global routing, redundant supervision and mesh-anchored depth calibration. v1's discussion of nonunique metric solutions and its UniDepth-failure caveat disappear. v2 instead identifies heavy occlusion as a limitation and acknowledges keypoint/patch limitations in routing analysis. These change both the interpretation and stated applicability boundaries.

D1.justification: v2 substantially expands implementation documentation: named encoders, expert configuration, 256-by-256 crops, one A100 GPU, SynFocal construction, and detailed depth-refinement architecture, anchor filtering, normalization and affine constraints. These are disclosures, not evidence that every corresponding setting changed. Some specificity is lost: v1 explicitly identifies Masked-DROID for its trajectory evaluation, while v2 does not specify its corresponding extrinsic-estimation procedure.

E1.justification: The reported training mix replaces Human3.6M and MPI-INF with BEDLAM, AIC, COCO and MPII, retaining 3DPW. Static-camera trajectory evaluation changes from Human3.6M to RICH. v2 adds PROX depth training/evaluation and SynFocal evaluation under varying focal lengths. Local-pose evaluation on 3DPW/EMDB-1 and trajectory evaluation on EMDB-2 remain.

E2.justification: The matched local-pose comparison adds PersPose, Human3R, CameraHMR and PromptHMR, while removing SPIN, CLIFF, ReFit and TRACE. EMDB-2 comparisons expand to additional methods including PromptHMR-vid, TRACE, GLAMR, SLAHMR and Human3R, with membership depending on camera settings. New depth comparisons evaluate Metric3D, UniDepth and MapAnything; SynFocal compares against Human3R.

E3.justification: Although AdamW, 40 epochs and batch size 64 remain, weight decay changes from 0.01 to 0.0001, and differentiated learning rates become a stated uniform 0.00001. New protocols include a 9:1 PROX train/test split with AbsRel, MAE and delta1 evaluation, and controlled focal-length variation assessed with RPSD and RDE. Existing pose and trajectory metrics remain.

E4.justification: v1's Bbox+K versus ray ablation on 3DPW/Human3.6M is replaced by image-only, added-ray and added-MoE comparisons on 3DPW/EMDB-2. v2 adds focal-length robustness tests and expert-routing analyses by body region, bounding-box scale and dataset. Conversely, v1's height-conditioned pose/depth ambiguity experiment in Section 3.2 and Figure 4 is removed.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals or significance tests. v2's RPSD measures positional dispersion across focal-length conditions; it is a robustness metric rather than uncertainty reporting for estimated performance.

E6.justification: Under revised architecture and training, reported 3DPW PA-MPJPE/MPJPE/PVE changes from 37.5/60.5/72.1 to 33.6/53.0/62.7; these are not controlled same-setting gains. EMDB-2 ground-truth-camera ERVE instead rises from 8.9 to 9.4. New results include PROX MAE 0.46 versus MapAnything's 0.58 and SynFocal RPSD 1.1 cm versus Human3R's 21.6 cm. v2's HMR2.0a row also reproduces v1's SPIN 3DPW triplet without explaining the attribution.

M1.justification: v1's concatenated image/ray features and iterative MLP regressor become Patch and Global Human MoE with routed, shared and ray experts. v2 adds explicit 3D-joint, vertex, height and load-balancing losses. It also introduces mesh-guided UNet–ViT depth refinement over MapAnything, substantially extending v1's human reconstruction and UniDepth point-cloud overlay pipeline.

P1.justification: The title and author information change, and the abstract, introduction, related work, method and conclusion are extensively rewritten around MetricHMSR. The standalone Metric Pose Bias section disappears, with its camera explanations transferred to supplementary implementation material. A substantial supplement organizes implementation, additional results and limitations, changing the narrative structure beyond merely adding experiments.

P2.justification: The pipeline is redrawn with MoE and depth-refinement branches, accompanied by new expert diagrams, routing plots, SynFocal examples and positional-distribution graphics. EMDB results are split into predicted/ground-truth-camera tables with online/offline groups. Original camera illustrations largely reappear as Figures 9–11, and COCO overlays are reused in Figure 14; these are relocations, not wholly new evidence.

R1.justification: Research positioning expands to MoE specialization and joint human-scene reconstruction, incorporating DeepSeekMoE, VIMoE, VGGT, MapAnything, CUT3R and Human3R, alongside newer perspective-aware HMR methods. v2 explicitly credits NeRF-inspired camera rays and recognizes CLIFF's full-perspective projection usage. This substantially revises v1's predominantly camera-model and metric-depth framing.

T1.justification: The documented cropped-intrinsic equation is corrected: v1 Equation 4 subtracts crop offsets from focal lengths, whereas v2 Equation 2 subtracts them from principal-point coordinates. v2 also introduces short mathematical definitions for expert balancing, depth correction and RPSD/RDE. These are limited formal additions and corrections, without a substantial theorem or proof development.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens assessment of the central metric-reconstruction claims: it corrects the cropped-camera equation, adds controlled focal-length tests and staged component ablations, and quantitatively evaluates scene depth where v1 mainly showed overlays. Expanded implementation details and stronger comparison methods further improve assessability. Removing the ambiguity discussion and leaving the HMR2.0a/SPIN score overlap unexplained are weaknesses, but the targeted validation and mathematical correction provide a substantial net improvement. Higher cross-version scores alone do not establish this judgment.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe successive versions of the same camera-ray-conditioned monocular reconstruction work, expanded from MetricHMR to MetricHMSR. Text, equations, tables and figures support comparison throughout. v1 has no appendix; v2 includes readable Supplementary Material, Sections 6–8.

after.justification: v2 reports original pose, trajectory, focal-length robustness and depth-estimation results, together with component ablations and expert-routing analyses in the main text and supplement.

before.justification: v1 reports original human-pose and trajectory evaluations, a pose-ambiguity experiment, and a camera-ray ablation, including Tables 2–5.

results.title: MetricHMSR: Metric Human Mesh and Scene Recovery from Monocular Images

C1.justification: V1 claims the first training-free score-based importance-sampling framework and emphasizes industrial and natural-image applications. V2 drops that priority claim and centers its contributions on lightweight guidance plus uncertainty-adaptive scheduling. Its abstract and introduction now claim matching or superior task performance with approximately 1.2–4.7× speedups over competing guidance methods.

C2.justification: V2 extends the approximation-error discussion into an explanation of early-step instability and guidance scheduling. Appendix C.2 introduces substantive interpretations of reward–diversity and reward–realism tradeoffs, metric disagreement and projection effects. Comparisons are explicitly restricted to training-free guidance, while v1's CSI failure-mechanism interpretation is removed.

D1.justification: Appendices B.3 and C add discrete sampling updates, noise schedules, architecture specifications, optimizer settings, training budgets, weight formulas and baseline configurations. Retained CelebA and StableCascade experiments receive checkpoint, classifier-training and Fourier-mask details absent from v1. The listed source-code repository address also changes; its availability cannot be verified from the PDFs.

E1.justification: V2 replaces the Circles, Spiral, Pinwheel and 8-Gaussians benchmarks with a 25-Gaussian base distribution and shaped target distributions, and removes the CSI compression task. It adds SD/SDXL human-preference alignment and MNIST class suppression/balancing. CelebA and StableCascade frequency control remain, with additional RGB-bias and low-frequency-control scenarios.

E2.justification: V1 evaluates MADE-MAA, NIS, NSF, CSF and TNA in Table 1; these comparisons disappear. V2 evaluates DPS, FreeDoM and DAS in the synthetic comparisons, and additionally DAS-1p in image alignment. DPS was previously cited but not evaluated as a baseline.

E3.justification: V1's synthetic evaluation uses Jensen–Shannon divergence and DDPM-based SDE sampling. V2 introduces DDIM evaluation using Wasserstein distance and runtime for 10,000 generated samples. The new image-alignment protocol specifies 100 diffusion steps, shared 8×PickScore weighting, and multiple alignment, perceptual-quality and diversity metrics. These are new evaluation designs, not evidence of same-setting reruns.

E4.justification: V2 adds scheduler-coefficient sensitivity studies, projected versus standard guidance comparisons, reward–diversity analysis and qualitative investigations of alignment versus realism in Appendix C.2. These substantially extend the analysis beyond v1's demonstrations. Conversely, v1's CSI high-distortion failure analysis is removed.

E5.justification: V1 reports unexplained ± quantities in its synthetic-results table. V2 explicitly identifies mean ± standard deviation in Tables 1 and 4 and newly documents matched seeds or noise for paired visual comparisons. Neither version specifies repeated-run counts or significance testing; the additional reporting does not establish that more runs were performed.

E6.justification: V1's synthetic divergence results and Spiral/CSI/StableCascade mean-weight entries disappear. V2 adds WD/runtime, preference, quality, diversity and MNIST results: Figure 1 reports LAGS WD 0.33, and Table 1 reports 85 seconds per SDXL image versus 4.722 times that runtime for DAS. These are new-setting results. CelebA's 35.1% to 51.2% result and the original StableCascade frequency examples are retained.

M1.justification: The finite-difference guidance approximation is retained, but v2 adds time-dependent guidance scaling through the LAGS scheduler in Section 3.3 and a hard-gating alternative in Appendix B.2. Appendix C.2.2 also implements an optional projection of guidance perpendicular to the DDIM drift. These additions change the sampling procedure beyond the ISSGM-to-LAGS renaming.

P1.justification: V2 extensively rewrites the abstract, introduction and conclusion around guidance efficiency, reorganizes the method and experimental narrative, and changes terminology from importance sampling/ISSGM to weighted sampling/LAGS. Retained applications move into structured appendices, accompanied by expanded explanations and a contents page.

P2.justification: The main text changes from single-column to two-column layout, with new density/runtime panels, alignment plots, sensitivity curves, quality/diversity tables and image grids. V1 Figures 4 and 5 reappear as v2 Figures 13 and 21 with presentation changes. The conceptual, Spiral and CSI figures and original table structures are removed.

R1.justification: V1 stresses separation from conditional sampling and says no prior baselines exist for its setup. V2 instead explains connections and adaptations to posterior guidance, positioning the contribution around inference efficiency. Appendix A substantially expands related work, including FreeDoM, DAS, particle sampling and fairness; Appendix C also introduces Adaptive Projected Guidance.

T1.justification: V1 states Theorem 1 without a proof and assumes an approximate second-order expansion. V2 revises the assumptions, including bounded support and a bounded Hessian of the weight itself, changes the error bound and supplies a proof in Appendix B.1. It adds Proposition 1 under an error-orthogonality assumption, plus a hard-gating derivation without that assumption.

improvement.justification: V2 addresses a central weakness of v1 by comparing against competing training-free guidance methods, with explicit runtime and quality evidence, rather than relying on separately trained density models. Added proofs, sensitivity/tradeoff analyses and implementation details substantially strengthen the paper's support and reproducibility. Removing CSI narrows application evidence, and some superiority claims remain overstated: Figure 6's rings example favors FreeDoM at WD 0.37 over LAGS at 0.48 despite its caption. These shortcomings temper but do not outweigh the substantial gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs are readable and describe the same reweighted diffusion-sampling work, despite substantial revision and renaming. Text, equations, tables and figures support comparison. V1 has no appendix; v2's Appendices A–C were included.

after.justification: Section 4 and Appendix C report original synthetic sampling, SD/SDXL preference alignment, ablations, MNIST class reweighting and image-control results.

before.justification: Section 4 reports original synthetic-distribution experiments, CSI compression analysis, CelebA class reweighting and StableCascade image-generation results.

results.title: Efficient Weighted Sampling via Score-based Generative Models

C1.justification: v3 broadens the headline claims to superiority over dedicated moderation tools and generalization across external safety benchmarks. Its contribution list replaces v1's explicit first-formalization contribution with a systematic vulnerability and component-analysis contribution. The MMDS dataset and joint user/assistant moderation contributions remain central.

C2.justification: v3 adds interpretations of image-driven risk, dialogue progression, and MCTS effectiveness. It qualifies late-turn trends because samples become sparse, retains rationales chiefly for interpretability despite modest performance effects, and distinguishes augmentation benefits on targeted scenarios from ordinary MMDS performance. New limitations address long-context computational cost and false positives, supported by WildChat results.

D1.justification: The expanded appendix supplies generation, annotation, moderation, attacker, and evaluator prompts; detailed policy specifications; image-resolution thresholds and CLIP configuration; three-expert annotation procedures; and role-specific rationale-generation instructions. v3 also adds a project-page link, although Appendix F still describes data/model release as planned. These disclosures substantially exceed v1's training and MCTS settings.

E1.justification: v1 evaluates moderation on MMDS and its policy-relaxation subset. v3 adds MM-SafetyBench, VLGuard-Test, ActorAttack, SafeDialBench (English), and benign WildChat dialogues, extending evaluation to single-turn multimodal and external text-only multi-turn settings. Appendix D.4 also adds human-crafted multimodal dialogues.

E2.justification: Table 1 adds InternVL3.5-38B, Qwen3-VL-30B-A3B-Instruct, Gemini-2.5-Pro, OpenAI Moderation, and Llama Guard-4-12B. Additional comparisons introduce LlavaGuard, Qwen3Guard-Gen-8B, their combined OR baseline, and linear search against MCTS. These are evaluated comparators, beyond additions to related-work citations.

E3.justification: v3 introduces rationale retraining/inference ablations, paired image-removal tests with regenerated target responses, and four 100-sample augmentation evaluations. Existing MMDS splits and principal training settings remain unchanged. The reported malicious-intent count changes from 350 to 348, and the attack target changes from Claude-3.5-Sonnet to Claude-3.7-Sonnet without establishing reruns. Policy adaptation now uses FPR instead of safe-class recall.

E4.justification: Beyond v1's policy-adaptation and per-dimension analyses, v3 adds rationale ablation, leave-one-out augmentation ablations, image-removal and dialogue-length analyses, MCTS-versus-linear search, safeguard-combination analysis, generated-image quality assessment, and a human-versus-synthetic generalization check. Figures 17–19 also add comparative case studies.

E5.justification: Both versions report point estimates without repeated-run summaries, random seeds, confidence intervals, or significance tests. v3 acknowledges that sparse late-turn observations have high variance, but does not introduce an uncertainty-estimation procedure.

E6.justification: LLaVAShield's MMDS F1 remains 95.71%/92.24%, and Table 2 is unchanged. Table 1 revises Qwen2.5-VL-72B F1 from 33.50%/27.03% to 33.33%/28.00%. Substantial new results include 97.62% average MM-SafetyBench recall, 15/16 human-crafted attacks detected, and extensive ablation results. The policy-test FPR values merely re-express v1's safe-recall outcomes.

M1.justification: The LLaVA-OV-7B model, supervised objective, structured outputs, and core MCTS procedure remain intact. One explicit procedural revision concerns augmentation: v1 Section 3.4 says policy relaxation is not used independently, whereas v3 Appendix A.3.2 describes both independent and combined use. Expanded rationale-generation details otherwise do not establish that the original model was changed or retrained.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and related work are substantially rewritten, with the introduction organized around three risk characteristics. Detailed MCTS and dataset explanations move into a much broader appendix structure. Main-text method sections are consolidated, discussion is reorganized, and MMRT-MCTS is generally renamed MMRT.

P2.justification: The document changes from single-column to two-column layout. Figure 1 gains explicit risk annotations; the taxonomy is recolored and relocated, with a new main-text summary and intent-distribution plot. Test distributions are reorganized across appendix displays, and numerous experimental tables, component plots, prompt panels, and case-study figures are added. The old policy-adaptation table becomes prose.

R1.justification: Related work expands from multi-turn attacks and VLM moderation to broader black-box search, visual jailbreaks, industrial moderation, and newer safeguards. v3 explicitly credits IDEATOR as inspiration and acknowledges Llama Guard-4's multi-image/multi-turn capabilities, refining the claimed gap. This materially changes research positioning beyond bibliographic updates.

T1.justification: The conditional-generation objective and MCTS selection and reward mathematics are retained under revised notation and placement. Added dialogue-state notation, standard cosine similarity, and an average-score metric do not introduce substantive theoretical reasoning. Neither version provides theorems or proofs.

improvement.justification: v1's evidence relied mainly on MMDS and lacked component ablations and direct comparisons with dedicated safeguards. v3 substantially addresses these weaknesses through external benchmarks, stronger comparator coverage, controlled analyses, and extensive reproducibility details. New benign-dialogue results expose a meaningful false-positive tradeoff, acknowledged in the limitations. Although uncertainty remains unquantified and some rollout pseudocode is inconsistent, the empirical support and transparency improve substantially.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe LLaVAShield, MMDS, and the same MCTS-based red-teaming framework. Their main text and complete appendices are readable, including figures and prompt templates inspected visually, and support reliable comparison.

after.justification: v3 retains original experiments and adds external benchmark evaluations, ablations, image and dialogue-turn analyses, and human-crafted dialogue results.

before.justification: v1 reports original MMDS moderation experiments, policy-adaptation tests, and red-teaming attack success rates in Tables 1–4.

results.title: LLaVAShield: Safeguarding Multimodal Multi-Turn Dialogues in Vision-Language Models

C1.justification: The central dataset, mask-aware model and improved findings-generation claims remain. V2 adds an explicit novelty claim in the abstract that its five-physician evaluation is the first human study of automated PET reporting.

C2.justification: V2 explicitly acknowledges hallucinated numerical measurements and qualifies the reader evaluation by explaining their exclusion. It also discusses PET domain shift, possible overrating by automated metrics and external generalization. Dependence on supplied masks and a future fully automated reporting pipeline were already discussed in v1.

D1.justification: V2's supplement supplies acquisition and deidentification details, the formatting prompt, software libraries, LoRA placement, precision, batch size, learning rate and other hyperparameters. It also documents reader blinding, numerical masking, viewing software and scoring rubrics. These are substantial new disclosures, although conflicting epoch counts and training descriptions limit reproducibility.

E1.justification: V2 adds evaluation on 32 external autoPET instances, extending coverage beyond the internal PET/CT dataset. The supplement identifies an additional imaging difference: primarily contrast-enhanced CT externally versus primarily non-contrast CT internally. Renaming PETAR-11K to PETARSeg-11K does not itself change coverage.

E2.justification: Compared with v1 Table 3, v2 Table 2 adds QoQ-Med and fine-tuned Qwen3-VL-8B and MedGemma-4B comparisons. The added fine-tuned 2D baselines materially strengthen comparisons under dataset adaptation. Expanded names for retained baselines are not counted as new methods.

E3.justification: The reported internal test size changes from 1,170 to 1,175, and the stated anatomical pretraining size changes from approximately 5,000 to 100,000 segmentations. V2 reports ten epochs for all stages instead of five for initial pretraining, although supplementary Table 9 still lists five. It also specifies three-view inputs for the new fine-tuned 2D comparisons and changes retained ablation rows' TS flags from enabled to disabled. These are reported setting revisions, not evidence that all experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: V2 adds an explicit full-model comparison with and without TotalSegmentator pretraining, which v1's populated ablation rows did not isolate. It also adds external distribution-shift evaluation, replaces the original qualitative cases with broader baseline error comparisons in Figure 4, and supplies autoPET examples in supplementary Figure 5.

E5.justification: V1 reports point estimates, whereas v2 Table 5 adds plus/minus quantities to physician ratings. Their statistical meaning is not specified. Neither version reports training-run uncertainty, seed counts, confidence intervals or significance tests.

E6.justification: PETAR's reported BLEU, CIDEr and GREEN change from 0.531, 0.415 and 0.246 to 0.535, 0.457 and 0.257; changed settings prevent interpreting these as controlled performance gains. GREEN's human correlation changes from 0.608 to 0.592, and other metric correlations and rankings change. V2 additionally reports new comparator results, internal physician scores and preference counts (15 preferred, 54 tied, 47 not preferred), external ratings and cohort statistics.

M1.justification: The core encoding, focal cropping, feature fusion and autoregressive objective remain unchanged. Section 4.4 changes the stated alignment order from mask-then-projector to projector-then-mask and describes repeating the three-stage sequence on both training datasets. However, v2's stage headings contradict their descriptions, leaving the implemented order uncertain.

P1.justification: V2 extensively rewrites the abstract, introduction, results and explanatory passages. It reorganizes experimental setup and human evaluation, replaces the standalone PETAR-Bench and Discussion sections with revised setup and limitations sections, renames the dataset, and adds a structured supplement.

P2.justification: Figures 1–3 are substantially redrawn, and Figure 4 becomes a larger comparison matrix with anatomical error annotations. V2 removes the model-capability table, redesigns the dataset comparison table, reorganizes experimental tables and adds physician-results and supplementary displays. These changes extend well beyond numerical updates and renumbering.

R1.justification: V2 substantially expands citations supporting baseline models, PET datasets, evaluation metrics, implementation tools and segmentation workflows. It sharpens the distinction from Reg2RG's organ-level, single-modality setting and develops the relationship to Describe Anything's focal prompting; Describe Anything was already cited in v1.

T1.justification: The cropping, encoding, fusion and likelihood equations retain their mathematical substance. V2 makes mask embeddings and notation more explicit and numbers more equations, but introduces no substantive theoretical result, proof or changed formal assumption.

improvement.justification: V2 resolves a major evidential gap by publishing quantitative physician outcomes that v1's clinical-utility claims lacked, adding a limited external evaluation and testing fine-tuned 2D competitors. Its supplement materially improves methodological transparency, including disclosure that numerical hallucinations were excluded from reader scoring. Conflicting training-stage descriptions, epoch counts and some prose/table values remain, but the strengthened clinical evidence and documentation provide a substantial net improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe PETAR-4B and the same core dataset of 11,356 lesions from 5,126 exams. Their text, equations, figures and tables support comparison. V2 includes supplementary material absent from the supplied v1, despite v1 referring to supplementary details.

after.justification: V2 reports original model comparisons, ablations, metric correlations and physician evaluations on internal and external data in Tables 2–5, with additional analyses in its supplement.

before.justification: V1 reports original model comparisons, component ablations and correlations between automated metrics and physician scores in Tables 3–5.

results.title: PETAR: Localized Findings Generation with Mask-Aware Vision-Language Modeling for PET Automated Reporting

C1.justification: The central claims about a diverse, physically simulated multi-body dataset with ground-truth trajectories and parameters remain stable. v2’s introduction explicitly adds novel evaluation metrics to the contribution, while its conclusion broadens the demonstrated applications from DyNVS evaluation to several tasks, including inverse physics.

C2.justification: v2 expands explanations of representation-specific reconstruction failures and interprets underestimated stiffness as excessive deformation used to fit multi-object observations. Appendix F replaces v1’s synthetic-to-real transfer discussion with limitations concerning constitutive simplifications, numerical discretization, and missing fine-scale dynamics. These materially revise both interpretation and applicability qualifications.

D1.justification: Appendix E newly identifies baseline configuration choices, public implementation links, training times, and a depth-scaling recommendation. Hardware reporting changes from four Titan Xp GPUs to one for simulation and from A6000 to A5000/A6000 for experiments. Most camera, rendering, and solver parameters are retained; these disclosures do not establish experimental reruns.

E1.justification: The same 17 scenes and monocular/multiview reconstruction tasks are retained. However, v2 actually evaluates Young’s modulus and Poisson’s ratio estimation on bouncing balls, previously discussed only as a potential application. It also empirically analyzes other physics and DyNVS datasets for motion complexity and visual distribution similarity, using TinyImageNet as the latter reference.

E2.justification: MoSca, previously only cited, joins the monocular quantitative and qualitative comparisons alongside D-3DGS, 4DGS, STG, and SoM. The new inverse-physics experiment evaluates PAC-NeRF and GIC, and trajectory evaluation includes a GT-GT oracle reference. The multiview reconstruction comparator set remains unchanged.
