E3.justification: Beyond the retained PSNR/SSIM/LPIPS evaluation, v2 introduces initial-frame trajectory matching, TD and cumulative-outlier AUOP evaluation, and an oracle control. It also adds Dynamic Score comparisons, FID/KID against TinyImageNet, and physics-parameter estimation evaluation. These substantially expand the evaluation design; existing camera configurations and image-quality protocols are retained.

E4.justification: v1’s physical-motion diagnosis relies on qualitative trajectory examples. v2 adds a low- versus high-dynamics comparison in Table 6, time-resolved outlier diagnostics in Figure 8, and a multi-object inverse-physics failure case in Section 5.3. Appendix E.2 also adds a dense-versus-sparse COLMAP depth-scaling observation.

E5.justification: Neither version reports experimental seed counts, repeated-run variability, confidence intervals, or significance tests. The new outlier percentages and oracle comparisons measure reconstruction errors and reference performance, rather than statistical uncertainty.

E6.justification: All retained per-scene and aggregate image-quality scores are unchanged. v2 adds MoSca results, including monocular averages of 19.5 PSNR, 0.76 SSIM, and 0.34 LPIPS, plus dataset-comparison and trajectory scores. Table 7 newly reports Young’s modulus estimates of 1,700 for PAC-NeRF and 23,400 for GIC against ground truth of 100,000.

M1.justification: The Houdini pipeline, FLIP/Pyro/MPM/Vellum solvers, and scene interaction procedures remain unchanged. The new Gaussian-splatting background, governing equations, and XPBD pseudocode expand documentation without establishing a changed generation algorithm or proposed reconstruction model. The new evaluation metrics are assessed under E3 and T1.

P1.justification: The main narrative is extensively rewritten and reorganized. Dataset construction moves from the main text into expanded appendices, a metrics section takes its place, and empirical analysis is reorganized around benchmark comparison, reconstruction, and inverse physics. Terminology shifts from dataset toward benchmark and from viscoelastic toward rheological materials.

P2.justification: v2 adopts a two-column main layout, moves v1’s Figure 3 to the opening teaser, reorganizes material-result tables, and introduces colored rankings and MoSca columns. New motion-score and outlier plots accompany new evaluation tables. Existing scene and qualitative panels are extensively redistributed, including moves into the appendix.

R1.justification: v2 adds references including FluidNexus, GIC, Vid2Sim, GP-4DGS, and evaluation-metric sources, and adds Phystwin to the dataset comparison table. Syn2Real disappears with the rewritten limitations discussion. The principal positioning against datasets with restricted materials, interactions, or physical ground truth remains unchanged.

T1.justification: Section 4 introduces mathematical definitions for matched-trajectory TD and the persistent outlier process underlying AUOP, absent from v1. Appendix D additionally states constitutive assumptions, including linear elasticity and Kelvin–Voigt viscosity, and removes v1’s explicit non-Newtonian liquid qualification. These expand the formal specification; no new theorem or proof is presented.

improvement.justification: v1 provides physical ground truth but assesses reconstructed physical motion only qualitatively. v2’s explicit metrics, oracle-referenced trajectory results, and temporal error analysis substantially strengthen validation of the benchmark’s central purpose; the inverse-physics experiment also demonstrates a previously proposed application. Validation remains limited to two trajectory scenes, and the AUOP threshold is unspecified, but these limitations do not outweigh the substantial gain in empirical support.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe PhysGaia, retaining the same 17 scenes and underlying simulation pipeline. The complete main texts and appendices, including equations, tables, and figures, are readable and support reliable comparison despite substantial reorganization.

after.justification: v2 retains those experiments and adds original dataset comparisons, quantitative trajectory evaluation, MoSca results, and physics-parameter estimation experiments.

before.justification: v1 reports original monocular and multiview reconstruction experiments, per-scene results in Tables 9–10, and qualitative trajectory analyses.

results.title: PhysGaia: A Physics-aware Benchmark with Multi-Body Interactions for Dynamic Novel View Synthesis

C1.justification: The central claims remain a plug-and-play edit-aware loss, improved edited-sRGB fidelity with reported gains up to 1.5-2 dB, and target-edit fine-tuning for metadata-assisted reconstruction. The added experiments support these existing contributions without redefining them.

C2.justification: v2 explicitly clarifies independence from the actual capture and inference ISPs, interprets the new results as supporting image-specific editing and limited lambda sensitivity, and identifies failures under extreme low light or unfamiliar illumination such as green LEDs. These concrete failure conditions replace v1's closing future-work discussion.

D1.justification: v2 quantifies training overhead at approximately 15% and newly specifies an ASN-neighborhood threshold of L1 <= 0.05. v1 mentions both overhead and neighborhood restriction without these values. The new L1 specification conflicts with the Euclidean wording retained in Section 3.2, leaving the precise norm ambiguous.

E1.justification: v1 evaluates the Samsung S24 Ultra dataset. v2 additionally evaluates NUS data from Samsung NX2000, Olympus E-PL6, and Sony SLT-A57 cameras in Section S4. Section 4.4 also adds manual, image-specific edits, substantially broadening camera coverage and editing scenarios.

E2.justification: The corresponding comparisons retain CAM, RAW Diffusion, UNet, and the CIE XYZ Net cyclic-loss comparison. The latter moves from Table S4 to S6. New experiments reuse existing comparison methods without introducing a new competing reconstruction method.

E3.justification: Section 4.3 introduces a blind forced-choice study with 25 users judging 20 images for three methods, yielding 1,500 responses. Additional protocols cover manual edits on 50 challenging images, NUS evaluation following the CAM protocol with two specified edits, and a lambda sweep over 1, 2, 4, and 8. Existing smartphone splits and evaluation settings remain unchanged.

E4.justification: Table S5 adds loss-weight sensitivity analysis for CAM and RAW Diffusion, while Section 4.4 tests robustness to image-specific edits. These extend the retained component, sampling-range, cyclic-loss, dehazing, and local-tone-mapping analyses.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, or significance tests. The new participant counts describe evaluation design; preference percentages and hyperparameter sweeps do not introduce uncertainty estimation.

E6.justification: All retained quantitative table entries are unchanged, including v1 Table S4 matched to v2 Table S6. New outcomes include 83% overall user preference, manual-edit results such as CAM's 22.11 dB baseline versus 24.36 dB with edit-aware loss, and NUS and lambda-sweep scores. NUS results also show reduced RAW PSNR and a Sony Edit B PSNR tie at 33.26 dB. These are additional experiments, not improvements to previously reported scores.

M1.justification: The four-module sampled ISP, reconstruction objectives, and target-edit fine-tuning procedures remain unchanged in Equations (1)-(11) and (S1)-(S3). The additional sampling-threshold disclosure does not establish an actual algorithm revision.

P1.justification: Local rewrites clarify ISP access and shorten related work. v2 adds Sections 4.3, 4.4, and supplementary Section S4, renumbers additional ablations to S5, and revises the conclusion. The abstract, overall narrative, and method exposition remain largely intact.

P2.justification: v2 adds Tables 5, S4, and S5 and renumbers the existing cyclic-loss table to S6. Figures 3 and 4 each shrink from six examples to four; the two displaced RAW Diffusion examples move into Figure S2, replacing two previous examples. Figure 5 moves from page 8 to page 7. The overall visual format and core diagrams remain unchanged.

R1.justification: v2 adds Cheng, Prasad, and Brown's 2014 work as the NUS dataset reference. Existing research positioning against RAW-fidelity objectives and unedited cyclic consistency remains substantially unchanged.

T1.justification: The mathematical formulations and assumptions, including normalized, demosaiced, denoised three-channel RAW inputs, are retained. Neither version adds or revises a theorem, proof, or substantive derivation.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens validation of the paper's practical editing claims: NUS experiments extend the single-camera evidence, the blind user study directly tests perceptual matching, and manual image-specific edits address the restriction to fixed edit recipes. Failure conditions and quantified training overhead also improve transparency. These gains address important evidentiary gaps in v1, despite limited uncertainty reporting and the inconsistent white-balance norm specification.

A1.justification: Both PDFs contain the same work, Edit-aware RAW Reconstruction, with readable main text, equations, figures, tables, and complete supplementary material. Content can be matched across layout changes and appendix renumbering.

after.justification: v2 retains those empirical results and adds a user study, image-specific editing experiments, NUS camera evaluations, and loss-weight sensitivity results.

before.justification: v1 reports original reconstruction experiments, target-edit fine-tuning, and ablations, including Tables 2-4 and S1-S4.

results.title: Edit-aware RAW reconstruction

C1.justification: The abstract, contribution list, and conclusion retain the same novelty and transferability claims for UPA-RFAS and its components. The added supporting material does not redefine those claims. The abstract's new code pointer is an access-information change.

C2.justification: Appendices E–G substantially expand interpretation: patch capacity versus visibility, contrastive-weight saturation, and why excessive perturbation budgets may hurt transfer. They also attribute harder physical transfer to clutter, blur, perspective distortion, trajectory smoothing, and mechanical redundancy. These are new qualitative mechanism explanations and applicability qualifications beyond the retained main-text discussion.

D1.justification: Appendix B supplies essential reproducibility information absent from v1, including 50×50 patches, 224×224 inputs, batch size, inner/outer steps, learning rates, 2000 optimization iterations, loss weights, temperatures, and attention-selection settings. Appendix E discloses coefficient rescaling, and the abstract adds a code-repository link. These are documentation additions rather than established changes to implementation.

E1.justification: BridgeData V2 and the four LIBERO task families remain the datasets and tasks. Both versions already claim physical manipulation evaluations; v3 provides concrete examples within that scope. The newly supplied π0 results concern another model on retained LIBERO coverage, rather than a new dataset or task.

E2.justification: The six UMA, UADA, and TMA objectives in the main transfer comparisons are retained. Newly supplied white-box Table 4 additionally includes Random Noise and UPA comparators and reports aggregated TMA results. Table 5's DOF1/DOF7 labels correspond to the existing TMA variants.

E3.justification: The retained LIBERO protocol still uses success rate, ten tasks per suite, ten trials per task, and predetermined patch placements. Appendix E adds controlled sweeps over patch area, contrastive weight, and perturbation budget. Appendix B's default training settings are newly disclosed, with no demonstrated revision to existing experiments.

E4.justification: The original component, text-probe, and patch-pattern analyses are retained. Appendix E adds substantive sensitivity analyses of patch size, contrastive weighting, and inner perturbation strength in Tables 6–8. Appendix F also supplies physical-robot case evidence and observations across patch positions, substantially extending the available robustness analysis.

E5.justification: V3 Table 4 introduces ± terms for white-box scores, although their statistical meaning and run/seed basis are unspecified. Appendix F newly states physical-trial repetition information using '3 times.' The original ten independent trials per LIBERO task remain unchanged; an increased run count is not established.

E6.justification: V1 Tables 1–4 retain their numerical values in v3 Tables 1–3. Substantial additional results appear: white-box average success rates of 0.5% and 2.75%, π0 transfer rates of 86.0% and 83.5% against 92.0% benign performance, parameter-sweep results, and physical failure examples. These are newly reported outcomes, not improvements over matched v1 scores.

M1.justification: The feature-space objective, repulsive InfoNCE term, inner perturbation minimization, outer patch optimization, PAD, PSM, and Algorithm 1 remain substantively unchanged. Appendix B discloses implementation choices without establishing a revised method.

P1.justification: Most main-text prose is retained almost verbatim. V3 resolves appendix placeholders, folds the experiment-setup subsection into Section 4, updates cross-references, expands affiliations, and adds acknowledgements and Appendices A–G. The scientific additions do not amount to extensive rewriting of the existing narrative.

P2.justification: V1's two main transfer tables are merged into one table with grouped victim-model columns. V3 adds five appendix tables and two frame-sequence figures showing physical executions and training examples. Figure 1's PAD/PSM section references are corrected, while the original patch images and ablation displays are retained.

R1.justification: The bibliography expands from 67 to 89 works, adding background on query-based attacks, SAM/video/MLLM transfer attacks, and adversarial training, including DIFAttack and DIFAttack++. These additions broaden citations within existing categories; the related-work taxonomy and positioning as the first universal transferable VLA patch framework remain substantially unchanged.

T1.justification: Appendix A supplies the previously missing proof of Proposition 1 using the reverse triangle inequality, the smallest singular value, and norm inequalities. The assumption, proposition, lower bounds, and corollary themselves are unchanged; the theoretical addition is confined to proving an existing result.

improvement.justification: V1 leaves important supporting material behind unresolved appendix references. V3 supplies the lower-bound proof, essential optimization settings, π0 and white-box evidence, sensitivity analyses, and physical examples, substantially improving completeness, reproducibility, and assessment of the existing claims. The main results remain unchanged. Undefined uncertainty terms and limited physical-trial documentation constrain the additions, but do not outweigh the substantial gains from making this previously unavailable support inspectable.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same UPA-RFAS work, and their text, equations, tables, and figures support reliable comparison. The complete v1 PDF ends after references despite unresolved appendix references; v3 supplies Appendices A–G. This is an observable difference in supplied content, not an extraction gap.

after.justification: V3 retains those empirical results and additionally reports white-box and π0 results, parameter sensitivity experiments, and qualitative physical-robot outcomes.

before.justification: V1 reports original LIBERO transfer experiments, component and text-probe ablations in Tables 1–4, and feature-alignment analysis.

results.title: When Robots Obey the Patch: Universal Transferable Patch Attacks on Vision-Language-Action Models

C1.justification: The central contribution changes from direct ODE editing with spatial masking and semantic guidance to three corrections targeting appearance transformation, motion preservation, and stability. Abstract and conclusion add explicit motion-energy and variance-reduction claims. V1's explicit claim to be the first inversion-free editing work using pretrained T2V models is dropped.

C2.justification: V2 attributes stronger transformations to directional correction and reframes DAG primarily around noise suppression and trajectory stability, rather than overcoming structural-preservation bias. It adds interpretations of skipping versus full sampling, motion/appearance tradeoffs, and why DAG's visible benefits yield modest metric gains. The incomplete-prompt failure and limited style-transfer applicability are retained.

D1.justification: V2 supplies full inference pseudocode instead of mask-only pseudocode, documents attention aggregation and upsampling, and adds timestep-shift, correction, and noise-schedule settings plus hardware/memory information. However, v1's explicit 832x480 resolution is omitted. Reproducibility remains weakened by three-versus-four DAG sample descriptions and the reversed anchor-difference sign between Equation 11 and Algorithm 1. Code release remains promised through the same project link.

E1.justification: V1 describes Internet and Wan-generated videos; v2 explicitly evaluates Internet/DAVIS pairs. Demonstrated coverage expands to black-and-white colorization, prolonged occlusion, and combined identity/gesture changes (Figures 4 and 20–22). These introduce substantive task and input-condition coverage beyond the retained object, material, and local-attribute edits.

E2.justification: The five main baselines remain FateZero, FLATTEN, TokenFlow, RAVE, and VideoDirector. However, the appendix efficiency comparison expands beyond DAG versus conventional averaging to measured FLATTEN, TokenFlow, and RAVE comparisons in v2 Table 4. FateZero and VideoDirector have missing measurements there because of memory limits.

E3.justification: Main evaluation changes from 8/22/36 to 41/81 frames, removes Frame-Acc, and adds a 14B configuration. V2 uses all 50 denoising steps instead of skipping ten, disables source CFG previously set to 3.5, and changes mask smoothing from 11 to 9. Its principal DAG setting uses three rather than four samples, although Appendix F still describes four. Efficiency testing changes from four 4090 GPUs to one H800.

E4.justification: V2 adds quantitative component-removal and DA-FC strength ablations (Tables 2–3), motion-correction case studies, attention-block comparisons, and sensitivity studies for motion-correction parameters, DAG strength, and ensemble sizes. It expands efficiency analysis with memory measurements and source-CFG discussion. V1's dedicated SAFC ablation and Porsche WarpError case analysis disappear; the DAG averaging and incomplete-prompt examples remain.

E5.justification: Neither version reports evaluation seed counts, repeated-trial uncertainty, confidence intervals, or significance tests. The changing numbers of stochastic DAG samples concern the inference procedure, not statistical uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: Table 1 replaces the earlier scores with results under different video lengths and evaluation settings. For example, 1.3B CLIP-T changes from 33.72/33.79/33.84 for 8/22/36 frames to 34.64/34.63 for 41/81 frames; this does not establish a same-setting gain. V2 adds 14B, quantitative ablation, and resource results, while removing Frame-Acc entries and the Porsche WarpError table.

M1.justification: V2 adds Direction-Aware Flow Correction through velocity decomposition and Motion-Appearance Decoupling through a motion-energy correction. DAG changes from averaging differences against subset estimates to selecting the least cosine-aligned candidates, and late-stage noise is frozen. V1's attention masking and edge softening remain within the revised framework; they are not newly introduced.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, method narrative, ablation discussion, and conclusion are extensively rewritten. Appendices are reorganized around full inference and separate correction analyses, while Broader Impacts and the standalone extended baseline-comparison section disappear. The author list and affiliations also change.

P2.justification: V2 adopts a two-column layout, replaces the original framework diagram with trajectory and vector diagrams, restructures Table 1, and adds ablation tables, attention maps, and parameter-study figures. Qualitative montages are substantially rearranged and refreshed. The earlier DAG and prompt-failure figures are retained with relocation and formatting changes.

R1.justification: The related-work organization and principal editing references remain. V2 adds DAVIS and a FlowAlign discussion, although FlowAlign has an unresolved citation, and removes several dataset and guidance references, including classifier-free guidance and guiding with a bad model. The explicit first-work positioning is softened without changing the overall research area.

T1.justification: V2 introduces the formal parallel/orthogonal decomposition and piecewise correction in Equations 5–6, plus motion residuals, an energy function, and an approximate gradient update in Equations 9–11. Its DAG definition also changes substantively: selecting least-aligned candidates avoids the cancellation implied by averaging all subset differences in v1 Equations 5–7. No theorem or proof is added.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially strengthens methodological coherence and empirical support: its selected-baseline DAG avoids the cancellation in v1's written formulation, while Tables 2–3 provide quantitative component evidence previously supported largely by qualitative examples. Motion-focused cases, sensitivity studies, and resource measurements further substantiate the revised framework. These gains outweigh reporting regressions, although the MAD-FC equation/pseudocode disagreement, inconsistent DAG sample descriptions, and omitted resolution still impede reproducibility. Changed evaluation conditions prevent interpreting the new headline scores as direct performance improvements over v1.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe FlowDirector and contain readable main text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices. The shared editing framework and retained examples support reliable comparison despite substantial revision.

after.justification: V2 reports original benchmark results, quantitative component ablations, parameter studies, runtime and memory measurements, and qualitative results for two model sizes.

before.justification: V1 reports original quantitative baseline comparisons, qualitative editing results, component ablations, and an appendix efficiency comparison.

results.title: FlowDirector: Training-Free Flow Steering for Precise Text-to-Video Editing

C1.justification: v3 redefines a main contribution around jointly using segmentation loss and semantic reward for predicted-mask adaptation, replacing the earlier emphasis on the auxiliary segmentation objective alone. It explicitly claims the first lightweight RGB-only demonstration of strong unseen-category generalization and reduces the headline collision-reduction claim from twofold to 10%.

C2.justification: v3 explains why low PPO collision counts can reflect early failure, interprets calibration and fine-tuning through recognition errors and improved viewpoints, and discusses the increased collisions accompanying predicted-mask adaptation. Appendix J adds a concrete near-goal safety limitation attributed to the reward balance. The earlier segmentation-dependence and free-form-instruction limitations remain.

D1.justification: v3 newly specifies a 15M-step fine-tuning budget, reward coefficient and clipping, lighting-augmentation parameters, and deployment hardware and camera details. v2 leaves its adaptation budget unspecified. Core hyperparameter tables and the code URL remain, but v2's CPU, Ubuntu version, and system-RAM disclosure are removed.

E1.justification: The retained HM3D-OVON coverage is extended with controlled lighting perturbations in Appendix H and physical iRobot Create 3 demonstrations involving visible and initially hidden targets in Appendix J. v2 contains simulation evaluations without these additional environmental conditions or physical-robot scenarios.

E2.justification: The benchmark baselines and switching-strategy comparators in Tables 1 and 2 retain the same membership, including Uni-NaVid, VLFM, TANGO, MTU3D, and EarlySwitcher. DagRL is reused in the new failure analysis; the additional entropy-related methods discussed in Appendix K are not evaluated as baselines.

E3.justification: Table 3 changes component evaluation from ground-truth to YOLOE masks. The observation ablation replaces the dummy 'table' text embedding with zeros, and the reported success reward changes from +1 to +2.5. New protocols include entropy-threshold sweeps, photometric perturbations, segmentation-error metrics, and training a 105-degree camera-FoV variant for robot demonstrations.

E4.justification: v3 adds entropy-threshold sensitivity analysis, a navigation-failure taxonomy, segmentation-error and lighting-robustness tests, and real-robot case studies. Table 3 also tests the separate and combined contributions of semantic reward and segmentation loss under predicted segmentation. Existing training curves and detector-confidence analyses are retained.

E5.justification: Both versions report three-seed means and standard deviations and describe three-run, one-sided unpaired t-tests. Revised p-values and additional statistical result rows accompany changed experiments without establishing a different uncertainty-estimation procedure or increased run count.

E6.justification: For the revised final configuration, Table 1 changes val-unseen SR/SPL from 40.1%/20.9% to 44.7%/20.6%, while Table 4 changes collisions from 24.7 to 45.4. Component and observation-ablation outcomes also change, and failure, robustness, hardware, and robot results are added. These replacements involve different training and adaptation configurations.

M1.justification: v3 introduces a semantic reward combining geodesic progress and changes in ground-truth target-mask area. It replaces v2's adaptation using size-filtered ground-truth masks with PPO fine-tuning on YOLOE predictions, jointly using semantic reward and auxiliary segmentation supervision. The architecture and EALM gate remain substantially unchanged.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, contribution list, and conclusion are substantially rewritten, with introductory arguments condensed and reordered. v3 introduces a numbered section hierarchy, an appendix guide, a lettered supplement, and acknowledgments, while removing the reproducibility checklist. These changes reorganize substantial retained material.

P2.justification: v3 adds entropy-sensitivity plots, robot photographs and trajectories, and failure, segmentation-error, augmentation, and hardware tables. Tables 3 and 4 gain reward and latency columns. Existing confidence-threshold plots are regrouped horizontally, and tables throughout are restyled and reduced in size.

R1.justification: New Appendix K substantially expands EALM's positioning against entropy-guided augmentation, distillation, curriculum learning, test-time adaptation, SAC, and SafeDAgger. v3 also attributes the semantic reward to Staroverov et al. (2025) and adds PPO and generalized-advantage-estimation references.

T1.justification: v3 adds a mathematical semantic-reward definition, an action-space-dependent rationale for entropy thresholds, and formal augmentation and IoU-based segmentation-event definitions in Appendix H. These are limited formal additions; the existing PPO/EALM equations remain substantially unchanged, and neither version supplies theoretical proofs.

improvement.justification: The predicted-mask component ablations in v3 Table 3 address v2's reliance on ground-truth masks to establish component benefits. New sensitivity, failure, lighting, and deployment studies substantially strengthen validation, while increased collisions and near-goal risks are explicitly discussed. Robot evidence remains qualitative, and reporting problems such as Table J's memory units limit particular claims, but the stronger evidence and clearer limitations provide a substantial overall improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe OVSegDT and retain identifiable architecture, training, and HM3D-OVON experiments. The main text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices are readable and support comparison across the reorganization.

after.justification: v3 reports revised navigation experiments and additional entropy-sensitivity, lighting-robustness, hardware-performance, and real-robot results.

before.justification: v2 reports original navigation results, training-strategy comparisons, component ablations, training curves, and observation-removal experiments in its main text and appendix.

results.title: OVSegDT: Segmenting Transformer for Open-Vocabulary Object Goal Navigation
